question: An American mathematics professor brought out a brand-new kind of game in 1993, in which each player builds a deck of magical spells, creatures and lands and duels a rival from 20 life to zero. He called it Magic: the Gathering. What was the mathematician's name?
context: Garfield earned his PhD in combinatorial mathematics at the University of Pennsylvania. He pitched the game to Peter Adkison's tiny Wizards of the Coast outfit in 1991.

question: A Magic: the Gathering player casts her spells from five colors of mana. One is peaceful and heals; one is clever and draws cards; one is ruthless and kills; one is fast and burns; one is wild and full of growing life. What are the five?
answer: White, blue, black, red, and green
choices: White, blue, black, red, and green
Red, blue, yellow, green, and orange
Gold, silver, bronze, copper, and iron
Fire, water, earth, air, and spirit
context: The five colors form the Color Pie. Each color has a flavor identity: white law, blue knowledge, black ambition, red passion, green nature.

question: Magic: the Gathering's designer pitched his new card game to a tiny company run from its founder's basement outside Seattle. The founder, a computer programmer who had started it in 1990, agreed to publish it. What is the company called?
context: Adkison founded WotC in 1990. Garfield brought him the prototype of Magic in 1991. WotC was acquired by Hasbro in 1999.

question: A Magic: the Gathering player pays one red mana and deals three damage to any creature or player, with the most famous cheap spell in the color of fire and fury. It was in the game's first set. What is it called?
context: Lightning Bolt printed in Alpha at common. It became the gold standard for cheap red removal in every format that allowed it.

question: Two Magic: the Gathering players are dueling, and one lays down a fresh creature. It cannot attack that turn. It has to wait for the next one unless it has haste, a rule that stops first-turn kills. What is this waiting rule called?
context: Garfield introduced the rule to prevent first-turn one-shot kills and to give the opponent a chance to respond before a new creature swings.

question: A Magic: the Gathering player turns a land card 90 degrees sideways on the table and gets one mana for casting a spell. A creature turned the same way has gone on the attack, and both straighten up at the start of the next turn. What is this sideways turn called?
context: Tapped cards are turned 90 degrees to show they have been used. They straighten back up — untap — during the controller's next untap step.

question: A wrestler with a bushy blonde mustache and a red bandanna tore off his yellow tank top in the 1980s World Wrestling Federation ring, cupped his ear to hear the crowd and called his huge biceps his '24-inch pythons.' He beat the Iron Sheik for the title in 1984. Who was he?
context: Hogan's real name is Terry Bollea. He won his first WWF title from the Iron Sheik on January 23, 1984, at Madison Square Garden.

question: Hulk Hogan body-slammed a seven-foot-four French wrestler of over 500 pounds in front of 93,000 fans at the Silverdome in Michigan in 1987. The same man also acted in the 1987 movie The Princess Bride, as the gentle, poetry-loving strongman Fezzik. What was his ring name?
context: Andre's huge size came from acromegaly. Hogan body-slammed him at WrestleMania III in front of a Pontiac Silverdome crowd announced as 93,173.

question: Miss Elizabeth, a graceful manager, walked a 1980s wrestler to the ring in his neon sunglasses and feathered cowboy hat while he shouted 'Ooh yeah!' in a raspy voice. Fans called him Macho Man, and he yelled 'Snap into a Slim Jim!' in TV commercials. What was his ring name?
context: Randy Savage's real name was Randy Poffo. He held the Intercontinental Championship in 1986-87, with a classic match against Ricky Steamboat at WrestleMania III.

question: Steve Austin, a bald Texan in a black vest, grabbed his opponent by the head in the late-1990s World Wrestling Federation, kicked him in the gut and dropped to his knees, slamming the man's jaw across the top of his own shoulder. What was this finishing move called?
context: Austin would kick the opponent in the gut, drop to a seated position, and bring the opponent's jaw down across his shoulder. The move was almost impossible to make look fake.

question: A third-generation star of the World Wrestling Federation raised one eyebrow like nobody else in the late 1990s, called himself the People's Champion and asked fans if they could smell what he was cookin'. He later became a huge Hollywood action-movie star. Who was this star?
context: The Rock's real name is Dwayne Johnson. His father was 'Soulman' Rocky Johnson; his grandfather was High Chief Peter Maivia. He debuted in 1996 as Rocky Maivia.

question: A wrestler almost seven feet tall walked to the World Wrestling Federation ring in near-total darkness while a slow bell tolled, in a long black duster coat and a wide-brimmed black hat. For years he won every single match he wrestled at the company's biggest show of the year. Who was he?
context: The Undertaker debuted at Survivor Series in November 1990. His WrestleMania streak began at WrestleMania VII in 1991 and became one of the longest-running stories in the company.

question: Singer Cyndi Lauper joined the ring at the biggest wrestling event of the year, a super-show held every spring since 1985 and watched on pay-per-view worldwide. A hero body-slammed a giant at the third one, and one black-coated wrestler built an unbeaten streak at it. What is this yearly super-event called?
context: WrestleMania I took place March 31, 1985, at Madison Square Garden. Mr. T tag-teamed with Hulk Hogan in the main event.

question: Stu Hart trained his son in a brutal basement gym called the Dungeon in Calgary, Canada, and the boy became a World Wrestling Federation favorite in pink and black tights. He boasted he was 'the best there is, the best there was, and the best there ever will be.' Fans nicknamed him the Hitman. Who was he?
context: Bret Hart was part of the wrestling Hart family from Calgary. He held the WWF Championship five times. His pink-and-black gear became iconic merch.

question: Ted Turner, a billionaire cable-TV owner, bought a Georgia pro wrestling company in 1988 and grew it into a national rival to the World Wrestling Federation. Its Monday Nitro show fought Monday Night Raw head-to-head from 1995 to 2001 and led the ratings for 83 straight weeks. What was the company called?
context: World Championship Wrestling launched Monday Nitro in September 1995 to compete directly with WWF Raw. Vince McMahon purchased WCW in March 2001 when it folded.

question: Mick Foley pulled on a torn brown leather mask, drooled and spoke to a sock puppet called Mr. Socko, the third of his World Wrestling Federation characters. The others were Dude Love, a 1970s lover-boy in tie-dye, and Cactus Jack, a wild bearded bruiser. What was the masked character called?
context: Mick Foley's leather-mask Mankind persona debuted in 1996. He won the WWF Championship for the first time on Raw, January 4, 1999. His memoir 'Have a Nice Day' was a 2000 bestseller.

question: A wrestler nicknamed the Heartbreak Kid won a 60-minute non-stop Iron Man Match for the world heavyweight title in 1996. He finished opponents with a jumping super-kick to the jaw that he called Sweet Chin Music. What was his ring name?
context: Shawn Michaels — real name Michael Hickenbottom — won his first WWF title from Bret Hart at WrestleMania XII in March 1996. He founded D-Generation X in 1997 with Triple H.

question: A Seattle fan pulls on a blue, green and silver jersey and heads for Lumen Field to watch a National Football League (NFL) game. The crowd there is so loud it once set a world record for stadium noise. What is this Seattle NFL team called?
context: The Seahawks joined the NFL as an expansion team in 1976. They played at the Kingdome from 1976 to 1999, briefly at Husky Stadium, then at Seahawks Stadium (Qwest/CenturyLink/Lumen) from 2002.

question: A bruising Seattle running back sits on the sideline between plays in the early 2010s, munching Skittles candy. He runs through National Football League (NFL) defenders like a wrecking ball, and his nickname is 'Beast Mode.' Who is he?
context: Marshawn Lynch came to Seattle in 2010. His 'Beast Quake' 67-yard touchdown against the Saints on January 8, 2011, registered on a real seismograph at the University of Washington.

question: A young Seattle quarterback led his team to crush the Denver Broncos 43-8 in Super Bowl XLVIII, the National Football League (NFL) championship, in February 2014. He kept starting for Seattle for years, and then in 2022 the club traded him away to those same Broncos. Who was he?
context: Russell Wilson was a third-round pick out of Wisconsin in 2012. He became the Seahawks' starter immediately and led them to two straight Super Bowls.

question: Kam Chancellor and his fellow Seattle defensive backs Richard Sherman, Earl Thomas and Brandon Browner hit ball-carriers so hard in the early 2010s that fans gave the group a scary nickname. What was the nickname?
context: The Legion of Boom shut down the Denver Broncos 43-8 in Super Bowl XLVIII on February 2, 2014. The name grew out of a 2012 radio interview in which Kam Chancellor talked about laying 'the boom' on ball-carriers, and fans supplied the rest.

question: A grinning, gum-chewing head coach arrived in Seattle from the University of Southern California (USC) college football team in 2010. Famous for his boundless energy, he would coach the team for more than a decade and win a Super Bowl. Who was he?
context: Pete Carroll took over after a successful run at USC. He won Super Bowl XLVIII in his fourth season and reached Super Bowl XLIX the next year.

question: Sports Illustrated magazine put a left-handed Seattle Mariners outfielder on its cover with his baseball cap on backward. He crushed 56 home runs in a single Major League Baseball season in 1997, one of the greatest power years ever. Who was this superstar?
context: Junior was drafted first overall by the Mariners in 1987. He debuted in April 1989 at age 19. His sweet swing made him the face of baseball in the 1990s.

question: A Japanese baseball star crossed the Pacific in 2001 to play right field for the Seattle Mariners in Major League Baseball. In his very first American season he collected 242 hits and won both Rookie of the Year and Most Valuable Player. Who was this outfielder?
context: Ichiro had been a superstar for the Orix BlueWave in Japan. His 242 hits in 2001 broke the major-league record for a rookie.

question: Seattle officially renamed a street next to the ballpark for one beloved Mariners hitter. He batted .312 over his career, was famous for driving in runs in clutch spots, and went into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 2019. Who was he?
context: Edgar Martinez played his entire career in Seattle from 1987 to 2004. The best-DH-of-the-year award was renamed the Edgar Martinez Award in his honor.

question: Not a single Detroit batter got a hit off a towering Seattle Mariners left-hander in a 1990 no-hitter. He stood 6 feet 10 inches tall, his fastball terrified every hitter who stepped in, and fans nicknamed him 'The Big Unit' for his enormous size. Who was he?
context: Randy Johnson came to the Mariners from Montreal in 1989. His no-hitter against the Tigers was the first in Mariners history. He won four straight Cy Young Awards after Seattle traded him.

question: A Venezuelan Seattle Mariners pitcher retired all 27 Tampa Bay Rays batters in a row in a 2012 perfect game. He was so dominant that fans packed a bleacher section called the King's Court in yellow shirts to cheer his starts. Who was he?
context: Felix Hernandez retired all 27 batters that day at Safeco Field, striking out 12. It was Major League Baseball's 23rd perfect game. He won the 2010 AL Cy Young Award.

question: Magic: the Gathering's makers rushed a third print run into shops in December 1993 to keep up with demand, after the first two, called Alpha and Beta. They called the third one Unlimited. How did Unlimited differ from Alpha and Beta?
answer: It used white borders instead of black
choices: It used white borders instead of black
It included 20 brand-new cards not in Alpha
It dropped all rare cards from the print run
It used a metallic foil finish on every card
context: Unlimited was meant to make the game more available; Wizards underprinted Alpha (about 2.6 million cards) and Beta. White borders distinguished a reprint from a first printing.

question: Garfield rushed the very first expansion for Magic: the Gathering to print in December 1993. He borrowed its whole flavor from old folktales, printing cards like Library of Alexandria that became instant collector prizes. What was this first expansion called?
context: Arabian Nights was designed by Richard Garfield as a tribute to the 1001 Nights. Library of Alexandria became one of the strongest lands ever printed.

question: Two brothers go to war in the ancient land of Terisiare in Magic: the Gathering's artifact-heavy expansion of March 1994. One is a brilliant tinkerer who builds weapons by careful engineering; the other seizes raw artifact power without truly understanding it. Their war shatters the world and cools the whole planet into an ice age. What are the two brothers named?
context: Antiquities introduced the Brothers' War storyline, which would dominate MtG flavor lore for years. Mishra fell to Phyrexian corruption; Urza survived as a planeswalker.

question: A Magic: the Gathering player opens a pack from the huge expansion of June 1994, at 310 cards the largest set the game had ever printed. Inside are unique named heroes and villains like Sivitri Scarzam, the game's first multicolored cards and an odd combat rule called banding. What is the set called?
context: Legends brought the first legendary creatures, such as Kei Takahashi and Sol'kanar the Swamp King, with the Elder Dragons among them. Revised, two months earlier, had 306 cards.

question: A duelist plays Mox Pearl, one of the small artifact stones called moxen and among the most valuable early cards in Magic: the Gathering. Each mox adds one mana of a single color. Which color of mana does Mox Pearl produce?
context: The five moxen — Pearl, Sapphire, Jet, Ruby, Emerald — each tap for one mana of white, blue, black, red, and green respectively. Mox Emerald is the green one.

question: A duelist pays five mana in the first set of Magic: the Gathering, Alpha, and lays down a famous white creature. She has 4 power, 4 toughness, flying and vigilance. What is this creature called?
context: Serra Angel appears on the box art of several Magic sets. Douglas Shuler painted the iconic Alpha version, and the card became a banner image for white.

question: A Magic: the Gathering player casts a spell, and her opponent spends two mana on a famous blue card and stops it before it can even happen. The card goes back to the original Alpha printing of 1993. What is this classic blue spell called?
context: Counterspell was printed in Alpha with a cost of two blue mana. Its simplicity made it the gold standard for blue control, and later sets have made the effect more expensive or conditional.

question: A player jump-starting a five-color Magic: the Gathering deck casts one tiny green creature for a single green mana, and it can add one mana of any color. It has been reprinted edition after edition since the game's 1993 debut. What is this creature called?
context: Birds of Paradise is a 0/1 flier from Alpha. The Mark Poole artwork showed a colorful tropical bird perched on a branch. Birds is the iconic green mana fixer.

question: Hulk Hogan, the muscular blond hero, beat the villainous Iranian wrestler the Iron Sheik at Madison Square Garden on January 23, 1984, and won his first World Wrestling Federation championship. He used one signature two-move combination to finish the Sheik. What were those two moves?
answer: The leg drop, after a big boot
choices: The leg drop, after a big boot
The piledriver, after a body slam
The pedigree, after a knee strike
The sleeper hold, after a clothesline
context: Hogan's act was simple: take a beating, 'Hulk up' as the audience cheered, then big boot and leg drop for the win. He held the title until February 1988.

question: Randy 'Macho Man' Savage defended his Intercontinental (IC) Championship against 'The Dragon' Ricky Steamboat in the semi-main of WrestleMania III, on March 29, 1987, in a fifteen-minute classic before a crowd announced at 93,173 at the Pontiac Silverdome in Michigan. How did the IC title match end?
answer: Steamboat won the IC title from Savage
choices: Steamboat won the IC title from Savage
Savage retained with help from Miss Elizabeth
Savage kept the belt by disqualification
The match ended in a double count-out
context: Steamboat-Savage at WrestleMania III is widely considered one of the best wrestling matches of all time. The two had rehearsed every spot in advance and called nothing on the fly.

question: Vince McMahon told the referee to ring the bell in the middle of the Survivor Series match in Montreal on November 9, 1997, on a hold Bret Hart had not tapped out of. Bret had been scheduled to drop the World Wrestling Federation Championship that night. What was that hold?
answer: The Sharpshooter, Bret's own signature submission
choices: The Sharpshooter, Bret's own signature submission
The figure-four leg lock, applied to the wrong leg
The sleeper hold, held until Bret went limp
The crossface, with Shawn pulling Bret's chin back
context: The Montreal Screwjob is wrestling's most infamous double-cross. McMahon's behind-the-scenes role created the heel character 'Mr. McMahon' that helped fuel the Attitude Era.

question: Stone Cold Steve Austin, a bald Texan, beat Jake 'the Snake' Roberts in the 1996 King of the Ring final. In his victory speech he mocked Roberts and coined a catchphrase that went on millions of T-shirts. What was the phrase?
context: Austin's exact line: 'You talk about your Psalms, you talk about John 3:16 — Austin 3:16 says I just whipped your ass!' The phrase put Austin's character over.

question: Mick Foley climbed the sixteen-foot Hell in a Cell structure covering the whole ring to fight The Undertaker, at the King of the Ring pay-per-view in Pittsburgh on June 28, 1998. He took one huge fall from it and climbed back up. The Undertaker chokeslammed him. What did Foley crash through next?
answer: The top of the cage, falling through to the ring
choices: The top of the cage, falling through to the ring
A stack of tables placed at ringside
The steel steps beside the ring post
A pile of steel folding chairs by the ring post
context: Foley was first thrown 16 feet off the top of the cell through the Spanish announce table. Later, he was chokeslammed THROUGH the top of the cell to the mat below. Both falls happened in the same match.

question: A group of real-life best friends hugged each other on stage in front of the whole arena at Madison Square Garden on May 19, 1996, and broke wrestling's oldest rule: never let fans see the good guys and bad guys hanging out. The moment became known as the Curtain Call, and the friends as the Kliq. Who were they?
answer: Shawn Michaels, Razor Ramon, Diesel and Hunter Hearst Helmsley
choices: Shawn Michaels, Razor Ramon, Diesel and Hunter Hearst Helmsley
Bret Hart, Owen Hart, the British Bulldog and Jim Neidhart
Hulk Hogan, Randy Savage, the Ultimate Warrior and Roddy Piper
Steve Austin, the Rock, Mankind and the Undertaker
context: Hunter Hearst Helmsley later became Triple H. The four hugged after Michaels's steel-cage match with Diesel, breaking kayfabe in front of the crowd. Sean Waltman, the fifth member of the Kliq, was in rehab and missed it, and only Helmsley was punished: he was pushed down the card for months.

question: Hulk Hogan walked to the ring at the Bash at the Beach pay-per-view on July 7, 1996, after 13 years as the biggest good-guy hero in the business. He dropped a leg on his own teammate and joined the villains Scott Hall and Kevin Nash as the mysterious third man. What was their faction called?
answer: The New World Order, or nWo
choices: The New World Order, or nWo
context: Hogan's heel turn — 'You can stick it, brother' — was one of the most iconic moments in wrestling. Fans threw garbage in the ring. The nWo dominated WCW programming for years.

question: Boxing heavyweight Mike Tyson took a shocking guest role at WrestleMania XIV, in Boston on March 29, 1998. In the weeks before, he had been running a television storyline with the rebellious wrestling faction D-Generation X. What was his official on-screen job at the main event that night?
answer: Special outside enforcer of the WWF Championship main event
choices: Special outside enforcer of the WWF Championship main event
Guest referee for the Undertaker vs Kane match
Special timekeeper at ringside during the main event
Special interviewer for the Raw post-show
context: Tyson's appearance was a major mainstream-attention coup. He counted the pin after Stone Cold's Stunner on Shawn Michaels — apparently switching loyalties from DX to Austin in the closing seconds. The Tyson-Austin angle reportedly drew the most media attention since Andre vs Hogan WM III.

question: Paul Heyman, a New York manager, filled a small bingo hall in South Philadelphia with barbed-wire matches and table-and-ladder brawls, as booking mastermind of a wild indie wrestling promotion that ran from 1993 to 2001. Its rowdy stars included the high-flyer Sabu, the hometown hero Tommy Dreamer and the shoot-fighter Taz. What was this promotion called?
context: ECW pioneered hardcore wrestling in the United States. Paul Heyman's edgy, indie-feel programming pressured WWF and WCW to push their content envelope. ECW folded in early 2001.

question: Triple H hooked both of an opponent's arms behind the man's back, tucked the man's head between his knees and fell forward, driving the face into the mat. It was his signature finishing move. What was the move called?
context: Triple H started using the Pedigree in 1995. He started as Hunter Hearst Helmsley, a snobby New England aristocrat character, before D-Generation X turned him into a tough heel.

question: The Rock fought the hero Stone Cold Steve Austin for the World Wrestling Federation title in the main event of WrestleMania X-Seven, at the Houston Astrodome on April 1, 2001. Late in the match a shocking figure jumped into the ring and helped Austin win. Who was that surprise helper?
answer: Vince McMahon, marking Austin's heel turn
choices: Vince McMahon, marking Austin's heel turn
Shane McMahon, after he ran in from the entranceway
Triple H, Austin's rival of the year before
Kurt Angle, mid-feud with both wrestlers
context: Austin's heel turn shocked fans. McMahon handed Austin chairs and helped him beat down The Rock. The booking was hotly criticized; Austin's heel run is widely seen as a major creative misstep.

question: Hulk Hogan came back to the World Wrestling Federation at WrestleMania X8, in Toronto's SkyDome on March 17, 2002, after its purchase of World Championship Wrestling. Booked as the villain, he faced the top hero The Rock in an 'Icon vs. Icon' match. The Toronto crowd surprised the bookers completely. What were the fans doing?
answer: Cheering Hogan as the face and booing The Rock
choices: Cheering Hogan as the face and booing The Rock
Booing both men equally throughout the match
Chanting for Stone Cold Steve Austin to come out
Sitting in silence during the entire entrance
context: Hogan was scripted as the heel; the Toronto crowd ignored the script and treated him like the legend he was. Hogan turned face on the spot; The Rock embraced it.

question: A small-and-slow wide receiver from Tulsa nobody wanted reported to Seattle after the club joined the National Football League (NFL) as an expansion team in 1976. He played his entire 14-year career there, retired in 1989 with then-NFL records in catches and yards, and later served in the US Congress. Who was he?
context: Largent was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1995. He later served as a US Representative for Oklahoma from 1994 to 2002. The Seahawks number 80 is retired in his honor.

question: Colin Kaepernick, the San Francisco 49ers quarterback, lofted a fade pass to the corner of the end zone in the final minute of the National Football Conference (NFC) championship game on January 19, 2014, with Seattle leading 23-17. Seattle cornerback Richard Sherman leaped up and tipped the ball away, and a teammate caught the deflection. Which 49ers receiver was Kaepernick throwing to?
context: Sherman tipped the pass to teammate Malcolm Smith for the interception. The Erin Andrews postgame interview where Sherman shouted that he was the best corner in the game became instantly iconic.

question: Seattle's quarterback threw a quick slant toward the goal line with 26 seconds left in Super Bowl 49, on February 1, 2015, in Glendale, Arizona, trailing the New England Patriots 28-24 and one yard from the winning touchdown. An unknown rookie Patriots cornerback stepped in front of the receiver, caught the ball and ended the game right there. Who was he?
context: Butler was an undrafted rookie out of West Alabama. The Seahawks' decision to pass instead of handing the ball to Marshawn Lynch became one of the most second-guessed calls in football history.

question: A running back just arrived in Seattle from Buffalo took a handoff late in a wild-card playoff game against the New Orleans Saints on January 8, 2011. He broke nine tackles on a single 67-yard touchdown run, and the fans inside Qwest Field jumped and screamed so hard that a University of Washington instrument a block away picked it up. What did the play get nicknamed?
context: The run helped the Seahawks upset the defending Super Bowl champion Saints 41-36. The University of Washington's Pacific Northwest Seismic Network confirmed the seismic signature.

question: Sportswriters named one Seattle running back National Football League (NFL) Most Valuable Player (MVP) for the 2005 season, after he rushed for 1,880 yards and scored 28 touchdowns, both leading the league. Then the Pittsburgh Steelers beat Seattle 21-10 in Super Bowl 40, a title game full of controversial referee calls. Who was this MVP running back?
context: Alexander played at Alabama before being drafted by Seattle in 2000. He set the then-NFL single-season touchdown record with 28 in 2005. Super Bowl XL was decided 21-10 with several controversial officiating calls against Seattle.

question: Joey Cora stood on third in the Kingdome in October 1995, in the 11th inning of the deciding Game 5 against the New York Yankees. A Mariners hitter lined a double down the left-field line, and Cora and a young teammate from first both raced home to win it. Which Yankees pitcher threw that pitch?
context: Edgar's Double saved baseball in Seattle. The 1995 'Refuse to Lose' campaign and that hit are credited with securing public funding for what became Safeco Field.

question: Cranky Frank Costanza, the father of George Costanza, shouts a legendary rant right at New York Yankees owner George Steinbrenner over the trade of Jay Buhner in a 1996 episode of the NBC comedy Seinfeld. Buhner really was a Seattle Mariners outfielder, and the Yankees really had traded him away in 1988. Who was the player the Yankees got back in that real-life trade?
context: The Yankees traded Buhner to Seattle in July 1988 for the aging Ken Phelps. Buhner hit more than 300 home runs for Seattle, and the Seinfeld scene immortalized the trade as a Yankees blunder.

question: Pat Gillick built a 2001 Seattle Mariners side that won 116 regular-season games, the most in a single Major League Baseball season by any team of the modern era. That total tied a record that had stood untouched since 1906, when one turn-of-the-century club also won 116 games in a season. Which team set the 1906 record?
context: The 1906 Cubs won 116 games in a 152-game season; the 2001 Mariners won 116 in 162. Both teams failed to win the World Series — the Mariners lost the ALCS to the Yankees 4-1.

question: George Sisler had held the single-season hits record since 1920, with a mark of 257, until a Seattle Mariners right fielder passed him during the 2004 Major League Baseball season. All summer the right fielder sprayed singles, choppers and bunts across American ballparks. How many total hits did he end that record-breaking season with?
context: Sisler's record of 257 had stood since 1920 — 84 years. Ichiro broke it on October 1, 2004. His 2004 batting average was .372. He hit 262 in 161 games.

question: A young pinch-hitter stepped in for the Seattle Mariners in the bottom of the ninth against Oakland on September 30, 2022, with the score tied 1-1. A win would end the longest active playoff drought in North America's major pro sports, twenty-one years long. His walk-off homer did it. Who was he?
context: The 2022 Mariners snapped a 21-year postseason drought — the longest active drought in the four major North American sports. They beat the Blue Jays in the AL Wild Card series.

question: Garfield finished his doctorate in mathematics at the University of Pennsylvania in 1993, the same year his card game Magic: the Gathering reached the shops. His branch of mathematics directly helped him give the game balanced odds. What branch was it?
answer: Combinatorial mathematics, the mathematics of counting and arranging
choices: Combinatorial mathematics, the mathematics of counting and arranging
Differential geometry, the mathematics of curved surfaces
Number theory, especially prime distribution and factorization
Topology, the mathematics of connectedness and continuity
context: Garfield's doctorate, supervised by Herbert Wilf, was in combinatorial mathematics. He became a visiting professor at Whitman College soon after. He had designed RoboRally years before Magic.

question: A small game publisher met Garfield in 1991, looking for something new to print. Garfield showed him one design first, but it cost too much to make, so the publisher asked instead for a cheap game that was portable and quick to play. Garfield came back with Magic: the Gathering. What was the first design?
choices: Talisman, a fantasy quest board game
context: Adkison liked RoboRally, but it was too costly for the tiny startup, so he asked Garfield for a portable game that played quickly, and Garfield designed Magic. Wizards of the Coast published RoboRally in 1994, after Magic's success.

question: Longtime Magic: the Gathering players rose up in fury in July 1995, when a cheap new set reprinted a big chunk of the most famous cards from earlier expansions and crashed the collector market. The makers answered in 1996 with the Reserved List, a promise never to reprint. What was the 1995 set called?
choices: Revised, the third edition of the base set
Collectors' Edition, a square-cornered gift reprint
context: Chronicles reprinted cards from Arabian Nights, Antiquities, Legends and The Dark in cheap white-bordered form. Collectors who had paid premium prices saw values drop overnight, and the Reserved List was Wizards' answer.

question: An experienced collector holds up two Magic: the Gathering cards of the same design, one from the first print run of about 2.6 million cards, called Alpha, and one from the next, called Beta. One physical difference in the card itself tells her which is which. What marks a card as Alpha?
answer: Rounder corners than Beta and all later printings
choices: Rounder corners than Beta and all later printings
Thicker cardstock than any later printing
Glossy front coating not used in later sets
Smaller text font on the rules box
context: Alpha cards have a noticeably larger corner radius than Beta cards. Beta sharpened the corners to standard playing-card dimensions. The Alpha rounded corners are the easiest visual tell of a 1993 first-run card.

question: Garfield set the colors of Magic: the Gathering on a wheel, each with two allies at its side and two enemies opposite. White, the color of order, counts green among its allies. What are white's two enemy colors?
context: The Color Pie matters mechanically — allied colors share more themes (white-blue control, blue-black graveyard, white-green lifegain) while enemy colors are designed in opposition. White's law-and-order conflicts with black's selfishness and red's freedom.

question: Magic: the Gathering's first Pro Tour came to New York City in February 1996, with real cash prizes on the table. Its winner beat, in the final, the same Frenchman who had lost the first World Championship two years before. Who won that first Pro Tour?
context: Loconto beat Bertrand Lestree, the runner-up of the 1994 World Championship, in the final and took home $12,000. Tom Chanpheng won the 1996 World Championship, the first Worlds run as a Pro Tour.

question: One villain pinned Bruno Sammartino at Madison Square Garden in January 1971 and took the World Wide Wrestling Federation belt from him. The Italian-American strongman had held it since May 1963 without losing it once, a run of nearly eight years and still the longest single title reign in pro wrestling history. Who pinned him?
choices: Pedro Morales, the Puerto Rican grappler
Superstar Billy Graham, the muscle-bound icon
context: Koloff pinned Sammartino on January 18, 1971, ending a 2,803-day reign. The MSG crowd was silent in shock. Koloff held the belt just 21 days before dropping it to Pedro Morales.

question: Rowdy Roddy Piper and 'Mr. Wonderful' Paul Orndorff lost the main event of the very first WrestleMania, at Madison Square Garden on March 31, 1985, to Hulk Hogan and a hugely famous celebrity. Who was Hogan's celebrity partner that night?
answer: Mr. T, fresh off Rocky III and The A-Team
choices: Mr. T, fresh off Rocky III and The A-Team
Cyndi Lauper, the pop star manager
context: Mr. T's involvement linked wrestling to mainstream Hollywood. Cyndi Lauper was at ringside; Muhammad Ali was the special outside enforcer; Liberace was the timekeeper. The whole night was a celebrity spectacular that legitimized the event.

question: Andre publicly turned on Hulk Hogan on the Piper's Pit talk segment on February 7, 1987, and the two were on-screen friends no longer. Their confrontation at WrestleMania III took years to build. What did Andre famously rip off Hogan?
answer: Hogan's crucifix necklace, leaving a cut on his chest
choices: Hogan's crucifix necklace, leaving a cut on his chest
Hogan's iconic yellow bandanna with the red H
The WWF Championship belt itself, in a shocking grab
A handful of Hogan's signature yellow beard
context: Andre, prompted by his new manager Bobby 'The Brain' Heenan, tore Hogan's crucifix off in a violent flourish. The on-camera blood from the chain digging in was reportedly real. The angle launched a year of buildup to WrestleMania III.

question: The Ultimate Warrior, a face-painted, tassel-wearing powerhouse, beat Hulk Hogan in a rare champion-versus-champion match at WrestleMania VI, in Toronto's SkyDome on April 1, 1990. Each man had walked to the ring wearing a different championship belt. After the match only one remained: the two titles had been unified. Which two belts were merged that night?
choices: WWF Championship and World Tag Team Championship
WWF Championship and World Television Championship
WWF Championship and King of the Ring crown
context: Warrior was the IC champion; Hogan held the WWF title. The Warrior won and held both belts for the first time in WWF history. He held the WWF title until SummerSlam 1990, when he lost it to Sgt. Slaughter.

question: Bret 'The Hitman' Hart defended his Intercontinental Championship at Wembley Stadium in London on August 29, 1992, in the main match of the SummerSlam pay-per-view. Most of the more than 80,000 fans cheered not for Bret but for his real-life brother-in-law, who took the belt from him that night. Who was Bret's opponent?
answer: Davey Boy Smith, the British Bulldog
choices: Davey Boy Smith, the British Bulldog
Jim Neidhart, his Hart Foundation tag partner
Mr. Perfect, his then-rival Curt Hennig
context: Davey Boy Smith was married to Bret's sister Diana. The Wembley match was a 26-minute classic. Bret carried Smith, who later admitted he had blanked on much of the choreography and that Bret called every spot in real time.

question: Mick Foley won the World Wrestling Federation Championship for the very first time on a taped Monday Night Raw that aired on January 4, 1999. The result had leaked, and that same night someone on the rival live show, Monday Nitro, read the spoiler on the air. Who delivered the spoiler?
choices: Eric Bischoff, the head of WCW
Ric Flair, the Four Horsemen leader
Mean Gene Okerlund, the WCW interviewer
context: Schiavone told Nitro's viewers that Foley, who had wrestled in WCW as Cactus Jack, was going to win the title, and sneered that it would put some butts in the seats. Roughly 600,000 viewers reportedly switched to Raw. Schiavone has expressed lasting regret over the announcement.

question: Stone Cold Steve Austin beat Shawn Michaels for his first World Wrestling Federation Championship in Boston on March 29, 1998. It was Shawn's last match for over four years. What caused Shawn's hiatus?
answer: A serious back injury, including a herniated disc
choices: A serious back injury, including a herniated disc
A torn rotator cuff that required reconstructive surgery
A career-ending concussion from a casket match
A torn ACL from a leap off the Hell in a Cell
context: Shawn had originally hurt his back at Royal Rumble 1998 during a casket match with the Undertaker. He held on to the title for WrestleMania despite barely being able to walk. He did not wrestle again until 2002.

question: Dwayne Johnson turned one sneering insult into a household word in the late 1990s, using it on wrestlers he considered nobodies. The term is usually traced to wrestling slang for a wrestler whose only work was to lose on purpose so that the top star would look strong. What was that losing role called inside the wrestling business?
answer: A jobber, the man who does the job
choices: A jobber, the man who does the job
A heel or henchman in the locker room
A bumper, the rookie who took practice falls
context: A jobber does the job: he loses so that the star looks good. The Rock made jabroni a household insult in the late 1990s.

question: The Undertaker fought the first-ever Hell in a Cell match at the Badd Blood pay-per-view on October 5, 1997. It ran for 30 minutes, and then the lights went out. Who arrived in a red-and-black costume to attack the Undertaker?
choices: The Big Boss Man, freshly heel
context: Kane was Glenn Jacobs, who had played other gimmicks before (Isaac Yankem DDS, the fake Diesel). The Undertaker and Kane brother feud became one of the WWF's longest-running stories.

question: The Rock was cutting a promo in the ring on Monday Night Raw on August 9, 1999, when a mystery 30-second countdown clock ticked down. When it hit zero, the arena went into flashing lights, the crowd exploded, and a cocky new wrestler strolled out to cut The Rock off mid-sentence. What was this brand-new character called?
choices: Tazz, the WWF debut from ECW
context: Y2J — short for Year Two-Thousand Jericho — referenced the Y2K bug. Jericho had been WCW's star and chose to jump ship for a bigger role. He went on to become the first Undisputed Champion in WWF history in December 2001.

question: Kurt Angle signed with the World Wrestling Federation in late 1999 with a credential no other wrestler there could match: a real Olympic gold medal from the 1996 Summer Games in Atlanta. Fans mocked him with 'You suck!' chants, but he really was an Olympic champion. In what specific sport and weight class did Angle win his gold?
context: Angle won gold despite a broken neck — he wrestled with two cracked vertebrae. His credentials helped him transition into wrestling instantly. His three I's were Intensity, Integrity, and Intelligence.

question: A retired Seattle wide receiver ran for the U.S. House of Representatives as a Republican in 1994 and won his very first campaign. He had left the National Football League (NFL) five years earlier holding every major career record for pass catchers: most receptions, most yards, most touchdowns. Which state's congressional district did he go on to represent?
context: Largent was a four-term congressman until 2002, when he made an unsuccessful run for Oklahoma governor. He had been the all-time leader in catches (819), receiving yards (13,089), and TD catches (100) when he retired.

question: Matt Hasselbeck dropped back in Seattle behind one enormous Alabama-born left tackle, drafted sixth overall out of Florida State. That lineman anchored the offensive line for twelve straight seasons from 1997 to 2008. He made nine Pro Bowls, never played for another team and was elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2014. What was his name?
context: Walter Jones was inducted to the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2014. He famously held out three times as the franchise tagged him in consecutive years — and never missed a game from those holdouts. He blocked for Shaun Alexander's MVP season.

question: Seattle picked a quarterback in the third round of the 2012 National Football League (NFL) Draft, 75th overall. He had transferred for his final college season from one school to another after being passed over as the starter at his original school. Which two schools did he attend in football?
answer: NC State, then Wisconsin for his senior year
choices: NC State, then Wisconsin for his senior year
Virginia Tech, then Florida State for graduate transfer
Boise State, then Oregon for a transfer year
Stanford, then North Carolina for a transfer year
context: Wilson played quarterback and baseball at NC State. When Mike Glennon was named starting QB for 2011, Wilson used the graduate transfer rule to go to Wisconsin. He led the Badgers to the Rose Bowl that season.

question: Peyton Manning was still reading the defense on the very first play from scrimmage of the National Football League's title game on February 2, 2014, in New Jersey. The center hiked the ball early, and it flew past Manning into the end zone behind him. What did that opening play score for Seattle?
answer: A safety, the fastest in Super Bowl history at 12 seconds
choices: A safety, the fastest in Super Bowl history at 12 seconds
A touchdown after Lynch recovered the fumble
A field goal after Hauschka kicked from the 5-yard line
A touchdown after Malcolm Smith ran it back
context: Center Manny Ramirez snapped the ball before Manning was ready, and Knowshon Moreno recovered it in the end zone for a safety. The 12-second score was the fastest in Super Bowl history.

question: Cortez Kennedy played like a wrecking ball at tackle in 1992, on a Seattle team with only two wins and fourteen losses. He spent eleven seasons in the National Football League (NFL), and that year, even on a losing team, he took home one of its top honors. What was the award called?
answer: NFL Defensive Player of the Year
choices: NFL Defensive Player of the Year
Walter Payton Man of the Year Award
NFL Comeback Player of the Year
context: Cortez Kennedy was virtually impossible to single-block. He recorded 14 sacks from defensive tackle in 1992. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2012. He died unexpectedly in May 2017 at age 48.

question: The Seattle Mariners' star center fielder, a slugger with a gorgeous swing, went down on one play in 1995 and paid a huge price for it: he missed months of the season. What was the injury?
answer: He broke his left wrist crashing into the Kingdome wall making a catch
choices: He broke his left wrist crashing into the Kingdome wall making a catch
He tore his hamstring legging out an infield single
He suffered a season-ending concussion from a beanball
He shattered his ankle stealing third base
context: Griffey crashed into the wall on May 26, 1995 making a spectacular catch. He returned in August. The injury cost Seattle his presence for half a season, but his return helped fuel the 'Refuse to Lose' playoff push.

question: Ken Griffey Sr. joined the Seattle Mariners for the 1990 season and played beside his son in the same outfield. On September 14, 1990, father and son did something no other father-son duo had ever done in a Major League game. What was it?
answer: Hit back-to-back home runs in the same inning
choices: Hit back-to-back home runs in the same inning
Started a triple play together in the outfield
Each hit two home runs in the same game
context: Griffey Sr. and Jr. hit back-to-back homers off Kirk McCaskill of the Angels at Anaheim Stadium. Junior was 20; Sr. was 40. They had played together since August 31, 1990. No father-son duo has ever done it since.

question: A rookie from Japan joined the Seattle Mariners in 2001, collected 242 hits, batted .350 and won both the American League Rookie of the Year and the Most Valuable Player awards. Two more famous honors came his way that same season. Which two awards did he add?
answer: Gold Glove and Silver Slugger in right field
choices: Gold Glove and Silver Slugger in right field
Roberto Clemente Award and Cy Young Award
Hank Aaron Award and Babe Ruth Award
Comeback Player of the Year and All-Star MVP
context: Ichiro's 2001 was unprecedented for a rookie. He also led the league with 56 stolen bases, and he went on to win ten straight Gold Gloves.

question: Major League Baseball renamed its yearly award for the best designated hitter (DH) after one Seattle Mariners legend, who spent most of his career in that role and rarely played in the field. He was born in New York in 1963, raised in Puerto Rico, and made seven All-Star teams. What is the DH-of-the-year prize called now?
context: MLB renamed the Outstanding DH Award the Edgar Martinez Award in 2004, the year he retired. He won it five times during his career, before they renamed it for him.

question: A Seattle fan watches the 116-win Mariners of 2001 lose the American League Championship Series (ALCS) to the New York Yankees, 4 games to 1, a year after the 2000 club also fell to New York. The first Mariners side to reach that round, in 1995, went out to a different team. Which team eliminated them?
choices: The Red Sox, in a 4-1 series
context: Cleveland beat Seattle four games to two in the 1995 ALCS, days after Edgar's Double. The 2000 and 2001 Mariners both lost the ALCS to the Yankees, the 2000 side four games to two.

question: A collector lays out the Power Nine, the most coveted cards of Magic: the Gathering, all first printed in 1993: Black Lotus, the five moxen, Ancestral Recall and Time Walk. The ninth card makes every player shuffle hand, graveyard and library together, then draw seven fresh cards. What is the ninth card?
context: The Power Nine are Black Lotus, Ancestral Recall, Time Walk, Timetwister and the five moxen, printed in the game's first sets of 1993 and dropped from the base set in 1994. Wheel of Fortune, a red card from the same first set, also hands every player a fresh seven, but by discarding hands rather than shuffling them back.

question: Garfield laid the groundwork for Magic: the Gathering with an earlier card game of his own, Five Magics. He built it in the spirit of an older board game he had loved for years, where every player holds one special power that breaks the rules. Which game inspired it?
answer: Cosmic Encounter, a science-fiction negotiation game
choices: Cosmic Encounter, a science-fiction negotiation game
Diplomacy, the World War I negotiation board game
Settlers of Catan, the resource-trading board game
context: Cosmic Encounter gives each player an alien race with its own rule-breaking power. Garfield's Five Magics, inspired by it, laid the foundation for Magic. Garfield also designed RoboRally, King of Tokyo and others.

question: A duelist pays 8 mana to cast one of the five three-color Elder Dragons of 1994 in Magic: the Gathering. One of them, in blue-black-red, a scheming, primordial reptile, became the game's most famous recurring villain across the next thirty years of storylines. Which Elder Dragon is that villain?
context: Nicol Bolas is depicted with horns and golden eyes; the original Legends artwork by Mark Tedin became iconic. The Elder Dragon Highlander format (later renamed Commander) took its name from this cycle. Bolas became a planeswalker in lore, then de-sparked, then returned multiple times.

question: A duelist kills an opponent on turn one of Magic: the Gathering with Fireball, fed by a burst of colorless mana from one early card. The first banned-and-restricted list for tournament play came in 1994, and this card was eventually restricted to one per deck rather than banned outright. What was the card?
answer: Channel, the Alpha green sorcery converting life into mana
choices: Channel, the Alpha green sorcery converting life into mana
Mishra's Workshop, the Antiquities artifact land producing colorless mana
Strip Mine, the original land-destruction land from Antiquities
Bazaar of Baghdad, the Arabian Nights draw engine of choice
context: Channel and Fireball became a notorious first-turn kill. Channel itself remains restricted in Vintage.

question: Eric Bischoff, the head of World Championship Wrestling, decided to cut Steve Austin in 1995, with the Texan at home recovering from surgery on a torn triceps. Austin had joined in 1991 as a good-looking villain called 'Stunning' Steve Austin and won two titles there. Bischoff did not call. He did not visit. How did the firing reach Austin?
answer: A FedEx envelope delivered to Austin while he was injured
choices: A FedEx envelope delivered to Austin while he was injured
A phone call during Austin's recovery from triceps surgery
An in-person meeting at the WCW offices in Atlanta
A handwritten letter mailed to Austin's Texas home
context: Austin had torn his triceps tendon while wrestling in Japan. WCW released him because Bischoff said Austin couldn't draw. Austin used the firing as fuel — the bitter chip on his shoulder created the 'Stone Cold' character. He went to ECW briefly before debuting in the WWF in early 1996.

question: Mick Foley put out a New York Times bestseller in 1999, the autobiography 'Have a Nice Day: A Tale of Blood and Sweatsocks.' How he produced the manuscript became part of the book's mythology. What was unique about his method?
answer: He wrote the whole 500+ page book in pencil while flying coach between WWF house shows
choices: He wrote the whole 500+ page book in pencil while flying coach between WWF house shows
He dictated it to his wife, who transcribed it on a typewriter
He composed it in a hotel office during a year-long retirement
He emailed chapters to ghostwriter J.R. Moehringer for editing
context: Foley wrote in spiral notebooks during his constant travel. Editor Michael Wright assembled the chapters from Foley's handwritten pages. The book sold over 1 million copies. Foley dedicated it to his daughter Noelle. Three follow-up memoirs followed — Foley Is Good, The Hardcore Diaries, and Countdown to Lockdown.

question: Referee Earl Hebner called for the bell on a hold Bret Hart had not submitted to, at the Molson Centre on November 9, 1997. This was the Montreal Screwjob, at the Survivor Series in Bret's home country of Canada. What did Bret do to Vince McMahon after the show?
answer: Punched McMahon in the locker room, leaving him with a black eye
choices: Punched McMahon in the locker room, leaving him with a black eye
Walked out without a word and never spoke to McMahon again
Sent McMahon a handwritten resignation letter the next morning
Shoved McMahon off the stage at a Toronto press conference
context: McMahon came away with a black eye and a sprained ankle: Bret said the punch lifted him off his feet and he rolled the ankle landing, while McMahon and Gerald Brisco later said Brisco had stepped on his foot. Bret left for WCW and did not return to WWE until 2010.

question: Triple H and his D-Generation X partner shouted the question and the crowd shouted the answer, with crotch-chopping flourishes that became merch gold. It was the group's signature catchphrase. What was the call-and-response?
answer: Are you ready? — followed by 'two words: SUCK IT'
choices: Are you ready? — followed by 'two words: SUCK IT'
Whatcha gonna do? — followed by 'Hulkamania runs wild'
Can I get a hell yeah? — followed by Stone Cold's whoop
Who's the man? — followed by 'The Rock is the man'
context: DX formed in 1997 with Shawn Michaels, Triple H, Chyna, and Rick Rude. After Shawn's back injury in 1998, Triple H led the second iteration including X-Pac and the New Age Outlaws. Their crotch-chops and 'SUCK IT' became defining Attitude Era moments.

question: The Rock pinned Mick Foley in the finals of a 14-man tournament for the vacant World Wrestling Federation title, at Survivor Series on November 15, 1998. It began his first reign as champion. What controversial development in the match turned a hero into a villain?
answer: Vince McMahon switched alignment and helped The Rock cheat to win, forming the Corporation
choices: Vince McMahon switched alignment and helped The Rock cheat to win, forming the Corporation
The Rock low-blowed Mankind without a referee seeing it
Mankind tapped out to a fake submission for a cash payoff
Shawn Michaels returned to interfere on The Rock's behalf
context: The Rock had been a babyface; his joining the Corporation heel faction with McMahon was a major character pivot. McMahon called The Rock 'The Corporate Champion.' This set up the year-long Rock-Mankind-Austin triangle that defined late 1998 and 1999.

question: Goldberg lost at Starrcade on December 27, 1998, and an undefeated streak that had begun in September 1997 was over. The on-air announcers of World Championship Wrestling had claimed 173 wins with zero losses. Who beat him that night?
answer: Kevin Nash, with help from Scott Hall using a stun gun
choices: Kevin Nash, with help from Scott Hall using a stun gun
Hulk Hogan, in a one-on-one match without interference
Sting, with a Scorpion Death Lock submission
Bret Hart, after a Sharpshooter that Goldberg verbally submitted to
context: Scott Hall ran in disguised as a security guard and hit Goldberg with a taser disguised as a cattle prod. Kevin Nash then pinned him with a Jackknife Powerbomb. Goldberg's real win-loss record in WCW was much lower than 173-0, but the kayfabe number is the famous one.

question: Sting changed everything in 1996. For years the smiling, face-painted good-guy hero of World Championship Wrestling, with bright colors and a blond flat-top haircut, he grew silent, switched to black leather and white face paint, and started appearing high in the arena rafters holding a black baseball bat. His new look was copied directly from a 1994 movie about a rock musician who returns from the dead. Which movie?
choices: Phantom of the Opera, the Broadway revival
context: Sting hid in the rafters of WCW arenas for months in 1996-97, watching events without intervening. He finally returned at Starrcade 1997 to face Hollywood Hogan for the WCW World title. The Crow-inspired character became Sting's most iconic look.

question: The World Wrestling Federation brought the boxer Mike Tyson to WrestleMania XIV in March 1998 for the main event between Shawn Michaels and Stone Cold Steve Austin, after weeks of siding on TV with Michaels's faction D-Generation X. Austin landed the Stunner with the referee down, and Tyson slid into the ring. What did he do?
answer: Counted the three for Austin, then knocked Michaels out
choices: Counted the three for Austin, then knocked Michaels out
Refused to count, then dragged Austin out of the ring
Woke the referee, then held Austin for a Michaels kick
Raised Michaels's hand, then walked out with D-Generation X
context: Tyson made a fast three count after the Stunner, giving Austin his first WWF Championship. When Michaels confronted him, Tyson floored him with one punch, and Austin celebrated by tossing him an Austin 3:16 shirt.

question: Vince McMahon Jr. inherited control of Capitol Wrestling Corporation from his father in 1982, and he made an aggressive move that altered the business permanently: he ignored the unwritten rule that promoters did not poach other territories' top talent. Who was the first major star he poached, kicking off his national expansion?
answer: Hulk Hogan, who had been working for Verne Gagne's AWA
choices: Hulk Hogan, who had been working for Verne Gagne's AWA
Andre the Giant, who had been a Vince Sr loyalist
Bob Backlund, who was already WWWF champion
Roddy Piper, from Stampede Wrestling in Calgary
context: Hogan had been working for Verne Gagne's AWA and had developed Hulkamania there. Vince Jr signed him in December 1983 and immediately put the WWF title on him in January 1984. The territorial system collapsed within a few years; Vince had bought the country.

question: Chyna, billed as the Ninth Wonder of the World, became the first woman to enter the Royal Rumble in 1999. Later that year she became the first to win the Intercontinental Championship, at the No Mercy pay-per-view. Whom did she defeat for that belt?
answer: Jeff Jarrett, in a 'Good Housekeeping' gimmick match
choices: Jeff Jarrett, in a 'Good Housekeeping' gimmick match
Chris Jericho, in a singles match with no time limit
Triple H, in a stipulation match on Raw
X-Pac, in a no-disqualification gimmick match
context: Jarrett had been champion. The Good Housekeeping match involved household objects (irons, vacuum cleaners, frying pans) as weapons. Chyna's real name was Joan Laurer. She passed away in April 2016.

question: Eddie Guerrero grew up in a family of wrestlers: his father, the lucha libre legend Gory Guerrero, and his brothers Chavo, Mando and Hector all worked the ring. Gory staged his own shows, and as a boy Eddie wrestled his nephew, the younger Chavo, in the intermissions. Where did Gory hold those shows?
context: Gory Guerrero promoted shows at the El Paso County Coliseum, and Eddie, raised in El Paso, wrestled young Chavo there during intermissions. Eddie debuted in 1986 and wrestled in Mexico as the original Mascara Magica before ECW, WCW and the WWF.

question: Bill Leavy refereed Super Bowl XL on February 5, 2006, in Detroit, where the Pittsburgh Steelers beat Seattle 21-10 in a game marred by officiating controversies. In the fourth quarter a holding flag on Sean Locklear wiped out a long Seattle catch. Years later, what did Leavy publicly admit about his officiating in that game?
answer: He had 'kicked' two specific calls and the controversy haunted him
choices: He had 'kicked' two specific calls and the controversy haunted him
His crew had been improperly trained on the rules in effect
He stood by every call his crew had made that night
He had lost sight of the ball on the Pittsburgh touchdown run
context: Leavy spoke up at Seahawks training camp in August 2010: he said he kicked two calls in the fourth quarter, that he had impacted the game, and that it had left him with a lot of sleepless nights. He did not say which two calls he meant.

question: Beast Mode, Seattle's bruising running back, arrived at the podium in the days before Super Bowl 49 in early 2015, for the required media sessions he famously hated. He answered every single reporter's question with one identical repeated sentence. What was the sentence?
answer: I'm just here so I won't get fined
choices: I'm just here so I won't get fined
Beast Mode, that's all I got
context: Lynch had been fined repeatedly by the NFL for refusing to speak to media. At Super Bowl XLIX media day, he attended for less than five minutes and used the line as his only response. The NFL eventually changed media-availability rules after the Lynch saga.

question: Darrell Bevell, Seattle's offensive coordinator, called a slant pass to Ricardo Lockette instead of a run at the end of Super Bowl 49, with one yard to go and 26 seconds left, on second down. It became one of the most famous play calls in football history. Why did Bevell later say the team didn't run the ball there?
answer: To save time and avoid a third-down clock issue
choices: To save time and avoid a third-down clock issue
Wilson had audibled out of the planned run call
The Patriots had only one timeout left and Seattle panicked
Lynch was injured and needed a play to catch his breath
context: Bevell took heat from fans for the call. Pete Carroll defended it, saying the Patriots' goal-line stack expected a run. Malcolm Butler recognised the formation from practice, where the scout team had beaten him on the same play.

question: The Seattle crowd at Qwest Field roared on January 8, 2011, as a running back broke tackle after tackle on a 67-yard touchdown run against the visiting New Orleans Saints in a National Football League (NFL) playoff game. The noise shook the stands so hard that nearby University of Washington seismographs, the instruments that measure earthquakes, registered real ground movement. What did they read?
context: The seismograph that registered the Beast Quake was a station near Qwest Field (now Lumen Field) operated by the UW Pacific Northwest Seismic Network. The magnitude was measured at roughly 2.0 — equivalent to a very small earthquake. The 67-yard run featured Lynch breaking nine tackles, including the famous stiff-arm of Tracy Porter at the 30-yard line. The tradition continues; subsequent Seahawks games have produced their own measurable quakes during big plays.

question: A new head coach took over Seattle in January 2010 after nine years at the University of Southern California (USC), where he had won national college football championships in 2003 and 2004. The club had just finished a losing 5-11 season and fired the head coach it had brought in the year before. Who was the man he replaced?
answer: Jim Mora Jr., who lasted only one season as head coach
choices: Jim Mora Jr., who lasted only one season as head coach
Mike Holmgren, who left after the 2008 season
Tom Cable, the interim head coach
Dennis Erickson, who returned for a season
context: Jim Mora Jr was Mike Holmgren's defensive backs coach who was promoted before Carroll arrived. He coached just the 2009 season (5-11). Holmgren left in 2008 after a decade. Carroll became GM and head coach, building the Legion of Boom defense from the ground up.

question: Dave Niehaus was calling the game on the radio on October 8, 1995, when a series-winning double in the 11th inning of Game 5, in baseball's divisional playoff round, scored Joey Cora from third and a Mariners teammate from first base. His call has become a Mariners legend. What words did Niehaus famously shout as the winning run scored?
answer: My oh my, and that the Mariners would play for the American League Championship
choices: My oh my, and that the Mariners would play for the American League Championship
Hot diggity, and that Seattle was going to the World Series
Holy mackerel, and that the Mariners had won the West
Goodness gracious, and that Seattle had won it all
context: Niehaus's full call: 'Right now the Mariners are going to play for the American League Championship! I don't believe it! It just continues! My oh my!' The call has been played thousands of times at Safeco Field. Niehaus was inducted into the Hall of Fame broadcaster wing in 2008. He died in November 2010 of a heart attack.

question: The baseball writers who left a Seattle Mariners center fielder off their Hall of Fame ballots in January 2016 have never said why. The rest elected him to Cooperstown with a then-record vote percentage, just short of unanimous. What exact percentage did he receive?
context: Griffey's 99.3% topped Tom Seaver's previous record of 98.84%. The record stood until Mariano Rivera became the first unanimous Hall-of-Famer in 2019. Derek Jeter then missed unanimity by one vote in 2020 (99.7%). The three writers who did not vote for Griffey never revealed themselves publicly.

question: Woody Woodward, the Seattle Mariners general manager, called Montreal in May 1989 about a wild young Expos starter, a lanky 6-foot-10 left-hander who would later win five Cy Young awards. He worked out a trade, sending one of his own pitchers north in exchange. Which pitcher did Woodward give up to land the future Hall of Famer?
context: The Langston-for-Johnson trade is regarded as one of the most lopsided in baseball history in Seattle's favor. Johnson went on to win five Cy Youngs, the first in 1995 with Seattle. The Mariners also got Brian Holman and Gene Harris in the deal.

question: A right fielder who came to the Seattle Mariners after nine seasons with Japan's Orix BlueWave retired as the holder of a world baseball record no other player has ever matched: his Japanese pro-league hits and his Major League hits added together. How many career hits did he finish with in all?
context: His 1,278 hits in Japan and 3,089 in the majors make 4,367. The combined total passed Pete Rose's major-league record of 4,256 on 15 June 2016, though Rose still holds the official major-league mark, and Ichiro played on until 2019, back with Seattle.

question: A fan in the King's Court, the yellow-shirted bleacher section at Safeco Field, watches the 27th straight Tampa Bay Ray go down on August 15, 2012. It is the 23rd perfect game in Major League Baseball history and the third in 2012 alone. Which other two pitchers threw perfect games that season?
context: Philip Humber's perfect game came on April 21 against the Mariners, and Matt Cain's on June 13 against Houston. No season before 2012 had held three perfect games.

question: Magic: the Gathering's first print run, Alpha, came out in 1993 with nine of the ten original dual lands, which each make two colors of mana. The tenth was missing from the print sheets and first appeared in the second run, Beta, so no Alpha copy of it exists. What was the missing land?
answer: Volcanic Island, the red-blue dual land
choices: Volcanic Island, the red-blue dual land
Underground Sea, the blue-black dual land
context: Volcanic Island and Circle of Protection: Black are the two cards that never made it into Alpha, by one account because their art was not finished in time. Both first appeared in Beta, and the dual lands joined the Reserved List in 1996.

question: Suppose you cast one of the five Elder Dragons from Magic: the Gathering's June 1994 expansion, a legendary three-color dragon that cost 8 mana. The cycle had a notorious design quirk that made these dragons hard to keep on the table despite their power. What was that quirk?
answer: Each upkeep, you paid 3 mana of their colors or sacrificed them
choices: Each upkeep, you paid 3 mana of their colors or sacrificed them
Each upkeep, you discarded a card from your hand or lost 5 life
Each turn, you skipped your draw step or sacrificed two lands
Each combat, you attacked with them or paid 5 generic mana
context: The upkeep tax of three colored mana made the Elder Dragons hard to keep in any deck without plenty of mana fixing. Their design legacy is large: the Elder Dragon Highlander format, later renamed Commander, takes its name from this cycle.

question: Players at Magic: the Gathering's first Pro Tour, in New York City in February 1996, built decks from the sets then in print, the usual tournament format of the day. The organizers added one rule of their own on top, and it shaped every deck in the room. What did the rule require?
answer: At least five cards from each legal set
choices: At least five cards from each legal set
At least one card of each of the five colors
No more than one copy of any rare card
Exactly twenty lands among sixty cards
context: The format, nicknamed New York Style, was a modified Type II: each deck, counting its sideboard, had to hold at least five cards from every set legal at the time.

question: Fans furious over reprints won a promise in 1996: the Reserved List of more than 500 Magic: the Gathering cards that would never be reprinted. The makers went back to the list in 2002 and removed one specific category of card. What category did they remove?
answer: The commons and uncommons of Alpha and Beta, Demonic Tutor among them
choices: The commons and uncommons of Alpha and Beta, Demonic Tutor among them
All multicolor cards, the Elder Dragons among them
All the rares of Antiquities, the March 1994 artifact set
All five basic-land variants printed only in early black-bordered sets
context: The 2002 revision took the Alpha and Beta commons and uncommons off the list after a poll found overwhelming support, and Demonic Tutor was the most important card freed. The rares stayed.

question: A duelist lays down one rare card of June 1994 in a game of Magic: the Gathering, and from then on each creature's controller must pay one mana per upkeep or lose it. Played copies command thousands of dollars, more than any other card in the set. What is the card?
answer: The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale, a legendary land
choices: The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale, a legendary land
Moat, a four-mana enchantment with a flying clause
Mirror Universe, an artifact that swaps life totals
Eureka, a sorcery that puts permanents into play
context: The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale gives every creature an upkeep cost of one mana, and any creature whose controller does not pay is destroyed. It is brutal against creature decks, and as a Reserved List card it will never be reprinted.

question: Stone Cold Steve Austin pitched the design of his first catchphrase T-shirt himself after his 1996 King of the Ring win: the slogan on the front, his name on a skull on the back. As Austin later told it, Vince McMahon feared the skull might look like gimmick infringement, so one other wrestler had to clear it first. Who was he?
context: Austin told the story on Busted Open Radio in 2021: the WWF's Jimmy Miranda had asked him for ideas, and the Undertaker gave the skull his blessing. The shirt became one of the best-selling in wrestling history.

question: Eric Bischoff, boss of World Championship Wrestling, later said he personally ordered the spoiler on live Nitro on January 4, 1999, when an announcer gave away Mick Foley's first title win on a taped Raw. The spoiler reportedly drove 600,000 viewers to flip channels to Raw, and the win became a turning point in the Monday Night Wars. What was Bischoff's reasoning, according to his own later interviews?
answer: He thought no one would care about Mankind winning and the spoiler would actually retain Nitro's audience
choices: He thought no one would care about Mankind winning and the spoiler would actually retain Nitro's audience
He thought the spoiler would alienate WWF fans into watching WCW long-term
He had been pressured by Ted Turner to attack Vince McMahon directly on-air
He thought the spoiler would draw a lawsuit that would publicize WCW Nitro
context: Bischoff's miscalculation is one of the most-quoted strategic errors in the Monday Night Wars. The flip-over moment is often cited as the night WWF won the war for good. Schiavone later said he had no choice — the spoiler was Bischoff's call. He has expressed regret in multiple later interviews.

question: Paul Jay was filming Bret Hart for the documentary Wrestling with Shadows when the Montreal Screwjob happened on November 9, 1997. Seconds after the referee called for the bell, Bret got to his feet and walked over to Vince McMahon at the ring apron. What did he do to McMahon?
choices: He shoved McMahon into the front row
He ripped the headset off McMahon's head
He hurled a steel chair at McMahon
context: Hart spat in McMahon's face, then smashed ringside monitors and traced the letters W-C-W in the air for the fans. The punch backstage came later, and Jay's documentary chronicles part of that night.

question: Mick Foley kept wrestling through the Hell in a Cell match at the June 1998 King of the Ring, after two of the most infamous falls in wrestling history, and he even climbed off a stretcher to do it. One of his injuries was plain for the TV cameras to see. What was it?
answer: A knocked-out tooth sticking out beneath his nose
choices: A knocked-out tooth sticking out beneath his nose
A broken nose knocked flat to one side of his face
A torn ear held on with strips of white tape
A broken finger bent back at the knuckle
context: The steel chair that fell through the roof with Foley struck his face, costing him several teeth and briefly knocking him unconscious; one tooth ended up hanging beneath his nose. He kept wrestling, even taking a fall onto thumbtacks, while Jim Ross shouted on commentary for somebody to stop the match.

question: Eric Bischoff brought former World Wrestling Federation stars Scott Hall and Kevin Nash into World Championship Wrestling in 1996, to pretend they were attacking the company from outside. The federation filed a legal challenge against Bischoff's company that year. What specific legal issue did it raise?
answer: Trademark infringement, because the gimmicks evoked Razor Ramon and Diesel
choices: Trademark infringement, because the gimmicks evoked Razor Ramon and Diesel
Antitrust, alleging WCW had violated talent-poaching agreements
Defamation, claiming Bischoff had falsely promoted Vince McMahon
Copyright infringement on the WWF logo as used in promotional spots
context: WWF sued WCW in 1996 over the presentation of Scott Hall, whose 'bad guy' talk evoked his Razor Ramon character, and Kevin Nash, whose look evoked Diesel. The fight is told in The Death of WCW by R.D. Reynolds and Bryan Alvarez.

question: Stone Cold Steve Austin pinned The Rock in the main event of WrestleMania X-Seven, at the Houston Astrodome on April 1, 2001, a match often called the greatest main event in WrestleMania history. The last moment of the night was caught on broadcast and became iconic. What did Austin do as the night was ending?
answer: Shook hands and shared beers with Vince McMahon as the show went off the air
choices: Shook hands and shared beers with Vince McMahon as the show went off the air
Sprayed beer on The Rock's prone body in the center of the ring
Lifted McMahon onto his shoulders as the ramp's pyrotechnics went off
Hurled McMahon out of the ring as the show went off the air
context: The handshake over beers confirmed Austin's heel turn: McMahon had handed him the steel chair he used on the Rock. Austin's heel run that followed is widely seen as a creative disappointment, though the match itself is often called a classic.

question: Vince McMahon purchased World Championship Wrestling in March 2001, and Hulk Hogan met The Rock in the Icon vs Icon main event of WrestleMania X8, at Toronto's SkyDome on March 17, 2002. Hogan was scripted as the villain, and the Toronto crowd ignored the script. What scramble did that unscripted reaction set off during the match itself?
answer: The Rock and Hogan called audibles to swap multiple key spots so Hogan could absorb the crowd's love as he faced his exit
choices: The Rock and Hogan called audibles to swap multiple key spots so Hogan could absorb the crowd's love as he faced his exit
Vince McMahon ran to the gorilla position to demand Pat Patterson change the finish to a Hogan win
The Rock walked out of the match mid-stride, demanding a script revision before continuing
Hogan tore up the rest of the script and ad-libbed his entire remaining offense
context: The match is widely considered one of the most emotional in WrestleMania history because of the unscripted crowd reaction. Hogan's post-match handshake with The Rock and 'do the right thing' gesture mid-fight created an organic face turn for Hogan. He went on to win his sixth WWF Championship a few weeks later at Backlash 2002.

question: One wrestler founded Frontier Martial-Arts Wrestling (FMW) in 1989, the company that started the deathmatch style of barbed wire and exploding rings. Paul Heyman brought Japanese stars to his wild shows in Philadelphia, and this founder later appeared there. Who was he?
context: Atsushi Onita founded FMW (Frontier Martial-Arts Wrestling) in 1989. His no-rope barbed-wire and exploding-ring matches stunned audiences. Sabu, Terry Funk, and other ECW stars regularly worked Japanese deathmatch tours. Onita's influence on Heyman's Philadelphia hardcore booking is well documented in the wrestling press.

question: The Undertaker faced Mick Foley at King of the Ring in Pittsburgh on June 28, 1998, inside a Hell in a Cell, a huge steel cage with a roof suspended over the ring. Wrestlers are allowed to climb onto its flat top, sixteen feet in the air. In the opening moments the Undertaker did something to Foley that became the most-replayed bump in wrestling history. What did the Undertaker do?
answer: Threw him off the top of the 16-foot cell, crashing through the Spanish announce table
choices: Threw him off the top of the 16-foot cell, crashing through the Spanish announce table
Powerbombed him through the ringside timekeeper's table in the first minute
Tombstone-piledrove him on the steel floor as the match's opening move
Hit him with a steel chair as Foley climbed in through the top hatch
context: Foley took two of the most famous falls in wrestling in this match. The throw from the top through the table was planned; the second, when the Undertaker chokeslammed him through the roof of the cell into the ring, was not. A chair fell on him as he landed.

question: Bill Belichick kept his goal-line defense on the field at the end of Super Bowl 49, on February 1, 2015, and his undrafted rookie cornerback from West Alabama jumped Seattle's slant and intercepted it at the goal line. The rookie said he knew the play the moment Seattle lined up. Where had he seen it before?
answer: In practice before the game, when the scout team ran it and beat him for a touchdown
choices: In practice before the game, when the scout team ran it and beat him for a touchdown
In Seattle's NFC Championship film, where the same play had scored against Green Bay
In college at West Alabama, where his own team had run the same slant
On Seattle's regular-season tape, where the slant had been run three times
context: Belichick kept three cornerbacks on the field in his goal-line defense, and Butler, who recognised the formation from practice, jumped the slant meant for Ricardo Lockette. The interception sealed a 28-24 Patriots win.

question: An analyst freezes the tape on one moment of a 67-yard Seattle touchdown run against the Saints on January 8, 2011, in a playoff game Seattle won 41-36. The runner broke nine tackles, but one physical move is often cited as the defining move of the run. Which move is it?
answer: A stiff-arm that put a cornerback flat on the ground
choices: A stiff-arm that put a cornerback flat on the ground
A spin move that left two tacklers grabbing air
A hurdle over a diving safety near midfield
A cutback across the whole field at the 20
context: Lynch stiff-armed cornerback Tracy Porter to the ground as he angled toward the right sideline, one of nine tackles he broke on the run. The touchdown put Seattle ahead 41-30, and the Saints scored once more before the end.

question: A 5-foot-11 rookie quarterback beat out a free agent in Seattle's training camp in 2012. He had gone 75th overall in the third round, at the time considered a major reach because of his height, and the pick is widely cited as one of the great steals in National Football League (NFL) history.
