The Saigon-born boy who played him left acting for decades to work on stunts behind the camera, then came back to win an Oscar in 2023. What is his name?
context: Ke Huy Quan also played Data in The Goonies (1985). He stepped away from acting in the 1990s and worked as a stunt coordinator. He made a major comeback as Waymond Wang in Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022), winning the Oscar.

question: James Cameron's early-1980s script The Terminator sends a killer robot back in time to murder a young waitress named Sarah Connor. Cameron sold the rights to the producer Gale Anne Hurd on one condition: that he would direct the film himself. What did he take for them?
context: Cameron sold the rights to Gale Anne Hurd for $1 on her promise to produce the film only if he directed it, a sale he later regretted. The Terminator made about $78 million on a $6.4 million budget and launched both Cameron's and Arnold Schwarzenegger's A-list careers.

question: Ridley Scott spotted the airbrushed art book Necronomicon and hired the Swiss surrealist painter behind it for his 1979 space-horror film Alien, advertised with the tagline 'In space no one can hear you scream.' The nightmare stalking the towing ship Nostromo was a skeletal black beast with a second inner mouth. Who designed the alien?
context: Giger was a Swiss surrealist whose 1977 art book Necronomicon (no relation to Lovecraft) caught Scott's eye. The 'biomechanical' aesthetic — fusion of skeletal and machine forms — defined the franchise. Giger won the Oscar for Visual Effects.

question: Raiders of the Lost Ark opens with Indiana Jones creeping through a booby-trapped Peruvian temple toward a small gold idol on a stone pedestal. He knows the pedestal is weight-triggered, so he has brought something to set down on it the instant the idol comes away. What does he swap onto the pedestal?
context: Indy underestimates the weight; the trap triggers anyway. The giant rolling boulder sequence followed. The opening was inspired by old Republic Pictures Saturday-morning serials Lucas and Spielberg loved as kids.

question: Rutger Hauer reportedly cut Roy Batty's monologue in Ridley Scott's 1982 Blade Runner down to its iconic length, ending on 'All those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain.' Most of those famous lines were not in David Peoples's shooting script. When did Hauer write his version?
answer: The night before shooting, in his hotel room
choices: The night before shooting, in his hotel room
During the table read three weeks before filming
On set between takes with Scott approving each line
Two months after wrap, for the redubbed director's cut
context: Hauer cut Peoples's longer speech down and added the 'tears in rain' image. The film crew reportedly applauded after the take. The speech is one of cinema's most-studied scenes.

question: Fred Savage played the boy in bed with a baseball video game at the start of Rob Reiner's 1987 film The Princess Bride, while Peter Falk played the grandfather who comes to read to him. Within months Savage was starring in a television show that began the following January and ran six seasons. What was the show?
context: The Wonder Years premiered on ABC in January 1988, with Savage as Kevin Arnold and Daniel Stern as the voice of the grown-up narrator. Savage was ten when The Princess Bride was shot in 1986.

question: Rob Reiner recorded all of Andre the Giant's lines for The Princess Bride on cassette, so the 7-foot-4 wrestler could learn them by ear. Andre played Fezzik there, and a few years earlier he had played a horned brute for another famous filmmaker. In what earlier film did Andre play that brute?
context: In Conan the Destroyer (1984) Andre played Dagoth, the horned god, under heavy costume. He had played Bigfoot in The Six Million Dollar Man in 1976, and he died of heart failure in Paris on January 27, 1993, at 46.

question: Gideon Graves, Ramona's seventh and last evil ex, runs a record label and owns the club where Scott Pilgrim finally fights him, in Bryan Lee O'Malley's six-volume comic and Edgar Wright's 2010 film alike. The club's name is a nod to the video game EarthBound. What is it called?
context: Gideon owns the Chaos Theatre in New York and is opening one in Toronto, with Envy Adams's band as its opening act. Jason Schwartzman played Gideon in the 2010 film.

question: Mrs. Brisby, a field mouse, discovers a colony of super-intelligent rats in the farmer's rosebush in Don Bluth's first independent film. The rats have escaped from a real government mental-health laboratory that experimented on them. The film follows a 1971 children's novel that won the Newbery Medal. Who wrote the book?
context: O'Brien (pen name for Robert Leslie Conly) died in 1973 before seeing the film. The novel was titled 'Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH.' Bluth changed Frisby to 'Brisby' to avoid trademark conflict with the Wham-O flying disc.

question: Don Bluth's knight Dirk the Daring pulled huge crowds in 1983 at 50 cents a play, double the normal quarter. Every frame of the cartoon sat on a laserdisc inside the arcade cabinet. Yet the cabinets turned into a costly headache. Why?
answer: The laserdisc players kept breaking down and needed frequent repairs
choices: The laserdisc players kept breaking down and needed frequent repairs
Players completed the game in ten minutes so cabinets couldn't generate enough revenue
Nintendo's Donkey Kong released the same month and dominated arcade floor space
The cabinets weighed 600 pounds, requiring two-person installation in most arcades
context: Early cabinets used a Pioneer PR-7820 laserdisc player, later replaced by the sturdier LD-V1000, and discs skipped as they wore. The constant field servicing strained Cinematronics' finances. Sequels (Space Ace in 1984, Dragon's Lair II: Time Warp in 1991) tried to recapture the magic.

question: Stuntman Bill Bryan climbed into a suit for the giant mascot monster of 1984's Ghostbusters and walked through a tabletop New York, filmed at miniature scale to look a hundred feet tall. That one sequence cost more than all the film's other effects combined. A Hollywood special-effects veteran directed the work, and his other 1980s credits included Return of the Jedi and Poltergeist. Who was that veteran?
answer: Richard Edlund and his Boss Film Studios
choices: Richard Edlund and his Boss Film Studios
Stan Winston and his creature shop in Van Nuys
Phil Tippett and his stop-motion animation team
Rob Bottin and his The Thing prosthetics company
context: Stay-Puft was a suit worn by stuntman Bill Bryan, filmed at miniature scale to make him look 100 feet tall against tabletop New York buildings. Edlund had been ILM's visual-effects supervisor on the Star Wars OT before founding Boss Film. The Stay-Puft sequence cost more than the rest of the film's effects combined.

question: A lead animator moved the AT-AT walkers across the snow of Hoth one frame at a time, blurring every frame with motion-control rods so the stop-motion would not judder. He called the trick go-motion. Years later Steven Spielberg switched Jurassic Park to computers, and the man supervising its dinosaurs said he thought he had gone extinct. Who is he?
context: Tippett's go-motion technique used motion-controlled rods to slightly blur each frame, eliminating the jerky look of pure stop-motion. He was set to do Jurassic Park's dinosaurs in stop-motion until Spielberg switched to CGI. Tippett's quote: 'I think I'm extinct.' He got 'Dinosaur Supervisor' credit instead.

question: Charlie, the love interest of Tom Cruise's hotshot pilot in Top Gun, began as an enlisted member of the Navy in the early script. That ran straight into the military's ban on officers dating enlisted personnel, and because the film needed real F-14 Tomcats, the Navy had a say over the script. What was she rewritten as?
answer: A civilian contractor working with the Navy
choices: A civilian contractor working with the Navy
A fellow officer on the Top Gun staff
A British exchange pilot at Miramar
context: The Navy's script approval changed several things: the opening dogfight moved from Cuba to international waters, the language was toned down, a crash on a carrier deck was cut, and Charlie went from an enlisted woman to a civilian contractor because the military forbids fraternization between officers and enlisted personnel. In the film she is a civilian astrophysicist who instructs at the school.

question: Marty McFly reaches 1955 in Robert Zemeckis's Back to the Future wearing a bright red down-filled puffer vest, a design the townsfolk have never seen. They mistake it for a completely different kind of garment. Seeing his underwear label later, they even start calling him Calvin Klein. What do the locals think the vest is?
answer: A life preserver (they think he's a sailor who fell off a boat)
choices: A life preserver (they think he's a sailor who fell off a boat)
A fireman's life vest from the local volunteer station
A Russian air-force flight survival vest from the Eisenhower era
A cowboy-inspired buoyancy aid worn by 1955 rodeo participants
context: The famous Calvin Klein joke wasn't accidental — Calvin Klein launched his eponymous brand in 1968 and had become a household name by the 1985 production. Robert Zemeckis specifically wrote the gag to land with 1985 audiences. The puffer vest itself was a then-current style.

question: Jeff Cohen lifted his shirt and shook his belly on Mikey's doorstep as Chunk in The Goonies in 1985, doing the truffle shuffle to gain entry to the house. The role typecast him, and he left acting in his teens. He grew up to be a successful Hollywood professional. In what field?
answer: Entertainment law (he became a major-studio attorney)
choices: Entertainment law (he became a major-studio attorney)
Film direction (he directed three indie thrillers in the 2010s)
Restaurant ownership (he opened a Beverly Hills steakhouse)
Real-estate development (he built a luxury hotel chain)
context: Jeff Cohen graduated from UCLA Law School and became founding partner of Cohen Gardner LLP, representing major Hollywood talent and studios. He stopped acting in his teens.

question: John Milius's 1982 film Conan the Barbarian shows Conan's father teaching him the riddle of steel before Thulsa Doom kills the man. That riddle is Milius's own creation, but the line of text on screen before anything happens comes from somewhere else. Where does it come from?
choices: Robert E. Howard's first Conan story
L. Sprague de Camp's Conan pastiches
The Hávamál, the Norse poem of proverbs
context: The line is 'That which does not kill us makes us stronger', from Twilight of the Idols (1888), aphorism 8 of Maxims and Arrows. The riddle of steel, 'what is steel compared to the hand that wields it', is Milius's own invention for the film, not Howard's.

question: Kenny Baker fell ill, and a young British actor named Warwick Davis got the part of Wicket W. Warrick, the little Ewok scout who befriends Princess Leia in the woods in George Lucas's 1983 movie Return of the Jedi. Standing only 2 feet 11 inches tall, Davis was cast for his height in his very first movie role. How old was he when he took the part?
context: Davis later starred in Willow (1988) and Leprechaun (1993) and played Professor Flitwick and Griphook in the Harry Potter films. He was first cast as a different Ewok and only got the Wicket role when Kenny Baker fell ill.

question: Cary Elwes and Mandy Patinkin fought a long, witty sword duel on the edge of a cliff in The Princess Bride, and they performed most of the swordplay themselves. Their teacher was Bob Anderson, a former British Olympic fencer who spent decades secretly choreographing movie duels around the world. Anderson also helped train the sword-fighting cast of another huge film franchise. Which series did he work on?
context: Anderson fenced for Great Britain at the 1952 Olympics in Helsinki and became cinema's sword master of choice. He wore Darth Vader's costume for the lightsaber duels of The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi, while David Prowse played Vader elsewhere, and he later trained the casts of The Lord of the Rings and Pirates of the Caribbean.

question: Don Bluth's 1979 walkout left Disney's animation department thin for the films that followed, among them a fantasy from Lloyd Alexander's Prydain Chronicles. Its Horned King raises an undead army of skeleton warriors, scenes that made it the first Disney animated feature rated above G. Which film is it?
context: The Black Cauldron was one of the most expensive animated features of its time and bombed. The Horned King's army of cauldron-born undead earned the PG. Bluth had no part in the film; he had walked out six years earlier, and his departure thinned the studio's animation ranks.

question: Steven Spielberg's studio Amblin backed Don Bluth on The Land Before Time, the story of a young dinosaur named Littlefoot on a dangerous journey to find safety. Bluth and Amblin had teamed up two years earlier on another beloved animated film. Which film was it?
context: American Tail's Fievel was named after Spielberg's grandfather. Spielberg did not produce Anastasia (Fox Animation) or All Dogs Go to Heaven (Goldcrest Films), later Bluth projects. The Land Before Time's 13 direct-to-video sequels were not Bluth's work.

question: The Earp brothers and Doc Holliday faced the Cowboys faction in a narrow vacant lot in Tombstone, Arizona, in 1881, and the shootout lasted about 30 seconds. Three of the Cowboys were killed, and the 1993 film Tombstone restages the moment. Which of these four men lived?
context: Ike Clanton had instigated the fight by drunkenly threatening the Earps the night before but ran when shooting started. Tom McLaury, Frank McLaury, and Billy Clanton were killed. Virgil and Morgan Earp were wounded. Wyatt was untouched. Doc Holliday took a graze. The real fight is now reenacted in Tombstone, Arizona for tourists.

question: Todd Ingram draws his powers from being vegan in Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels. In the 2010 film the Vegan Police strip him of them after Scott tricks him into drinking half-and-half, and the officers read out two older offences, a late-night gelato and a plate of something else. What was on the plate?
context: Brandon Routh played Todd, and Thomas Jane and Clifton Collins Jr. played the Vegan Police. Told about the chicken, Todd asks in honest shock whether chicken is not vegan.

question: Nigel Godrich, Radiohead's producer, oversaw the music for Edgar Wright's 2010 film about Scott Pilgrim, and Scott's garage band performs all the way through it. Which musician wrote the band's original songs?
choices: Jack White of The White Stripes
context: Beck wrote 'Garbage Truck' and 'We Are Sex Bob-omb' for the film. Broken Social Scene's Brendan Canning and Kevin Drew also contributed. The Clash at Demonhead's songs (Envy Adams's band) were written by Metric's Emily Haines.

question: Donkey Kong's grumpy old father in The Super Mario Bros. Movie is Cranky Kong, who rules Kong Island from his throne. He is older than the film: he goes back to 1981 and Nintendo's first barrel-throwing coin-op, where Mario, then called Jumpman, climbed girders to rescue a woman named Pauline. Who was Cranky in that first cabinet?
answer: The original Donkey Kong from the 1981 arcade game
choices: The original Donkey Kong from the 1981 arcade game
King Kong from a separate Universal Studios franchise
Diddy Kong's grandfather from the SNES Donkey Kong Country games
An entirely new character invented for Donkey Kong 64
context: Cranky's identity as the original Donkey Kong was set up in Donkey Kong Country (1994). In the 1981 arcade game the ape carries off Pauline, and Jumpman, later renamed Mario, climbs the girders after her.

question: Littlefoot, the young dinosaur of Don Bluth's 1988 film The Land Before Time, sets off with his friends across a dying land to find the Great Valley. A child actor speaks every one of his lines in the film. Who voices Littlefoot?
context: Damon's other notable credit was Newsies (1992). The Land Before Time spawned 13 direct-to-video sequels (1994-2016) without Bluth's involvement.

question: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade ends its hunt in a chamber lined with dozens of cups, one of them the Holy Grail, and an immortal knight stands guard over them. The greedy financier Donovan, played by Julian Glover, seizes the gaudiest goblet and drinks from it. It is the wrong one. What does the knight say?
choices: He picked the cup of pride
context: Robert Eddison played the immortal Grail Knight; Laurence Olivier had been considered first but was too ill. The knight's three words became one of the most quoted lines of the series.

question: John G. Avildsen took on The Karate Kid in 1984 knowing how an underdog story goes: Daniel LaRusso, a bullied teenager, learns karate from his apartment building's handyman, Mr. Miyagi. Avildsen had already won the Academy Award for Best Director for a sports film about a poor boxer given one shot at the heavyweight title. Which film was that?
context: Rocky won Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Film Editing in 1977. Karate Kid's emotional structure mirrors Rocky's — the unlikely mentor, the romantic subplot, the climactic tournament. Pat Morita's performance as Mr. Miyagi earned a Best Supporting Actor nomination.

question: An invisible alien hunter stalks Arnold Schwarzenegger's commandos through the Central American jungle in John McTiernan's 1987 film Predator, and it hunts by heat rather than by sight. The audience has to see through its eyes, in a false-color picture of that jungle. How did McTiernan's crew film those shots?
answer: A real Inframetrics 525 thermal imaging camera, normally used for industrial inspection
choices: A real Inframetrics 525 thermal imaging camera, normally used for industrial inspection
Stop-motion overlays composited frame-by-frame in post-production
False-color time-lapse photography exposed through dichroic filters
A custom video feedback loop with chromatic separation lenses
context: The Inframetrics 525 cost approximately $80,000 in 1986. The Predator's thermal POV had to be filmed separately and then matted in. The technology had previously been used to identify roof leaks and electrical equipment failures.

question: A different director worked on Total Recall for a while and then quit, years before Paul Verhoeven took the job and filled the 1990 film with Martian mutants and exploding heads. The finished movie starred Arnold Schwarzenegger as a construction worker who may or may not really be a spy on Mars with fake memories. Who was that first director?
answer: David Cronenberg, fresh from The Dead Zone
choices: David Cronenberg, fresh from The Dead Zone
Ridley Scott, fresh from Blade Runner
John Carpenter, fresh from The Thing
context: Dino De Laurentiis hired Cronenberg in 1984, and he wrote twelve drafts in a year before leaving: he did not want the Raiders of the Lost Ark on Mars that the producers wanted. Seven directors were attached over the years before Carolco hired Verhoeven.

question: Colonial Marines reach a lost human colony in James Cameron's 1986 sequel Aliens and find every colonist dead or missing, except one terrified little girl hiding alone in the air ducts. Sigourney Weaver's warrant officer has come with them, after 57 years of hibernation drifting in space. What is that girl's name?
context: Carrie Henn played Newt; this was her only film role. Newt's family had named her Rebecca but her brother called her Newt because she could 'fit into all the small places.'

question: Orion wanted Arnold Schwarzenegger to play the hero Kyle Reese in James Cameron's The Terminator. Cameron, by his own account, met him for lunch meaning to pick a fight and sink the idea, but ended up sketching Arnold's face instead and left sure that Arnold should play the killer cyborg. What did Arnold keep talking about?
answer: How the villain ought to be played
choices: How the villain ought to be played
How the hero ought to be played
His plans for a Conan sequel
His years as a champion bodybuilder
context: Orion had approached Schwarzenegger for Kyle Reese, the human soldier sent back to protect Sarah Connor. Cameron asked him to stop talking and hold still while he sketched, and afterwards told the producer John Daly that Arnold would not play Reese but would make a hell of a Terminator. Lance Henriksen, who had helped Cameron pitch the film by turning up dressed as the Terminator, was given the part of Detective Vukovich.

question: Hulk Hogan body-slammed Andre the Giant, billed at 520 pounds, at WrestleMania III in March 1987, before a crowd announced at 93,173. Months earlier, in 1986, Andre had played the friendly giant Fezzik in The Princess Bride. Rob Reiner had to work around one medical problem during the shoot. What was it?
answer: Andre had just had back surgery, so hidden ramps and cables took the weight of his lifts
choices: Andre had just had back surgery, so hidden ramps and cables took the weight of his lifts
Andre's eyesight was failing, so every set had to be marked with bright tape
Andre needed dialysis three times a week at a hospital near the studio
Andre's hands were so swollen that he could not grip a sword or a rope
context: Andre had major back surgery before filming and could not take anyone's weight: when Fezzik seems to carry Buttercup, Robin Wright hung on cables, and in his fight with Westley he walked on ramps below the camera. Andre died of heart failure in Paris in January 1993.

question: Edgar Wright, the British director who had just made Shaun of the Dead, agreed to make a film of Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim books while the series had hardly started. The small black-and-white paperbacks looked and read like Japanese manga, and Wright's film took its title from the second book. What was the book called?
choices: Scott Pilgrim and the Infinite Sadness
context: The six volumes: Precious Little Life (2004), vs. the World (2005), and the Infinite Sadness (2006), Gets It Together (2007), vs. the Universe (2009) and Finest Hour (2010). Wright's film took the title of volume 2; the last volume was not yet finished when the film was made.

question: Mario and Luigi advertise their new plumbing business in a commercial made for The Super Mario Bros. Movie and aired during the 2023 Super Bowl, styled like a cheap local TV spot. Its jingle brings back the rap theme of an older Mario show from 1989. Which show?
answer: The Super Mario Bros. Super Show!
choices: The Super Mario Bros. Super Show!
The Adventures of Super Mario Bros. 3
context: The spot's jingle reworks the rap theme of The Super Mario Bros. Super Show!, in which Lou Albano and Danny Wells played Mario and Luigi in 1989. The advert sent viewers to a real Super Mario Bros. Plumbing website, and its phone number played a message from Charlie Day, the film's Luigi.

question: Steven Spielberg named a cartoon mouse for his grandfather, borrowing the old man's Yiddish name. The mouse was Fievel, a young Russian-Jewish immigrant who loses his family on the voyage to America, in the 1986 film Spielberg made with Don Bluth. What was that grandfather's surname?
context: Spielberg's maternal grandfather, Philip Posner, had the Yiddish name Fievel. The film's central song, 'Somewhere Out There', sung by Linda Ronstadt and James Ingram, was a major hit and won two Grammys. American Tail spawned a sequel (Fievel Goes West, 1991) and a TV series. Bluth left the franchise after the first film.

question: Robert Zemeckis filmed for four to five weeks with a different actor as Marty McFly in Back to the Future, then replaced him. The Amblin team realized the chemistry wasn't working, paid out the original actor and refilmed everything with a new lead. Who was the original Marty?
context: Eric Stoltz had just come off the Oscar-buzzy Mask (1985, where he played a young man with cranial dysplasia). The BTTF team felt he was too dramatic for the comedic tone the film needed. Michael J. Fox was the original first choice but had been unavailable due to his Family Ties shooting schedule. After the swap, Family Ties producer Gary David Goldberg let Fox shoot BTTF during Family Ties production gaps — Fox filmed late nights and weekends for months. Stoltz was paid in full for his weeks of work and went on to a strong indie-film career.

question: Don Bluth left Walt Disney Animation in 1979, and about a dozen animators followed him. He had been at Disney since 1955, when he worked on Sleeping Beauty as a 17-year-old in-betweener, and he had been lead animator on The Rescuers (1977). What had frustrated him at the studio?
answer: Disney was using xerography to cheapen the animation process and cutting fluid hand-drawn detail
choices: Disney was using xerography to cheapen the animation process and cutting fluid hand-drawn detail
Disney was outsourcing in-between animation work to a studio in Tokyo
Disney was about to license its characters to a kids' meal partnership at McDonald's
Disney was reorganizing its Burbank studio to share space with the theme parks
context: Bluth specifically named the loss of inking-by-hand and the elimination of multi-plane camera shots. Xerography (the photocopy-style process pioneered on 101 Dalmatians in 1961) gave a rougher line quality. Bluth's later films restored multi-plane and hand-inking. The Disney Renaissance starting with The Little Mermaid (1989) partly addressed his original grievances.

question: Don Bluth went back to the laserdisc in 1984 for a follow-up to his first arcade cartoon, again sold by Cinematronics but this time with a science-fiction theme. The first game's cabinets had sold for about $4,300 each, and players had paid 50 cents a play, double the standard quarter. What was the 1984 follow-up called?
context: Space Ace stars Ace, a hero shrunk back into the boy Dexter by the villain Borf's Infanto Ray. Both Dragon's Lair and Space Ace ran on laserdisc players and branched between scenes as the player chose.

question: Test crowds in Denver and Dallas turned hostile toward Blade Runner's pacing and lack of narration in May 1982. Warner Bros. forced Ridley Scott to add a Harrison Ford voiceover before the June 25 release, and Ford reportedly delivered it badly on purpose, hoping it would be cut. What was added besides the voiceover?
answer: A 'happy ending' featuring outtake footage from Stanley Kubrick's The Shining
choices: A 'happy ending' featuring outtake footage from Stanley Kubrick's The Shining
An opening expository newsreel explaining the off-world colonies
A wisecracking new partner for Deckard in the street scenes
A live-action prologue with Edward James Olmos's Gaff explaining the case
context: The aerial footage flying over forests was originally shot by Kubrick for The Shining's opening but unused. Scott borrowed the footage for the 1982 theatrical 'happy ending.' The 1992 Director's Cut and 2007 Final Cut removed both the voiceover and the happy ending and restored the unicorn dream sequence.

question: John Milius sent his composer a cut of the 1982 movie Conan the Barbarian with its scenes set to Wagner and other composers, to show the feeling he wanted. The score was recorded in Rome over three weeks, with a choir and an orchestra. What sound opens its famous main theme, Anvil of Crom?
answer: The brassy blast of twenty-four French horns
choices: The brassy blast of twenty-four French horns
A lone trumpet over pounding war drums
A massed choir singing over timpani
A solo cello over a hushed string section
context: Basil Poledouris spent three weeks recording the score in Rome late in 1981, with a 24-member choir from the Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia and a RAI orchestra. Anvil of Crom is the film's main theme. Poledouris died in 2006 at age 61.

question: Val Kilmer's coughing, card-playing Doc Holliday was widely seen as the standout performance of the 1993 Western Tombstone, eclipsing its star, Kurt Russell. Behind the camera, the film's original director lasted about a month of shooting before he was fired. Who was he?
answer: Kevin Jarre, who also wrote Glory (1989) and the Tombstone screenplay itself
choices: Kevin Jarre, who also wrote Glory (1989) and the Tombstone screenplay itself
John Carpenter, who left over budget disputes with Disney's Hollywood Pictures
Andy Garcia, in his first attempted directorial debut after a delayed Godfather Part III
Steve Beck, the visual-effects supervisor who had directed second-unit work
context: Producer Andrew Vajna fired Jarre about a month into filming, after he was quickly overwhelmed by the job, and George P. Cosmatos replaced him. Jarre had written a much longer epic screenplay, and his screenplay credit remained intact. Russell later said Cosmatos had been a ghost director and that he himself did much of the directing.

question: Edgar Wright cast Brandon Routh as Todd Ingram and Chris Evans as Lucas Lee in his 2010 film, which lost money in cinemas and only later became a cult favorite on home video. Routh had already played a famous comic-book hero before the film, and Evans went on to play another the next year. Which two heroes?
answer: Superman for Routh, Captain America for Evans
choices: Superman for Routh, Captain America for Evans
Green Lantern for Routh, Thor for Evans
Batman for Routh, Daredevil for Evans
The Atom for Routh, the Human Torch for Evans
context: Routh played Superman in Superman Returns (2006), and Evans became Captain America in Captain America: The First Avenger (2011); he had already played the Human Torch in Fantastic Four (2005). Routh later played the Atom on television, and Brie Larson, the film's Envy Adams, became Captain Marvel in 2019.

question: James Cameron made Aliens in 1986, turning Ridley Scott's 1979 horror film into an action-heavy war picture, and earned Sigourney Weaver an Oscar nomination for Best Actress. The sequel became one of the most celebrated in cinema, and fans expected him to jump straight into a third. What did Cameron do next?
answer: Cameron's next film was The Abyss (1989), not an Aliens sequel
choices: Cameron's next film was The Abyss (1989), not an Aliens sequel
Cameron immediately directed Alien 3 (1992) before The Abyss
Cameron directed Aliens 4 in 1995 before True Lies
Cameron made a Working Title Aliens 2.5 between Aliens and T2
context: Alien 3 (1992) was directed by David Fincher (his directorial debut, an experience he has called a 'horror story'). The Abyss followed Aliens for Cameron. Weaver's involvement in Alien 3 was strange — she was a producer.

question: John McTiernan had Arnold Schwarzenegger's commando hunted through the jungle by an alien in Predator in 1987, at the start of one of the greatest runs in action-movie history. He followed it with two more iconic action films, back to back, one starring Bruce Willis and the other starring Sean Connery. What were those two films?
answer: Die Hard (1988) and The Hunt for Red October (1990)
choices: Die Hard (1988) and The Hunt for Red October (1990)
Die Hard (1988) and Last Action Hero (1993)
Lethal Weapon (1987) and The Russia House (1990)
RoboCop (1987) and Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989)
context: McTiernan's Predator-Die Hard-Hunt for Red October trio is one of the great action-director runs in cinema.

question: Ron Howard, the redheaded kid who grew up playing Opie on The Andy Griffith Show, made the sci-fi drama Cocoon, where a group of retirement-home men swim in a pool full of glowing alien pods and suddenly feel young and strong again. Don Ameche won the Best Supporting Actor Oscar for it. What Disney movie had Howard directed the year before?
answer: Splash (1984), with Tom Hanks and Daryl Hannah as the mermaid
choices: Splash (1984), with Tom Hanks and Daryl Hannah as the mermaid
Night Shift (1982), with Henry Winkler and Michael Keaton
Gung Ho (1986), with Michael Keaton at the Japanese auto plant
Willow (1988), with Warwick Davis and Val Kilmer in the lead roles
context: Splash was Touchstone Pictures' first release, Disney's adult-oriented label. Howard's career took off after Splash. He had been Opie on The Andy Griffith Show and Richie on Happy Days before moving into directing in the late 1970s.

question: The author of The Princess Bride dressed his 1973 novel as his own abridgement of a fictional classic by S. Morgenstern, and in the book he made readers a famous offer. What did he promise the readers who wrote in?
answer: The reunion scene between Westley and Buttercup that he had cut
choices: The reunion scene between Westley and Buttercup that he had cut
A page of Morgenstern's original manuscript, in its Florinese text
A map of Florin and Guilder drawn by Morgenstern himself
A photograph of Morgenstern's grave in his native Florin
context: Readers who wrote to the publisher received a polite form letter explaining that the Morgenstern estate would not allow the scene to be printed. Morgenstern, his classic and his estate were all Goldman's inventions.

question: Vigo the Carpathian, a 16th-century tyrant, waits with his spirit trapped in a self-portrait at a Manhattan art museum in the 1989 sequel Ghostbusters II. A towering former heavyweight boxer plays him. What is that actor's name?
context: Homburg, born Norbert Grupe in Berlin, wrestled professionally before boxing as a heavyweight and light heavyweight through the 1960s. Ivan Reitman had Max von Sydow dub all of Vigo's lines. Homburg died in 2004, aged 63.

question: Back to the Future stages the DeLorean's first time jump at Twin Pines Mall, and the name sets up a small pine-tree gag. Robert Zemeckis shot the scene at a real Southern California shopping center that went by another name. Which real location was it?
answer: Puente Hills Mall, in the city of Industry
choices: Puente Hills Mall, in the city of Industry
Sherman Oaks Galleria, in the San Fernando Valley
Glendale Galleria, a few miles from Burbank
Fox Hills Mall, out in Culver City
context: Puente Hills Mall stands in the city of Industry, east of Los Angeles, and has hosted several Back to the Future reunions. The Twin Pines name sets up one of the film's many small payoffs.

question: The filmmakers behind Daniel LaRusso and Mr. Miyagi could not simply use the title The Karate Kid in 1984. A comic-book publisher already owned a superhero of that name, a martial-arts member of the Legion of Super-Heroes since 1966, so they needed its permission. Which publisher was it?
context: DC Comics owns Karate Kid, a member of the Legion of Super-Heroes created in 1966, and in 1984 the filmmakers received DC's permission to use the title for the film and its sequels.

question: Jean-Claude Van Damme wore the first alien suit, a skinny insect with a long red neck, on the set of the 1987 film Predator. Arnold Schwarzenegger and director John McTiernan both hated the design and demanded a full redo. It went to a legendary special-effects sculptor who had also built the creatures for Aliens and The Thing. Who was he?
context: Stan Winston Studio became the go-to creature-effects shop in the 1980s and 90s — also doing Terminator (1984), Aliens (1986), Predator (1987), Jurassic Park (1993), and Edward Scissorhands (1990). Winston died of multiple myeloma in 2008 at age 62. Jean-Claude Van Damme had originally been cast as the Predator but quit after one day.

question: Stan Winston's crew built James Cameron's Alien Queen as a real costume for the 1986 film Aliens. Sigourney Weaver drove the yellow power loader herself after a few rehearsals, and four trained cats took turns as Jonesy the cat. How tall was the Queen costume, and how was it worked?
answer: Fourteen feet, operated by two puppeteers inside and a crane for movement
choices: Fourteen feet, operated by two puppeteers inside and a crane for movement
Twelve feet, with rod puppeteers controlling only the upper body
Eighteen feet, with hydraulics controlled by joystick offstage
Sixteen feet, with three suit performers stacked vertically inside the costume
context: The Queen costume was designed by Stan Winston and operated by 14-16 people total when the rod-and-puppet team was counted. Sigourney Weaver insisted on doing her own Power Loader stunts after a few rehearsals. The cat Jonesy was played by four trained cats.

question: Nicholas Pileggi, an American journalist, taped hundreds of interviews with Henry Hill, a real New York mobster who spent decades inside the Lucchese crime family. His 1985 book became Martin Scorsese's 1990 film Goodfellas, with Ray Liotta as Hill. What was Pileggi's book called?
answer: Wiseguy: Life in a Mafia Family
choices: Wiseguy: Life in a Mafia Family
The Goodfella's Tale: Henry Hill's Story
The Mob: A Made Man's Memoir
context: Pileggi co-wrote the screenplay with Scorsese. The book's title could not be used for the film because of an unrelated TV series called Wiseguy (1987-90). Joe Pesci's 'Funny how?' scene became one of the film's most quoted.

question: Marty McFly tries to order a soft drink in a 1955 diner in Robert Zemeckis's Back to the Future, the film that earned $381M worldwide on a $19M budget. Both names he gives the soda clerk mean nothing to the man, which is the famous gag. Which two drinks does Marty try to order?
answer: Tab and Pepsi Free, neither of which existed in 1955
choices: Tab and Pepsi Free, neither of which existed in 1955
Diet Coke and Sprite Zero, Coca-Cola products from later decades
Mountain Dew and Sunkist, brands that hadn't yet been launched
Coca-Cola Classic and New Coke, distinguishing the 1985 confusion
context: Marty asks for a Tab — the soda clerk responds 'I can't give you a tab unless you order something.' Marty then asks for a Pepsi Free — the clerk says 'You want a Pepsi, pal, you're gonna pay for it.' Tab and Pepsi Free were both real Pepsi/Coca-Cola products in 1985 (diet variants). The gag plays on 1955 versus 1985 vocabulary differences.

question: Mel Brooks spoofed Star Wars in his 1987 movie Spaceballs. His hero Lone Starr piloted a Winnebago spaceship across the galaxy with his best friend Barf, a big lovable half-man, half-dog creature called a Mawg, with floppy ears, a wagging tail and a huge appetite. A warm-hearted, heavyset Canadian comedy actor famous for Uncle Buck and Planes, Trains and Automobiles played Barf. Who was he?
context: Candy died in 1994 at age 43 from a heart attack. Rick Moranis played Dark Helmet (the Vader parody). Bill Pullman played Lone Starr (the Han Solo parody). Spaceballs took Star Wars to task for marketing itself through merchandise — the 'Spaceballs the Lunchbox' running gag was prescient.

question: Scott Pilgrim squares up to the only female fighter he has to face in Bryan Lee O'Malley's six-volume graphic novel series: Ramona Flowers's fourth evil ex, a katana-wielding young woman Ramona briefly dated during college. What is this fourth ex's name?
context: Roxie Richter is Ramona's fourth evil ex and her only female one. Mae Whitman played her in the 2010 film and is also the voice of Katara in Avatar: The Last Airbender. Envy Adams is Scott's own ex, Lisa Miller his old friend from high school, and Kim Pine his band's drummer.

question: Mario clips through a wall in World 1-2 of the original 1985 NES cartridge and lands in a copy of World 7-2's underwater level that loops with no exit. The Japanese Famicom Disk System version does something else with the same glitch. What happens on the Famicom Disk version?
answer: The Minus World becomes three glitch levels in a row, and they can be finished
choices: The Minus World becomes three glitch levels in a row, and they can be finished
The Minus World shows the title screen in distorted colours, then freezes
The Minus World becomes World 0, an upside-down copy of World 1-1
The Minus World ends on a hidden screen crediting Shigeru Miyamoto
context: On the cartridge the Minus World is a copy of World 7-2 that loops its end back to its beginning, so it can never be beaten. On the Disk System it runs through three different levels, the last an underground stage with an axe at the end, and finishing them reaches the game's ending.

question: Khary Payton, who voiced Cyborg on Teen Titans for years, plays the Penguin King in The Super Mario Bros. Movie, defending his Snow Kingdom against Bowser. Its penguins are a Mario species that first turned up in a snowy world of Super Mario 64, the 1996 game, where Mario returns a lost baby penguin to its mother. Which world?
context: In Cool, Cool Mountain Mario carries a lost baby penguin back to its mother and races a big penguin down an icy slide, the first penguins of the Mario games. Sherbet Land is a Mario Kart 64 course, Freezeflame Galaxy a level of Super Mario Galaxy, and Snowman's Land the other snow world of Super Mario 64.

question: Christopher Lloyd's Doc Brown dangles from the hands of the courthouse clock in the climax of Back to the Future, high above a town square on the Universal Studios backlot that had served To Kill a Mockingbird (1962). How were the wide shots of Doc up on the tower made?
answer: Lloyd hung up there himself, in a harness hidden under his costume
choices: Lloyd hung up there himself, in a harness hidden under his costume
A stunt double in Doc's wig and costume did every tower shot
A dressed dummy of Doc was hung from the real clock's hands
The tower was a half-scale model, shot from a low camera angle
context: In his memoir Lloyd recalls that a crane lifted him to the top of the building and that, for the distance shots, it really was him up there, hanging on to the clock hands in a harness under his costume; the close-ups were filmed on a full-size copy of the clock on a soundstage. The courthouse square was built in 1948 for An Act of Murder and was long known as Mockingbird Square.

question: Mars Inc. famously passed on putting M&Ms in Steven Spielberg's 1982 film E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, and Hershey signed a $1 million deal with Universal instead, for another candy to lure the alien. Within weeks of release, sales of that candy jumped. By how much did they rise?
context: The Mars Inc. rejection of M&Ms is one of the most-cited examples of a marketing misstep. Hershey's $1 million deal was modest by today's standards but groundbreaking in 1982, and E.T. went on to become the highest-grossing film of its time.

question: Darth Vader marches to the main title theme in George Lucas's 1977 Star Wars, because the famous 'Imperial March' does not appear in that film. John Williams had borrowed a Wagnerian trick for his score, assigning specific themes to specific characters, but Vader's own music had to wait. When did it debut?
answer: The Empire Strikes Back (1980), where Williams introduced it as Vader's leitmotif
choices: The Empire Strikes Back (1980), where Williams introduced it as Vader's leitmotif
Return of the Jedi (1983), where it premiered in the throne-room confrontation
The original 1977 film, in a slower, less-recognizable form during the Death Star scenes
The 1997 Special Edition rerelease, which added the Imperial March to several Vader scenes
context: The Imperial March premiered in The Empire Strikes Back (1980). The original 1977 Star Wars used the Main Title theme for Vader's appearances.

question: John Carpenter's The Thing opened two weeks behind E.T. in June 1982, and its Antarctic shape-shifter was built by hand from rubber, slime and hidden machinery. The young effects designer who led that work drove himself so hard that he ended up in a hospital bed with exhaustion, pneumonia and a bleeding ulcer. Who was he?
context: Rob Bottin, barely into his twenties, designed most of the film's creatures and led a large crew. When time ran short, Stan Winston finished the Dog-Thing as a hand puppet and asked to go uncredited. The film sank at the box office and has since been reassessed as one of the great horror films.

question: Ray Parker Jr. wrote the theme song for the 1984 comedy Ghostbusters, and it became one of the year's biggest hits, three weeks at number one on the Billboard chart. It immediately triggered a famous copyright-infringement lawsuit as well. Who sued Parker for plagiarism, and what was the disputed song?
answer: Huey Lewis sued for similarity to 'I Want a New Drug' (1984); the case settled out of court
choices: Huey Lewis sued for similarity to 'I Want a New Drug' (1984); the case settled out of court
Lionel Richie sued for similarity to 'All Night Long' (1983); won damages on appeal
Tina Turner sued for similarity to 'What's Love Got to Do With It' (1984); was dismissed
Prince sued for similarity to 'When Doves Cry' (1984); settled for publishing royalties
context: The settlement included a confidentiality agreement; when Lewis discussed the case on VH1's Behind the Music in 2001, Parker sued him for breaching it. The theme reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 on August 11, 1984, and stayed three weeks. Ray Parker Jr. was also a respected session guitarist who had played on records by Stevie Wonder and Barry White.

question: James Cameron clashed extensively with the British crew at Pinewood Studios while shooting his 1986 film Aliens, over American versus British filmmaking practices. The story still told from that set has him firing the entire crew on the first day. What did he really do?
answer: He fired the first assistant director, then talked the crew back after a walkout
choices: He fired the first assistant director, then talked the crew back after a walkout
He flew in his own American crew from The Terminator to replace the British one
He moved the whole shoot to a Los Angeles soundstage for the rest of the film
He handed the set to producer Gale Anne Hurd and directed from the editing room
context: The assistant director Cameron and Gale Anne Hurd fired was Derek Cracknell; Hurd also talked Cameron out of moving the shoot out of England, and the crew agreed to back him if he kept to their working hours. He has said in interviews that the crew was unaccustomed to working at the pace he wanted. Sigourney Weaver was famously paid $1M for Aliens (a then-record for a female lead in an action film). The film's $18M budget was modest by 1980s standards. Aliens received seven Oscar nominations and won two.

question: Paul Verhoeven had to recut his 1990 film Total Recall before the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) would give it an R rather than an X. Its violence was typical of his RoboCop-era Hollywood work. Which scene gave the MPAA the most trouble?
answer: Schwarzenegger using a human body as a shield in the subway shootout
choices: Schwarzenegger using a human body as a shield in the subway shootout
Quaid's eyes bulging as the Mars atmosphere reaches him
Quaid pulling a tracking bug out through his nose
Quaid's disguise splitting open at the Mars customs gate
context: In the subway scene Quaid holds a dead man's body in front of himself as bullets riddle it. The first cut drew an X for its violence, and Verhoeven trimmed the gore to get the R. Total Recall earned $261M worldwide.

question: Pat Morita drew a Best Supporting Actor nomination for his Mr. Miyagi, a gentle Japanese-American handyman who carries painful memories of the Second World War, in the 1984 film The Karate Kid. Morita knew that era first-hand, because as a child he and his family were interned in America during the war. Where was he held?
answer: Gila River, Arizona (then transferred to Tule Lake, California for security reclassification)
choices: Gila River, Arizona (then transferred to Tule Lake, California for security reclassification)
Manzanar, California (the best-known camp of the war)
Heart Mountain, Wyoming (the highest-altitude camp in the system)
Topaz, Utah (where Morita's family had owned a Sacramento Valley restaurant)
context: Morita was born in Isleton, California in 1932 to immigrant parents. He had spinal tuberculosis as a child and spent nine years in a Sacramento hospital. After the war, his family ran restaurants. He moved into stand-up comedy in the 1960s as 'The Hip Nip' and broke into TV with Happy Days. The Karate Kid (1984) was his career-defining role. He died in 2005 at age 73.

question: Kurt Russell gave True West magazine his own account of the 1993 Western Tombstone in 2006. Its first director had been sacked about a month into a famously chaotic shoot, and George P. Cosmatos was hired to take over. What did Russell say about Cosmatos's part in the film?
answer: That Cosmatos was brought in as a ghost director while Russell directed
choices: That Cosmatos was brought in as a ghost director while Russell directed
That Cosmatos had a longer cut the studio never released
That Val Kilmer had directed all of his own scenes
That Wyatt Earp's grand-niece had rewritten the script
context: Russell told True West that the producers wanted him to take over the film and that he agreed on condition his name stayed off it. Val Kilmer later wrote that Russell was solely responsible for the film's success, though he stopped short of saying Russell did the directing. Cosmatos had directed Rambo: First Blood Part II (1985) and Cobra (1986).

question: Temple of Doom opens in a glittering Shanghai nightclub in 1935, with a song-and-dance number, a poisoned drink and a diamond deal gone wrong. Raiders had already hidden George Lucas's droids on a tomb wall, C-3PO and R2-D2 carved among the hieroglyphs. This film slips in another Star Wars nod: the name of the club. What is it called?
context: In a nod to Star Wars, the Shanghai nightclub where Temple of Doom begins is called Club Obi-Wan. Raiders of the Lost Ark had already hidden R2-D2 and C-3PO among the hieroglyphs in the Well of Souls.

question: The crew of The Goonies built One-Eyed Willy's pirate ship as a full-scale practical effect for the film's climax, for a young cast that included Sean Astin, Josh Brolin, Corey Feldman, Jonathan Ke Quan and Martha Plimpton. What happened to the ship after filming?
answer: It was scrapped after shooting, because no one could be found who wanted it
choices: It was scrapped after shooting, because no one could be found who wanted it
It was sold to Universal Studios theme park and became part of the Earthquake ride decoration
It was donated to the Astoria Maritime Museum in Astoria, Oregon (the filming location)
It was burned for the Goonies' 20th-anniversary 2005 ceremony with Donner's blessing
context: The full-size ship was scrapped after shooting because no one could be found who wanted it. Donner kept the young cast from seeing it until their characters first did, and the first take of that reveal was reshot. The Astoria, Oregon film locations have become a tourist attraction.

question: Tony Scott was filming F-14 Tomcats aboard a real Navy carrier for Top Gun, in exactly the light he wanted, when the commanding officer changed course and the light shifted with the ship. Scott asked to swing back to the old heading and was told that turning the carrier would cost $25,000. What did he do?
answer: Wrote the captain a check and kept shooting
choices: Wrote the captain a check and kept shooting
Waited a day for the same light to return
Moved the scene over to the second carrier
Relit the deck with the crew's own lamps
context: When Scott asked the carrier to keep its earlier course, he was told it cost $25,000 to turn the ship, so he wrote the captain a check and kept filming. The carrier sequences were shot aboard the Enterprise and the Ranger, and the film's enemy MiG-28s were really Northrop F-5s.

question: Edward Furlong was a total unknown, picked from hundreds of hopefuls, when he took on John Connor, the rebellious teenage hero of James Cameron's 1991 action film Terminator 2: Judgment Day. Its shape-shifting liquid-metal villain was one of the first big Hollywood uses of computer-generated imagery (CGI). How was Furlong first discovered for the film?
answer: Casting director Mali Finn spotted him while visiting a Boys and Girls Club in Pasadena
choices: Casting director Mali Finn spotted him while visiting a Boys and Girls Club in Pasadena
He was a child model who had appeared in Sears catalogs and was already on Cameron's shortlist
His mother sent his school photo to the production office along with thousands of others
His uncle was a stunt coordinator at Stan Winston Studios who recommended him
context: Mali Finn wanted a boy without acting experience, because none of the child actors who auditioned seemed streetwise enough. Furlong had to take acting lessons, learn Spanish and learn to ride a motorcycle for the part, and he won the MTV Movie Award for Best Breakthrough Performance. Robert Patrick (the T-1000) was a relatively obscure character actor who broke through with T2.

question: Nega-Scott, the dark double of Scott Pilgrim, turns up in Edgar Wright's 2010 film only after the last fight, and the two become friends. In Bryan Lee O'Malley's last graphic novel the meeting matters more: Scott settles things by accepting him rather than beating him. What does Nega-Scott stand for?
answer: Scott's buried memories of all the mistakes of his past
choices: Scott's buried memories of all the mistakes of his past
Scott's secret fear that Ramona will leave him for Gideon
Scott's hidden jealousy of his more talented bandmates
Scott's quiet wish to give up music and go back home
context: Nega-Scott is the dark side of Scott, a reminder of all the mistakes he has made. In the last book Scott learns that his own memories of his past had flattered him, and accepting Nega-Scott is how he owns up to it.

question: Robert Patrick, a lean, little-known actor then living in his car, won the part of the liquid-metal cyborg that pours through bars after young John Connor in James Cameron's Terminator 2, on the strength of his intense presence. But Cameron's first choice had been a sneering, spiky-haired British rock singer, until a motorcycle crash badly injured the singer's leg. Who was he?
context: Billy Idol was originally cast as the T-1000 before a motorcycle crash seriously injured his leg; Cameron later said he probably would not have cast him in hindsight. Casting director Mali Finn felt Robert Patrick had the intense presence the part needed.

question: Robert Zemeckis and Bob Gale sent Marty McFly and Doc Brown to October 21, 2015 in the 1989 film Back to the Future Part II, and filled that fictional 2015 with silly guesses: hoverboards floating over sidewalks, Nikes that laced themselves up, a nineteenth Jaws sequel. Only one guess about the real world came true, and it stunned Gale years later. Which one?
answer: The Cubs winning the World Series in 2016 (just one year late from the film's October 21, 2015 prediction)
choices: The Cubs winning the World Series in 2016 (just one year late from the film's October 21, 2015 prediction)
Hoverboards becoming an actual consumer product (the 2015 self-balancing scooter)
Video calls with multi-channel interfaces (similar to Marty's TV-call scene)
Movies running 19+ sequels (the Jaws 19 joke poster in the film)
context: The Chicago Cubs hadn't won a World Series since 1908. Their 2016 victory broke the longest drought in major American sports. Bob Gale's screenplay had positioned the joke as the most-impossible thing about 2015. Other predictions in BTTF Part II have come partially true — video calls (FaceTime), self-tying shoes (Nike's 2016 release), Pepsi Perfect (released as Pepsi Perfect for the 2015 anniversary).

question: The Grail temple in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade has a real rose-red front: a tomb face carved into a cliff at Petra, in Jordan, by Nabataean masons two thousand years ago. Local Bedouins believed a pharaoh had hidden riches in the stone urn at its top and fired rifles at it to crack it open; the bullet scars still show. What does the tomb's Arabic name, Al-Khazneh, mean?
context: Al-Khazneh means the Treasury in Arabic, a name the area's Bedouins gave it in the early nineteenth century from a legend that riches lay in its urn, which is solid sandstone. The film used the façade as the entrance to the Grail temple and shot the interior at Elstree Studios in England.

question: Fievel and his family board a ship leaving Russia in the 1986 cartoon Don Bluth made with Steven Spielberg, a story based on Spielberg's family history of Russian-Jewish immigration. Their flight is historical. What real event forces this wave of Jews to flee?
answer: The pogroms that swept the Russian Empire in the early 1880s
choices: The pogroms that swept the Russian Empire in the early 1880s
The Russo-Japanese War, which emptied villages in 1904-1905
The Bolshevik Revolution that seized power in 1917
The Russian Civil War between Reds and Whites, 1918-1922
context: The film opens in 1885 in Shostka, in the Russian Empire, where Cossacks and their cats raid the village. A wave of pogroms broke out across the Russian Empire in 1881, after the assassination of Tsar Alexander II. Fievel is separated from his family during a storm on the crossing to America.

question: One orange-masked turtle swings two wooden sticks joined by a chain in the 1987 Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles cartoon and yells 'Cowabunga' whenever he does something cool. He and his three teammates are named after Renaissance artists. Which turtle is he?
context: The four turtles are named after Italian Renaissance masters: Leonardo (blue, katanas), Raphael (red, sai), Donatello (purple, bo staff), Michelangelo (orange, nunchucks). 'Cowabunga' became Mikey's signature exclamation through the cartoon.

question: ThunderCats (1985) crash-lands a group of cat-like warriors on a strange world after they flee their dying home planet of Thundera. Their young leader sees far-off dangers through the Sword of Omens and raises it to cry 'Thundercats, ho!' Who is he?
context: Lion-O leads the Thundercats on Third Earth after fleeing the dying planet Thundera. Other team members include Panthro (panther engineer), Cheetara (cheetah speedster), Tygra (tiger), and the twin cubs WilyKit and WilyKat.

question: Giant living robots from the planet Cybertron come to Earth in the 1984 cartoon The Transformers, disguised as regular vehicles. The Autobot leader, a wise, brave commander, transforms into a red-and-blue Freightliner semi truck and cries 'Autobots, roll out.' Who is he?
context: The Transformers cartoon launched in September 1984 alongside the Hasbro toy line. Optimus Prime leads the Autobots; Megatron leads the Decepticons. The tagline 'More than meets the eye' became cultural shorthand.

question: An elite team of American soldiers leaps from jets to battle the evil terrorist group Cobra in the 1985 cartoon A Real American Hero. Every time the team charges into action, every soldier shouts the same two-word rallying cry. What is the battle cry?
context: G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero ran 1985-1987 with 95 episodes. Cobra Commander led the terrorist organization Cobra alongside Destro and the Baroness. Each episode famously closed with a PSA — 'Knowing is half the battle.'

question: A black-gloved hand pets a mean, growling cat named Mad Cat beside a big leather chair in the 1983 cartoon Inspector Gadget, and that is nearly all viewers ever see of the criminal mastermind behind every scheme. Who is this hidden villain?
context: Inspector Gadget's niece Penny and dog Brain solve most of the cases while Gadget bumbles around with his cybernetic gadgets. Dr. Claw's face was never shown — viewers only saw his armored gauntlet and his white cat. The line 'I'll get you next time, Gadget — NEXT TIME' closed many episodes.

question: Scrooge McDuck and his nephews Huey, Dewey and Louie hunt gold and treasure around the world in Disney's 1987 afternoon cartoon DuckTales. Its catchy theme song is famous for a short, punchy, two-syllable cheer right after the singers sing the title. What is the cheer?
context: DuckTales followed Scrooge McDuck, his nephews Huey, Dewey, and Louie, and a cast including Webby and pilot Launchpad McQuack. The theme song's 'DuckTales — Woo-oo!' hook lodged in a generation's heads. Scrooge's vault of gold coins, where he swam in money, was iconic.

question: Animaniacs, from 1993, follows three black-and-white cartoon siblings, two brothers and a little sister, locked in a vault in the 1930s and now living atop the Warner Bros. water tower in Burbank. Their three names are shouted together in the theme song. What are they?
context: Animaniacs was produced by Steven Spielberg for Warner Bros. and Amblin Entertainment. The Warner siblings shared the show with recurring segments like Pinky and the Brain (two lab mice plotting to take over the world). Dot's full name was Princess Angelina Contessa Louisa Francesca Banana Fanna Bo Besca III.

question: Sergio Leone put the same tall, squint-eyed American in a poncho for three Westerns of the 1960s, from A Fistful of Dollars to The Good, the Bad and the Ugly. He plays a mysterious gunslinger known only as the Man with No Name. Who was the actor?
context: Eastwood played the Man with No Name in A Fistful of Dollars (1964), For a Few Dollars More (1965), and The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966). Sergio Leone directed all three. Ennio Morricone composed the scores. Eastwood went on to direct his own Westerns including Unforgiven (1992), for which he won Best Director.

question: Charlie Brown is sent to pick a Christmas tree for his school's play in the 1965 TV special A Charlie Brown Christmas. He walks past the fancy aluminum trees on the lot, and his friends laugh at his pick. What does he bring back?
choices: A perfect tall fir from the lot
A blue spruce decorated with tinsel
context: A Charlie Brown Christmas (1965) was the first Peanuts TV special and aired on CBS December 9, 1965. Vince Guaraldi composed the iconic jazz score including 'Linus and Lucy.' Linus's recitation of Luke 2:8-14 — 'And there were in the same country shepherds...' — became the most-remembered scene.

question: American families sat down in December 1964 for a new stop-motion TV special, Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, acted out by puppets. The little studio behind it went on to make Frosty the Snowman and The Year Without a Santa Claus. What was the studio called?
context: Arthur Rankin Jr. and Jules Bass formed Rankin/Bass Productions in 1960. Their stop-motion 'Animagic' technique was actually animated by Tadahito Mochinaga's studio MOM in Tokyo. Burl Ives narrated Rudolph as Sam the Snowman. Other Rankin/Bass classics: Frosty the Snowman (1969), Santa Claus is Comin' to Town (1970), The Year Without a Santa Claus (1974).

question: A fat orange tabby who hates Mondays and eats pans of lasagna dresses up as a pirate with his dog friend Odie and lands on a haunted island in a 1985 animated TV special. He comes from Jim Davis's comic strip. What is his name?
context: Garfield's Halloween Adventure aired on CBS October 30, 1985 and won a Primetime Emmy. Lorenzo Music voiced Garfield. The special's spooky pirate-ghost sequence features one of TV's eeriest narrated monologues, delivered by an unseen old man on the haunted island.

question: The 1990 comedy Home Alone sends a big family rushing for a plane to Paris at Christmas, and the panic leaves one son behind. The clever eight-year-old, played by Macaulay Culkin, fights off two bumbling burglars with booby traps. What is the boy's name?
context: Home Alone was directed by Chris Columbus, written by John Hughes, and starred Macaulay Culkin as Kevin. The two bumbling burglars Harry (Joe Pesci) and Marv (Daniel Stern) called themselves the 'Wet Bandits.' The film was the highest-grossing live-action comedy in history until 2011.

question: A niece does the real detective work for her clueless uncle in the 1983 cartoon Inspector Gadget. She carries a wristwatch that is really a two-way radio and a Computer Book that can hack machines, and she solves almost every case. What is her name?
context: Penny works with the dog Brain to solve the cases Inspector Gadget gets credit for. Her computer book contained a video phone, a printer, encyclopedic data, and other gadgets. Don Adams (Get Smart's Maxwell Smart) voiced Inspector Gadget; Cree Summer Francks voiced Penny in the first season.

question: Tiny Toon Adventures sends younger student versions of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck to a school called Acme Looniversity in 1990. Its executive producer is the film director who had already made E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial and would soon make Jurassic Park. Who is he?
context: Tiny Toon Adventures (1990-1992) featured Buster Bunny, Babs Bunny, Plucky Duck, Hamton J. Pig, and Elmyra Duff. Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment co-produced with Warner Bros. Animation. The success of Tiny Toons led directly to Spielberg producing Animaniacs (1993) and the Pinky and the Brain spinoff.

question: Splinter, a giant rat, trains four teenage turtles in the ninja arts in the New York City sewers in a 1987 cartoon. Between missions they order one junk food from delivery drivers up above the manhole cover. What food do they love above all others?
context: The pizza obsession was invented for the 1987 cartoon — Eastman and Laird's 1984 black-and-white comic had no special pizza fixation. The cartoon used it for kid-friendly humor and toy merchandise (the Turtle Van featured a Pizza Thrower weapon).

question: Prince Adam raises his glowing sword to the sky in the 1983 cartoon He-Man and the Masters of the Universe and shouts a magic phrase. Lightning strikes him, and he becomes the mightiest warrior in the universe. What does he shout?
choices: By the light of the Ancients
context: Filmation produced the Masters of the Universe cartoon as a syndicated half-hour show tied to the Mattel toy line. MAJOR AWARD — and he reads it as a German imperial title
FROM CLEVELAND — and he assumes a Polish manufacturer
DELICATE — and he calls it Russian craftsmanship
context: Darren McGavin played the Old Man. Director Bob Clark, working from Jean Shepherd's stories, had the leg lamp custom-built; the prop became an instant cultural icon. Replicas remain a popular Christmas decoration four decades later. The original 1983 lamp from the film was sold at auction in 2014 for over $100,000.

question: April O'Neil chases one more weird story across New York City in the 1987 cartoon Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and ends up needing the Turtles to save her from Shredder's Foot Clan. She is a news reporter, the human friend of the four sewer-dwelling heroes. What TV channel does she work for?
context: The 1987 cartoon introduced April as a television reporter for Channel 6 News. In the original 1984 comic she was a computer programmer for the scientist Baxter Stockman.

question: Gaia, the spirit of Earth, gives five kids from five different continents magic rings to fight pollution in the 1990 cartoon Captain Planet and the Planeteers. Kwame is from Africa, Wheeler from North America, Linka from Eastern Europe and Ma-Ti from South America. The fifth Planeteer is a girl named Gi. Where is she from?
context: Gi's ring controlled Water and she was a marine biologist. The five-continent representation was Ted Turner's idea — he wanted the show to feel globally inclusive. The voice cast was unusually star-studded: Whoopi Goldberg (Gaia), LeVar Burton (Kwame), Joey Dedio (Wheeler), then Captain Planet voiced by David Coburn. Eco-villains included Dr. Blight, Looten Plunder, and Hoggish Greedly.

question: Three sneaky, immortal witch sisters called the Weird Sisters scheme in the background of Disney's 1994 series Gargoyles, which borrows heavily from Shakespeare. The show follows a clan of stone warriors who sleep as statues by day and fly the skies of modern New York City by night. In which Shakespeare play do those three witches first appear?
context: Gargoyles also featured a major recurring character named Macbeth (the actual king of Scotland from history and from Shakespeare's play) and Demona, who was his immortal sometime-ally. Creator Greg Weisman built much of the mythology on Scottish history and folklore. Other Shakespeare-influenced characters included Oberon and Titania of the Third Race (the show's name for fairies).

question: Mel Blanc, the voice of Daffy Duck, Porky Pig and Yosemite Sam, lay in a two-week coma in January 1961 after a bad car crash on Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles, and doctors could not wake him. A famous hospital-room story says one thing a doctor tried finally reached him and got a reply. What did the doctor do?
answer: Asked 'How are you, Bugs Bunny?' and he answered in character
choices: Asked 'How are you, Bugs Bunny?' and he answered in character
Played a recording of his recent Daffy Duck sessions
Brought Warner Brothers animators in to read scripts at his bedside
Used voice-synthesis machines to play his prior performances at him
context: Blanc himself told versions of the story in interviews. By the usual account, after days with no response, one of his neurologists at the UCLA Medical Center asked how Bugs Bunny was feeling, and Blanc answered weakly in the rabbit's voice. After he recovered, Blanc kept voicing Bugs and dozens of other characters until his death in 1989.

question: Steve Barron directed the 1990 live-action Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movie for $13.5 million, with full-body animatronic turtle suits from the Jim Henson workshop in London. It was Henson's last finished project before his death that May, and the film grossed over $200 million worldwide. Who composed the score?
context: Du Prez had previously scored several Monty Python films. The animatronic turtle heads were filled with delicate radio-controlled servos worked by puppeteers including David Greenaway, Mak Wilson, and Robbie Williams. Corey Feldman provided Donatello's voice in the film while Leif Tilden performed in the suit. Brian Tochi voiced Leonardo. The film's tone, much darker than the cartoon, surprised many fans coming from the Saturday-morning version.

question: Hasbro needed names and personalities for its 1984 Transformers, and Bob Budiansky, a Marvel Comics writer, supplied most of them, Megatron, Starscream and Ratchet among them. The Autobot leader's name came from another Marvel man, a writer famous for reviving Batman in the 1970s. Who was he?
context: Budiansky conceived the names of most of the original Transformers, Megatron, Starscream, Ratchet and Ravage among them, and later wrote Marvel's Transformers comic for years. He credits Denny O'Neil, who had brought Batman back to his dark roots with the artist Neal Adams, with naming Optimus Prime.

question: Filmation Studios refused to send the art for its 1983 He-Man cartoon to Korea or Japan, as most 1980s studios did to save money. It kept all the art in California, even though it cost more. Which co-founder was the loud voice for keeping the work at home?
context: Scheimer co-founded Filmation in 1962 and ran it until it closed in 1989. Keeping the work at home made Filmation dearer than its rivals, and reusing stock animation across episodes was how it paid for that. Other Filmation shows include She-Ra, BraveStarr, Ghostbusters (1986, not the Bill Murray film) and Fat Albert.

question: Mark Hamill, long typecast as Luke Skywalker, won the part of the Joker on Batman: The Animated Series in 1992, and his Joker became the classic animated one. Hamill later said that, without realizing it at first, he had been imitating one old Universal horror performance. Which one?
answer: Claude Rains as the Invisible Man
choices: Claude Rains as the Invisible Man
Lon Chaney Jr. as the Wolf Man
context: Hamill has said Jay Leno and the sportscaster Howard Cosell were in the mix too. He went on to voice the Joker in many animated films and in the Arkham video games.

question: One artist made Scrooge McDuck in 1947 while drawing Donald Duck stories in secret for Western Publishing. The same man made most of the DuckTales cast: Magica De Spell, Flintheart Glomgold and the Beagle Boys. The 1987 cartoon came straight from his comics. Who was 'the good duck artist'?
context: Carl Barks worked anonymously because Disney's contractual standard didn't credit comic-book creators. Fans called him 'the good duck artist' to distinguish him from Disney's many lesser duck artists. Don Rosa was Barks's biggest fan and continued his story tradition with The Life and Times of Scrooge McDuck (1992-1996). Barks died in 2000 at age 99. The DuckTales pilot 'Treasure of the Golden Suns' adapted Barks's stories almost directly.

question: Alan Le May drew his 1954 novel from the real kidnapping of a nine-year-old Texas girl by Comanche raiders in 1836, and John Ford turned the book into a 1956 film frequently cited as the greatest American Western. She lived among the Comanche for 24 years, married a war chief and bore three children before Texas Rangers recaptured her in 1860. Who was the historical figure?
context: Cynthia Ann Parker's son with her Comanche husband Peta Nocona was Quanah Parker, who became the last great Comanche war chief. After her 1860 recapture by Texas Rangers, she repeatedly tried to return to her Comanche family and refused to assimilate. The film's Ethan Edwards (John Wayne) and his hunt for his abducted niece Debbie (Natalie Wood) explicitly drew on Parker's story.

question: A fly buzzes around Jack Elam for nearly three silent minutes at the start of Sergio Leone's 1968 Western Once Upon a Time in the West, where he is one of three gunmen at a train station. Leone made the whole scene as a tribute to an older film. Which 1952 Western was he honoring?
context: Fred Zinnemann's High Noon (1952), starring Gary Cooper, used real-time waiting for a noon train as its central tension. Leone's three gunmen are waiting at the station for Charles Bronson's Harmonica. The opening's soundtrack is spare (a creaking windmill, dripping water, the fly), with Ennio Morricone's full score saved for later. Bronson, Henry Fonda (cast against type as the villain Frank) and Claudia Cardinale led the cast.

question: Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, the real outlaws behind the 1969 film, rode back between robberies to a remote red-rock hideout. Their gang worked in Wyoming and Utah from 1896 to 1901 and took its name from that place. What was the hideout called?
answer: Hole in the Wall (Wyoming Big Horn Mountains)
choices: Hole in the Wall (Wyoming Big Horn Mountains)
context: Hole in the Wall, Robbers Roost and Brown's Hole were stops on the so-called Outlaw Trail, and at Castle Gate, Utah, Butch Cassidy robbed a mine payroll in 1897. Butch Cassidy was born Robert Leroy Parker; the Sundance Kid was Harry Longabaugh. George Roy Hill directed the 1969 film; Burt Bacharach wrote the score including 'Raindrops Keep Fallin' on My Head.'

question: John Henry 'Doc' Holliday earned his dental degree at the Pennsylvania College of Dental Surgery in Philadelphia in 1872. Soon after, he caught tuberculosis, and doctors told him he had to move west to a drier climate or the wet Georgia air would kill him fast. He set up his first dental office out west in a booming cattle town, before he drifted into gambling. In what city was it?
context: Holliday's coughing drove patients away from his Dallas practice, and he turned to gambling for income. He met Wyatt Earp in Fort Griffin, Texas, in 1877 and met him again in Dodge City, where in 1878 Doc is said to have come to his aid in a standoff with armed Texas cowboys; Earp testified in 1881 that Doc 'came to my rescue and saved my life when I was surrounded by desperadoes.' The two became close friends, and Doc later joined Wyatt in Tombstone. Doc died of tuberculosis in Glenwood Springs, Colorado, on November 8, 1887, aged 36.

question: Kevin Costner had every scene with Lakota characters in his 1990 epic Western Dances with Wolves played in the real Lakota language, with English subtitles. The film, about a Union Army lieutenant who slowly joins a Lakota Sioux band on the Great Plains, won seven Academy Awards. The cast needed a fluent Lakota coach to teach them how to say the words on camera. Who was hired?
answer: Doris Leader Charge of Sinte Gleska University
choices: Doris Leader Charge of Sinte Gleska University
Frank Waters of the Taos Pueblo writers
Russell Means of the American Indian Movement
N. Scott Momaday of the Kiowa Tribe writers
context: Doris Leader Charge taught Lakota language and culture at Sinte Gleska University in Mission, South Dakota. She translated the film's Lakota dialogue, coached the actors and played Pretty Shield on screen. The activist Russell Means later said that Lakota has a male and a female way of speaking, and that because a woman taught the actors, Costner and some of the Native actors spoke in the feminine way; watching the film with Lakota friends, he said, they laughed.

question: Disney's bosses hid The Nightmare Before Christmas, a stop-motion film produced by Tim Burton about Jack Skellington's plan to steal Christmas from Santa, behind a grown-up label they owned in October 1993. They feared the film and its skeletal hero would scare young families away from the main Disney brand. Which label released the film?
context: Touchstone had been launched in 1984 specifically for Disney's PG-13 and R-rated content. Other Touchstone releases included Pretty Woman (1990) and Pulp Fiction's Miramax distribution (1994). Disney rebranded Nightmare under the main Disney label in 2006 after years of cult-classic success made the original distribution decision seem absurd. Henry Selick directed; Tim Burton conceived and produced. Danny Elfman wrote 10 songs and sang for Jack Skellington's musical numbers.

question: Clark Griswold has been planning to use his Christmas bonus to buy his family a swimming pool in National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation, from 1989. When the envelope finally arrives, he opens it expecting a check and finds something else. What has his employer sent him as a bonus?
answer: A one-year membership in the Jelly of the Month Club
choices: A one-year membership in the Jelly of the Month Club
A signed photo of the CEO and a Christmas card
A coupon for the company cafeteria worth one hundred dollars
A stock certificate worth less than the framing it came in
context: Cousin Eddie (Randy Quaid) hears about Clark's lack of bonus and remarks, after Clark snaps about it being 'a one-year membership in the Jelly of the Month Club,' that 'that's the gift that keeps on giving the whole year, Clark.' The line and the Jelly of the Month Club phrase entered American holiday-comedy permanent rotation. Clark's profanity-laden meltdown after opening the envelope is one of the all-time great holiday-comedy monologues. John Hughes wrote the script.

question: Garfield's Halloween Adventure, from 1985, sends Garfield and Odie to trick-or-treat on an empty island. Ghost pirates are due back at midnight to dig up their treasure, and an old man in a shack warns Garfield with one creepy line that has scared kids for years. What does he say as midnight strikes?
answer: They're coming, they're coming, they're coming
choices: They're coming, they're coming, they're coming
Beware the pirates, dear child of mine
Run while you can, the dead don't tire
Listen, the bells, the bells, the bells
context: The line is whispered, then repeated with rising urgency. The animation cuts to Garfield's wide-eyed reaction in close-up — a moment cited by 90s kids as the most unexpectedly scary thing they ever saw on Saturday morning cartoons. Lorenzo Music voiced Garfield. C. Lindsay Workman voiced the old man.
