The TV special was produced by Phil Roman, who would also direct most of the subsequent Garfield specials and the cartoon series.

question: Chris Van Allsburg won the Caldecott Medal for his 1985 book The Polar Express, famously sparse at only a few thousand words, and he left its child without a name. Robert Zemeckis expanded the story dramatically for his 2004 motion-capture feature. What was the child called on screen?
answer: Hero Boy (his actual given name is never used in the film either)
choices: Hero Boy (his actual given name is never used in the film either)
Billy (named in the credits and several scenes)
Hero (his actual name said only once)
context: Zemeckis deliberately preserved the book's anonymity for the protagonist. Tom Hanks performed both Hero Boy and the Hero Boy's Father via motion-capture. Other unnamed roles: Hero Girl, the Lonely Boy. The bell that Hero Boy receives from Santa rings only for those who still believe. The book was inspired by Van Allsburg's childhood obsession with the Christmas-train sets in Grand Rapids, Michigan storefronts.

question: Ren, the scrawny chihuahua of The Ren & Stimpy Show, goes full psychotic in one early-1990s episode, drawn in the show's wild, sometimes disturbing style. Network executives at Nickelodeon, who censored several episodes, were so frightened by this one that they refused to broadcast it for the entire decade. It finally aired years later. Which banned episode was it?
context: 'Man's Best Friend' has Ren beating his owner, George Liquor, with an oar. Nickelodeon fired creator John Kricfalusi partly over this episode. 'Stimpy's Invention' introduced the song 'Happy Happy Joy Joy', and 'Sven Höek' gave Ren a Norwegian cousin as dim as Stimpy.

question: Jim Jinkins sold his studio, Jumbo Pictures, to Disney in 1996, and Doug, the cartoon he had made for Nickelodeon in 1991, moved to ABC Saturday morning. Fans said the Disney version looked and felt worse. What new character showed up in it?
choices: A new bully character named Boomer Bledsoe
Roger Klotz's mother as a recurring character
context: Doug's family in the Disney version expanded to add Cleopatra — usually called 'Dirtbike' — as a baby sister. Patti Mayonnaise was Doug's crush throughout the show. Quailman was his imaginary superhero alter ego, with the famous quail egg yolks of justice. Roger Klotz was the recurring bully. Jim Jinkins later also created PB&J Otter (1998) and Pinky Dinky Doo (2005) for kids' TV.

question: Arnold lives with his grandparents in a boarding house called the Sunset Arms in Nickelodeon's 1996 series Hey Arnold, set in a stylized big-city neighborhood inspired by Brooklyn and Seattle. His classmates call him 'Football Head' for the distinctive shape of his head. Who created the show?
context: Craig Bartlett had worked on Pee-wee's Playhouse and was Matt Groening's brother-in-law. Hey Arnold ran from 1996 to 2004, and the 2017 film Hey Arnold!: The Jungle Movie took up its unfinished story. Helga Pataki is Arnold's secret admirer, who torments him in public.

question: Six fourth-graders band together at Third Street Elementary School in Recess, a Disney One Saturday Morning cartoon of 1997. The cast is multicultural, and every kid has a clear role in the gang. One of the six is the brainy science whiz with glasses and a hand-held computer. Which kid is it?
context: Gus Griswald was the newcomer military-brat, Mikey the soft-hearted poet, Vince the athletic star, Spinelli the tough-girl, TJ the leader. Recess was created by Paul Germain (who also co-created Rugrats) and Joe Ansolabehere. It ran 1997-2001 on ABC with multiple theatrical and direct-to-video movies. The school's hierarchy — King Bob ruled the playground from a slide-throne — was a parody of medieval feudalism that snuck political satire into a kids' show.

question: Dexter Douglas, a teenager, turns into the superhero Freakazoid after a computer accident in the Warner Bros. Animation cartoon of 1995. The show was originally pitched as a much more serious, dark-tone project. What happened to make it the goofy fourth-wall-breaking comedy fans know?
answer: Tom Ruegger took it over after Timm left to work on Superman: The Animated Series
choices: Tom Ruegger took it over after Timm left to work on Superman: The Animated Series
Test screenings rejected the dark version and Warner rewrote it from scratch
Network executives demanded a comedy after Pinky and the Brain's success
Mark Hamill's involvement caused a shift in tone toward voice-actor comedy
context: Tom Ruegger had been the showrunner of Tiny Toons (1990), Animaniacs (1993), and Pinky and the Brain (1995). When Bruce Timm left Freakazoid to develop Superman: The Animated Series for the DC Animated Universe, Ruegger turned the project into a meta-comedy. The show featured cameo characters like the Lobe (Joe Leahy) and Cave Guy (Jeff Bennett). Paul Rugg voiced Freakazoid himself; Jonathan Harris (Lost in Space) voiced Professor Heiney.

question: Wyatt Earp drifted through gold rushes and gambling halls for decades and ended up in 1920s Los Angeles, where a silent-Western star became his friend. A young Fox prop boy of those years later said he had modelled his screen lawman's walk and talk on Earp. Who were the two film men?
answer: Tom Mix and the young John Wayne
choices: Tom Mix and the young John Wayne
William S. Hart and Buck Jones
context: Wyatt Earp died January 13, 1929 at age 80. Tom Mix and William S. Hart, leading silent-Western stars, were among his pallbearers. John Wayne, then a young prop boy at Fox, later told Hugh O'Brian that he had based his Western lawman on Earp; whether the two ever really met is uncertain. Stuart Lake's 1931 biography Wyatt Earp: Frontier Marshal, heavily fictionalized, established most of the Earp myth Americans know.

question: CBS bosses watched A Charlie Brown Christmas early, in November 1965, and hated it: a slow, sad show with jazz, Bible verses, real kid voices and no laugh track. They planned to air it once, on December 9, and never again. What saved it?
answer: It came second in the ratings, watched on 45 percent of TVs in use
choices: It came second in the ratings, watched on 45 percent of TVs in use
Charles Schulz personally bought the special back from CBS and sold it to NBC
It tied for highest rating only after an unprecedented critical Time magazine review
Coca-Cola sponsorship contracts mandated CBS air it for the next decade unchanged
context: About 45 percent of the televisions in use that night were tuned to it, some 15.5 million households, and only NBC's Bonanza beat it that week. It won the Peabody Award and an Emmy. CBS reran it every year until 2000; ABC carried it after that, and Apple TV+ took it over in 2020. Vince Guaraldi's jazz score and the children's-choir version of 'Hark! The Herald Angels Sing' both became Christmas standards.

question: The crew of Home Alone shot a black-and-white gangster movie in a single day, just so Kevin could scare off a pizza delivery boy with it on the video recorder. Plenty of viewers assumed its mobster and tommy gun came from a real 1930s picture. The title spoofed a real 1938 James Cagney crime film. What was the fake movie called?
context: Angels with Filthy Souls was made specifically for Home Alone, shot in one day before main filming began, and its title spoofs Angels with Dirty Faces (1938), starring James Cagney. Ralph Foody played the mobster Johnny, and Kevin watches a sequel, Angels with Even Filthier Souls, in Home Alone 2.

question: Skeletor and a goblin general trick He-Man into believing he has accidentally killed someone in one 1984 episode of Filmation's He-Man and the Masters of the Universe. Most episodes end on a moral lesson, but this one goes darker than the rest, leaving the strongest man in the universe sick with guilt. What is the episode called?
context: In The Problem with Power, Skeletor and the goblin General Tataran manipulate He-Man into believing he has killed someone by accident. Bob Forward, Leslie Wilson and Tom Tataranowicz wrote the episode, which first aired on 9 November 1984.

question: Unicron, the planet-devouring giant Transformer of The Transformers: The Movie (1986), speaks with a voice recorded on 5 October 1985, five days before the actor died. It was his last film role, and his voice was so weak that it had to be run through a synthesizer. What did he tell his biographer about the job?
answer: That he had played the voice of a toy, a planet
choices: That he had played the voice of a toy, a planet
That he had done it so his grandson could hear him
That he had asked to play the Autobot leader instead
That he had turned the part down twice before agreeing
context: Orson Welles recorded Unicron on 5 October 1985 and died on 10 October. He told his biographer Barbara Leaming that he had played the voice of a toy, a planet; the director, Nelson Shin, said Welles had been glad to take the part. Leonard Nimoy voiced Galvatron in the same film.

question: 'The Presidents,' a 1993 song from Animaniacs, sends Yakko Warner racing through all 41 American Presidents to date, Washington through Clinton, at extremely rapid tempo. The tune was lifted from a 19th-century light-classical piece and played roughly twice as fast. What was the source piece?
choices: Russian Easter Festival Overture by Rimsky-Korsakov
context: Rossini's 1829 William Tell Overture is also the Lone Ranger's theme. 'The Presidents' belongs to the show's run of fast teaching songs, alongside 'Yakko's World' and 'Wakko's America'.

question: Batman: The Animated Series turns Mr. Freeze, a goofy 1960s pun villain, into a sad figure in its 1992 episode 'Heart of Ice.' The episode won an Emmy, and DC Comics later made its story the official comic version. What is the new sad origin the episode sets up?
answer: Victor Fries was trying to save his terminally ill wife Nora when a lab accident left him needing sub-zero suits to live
choices: Victor Fries was trying to save his terminally ill wife Nora when a lab accident left him needing sub-zero suits to live
Victor Fries was a Russian defector whose family was killed in retaliation for his escape
Victor Fries was a polar climatologist who accidentally cryogenically froze himself solving climate change
Victor Fries was the test subject of a CIA cryogenics weapons program that froze him by mistake
context: Paul Dini wrote 'Heart of Ice', and Michael Ansara voiced Mr. Freeze with a haunting, flat delivery. The episode set the tone for the show's deep treatment of its villains, and the comics later took up the new origin.

question: Maurice LaMarche built the Brain's grand, booming voice mostly out of one actor, rehearsing on a famous outtake of him grumbling through a frozen-peas commercial. Pinky and the Brain, two genetically enhanced lab mice at Acme Labs, got their own show in 1995 after starring in Animaniacs. Who was the actor?
context: LaMarche has described the Brain's voice as 65 percent Orson Welles and 35 percent Vincent Price, and he honed his Welles impression on the actor's notorious frozen-peas commercial outtake. Rob Paulsen voices Pinky, and the pair first appeared as a segment of Animaniacs in 1993.

question: Blondie, Angel Eyes and Tuco face one another in a standoff in a circular Civil War cemetery at the close of Sergio Leone's The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, each racing to learn who has the buried gold. Ennio Morricone's score for this finale is among the most famous film music ever recorded. The track that plays during the standoff has a name in Italian. What is it called?
choices: Il Buono, il Brutto, il Cattivo (Main Title)
context: 'Il Triello' plays during the standoff itself. The piece before it, as Tuco runs through the cemetery looking for the grave, is 'L'Estasi dell'Oro' (The Ecstasy of Gold), which Metallica has used to open its concerts for decades. Morricone received an honorary Oscar in 2007 and won the Original Score Oscar for The Hateful Eight in 2016.

question: Jesse James stood on a chair in his rented home in St. Joseph, Missouri, on April 3, 1882, to straighten a picture on the wall. A member of his own gang shot him from behind, after Governor Thomas T. Crittenden had promised the man a Missouri pardon and a reward. Who fired the shot?
choices: Frank James, his brother on impulse
Cole Younger of the original gang
context: Jesse had been standing on a chair to straighten a picture on the wall, his guns set aside. Bob and his brother Charley Ford had been staying in his house as members of his gang. Ford pleaded guilty, was sentenced to hang, and was pardoned the same day by Governor Crittenden. The folk song 'The Ballad of Jesse James' calls Ford 'that dirty little coward'; James had been using 'Mr. Howard' as his alias.

question: Pat Garrett, a sheriff, shot Billy the Kid dead in Pete Maxwell's bedroom at Fort Sumner on July 14, 1881, two months after the outlaw had escaped from jail while awaiting hanging. The Kid was 21, he had used multiple aliases, and the record is genuinely unclear about what he was originally christened. What name appears on most surviving documents from his early years?
context: His mother was Catherine McCarty; his stepfather was William Antrim, hence Henry Antrim was also used. As an adult he chose William H. Bonney as his alias, which is the name carved on his original headstone. The Kid was charged in 1881 with the murder of Sheriff William Brady during the Lincoln County War. Pat Garrett's 1882 book The Authentic Life of Billy the Kid established most of the popular myths Americans know today. Sam Peckinpah's 1973 film Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid starred James Coburn as Garrett and Kris Kristofferson as the Kid; Bob Dylan composed the score (including 'Knockin' on Heaven's Door').

question: Linus recites Luke 2 from the Bible in A Charlie Brown Christmas, from 1965, to tell Charlie Brown what Christmas is all about. All through the show he carries his blanket. In the middle of this scene he does one small, quiet thing. What does he do?
answer: He drops his blanket at the line 'Fear not'
choices: He drops his blanket at the line 'Fear not'
He looks up and addresses the camera directly at the end
He raises his arms in a benediction gesture at the closing
He walks across the stage without his blanket the entire time
context: Linus lets go of his blanket at 'Fear not', the angel's first words to the shepherds, and many viewers read it as the message of Christmas taking away his fear. Charles Schulz insisted on keeping the Bible reading, although his producers worried that religion was too touchy for television.

question: Tim Burton wrote three pages in 1982, while working as a Disney animator, and they became The Nightmare Before Christmas. He pitched them as a TV special, a children's book and a half-hour holiday animation; Disney rejected all three. By 1990 he had clout from Beetlejuice and Batman, and Disney green-lit a stop-motion feature. The pages were published in 1993 alongside the film. What form did they take?
answer: It was a Dr. Seuss-style rhyming poem, much shorter and not yet sung
choices: It was a Dr. Seuss-style rhyming poem, much shorter and not yet sung
It was a free-verse epic in the style of Edgar Allan Poe's Annabel Lee
It was a haiku sequence with detailed pen-and-ink illustrations
It was a screenplay treatment in two acts with character bios
context: The original poem opens with Christopher Lee's later film narration — 'Twas a long time ago / Longer now than it seems / In a place that perhaps / You've seen in your dreams' — almost verbatim. The Dr. Seuss influence on Burton's early work was explicit. Henry Selick directed the film while Burton was occupied with Batman Returns (1992) and Ed Wood (1994). Danny Elfman wrote the 10 songs and sang Jack Skellington's singing parts; Chris Sarandon spoke his dialogue. The film's $24M budget produced a $76M box office, considered a disappointment at the time despite later cult-classic status.

question: Captain Planet, the green-haired, blue-skinned hero of the 1990 cartoon, speaks with one man's voice through all 113 episodes, across six seasons and a change of title to The New Adventures of Captain Planet, while stars such as Whoopi Goldberg voiced the spirit Gaia. Who voiced Captain Planet?
context: David Coburn voiced Captain Planet from 1990 to 1996. Whoopi Goldberg voiced Gaia for the first three seasons and Margot Kidder for the last three, and LeVar Burton voiced the Planeteer Kwame.

question: Marshal BraveStarr calls on the spirits of four animals when trouble starts on New Texas, a desert planet with three suns, in Filmation's 1987 space western. Each spirit lends him one power, from sharper eyes to superhuman speed. Which four animals?
context: BraveStarr calls on the Eyes of the Hawk for vision, the Ears of the Wolf for hearing, the Strength of the Bear and the Speed of the Puma. The show is set in the 23rd century on New Texas, a desert planet in a system with three suns.

question: Richard Donner cut a fully shot scene from The Goonies in 1985 and never explained why: deep in the caverns, the kids come face to face with a giant prop octopus. Data still mentions the creature in the finished film. What became of the scene?
answer: It aired in some TV versions and became a DVD bonus feature
choices: It aired in some TV versions and became a DVD bonus feature
Only as a still photo in the official Goonies coffee-table book
It was lost in a 1990s studio archive fire and never restored
It was reshot in 2015 with the original child actors as adults
context: Data's mention of an octopus near the end is all the theatrical cut kept of the deleted scene. Donner never explained the cut; asked about it in 2009, he answered, 'What octopus?' The Disney Channel put the scene back when it aired the film in the 1990s, the 2001 DVD carried it as a bonus feature, and the octopus also turns up in Cyndi Lauper's music video for 'The Goonies 'R' Good Enough'. Spielberg conceived the story and Chris Columbus wrote the screenplay.

question: J. Michael Straczynski wanted no promotion for Slimer, the green-glowing ghost of the 1986 cartoon The Real Ghostbusters. ABC executives demanded it anyway, for the ghost's appeal to younger viewers, and the 1988 season was retitled to reflect that bigger part. What was the show called from 1988 forward?
choices: Slimer and Friends: The Ghostbusters Show
context: J. Michael Straczynski (later the creator of Babylon 5) had been the showrunner of the first two seasons and considered the Slimer mandate creative interference. He quit the show in 1988. The cartoon ran 1986-1991 with 140 episodes. The voice cast included Maurice LaMarche (Egon), Frank Welker (Ray), Lorenzo Music (Peter Venkman), Arsenio Hall (Winston, then Buster Jones).

question: Elmer Bernstein wrote the galloping theme for The Magnificent Seven, the 1960 Western about seven hired gunmen defending a Mexican village, and it became one of the best-known Western themes ever. In the 1960s, a famous ad campaign reused the theme for which American product?
choices: Ford pickup trucks (the 'Built Ford Tough' campaign)
Coca-Cola (the 'Things Go Better with Coke' campaign)
Chevrolet (the 'See the USA in Your Chevrolet' campaign)
context: Marlboro's cowboy advertising took up The Magnificent Seven theme in the 1960s, from late 1963 by one account, and it became the sound of Marlboro Country. Bernstein's other Western scores include True Grit (1969). His score for The Magnificent Seven was nominated for an Oscar, and he won his only Oscar for Thoroughly Modern Millie (1967). The cast, Yul Brynner, Steve McQueen, Charles Bronson, Robert Vaughn, James Coburn, Brad Dexter and Horst Buchholz, was an unusually deep bench of star talent. Eli Wallach played the villain Calvera.

question: Bob Clark commissioned the leg lamp for A Christmas Story from a small Cleveland prop shop, a custom prop for the 1983 film that was not based on any real product. The original lamp, the Old Man's Major Award, went to auction in 2014. What did it sell for, and to whom?
choices: About $42,000 — to the Cleveland History Center
Just under $15,000 — to actor Peter Billingsley
context: The auction price for the original leg lamp was around $100,000 (specifically $109,995 at the 2014 Profiles in History auction). Several distinct prop versions of the lamp survive — the main filming prop, the smashed-and-glued version, and various stunt doubles. Replica leg lamps sell every Christmas season, making the lamp one of the most successful film-prop merchandise items in history. The 'fra-GEE-lay, must be Italian' line — delivered by Darren McGavin as the Old Man — also became a permanent piece of holiday-comedy quotation.

question: Disney's 1994 cartoon Gargoyles writes a real 11th-century Scottish ruler into its story, a man Shakespeare put on the stage. The show draws on real Scottish history for him. What was his actual 17-year rule widely thought to be like?
answer: Generally peaceful and prosperous, a reformist king beloved by his people
choices: Generally peaceful and prosperous, a reformist king beloved by his people
Constantly besieged by Norse raiders and dragon-incursions from the Hebrides
An era of harsh repression of Picts and Catholic clergy alike under his rule
A period of civil war between MacAlpin and Pictish royal claimants
context: The real King Macbeth (Mac Bethad mac Findlaích, reigned 1040-1057) was a Mormaer of Moray who defeated Duncan I in fair battle, not by midnight assassination. He went on pilgrimage to Rome in 1050 and showered the poor with money. He was killed in 1057 by Duncan's son Malcolm Canmore. Shakespeare's 1606 play (based on Holinshed's Chronicles) deliberately distorted him for political reasons — James I of England, Shakespeare's patron, descended from Banquo. Gargoyles creator Greg Weisman was a history major and integrated all this into the show.

question: John Ford opened his 1956 film about Ethan Edwards on a dark room framed by a doorway, with John Wayne riding in from Monument Valley and getting off his horse at the cabin. The last shot mirrors it from the same doorway. Fans call it one of the best shots ever. Who filmed Ford's famous look?
answer: Winton C. Hoch, Ford's longtime cinematographer
choices: Winton C. Hoch, Ford's longtime cinematographer
Gregg Toland, the genius behind Citizen Kane
James Wong Howe, two-time Oscar-winning innovator
Russell Metty, of Touch of Evil fame
context: Hoch won three cinematography Oscars, two of them for Ford films, She Wore a Yellow Ribbon (1949) and The Quiet Man (1952). His VistaVision Technicolor photography for The Searchers showcased Ford's beloved Monument Valley on the Arizona-Utah border, where Ford had filmed since 1939's Stagecoach. The doorway shot has been homaged in many later films.

question: Mother Brain, lifted from the 1986 NES game Metroid, turns chatty, bombastic and vain as the chief villain of the 1989 cartoon Captain N: The Game Master. The singer who voiced her had already voiced a famous carnivorous plant in a 1986 horror musical. Who was that singer?
answer: Levi Stubbs of the Four Tops
choices: Levi Stubbs of the Four Tops
Pat Carroll before her Ursula casting
Estelle Getty between Golden Girls episodes
context: Levi Stubbs, lead singer of the Motown group the Four Tops, voiced Mother Brain. He had already been the voice of Audrey II, the singing man-eating plant of the 1986 film Little Shop of Horrors.

question: Doc Holliday glanced down at his bare feet on the morning he died, November 8, 1887. The gambler and gunfighter had always expected to die in a gunfight, and here was tuberculosis finishing him in bed. His reaction became part of Western lore. What did he reportedly say?
choices: That he wanted his boots on
That Wyatt should be sent for
context: By the usual account, Holliday's nurse gave him a glass of whiskey; he looked at his bare feet and said 'This is funny,' meaning he had never expected to die in bed with his boots off. His friend Wyatt Earp outlived him by more than forty years, dying in Los Angeles in 1929.

question: Stuart Lake spread the tale in a 1931 book: Wyatt Earp carried a custom gun with a 12-inch barrel, the Buntline Special, given to him by the dime-novel writer Ned Buntline. What do today's historians say about it?
answer: Almost certainly a pure invention by Lake, with no contemporary record to support it
choices: Almost certainly a pure invention by Lake, with no contemporary record to support it
Confirmed by Earp's surviving personal letters at Harvard Houghton Library
Documented in an 1881 newspaper article during the Tombstone period
Verified by the actual revolver displayed at the Earp family museum
context: Stuart Lake's 1931 biography Wyatt Earp: Frontier Marshal was the source of many famous Earp myths, the Buntline Special among them. Wyatt Earp himself had talked with Lake before his 1929 death and likely embellished his own stories. Hugh O'Brian's 1955 TV show The Life and Legend of Wyatt Earp cemented the mythology in popular culture.

question: Bars and pizza parlors set a coin-operated cabinet in the corner in 1972, and players lined up to feed it quarters. It showed two white paddles and a small square ball bouncing between them like tennis. What was this first commercial video-game hit called?
context: Designed by Allan Alcorn under Atari co-founders Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney. The first prototype was installed at Andy Capp's Tavern in Sunnyvale CA in 1972 and broke down from too many coins jammed in the slot.

question: Pac-Man chomps little pellets inside a blue maze in Namco's 1980 arcade game, running from colored ghosts. He is a small round hero, a pizza shape with a wedge cut out for his mouth, all one bright glowing color. What color is Pac-Man?
context: Pac-Man's round shape came from designer Toru Iwatani looking at a pizza with one slice missing. The four ghosts are Blinky (red), Pinky (pink), Inky (cyan), and Clyde (orange).

question: A giant ape climbs a construction site with a woman over his shoulder in Nintendo's 1981 arcade game Donkey Kong. A mustached carpenter named Jumpman runs up girders and ladders, dodging rolling barrels, to rescue her, his kidnapped girlfriend. What is her name?
context: Designer Shigeru Miyamoto picked 'Donkey' to mean stubborn in English; the title literally means 'Stubborn Ape.' The hero, originally called Jumpman, was renamed Mario in 1982.

question: Sonic the Hedgehog dashes through zones, collects gold rings and races to stop the mustachioed villain Dr Robotnik from turning forest animals into robots, in the 1991 game Sega made to challenge Nintendo's Mario. What color is Sonic's spiky fur?
context: Designer Naoto Ohshima chose blue to match Sega's logo. The shoes were inspired by Michael Jackson's Bad-album cover and Santa Claus boots.

question: A short, mustachioed plumber in blue overalls and a red cap with the letter M hops on mushroom-shaped Goombas and rescues Princess Peach from a dragon-turtle king, in the game that launched the NES in North America in 1985. What is his name?
context: Super Mario Bros launched the modern console era in North America after the 1983 crash. Miyamoto picked the overalls and cap so animators could distinguish Mario's arms and hair on the limited NES sprite.

question: An elf-eared boy in a bright green tunic and a floppy green cap wields the shining Master Sword against the evil pig-monster Ganon to rescue a princess, in a Nintendo fantasy series that began on the NES in 1986. What is the hero's name?
context: Designer Shigeru Miyamoto named him Link because he is the link between worlds. Zelda — the princess — was named after F. Scott Fitzgerald's wife Zelda Fitzgerald.

question: A lone bounty hunter in a bulky orange power suit lands on the dangerous alien planet Zebes to hunt space pirates in Metroid, Nintendo's 1986 NES game. What is the hunter's name?
context: Players who beat the original Metroid in under five hours saw the iconic reveal that Samus was a woman underneath the suit — one of the first major female protagonists in console gaming.

question: A plump yellow electric mouse rides on Ash Ketchum's shoulder in the Pokemon anime, with red cheeks and a lightning-bolt tail. He is the mascot of a franchise that began in Japan in 1996 with Red and Green for the Game Boy. What is his name?
context: Pokemon Red and Green launched in Japan in 1996, and Red and Blue reached the United States in September 1998. In the anime Pikachu is Ash's partner from the very first episode.

question: A Soviet computer scientist wrote a simple puzzle game in 1984: seven falling block shapes, spun and stacked into rows that vanished. Nintendo bundled it with a handheld in 1989, and people played it on planes, in class and under blankets. What is the game called?
context: Alexey Pajitnov created it at the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. Nintendo bundled it with every Game Boy at the 1989 US launch.

question: A California company released a wood-grain-front home console in 1977 that let American families play arcade-style games on their living-room TV. It came with a black joystick with one red button, and cartridges held games like Combat, Space Invaders and Pitfall. Which company made it?
context: The Atari 2600 sold over 30 million units and was the dominant US console until the 1983 crash. Its game library included Combat, Pac-Man, E.T., and Pitfall!.

question: One designer released a small grey handheld console in 1989, with a green-tinted screen, a directional D-pad and paired A and B buttons. It ran for hours on four AA batteries and came with a falling-blocks puzzle right in the box. What was it called?
context: Gunpei Yokoi, who also produced Metroid, designed it. The Game Boy's monochrome screen and thrifty AA batteries outlasted the technically superior Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear.

question: A player loads a Compact Disc into a sleek gray console from a Japanese electronics giant, brand-new to video games in 1994. Its controller has four shape buttons on the right side, triangle, circle, square and X, instead of the A and B letter buttons Nintendo used. What is the system called?
context: The PlayStation began life as a Nintendo-Sony CD-add-on for the SNES; when Nintendo backed out in 1991, Sony took the hardware solo. The PS1 sold over 100 million units.

question: Microsoft, mostly known for the Windows computer operating system, shipped its very first video-game console in 2001. It was a chunky black machine with a bold green logo on top, and it launched with a shooter from a studio called Bungie. What was the console called?
context: The Xbox was nicknamed the Direct X-box for its underlying graphics API. Halo: Combat Evolved was the killer app — Bungie's first-person shooter that defined console FPS controls.

question: Midway of Chicago filmed real actors in 1992 and digitized them into the fighters of a bloody arcade game. Its brutal finishing moves made it famous: with a foe knocked senseless at the end of the round, the winner had a moment to end the fight. What was the finishing move called?
context: Mortal Kombat's Fatalities triggered the US Senate hearings that led to the ESRB rating system in 1994. The Genesis port preserved the blood with the ABACABB code; the SNES port stripped it out.

question: Ryu, a Japanese karate master in a white gi and red headband, cups both hands at his hip in Capcom's 1991 arcade fighter Street Fighter II. He shoves them forward and launches a bright blue ball of pure energy at his opponent. What is this signature fireball move called?
context: Performed by quarter-circle forward + punch. Hadoken means 'surging-wave fist.' Ryu's rival Ken (red gi, blond) shares the move. Both characters' costumes were designed by Akira Yasuda.

question: Hironobu Sakaguchi feared in 1987 that Square, the company he worked for, was going broke. As he later told it, he bet everything on one last NES game and meant to quit if it flopped. It saved the company instead. What is the series called?
context: Sakaguchi said the name reflected his mood: had the game failed, he would have left Square and gone back to finish his studies at Yokohama National University. It sold 400,000 copies in Japan. The title began as Fighting Fantasy, a name already taken by a series of gamebooks.

question: The evil pig-monster Ganon menaces Princess Zelda in the Nintendo series named for her, which began on the NES in 1986, and an elf-eared boy crosses her green fantasy kingdom to stop him. What is the kingdom called?
context: Hyrule's geography shifts between games. The Triforce — three golden triangles representing Power, Wisdom, and Courage — is the source of magic in Hyrule. Ganon seeks Power, Zelda holds Wisdom, Link bears Courage.

question: A spinning orange creature in jeans and giant sneakers dashes through tropical islands smashing wooden crates and battling the mad scientist Dr Neo Cortex, in a 1996 game from the small California studio Naughty Dog. Sony needs a mascot to fight Nintendo's Mario and Sega's Sonic, and he gets the job. What is he called?
context: Created by Naughty Dog's Jason Rubin and Andy Gavin. Sony used him as the unofficial mascot to challenge Mario and Sonic during the 32-bit era. He never spoke a real language — just yelled 'WOAH!'.

question: A wealthy British archaeologist explores ancient tombs armed with twin pistols in Tomb Raider, the 1996 adventure from the British studio Core Design and its publisher Eidos. She wears a long brown braid and short khaki shorts, and her body is famously blocky because 1996 polygon graphics were angular. What is her name?
context: Designed by Toby Gard at Core Design in Derby, England. Angelina Jolie played her in the 2001 film.

question: Four friends hunt each other through split-screen levels from the James Bond film GoldenEye in Rare's 1997 N64 shooter. The most-hated character pick is the short, bowler-hatted henchman from the earlier Bond film Goldfinger, because his tiny hitbox makes him almost impossible to shoot. Who is he?
context: Oddjob's shorter stature meant bullets often passed over his head — friends made house rules banning him. The split-screen four-player mode was added late in development and became the killer feature.

question: Cortana, a holographic AI, rides inside a hulking human super-soldier's helmet and guides him across a giant ring-shaped world in Halo: Combat Evolved, the first-person shooter Bungie made for the 2001 launch of Microsoft's brand-new console. He wears polished green metal armor and fights alien invaders called the Covenant. What is the hero called?
context: Master Chief's full designation is Spartan-117 — but he's only called by it once in the original game. His face is never shown in the trilogy. Voice actor Steve Downes recorded his lines while standing because he felt it sounded more authoritative.

question: Nintendo's 1986 game Metroid sent a lone bounty hunter in a bright orange power suit through the winding caves of the alien planet Zebes, after a space pirate boss. A player who finished fast enough learned a huge secret about the hunter under the helmet. What was the secret?
context: Satoru Okada and Masao Yamamoto directed Metroid for producer Gunpei Yokoi. The game has five endings, chosen by finishing time, and the three fastest show Samus without her suit, revealed as a woman.

question: A beaten fighter stands staggering with almost no health left in Midway's bloody 1992 arcade game Mortal Kombat. The deep-voiced announcer yells two famous words. What does the announcer yell?
context: The 'FINISH HIM!' prompt gave the player about five seconds to input the Fatality button-sequence specific to each character. Scorpion's Fatality — ripping off his mask and breathing fire — was the most replicated on schoolyards.

question: A Mortal Kombat fan punches in the uncensored blood code, which the Nintendo rival banned, on Sega's sleek black 16-bit home console, a machine that reached North America in 1989. In Japan and Europe the same console is the Mega Drive. What is it called in North America?
context: Known as the Mega Drive in Japan and Europe. Sega's 'Genesis does what Nintendon't' campaign was a generation-defining piece of console-war marketing. The system was discontinued in 1997.

question: Nintendo saved the American video-game business with a grey console in 1985, after the 1983 crash had gutted Atari. The machine came bundled with a plastic light gun called the Zapper, and its logo carried three big letters: NES. What do those letters stand for?
context: Nintendo designed the front-loading cartridge slot to look like a VCR so retailers — burned by the 1983 crash — would shelve it next to home video instead of in the toy aisle.

question: Namco's 1980 arcade game Pac-Man sends its round hero through a blue maze to eat every pellet on the screen. Ghosts with different personalities hunt him: some chase directly, some cut him off, some wander. In the classic game, how many ghosts chase him?
context: Blinky (red, direct chase), Pinky (pink, ambush ahead of Pac-Man), Inky (cyan, uses Blinky's position in a complex calc), and Clyde (orange, wanders randomly). Each ghost's personality was deliberate.

question: A huge spike-shelled turtle-dragon king breathes fire, roars and leads an army of little turtle Koopas through Nintendo's pipe-lined Mushroom Kingdom. In most of the games a mustached plumber has to rescue the kingdom's kind, pink-dressed Princess Peach from him. What is the king's name?
context: Known in Japan as Koopa. The princess he kidnaps was named Princess Toadstool in the US until Super Mario 64 (1996) renamed her Peach. The Bowser-Peach kidnapping plot is the franchise's running joke.

question: Don Bluth, a former Disney animator, drew a 1983 arcade game by hand, and the machine played his cartoon back off a laserdisc. A player flicked the joystick or hit the sword button in time to steer a bumbling knight, Dirk the Daring, past spike traps and collapsing floors. What was the game called?
context: Animated by the former Disney animator Don Bluth (The Secret of NIMH, An American Tail), the game played its cartoon back off a laserdisc, one of the first arcade games to do so.

question: A family slides a film on a digital video disc (DVD) into a new black Japanese game console in 2000, and the machine doubles as its first DVD player. It will sell over 155 million units, the best-selling home console ever. What is it called?
context: The PS2's DVD playback was a major selling point — DVD players still cost $300+ in 2000 and the PS2 played them at $299 plus games. Launch lineup included SSX, Tekken Tag, and Madden 2001.

question: Capcom's 1991 arcade hit Street Fighter II gives the fighting genre its first playable woman, an Interpol detective among eight world warriors. She wears a blue cheongsam dress with white boots, spiked bracelets and ox-horn hair buns, and her signature move is a rapid-fire kick. Who is she?
context: Designer Akira Yasuda based her costume on Chinese opera. Her signature move is the Hyakuretsukyaku — Hundred Rending Legs — a rapid kick performed by mashing the kick button. Her flip kick (Spinning Bird Kick) is iconic.

question: Heihachi, cruel head of the wealthy Mishima clan, feuds with his son Kazuya in Namco's 1994 3D arcade fighter, from the studio behind Pac-Man. Kazuya's own son Jin joins the family war in a later game. What is the series called?
context: Tekken means 'iron fist' in Japanese. Sega's Virtua Fighter (1993) beat it to the 3D fighter market, but Tekken's PlayStation port made the home transition smoother. Jin Kazama joined in Tekken 3 (1997), and the Mishima family feud has been the series' through-line since the original.

question: Seth Gordon's 2007 documentary follows Steve Wiebe, a mild-mannered Washington schoolteacher, as he goes after the Donkey Kong world record held by the hot-sauce tycoon Billy Mitchell. What is the film called?
context: Full title: The King of Kong: A Fistful of Quarters. The film became a cult hit and made household names of obscure arcade-scene figures Walter Day (Twin Galaxies founder), Billy Mitchell (the restaurant owner), and Steve Wiebe (the teacher).

question: Grandparents and kids swung a slim wand through the air when Nintendo released a small white console in 2006, hitting tennis balls, bowling strikes and throwing punches. A bar on top of the TV helped the wand find the screen. What is the system called?
context: Nintendo intentionally chose 'Wii' — pronounced 'we' — to signal a console for everyone, not just gamers. The blue-ocean strategy worked: Wii sold 101 million units, outselling the technologically superior 360 and PS3.

question: A Konami developer dreamed up a famous cheat code in the 1980s: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A. It became famous in North America on one NES run-and-gun shooter, where typing it in at the title screen gave the player thirty lives. Which game was it?
context: Kazuhisa Hashimoto created the code for the 1986 NES Gradius because he found his own game too hard. In Contra it gave thirty lives, and it went on to turn up in dozens of other games.

question: Mario runs into Princess Peach's castle in Super Mario 64, his first game in full 3D, and finds that a dragon-turtle king has captured her. Magic paintings carry him into hidden worlds to hunt 120 Power Stars. A player who finds every one can climb onto the castle roof. Who waits up there?
context: Only 70 Stars are needed to face Bowser in the final battle, but a player with all 120 can fire a cannon up to the castle roof, where Yoshi waits with 100 extra lives. Super Mario 64 launched the N64 in June 1996.

question: A Namco designer lifted a slice out of a pizza one lunchtime, by his own later account, and looked at the wedge missing from the pie. That, he said, gave him the round shape of Pac-Man, the hero of the company's 1980 arcade game. Who was the Namco designer?
context: Iwatani also designed the ghost AI: Blinky chases directly, Pinky tries to ambush, Inky uses a complex calc involving Blinky's position, and Clyde wanders randomly. Pac-Man became the first widely-licensed video-game character.

question: Nintendo's 1981 arcade game Donkey Kong called its jumping hero Jumpman and sent him up steel girders to rescue a woman from a big angry ape. By the time the sequel Donkey Kong Jr. arrived in 1982, he had the proper name Nintendo still uses for him today. What was he renamed?
context: Mario was named after Mario Segale, Nintendo of America's warehouse landlord in Tukwila WA, who reportedly stormed into a staff meeting demanding overdue rent. Miyamoto designed Mario's red hat and mustache to work around NES sprite limitations.

question: A co-founder of a young California game company oversaw the first commercial video-game success in 1972, the arcade hit that launched the whole industry. A few years later he started a family pizza-and-arcade restaurant chain built around an animatronic mouse mascot called Chuck E. Cheese. Who was he?
context: Bushnell tasked engineer Allan Alcorn with building Pong as a training exercise. Alcorn made it too good and it became Atari's first hit. Bushnell sold Atari to Warner in 1976 for $28M and later founded Chuck E. Cheese as a way to put arcade machines in front of kids.

question: Tomohiro Nishikado released a shooting game called Space Invaders in 1978. Row after row of aliens marched down the screen while the player fired a laser cannon to blast them. In arcades across Japan, kids and grown-ups lined up to play. What did people say the whole country ran out of?
context: Designer Tomohiro Nishikado. The story of the 100-yen shortage is partly folklore — coin production did rise in 1978 — but Space Invaders genuinely earned over $2 billion by 1982, making it one of the highest-grossing entertainment products in history.

question: One of the few women working on arcade games co-designed Centipede in 1981, a rare programmer who wanted a game her friends would enjoy playing. A rolling trackball steers a bug-shooter through a field of mushrooms, blasting a wiggling centipede that splits into smaller pieces every time it is hit. What was her name?
context: Bailey came to Atari from General Motors, where she had written 6502 assembly for embedded car systems. She designed Centipede with Ed Logg, intending the bright pastel colors and arcing screen movement to appeal to a broader audience than the prevailing shoot-em-up boys.

question: A designer at the American arcade company Williams built Defender in 1981, sending the player's ship sideways across an alien planet to rescue tiny humans, with a control panel famous for being hard. He went on to make another classic in 1982, a shooter with two joysticks. Who was he?
context: Jarvis designed Defender to be intentionally hard — the player flies a spacecraft over a horizontal landscape, rescuing humanoids from alien abductors while juggling thrust, fire, and smart bombs. Robotron 2084 (1982) was the dual-stick blueprint that Geometry Wars later popularized.

question: A bouncing smiley face named Evil Otto comes after any player who dawdles in Stern Electronics' 1980 maze-shooter, and he cannot be killed. The player runs through glowing rooms blasting boxy robots while a scratchy synthesized voice, one of the first in arcades, barks 'Got the humanoid! Got the intruder!' What was the game called?
context: Designed by Alan McNeil. Berzerk's electronic-voice chip set the player against robots Otto and lookalikes. In 1981, a 19-year-old player at a Calumet City IL arcade died of a heart attack after posting a high score — leading to a parental-panic episode and the 'Berzerk killed a man' urban legend.

question: A 1979 black-and-white arcade game drawn in glowing line vectors puts a small wedge-shaped ship among drifting boulders. Its pilot rotates to aim and fires, and each boulder, when hit, breaks into smaller ones. Little flying saucers pop in from the edges to shoot back. What is the game called?
context: Designed by Ed Logg and Lyle Rains. Players quickly discovered the 'lurking' exploit: clearing all but one small asteroid, then hiding while waiting for UFOs to shoot for high points. Atari later patched it by ramping UFO frequency.

question: Shigeru Miyamoto, Nintendo's young designer, wanted his first big arcade game in 1981 to star a licensed American comic-strip trio: a hero, his tall girlfriend and a huge bully. The licensing deal fell through, so he invented his own cast: a carpenter, the carpenter's girlfriend and a giant ape. Which comic strip had he wanted?
context: The Popeye license eventually came through and Nintendo released a Popeye arcade in 1982 — but by then DK was already an enormous hit. Designer Miyamoto's first game was DK; he was 28 years old.

question: Konami's 1981 arcade game sends a little frog hopping from the bottom of the screen to the top. It crosses a busy highway of cars and trucks, then a river, no swimming allowed, leaping between drifting logs and diving turtles to reach a lily pad. What is the game called?
context: Frogger was distributed in the US by Sega/Gremlin. Its eight-direction joystick (no diagonals) and one-life-at-a-time-on-a-lily-pad design influenced decades of crossing-style games. A Seinfeld 1998 episode 'The Frogger' was built around George trying to move an arcade cabinet across a street.

question: Q*bert, a little orange creature with a long tubular nose, hops from cube to cube across a pyramid in Gottlieb's 1982 arcade game, changing each cube's color as he lands. When he loses a life to a snake or a falling bad guy, a speech bubble pops up above his head. What does it show?
choices: A sad face with rolling tears
A red exclamation point in a triangle
context: Designed by Warren Davis and Jeff Lee. The @!#?@! grawlix cloud became a Q*bert signature. Lee also created the iconic sound chip noise Q*bert makes — generated by a coil-spring impact sensor mounted in the cabinet.

question: Namco's 1981 arcade shooter Galaga sends bug-like aliens swooping down the screen, and a boss ship can grab the player's fighter with a tractor beam. A rescued fighter doubles the firepower. Galaga was the sequel to an older Namco game from 1979 that started the swooping-formation style. What was that older game called?
context: Galaxian (1979) introduced the dive-bombing enemy pattern. Galaga added the dual-fighter recovery — letting the captured ship fly alongside the rescued one for double firepower. Galaga famously cameos in Joss Whedon's 2012 Avengers when a SHIELD employee on the helicarrier is caught playing it.

question: Two players take to a fantasy sky above lava pits in Williams Electronics' 1982 brawler, one on a white ostrich, the other on a blue-gray stork. Each mashes a flap button to gain altitude and tries to be the higher when they collide. What is the game called?
context: Designed by John Newcomer. Co-op two-player Joust was the killer two-player arcade experience of the era. Newcomer chose ostriches because the design needed an animal that visually communicated mid-air flapping while still looking heroic.

question: A little man in a white space suit tunnels through colored dirt in Namco's 1982 arcade game, chased by round red Pookas and fire-breathing green Fygars. His only weapon is a pump: he jams it into a monster and pumps until the creature bloats up and pops like a balloon. What is the game called?
context: Designed by Masahisa Ikegami. The protagonist's real name was Taizo Hori — a Japanese pun on 'horitai zo' meaning 'I want to dig.' Dig Dug's hero went on to become the father of Mr. Driller (1999), a Namco mid-sized franchise of its own.

question: Williams Electronics' brutal 1982 shooter hands its lone hero two joysticks instead of a stick and a fire button: the left stick moves him, the right aims and fires in eight directions. Endless waves of chunky enemies pour in to kill him and the last human family. What is the game called?
context: Jarvis designed Robotron's twin-stick controls after breaking his hand in a car accident — the simpler-than-keyboard scheme was easier for his recovering hand. The control scheme later defined Smash TV (1990), Geometry Wars (2003), and countless indie shooters.

question: The red ghost in Namco's 1980 arcade game Pac-Man heads straight for the hero along the shortest path in the maze grid, closing the distance every frame. Each ghost has its own color and its own personality coded into its behavior, and the red one's is the most aggressive. What is the red ghost's name?
context: Iwatani designed each ghost with a distinct AI: Blinky (red) — direct chase; Pinky (pink) — ambush ahead of Pac-Man's facing direction; Inky (cyan) — flanks using a vector from Blinky; Clyde (orange) — wanders randomly when close to Pac-Man. The personalities have been preserved across every port.

question: A Sega designer sat the player in a red Ferrari convertible with a blonde girl in the passenger seat for the 1986 arcade racer OutRun. The player chose a radio station and drove across European countryside, and at each checkpoint the road forked. The same designer later made Virtua Fighter and Shenmue. Who was he?
context: Suzuki had also designed Hang-On (1985) and would later design After Burner (1987), Virtua Fighter (1993), Shenmue (1999), and the Virtua series. OutRun's three songs — Magical Sound Shower, Splash Wave, and Passing Breeze — by Hiroshi Kawaguchi defined arcade-driving music.

question: Nintendo dropped the blood from its home version of Midway's bloody arcade fighter Mortal Kombat in 1993, but Sega kept it on the Genesis, hidden behind a secret code of button presses. What was the code?
context: The Genesis ABACABB code is a tribute to Genesis (the band) and their 1981 album of the same name. The SNES port lacked blood entirely until Mortal Kombat II (1994). The Genesis port outsold the SNES version, partly because of the code.

question: Nintendo took its NES across all of America in 1986 in a basic set with one game bundled in the box. That pack-in cartridge showed families exactly what the machine could do: smooth side-scrolling levels, catchy chiptune music and secret pipes that warped between worlds. What was the game?
context: The 1985 test launch in New York came as a Deluxe Set with the robot R.O.B., the Zapper, Gyromite and Duck Hunt; the cheaper 1986 set came with Super Mario Bros. Miyamoto designed it with Takashi Tezuka.

question: The plumber hero of Nintendo's 1985 NES game runs along the top of the pipes and out over the ceiling of World 1-2, the underground level, if he times his jumps right. Three green warp pipes wait there, each firing him to a much later world. Which three worlds do they lead to?
context: The other Warp Zone is in World 4-2 and leads to Worlds 5, 6 and 7. The Minus World is reached by a carefully timed crouching jump through the wall beside the exit pipe, instead of entering the Warp Zone normally.

question: A lead programmer at Sega had one goal for his 1991 game: make Sonic the Hedgehog run faster than any video-game hero before him. He wrote the physics code that let Sonic curl into a ball, blast through loop-de-loops, roll down hills and rocket back up the other side. Who was the programmer?
context: Designer Naoto Ohshima created Sonic's visual look; programmer Yuji Naka built the rolling-physics engine that made Sonic feel uniquely fast. Sega Technical Institute team (later including Mark Cerny, future PlayStation architect) produced Sonic 2 in 1992.

question: Shigeru Miyamoto's 1986 adventure came out in Japan on a Famicom floppy disk, and in America in 1987 it became one of the first console games with a save battery in the cartridge. Its green-tunic elf-boy hero roams a top-down overworld and clears nine hidden dungeons. What was the game?
context: Miyamoto credited his childhood exploration of caves and forests near Sonobe, Kyoto, as the inspiration. The gold-colored cartridge of the US release was a Nintendo of America marketing decision to make the box stand out on shelves.

question: Shigeru Miyamoto produced a Zelda game for the N64 in 1998, with Eiji Aonuma among its five directors, and reviewers at the time called it the best video game ever made. Its boy hero pulled a legendary sword from a stone pedestal to fight the dark king Ganondorf. Which game was it?
context: Ocarina of Time's Z-targeting, named for the N64's Z trigger, set the pattern for 3D combat cameras. Eiji Aonuma designed its dungeons, among them the Water Temple, which became the series' most cursed dungeon for its constant swapping of the iron boots.

question: Squaresoft could not fit Final Fantasy VII on one game disc when it took the huge role-playing game to Sony's new console in 1997. It had too many pre-rendered movie scenes and 3D battles, and players used to Nintendo cartridges holding a whole game on one chip were stunned. How many discs came in the box?
context: FF7's full data — pre-rendered backgrounds, FMV cutscenes, voice-light audio — wouldn't fit on a 64MB Nintendo 64 cartridge, which is why Square moved to Sony's PlayStation. The move broke the Nintendo-Square partnership and made FF a PlayStation flagship for two decades.

question: Hironobu Sakaguchi and Yuji Horii, two giants of the role-playing game, wrote Chrono Trigger, Squaresoft's 1995 SNES game about a boy who accidentally opens a time portal at a medieval fair. For the character art they hired a manga star famous for drawing Dragon Ball. Who was he?
context: Chrono Trigger's Dream Team was Hironobu Sakaguchi (Final Fantasy), Yuji Horii (Dragon Quest) and Toriyama (Dragon Ball), with director Takashi Tokita and music by Yasunori Mitsuda, his breakthrough work; Mitsuda fell ill with stomach ulcers during the score.

question: A GoldenEye 007 player in a dorm room sneaks an explosive onto a wall of the map and waits. In the legendary four-player split-screen mode of Rare's 1997 N64 shooter, the weapon goes off when any enemy wanders by. What is it called?
context: Designed by Martin Hollis's team at Rare, GoldenEye's multiplayer was added late in development as an experiment. The proximity-mine-only mode — players laying mines and waiting — was a Friday-night campus staple from 1997 through 2001.

question: An elite police officer creeps through Spencer Mansion, a spooky estate full of shuffling zombies, giant snakes and a room-sized carnivorous plant with a long whipping tongue, in Capcom's 1996 horror game Resident Evil. The Capcom director behind the game invented a new genre and called it 'survival horror.' Who was he?
context: Mikami also directed Resident Evil 4 (2005), which fundamentally redefined third-person shooter cinematography with its over-the-shoulder camera. The original RE was famous for its prerendered backgrounds, fixed camera angles, and infamously stilted voice-acting ('Jill sandwich').

question: Solid Snake sneaks into a snowy nuclear base in Alaska to stop a giant walking tank called Metal Gear in Konami's 1998 game Metal Gear Solid. Full voice acting, cinematic camera cuts and an orchestral soundtrack make it play more like a Hollywood movie than a video game. Who directed it?
context: Kojima had directed Metal Gear (1987) and Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake (1990) for the MSX2 home computer in Japan. MGS1's Psycho Mantis boss famously required the player to physically unplug the controller and re-plug it into Port 2 to defeat his mind-reading.

question: The founder of the studio Game Freak designed Pokemon Red and Green, which came out in Japan in 1996. As a boy in Tokyo he loved catching beetles and dragonflies in the creeks near his home, and he built Pokemon so kids could feel that same hunt through their Game Boy. Who was he?
context: Tajiri pitched the idea to Nintendo around 1990, and it took six years to ship. Ken Sugimori drew the original creatures, and Junichi Masuda composed the music.

question: Kids traded the first English Pokemon cards at recess in 1999, when booster packs cost about three dollars. Wizards of the Coast had printed this Base Set, and one holographic rare became the most-wanted card of all: collectors have paid tens of thousands of dollars for a mint copy. Which Pokemon is on it?
context: The Base Set Charizard holo sells for thousands of dollars, and far more in its Shadowless or 1st Edition printings. The first run had no thin shadow beside the art; later runs added one. A top-graded 1st Edition Shadowless Charizard has sold for over $400,000.

question: A young programmer at the Soviet Academy of Sciences built a falling-block puzzle on a boxy Elektronika 60 computer in 1984 and named it from the Greek word for four. Because he made it on a state computer, the Soviet government owned the rights for years, and he saw no royalties from the game's billions until the rights came back to him in 1996. What was his name?
context: Pajitnov developed it on an Elektronika 60 — a Soviet-built PDP-11 clone. The game escaped Soviet borders through ELORG (Electronorgtechnica), which licensed it via a labyrinth of disputes resolved by Henk Rogers and Nintendo in 1989, bundling it with the Game Boy. Pajitnov emigrated to the US in 1991 and worked for Microsoft and others before co-founding The Tetris Company with Henk Rogers in 1996. The 2023 Apple TV+ film 'Tetris' dramatizes Rogers' Moscow trip to wrest the rights from Robert Maxwell and Soviet apparatchiks.

question: Atari reportedly sent dump trucks to a New Mexico landfill with millions of unsold cartridges of its E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial game and buried them under concrete. The tale passed for an urban legend until diggers really did find the buried games, decades later. In what New Mexico city was the landfill?
context: The story was treated as urban legend until April 26, 2014, when a documentary team led by Zak Penn (writer of Ready Player One) excavated the Alamogordo city landfill and confirmed it — finding thousands of Atari cartridges, console parts, and crushed Atari paperwork.

question: Sega fans lined up outside stores overnight in 1999, holding empty controllers, for the company's very last home video-game console in America. Sega had picked a release date built to be unforgettable, and ads across the country counted down to it while the marketing slogan told everyone the date over and over. What was the Dreamcast's launch date?
context: Sega's 9/9/99 marketing campaign was a huge launch hit — the Dreamcast set first-day-sales records. It launched with NFL 2K, Sonic Adventure, and Soulcalibur. Sega discontinued the console in March 2001 after PS2 dominance crushed it.

question: Nintendo's signature composer of the 1980s wrote the bouncy underground theme of its 1985 plumber game and the heroic overworld theme of its 1986 elf-boy quest, two of the most famous tunes in games. He stayed with Nintendo for over forty years. Who was he?
context: Kondo joined Nintendo in 1984 as the company's first dedicated music composer. The SMB overworld theme is the most-recognized piece of video-game music ever written. Kondo also scored Star Fox 64, Super Mario 64, and most Zelda main themes.

question: Billy Mitchell, a Florida teenager whose family ran a restaurant, came to an Iowa arcade in November 1982, when Life magazine gathered top players there for a photo shoot. At the Donkey Kong cabinet he set a world-record score that stood for years and made him an arcade celebrity. What was his score?
context: Mitchell set 874,300 during the Life photo shoot, beating Steve Sanders, who had claimed 1.4 million and later admitted lying about his earlier scores. Twin Galaxies struck Mitchell's later million-point scores, among them a taped 1,047,200 from the mid-2000s, in 2018, ruling that the tapes could not have come from original arcade hardware; Guinness World Records restored his records in 2020.

question: Namco's Pac-Man sends its hero into a wrecked maze on the so-called 'kill screen'. At the level where the bonus-fruit table overflows, the right half turns into a garbled mess of letters, numbers and tile-bits that stops the hero from finishing the dot field. What level is the kill screen?
context: 256 is the 8-bit unsigned integer overflow — the level counter wraps around. Billy Mitchell achieved the first publicly verified perfect Pac-Man game in 1999 — every dot, every fruit, every ghost, on every level through 255, ending with a planned death on 256. Score: 3,333,360.

question: High-score chasers on Nintendo's 1981 Donkey Kong hit a strange bug: the bonus timer started far too low. The carpenter hero could barely climb a single rivet before the timer expired and killed him, so the chasers named the spot the 'kill screen'. What level is it?
context: DK has 117 distinct screens cycling across stages and levels — the kill screen is on the 117th screen, technically the first screen of level 22. The bonus timer is calculated as 0x10 * (level + 1) but with a sign-bit bug at level 22 yielding effectively 0 seconds.

question: Boston students at General Computer Corporation built an unauthorized hack of Pac-Man, and Midway licensed and rebadged it as Ms. Pac-Man, released in 1982. It became one of the highest-grossing arcade games in US history. What was the hack called before Midway rebadged it?
context: GCC's Doug Macrae and Kevin Curran built Crazy Otto as a maze game with leg-having characters. Midway approached them and licensed it as the official Pac-Man sequel, much to Namco's annoyance — Namco hadn't authorized any sequel and only later embraced Ms. Pac-Man as canon in 2002.

question: Walter Day ran an arcade in a small Iowa town from 1981 and began keeping a book of the top scores players hit on his machines. From that pastime grew Twin Galaxies, for decades the official keeper of arcade high scores. Which town was it?
context: Day's Twin Galaxies arcade was running in Ottumwa by November 1981, and its national scoreboard followed in 1982; from 1983 Twin Galaxies supplied verified scores to the Guinness Book of World Records. The 2007 documentary The King of Kong made Day a household name.

question: Arcade legend says men in dark suits showed up at a few arcades in Portland, Oregon, in 1981, unplugged a strange black cabinet and hauled it away. Players who tried it had reported headaches, memory loss and even seizures. Nobody has ever proven the story is real. What was that supposed cabinet called?
context: Polybius first appeared on coinop.org in 1998 as a speculative listing. No evidence supports its existence. The legend is widely treated as the foundational creepypasta of arcade culture, parodied in The Simpsons (S25 'Married to the Blob') with a black cabinet labeled 'PROPERTY OF U.S. GOV'T'.

question: Atari gave a single in-house programmer only about five weeks in 1982 to design and code a game of Steven Spielberg's hit movie E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, in time for the Christmas shopping season. The game sold poorly, unsold cartridges were later buried in a New Mexico landfill, and historians blame it as a major cause of the 1983 video-game crash. Which lone programmer got the rushed job?
context: Warshaw had also designed Atari's hit Yars' Revenge (1982). Atari paid $20-25 million for the E.T. license and ordered five million cartridges; only 1.5 million sold. Warshaw still defends the design publicly — it's a complex pit-falling collection game, not 'the worst game ever,' but the rush job and the public memory have stuck.

question: Nintendo launched the Famicom, its first home game console, in Japan on July 15, 1983, over two years before the Nintendo Entertainment System reached the US. The launch lineup was just three games, all home ports of Nintendo arcade hits. Which three games were they?
answer: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye
choices: Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr., and Popeye
Mario Bros., Super Mario Bros., and Mario Tennis
Excitebike, Ice Climber, and Balloon Fight
context: The Famicom (Family Computer) was designed by Masayuki Uemura and released for ¥14,800 — about $66 in 1983 USD. The 'NES' redesign for the US was a deliberate VCR-look to avoid the 'toy' aisle still poisoned by the 1983 crash.

question: A California company launched a home game console in 1977 that plugged into the family television, and kids popped in cartridges of Combat, Space Invaders and later Pac-Man. Its maker first called the machine by a three-letter name, the initials of what the console technically was. When the bigger 5200 model arrived in 1982, the old machine was renamed the 2600. What was the three-letter name?
context: Atari renamed the VCS to 2600 in 1982 after launching the more advanced 5200. The 2600's joystick had a single button and eight-direction stick. Combat was the pack-in game. Activision was founded in 1979 by Atari programmers angry that Warner Atari wouldn't credit them on cartridges.

question: Nintendo of America passed over the real Japanese sequel to Super Mario Bros., later called The Lost Levels, as too hard. For the 1988 North American Super Mario Bros. 2 it reskinned a different Japanese Famicom game. What was the original game?
context: Doki Doki Panic was a 1987 Famicom Disk System game with mascots from a Fuji TV festival. Nintendo redrew the player-characters as Mario, Luigi, Toad, and Princess Peach. The true Japanese SMB2 finally reached the West in Super Mario All-Stars on SNES (1993) as 'The Lost Levels.'

question: The snide teen villain of the 1989 movie The Wizard, a film that promoted Nintendo, puts on a strange new NES accessory and sneers that it is 'so bad.' Mattel released the accessory that year to let players control games by moving a hand through the air, with ultrasonic signals tracking the wearer's hand. What did Mattel name it?
context: The Power Glove worked poorly: only two games were made for it, Super Glove Ball and Bad Street Brawler. Its place in pop culture, thanks largely to The Wizard, is far larger than its use as a controller.

question: Nintendo wired both controllers of its 1983 Japanese console, the Famicom, short for Family Computer, straight into the machine, so a player could not unplug them. Controller 1 had a D-pad, two action buttons, Select and Start. Controller 2 had no Select or Start at all, but it carried one extra part that Controller 1 lacked, and some Famicom games used it. What was it?
context: Few games used the microphone. In The Legend of Zelda a shout into it defeats the rabbit-eared Pols Voice; the American NES controller had no microphone, so players there used arrows instead.

question: Sonic Team made Sonic Adventure, the first fully 3D Sonic the Hedgehog game, which came out in Japan late in 1998 and led the lineup when the Dreamcast reached North America. Its director had been lead designer on the dream-world platformer Nights into Dreams. Who was he?
context: Iizuka directed and Yuji Naka produced. Sonic Adventure came out in Japan on 23 December 1998, a month after the Dreamcast, and was a launch game in North America. Nights into Dreams had been directed by Naoto Ohshima, the artist who drew Sonic.

question: Rare based its 1997 N64 shooter GoldenEye 007 on the James Bond movie of the same name, and every player of its legendary multiplayer mode wanted one weapon above all others. It killed any opponent in a single shot but held only a few bullets at a time. What was this weapon called?
context: Based on the Scaramanga golden pistol from the 1974 Bond film. Holds one bullet; one-shot kills anything. Spawned in random multiplayer locations, leading to mad scrambles. Many multiplayer house-rules tournaments forbid camping the Golden Gun spawn — and forbid Oddjob entirely.

question: Psycho Mantis, a telepathic villain in the 1998 stealth game Metal Gear Solid, seems to read the player's mind, dodging every attack as if he sees each button press before it happens. Veteran players cracked the fight not by pressing new buttons but by doing something odd to the console hardware itself. What did they have to do?
answer: Move the controller from Port 1 to Port 2
choices: Move the controller from Port 1 to Port 2
Hold the dualshock motion sensors face-down
Insert a memory card into Slot 2 mid-fight
Press Start while the disc tray was open
context: Psycho Mantis 'read the player's mind' by reading the controller in Port 1, so switching ports cut him off. Earlier in the fight he also reads the memory card and comments on other Konami games saved there, such as Castlevania.

question: Nintendo finally brought The Lost Levels, the brutally hard real Japanese sequel to its 1985 plumber game, to the US in 1993. It never came over on its own: it shared an SNES cartridge with 16-bit remakes of the plumber's three American NES games. What was that cartridge called?
context: All-Stars rebuilt all four NES games with 16-bit graphics by Nintendo R&D4. The Lost Levels added poison mushrooms, wind, and brutal difficulty. The cartridge also came in a Mario World pack-in version. The 1996 Super Mario All-Stars + Super Mario World combined edition is one of the rarest SNES carts.

question: A Dreamcast owner pops a tiny card out of its slot on top of the controller and feeds a virtual pet, Tamagotchi-style, on the school bus. The card has its own small liquid crystal display (LCD) screen, a D-pad and buttons, so it plays as a standalone handheld. What did Sega call it?
context: The VMU had 200 blocks of memory and a 48x32 LCD. Sonic Adventure's 'Chao Garden' could be loaded onto the VMU and raised standalone. Sony's PlayStation 1 PocketStation (1999, Japan-only) had a similar concept. The Sega VMU defines a forgotten era of console-peripheral creativity.

question: A green dinosaur named Yoshi came in the box when Nintendo launched the SNES in North America on August 23, 1991. The single pack-in cartridge was the colorful side-scrolling adventure that introduced him, with a spinning cape to let its hero glide. The console followed the NES with sharper 16-bit graphics, a Mode-7 rotating background trick and a stereo sound chip. What was the launch title?
context: Super Mario World was developed by Miyamoto's team alongside the SNES hardware itself, debuting Yoshi the dinosaur. The launch lineup also included F-Zero, Pilotwings, SimCity, and Gradius III. Nintendo had been beaten to 16-bit in the US by Sega Genesis (1989), but the SNES caught up by 1993.

question: A 23-year-old Squaresoft programmer, determined to compose a score, threatened to quit if not given the chance. He got Chrono Trigger, the 1995 SNES game, slept in his studio for nights on end, and fell ill from overwork during the composition. Who was he?
context: Nobuo Uematsu, Square's main composer, stepped in to write ten of the game's 64 tracks when Mitsuda fell ill. Mitsuda went on to score Xenogears (1998) and Chrono Cross (1999).

question: A Sega player in 1994 plugs one cartridge into the top of another. The spin-off starring a red echidna has a passthrough slot, and the mainline Sonic sequel from that same year goes into it, so the two play as one combined game. What is the combined game called?
context: Plugging Sonic 2 into the S&K cartridge let the player play as Knuckles in Sonic 2 (no extra story). Plugging Sonic 1 or any non-Sonic cart yielded the 'No Way' or 'Blue Sphere' randomly generated minigame. The lock-on cartridge tech was an engineering one-off — Sega never used it again.

question: A secret green ninja waits on the Pit stage of the original 1992 Mortal Kombat arcade game, and only players who meet specific conditions can fight him. Arcade rumour talks of flawless rounds, no blocking and silhouettes crossing the moon. He cannot be selected in the first game, but the sequel makes him playable. What is the green ninja's name?
context: MK1's secret-character lore — silhouettes flying across the moon, double-flawless rounds, no-block challenges — was a closely-guarded arcade rumor. Reptile's combination of Scorpion's spear and Sub-Zero's freeze made him a fan-favorite. MK2 added Smoke, Noob Saibot, and Jade as similar secret-ninja characters.

question: Capcom hid a secret boss inside Super Street Fighter II Turbo in 1994, an update of its famous series of one-on-one duels, and only players who met specific arcade conditions could challenge him. He was a corrupted master of dark energy, the evil brother of the sensei who trained the heroes Ryu and Ken. Who was the hidden boss?
context: Akuma debuted as a secret boss in Super Street Fighter II Turbo (1994); the only way to fight him was a run of specific arcade conditions. In Japan the character is called Gouki. He is the brother of Ryu and Ken's sensei Gouken, and his Raging Demon (Shun Goku Satsu) became one of the series' signature moves.

question: Konami launched Dance Dance Revolution in Japanese arcades in 1998, opening an entirely new genre of rhythm games played on foot-pad controllers. The game belonged to a broader Konami brand that included Beatmania (1997) and Guitar Freaks (1999). What was the brand called?
context: Bemani is short for 'Beat Mania.' DDR reached the US in 1999 and exploded among gym-class fitness programs by the early 2000s. The game's combination of public-arcade visibility, calorie burn, and music-discovery appeal made it the rare rhythm game to cross into mass-culture awareness.

question: Sega rushed out a strange add-on in 1994, just as its more powerful Saturn console was about to launch. Shaped like a black mushroom cap, it plugged straight into the cartridge slot of the company's 16-bit console and boosted the machine's graphics power. It flopped, and Sega discontinued it within a year. What was it called?
context: The 32X had its own power supply, AV cables, and required the Genesis to function — a mushroom-tower of plastic. Only 40-ish games were ever released for it, including Doom (with weaker graphics than 3DO), Star Wars Arcade, and Virtua Racing Deluxe. The Sega Saturn launch six months later cannibalized 32X sales.

question: An N64 player in 1996 took hold of an unusual three-pronged controller and chose two of its three grips: the left with the D-pad, the right with the face buttons, or the new center one. What was the central component that decided which two grips to hold?
context: The N64 analog stick was the first analog stick on a major home console — Sony quickly responded with the DualShock (1997). Holding left+center vs left+right depended on what the game needed; Super Mario 64 used center+right, while Mario Party gripped left+right for D-pad-heavy mini-games.

question: A Seattle actress first voiced Cortana, the AI companion of Bungie's Halo: Combat Evolved, when the game launched with Microsoft's first console in 2001. She has kept playing Cortana in every mainline Halo game, all the way through Halo Infinite in 2021. Who is she?
context: Jen Taylor, a Seattle-area actress, first voiced Cortana in 2001 and has played her for more than twenty years. Jennifer Hale, Tara Strong and Grey DeLisle are major game-voice actresses too, but none of them has played Cortana.

question: Two friends who had met as boys at a weekend Hebrew school in Virginia started a game company in 1984, while still in high school, and later renamed it Naughty Dog. Twelve years later their studio gave Sony's new console its first blockbuster hero, an orange marsupial spinning through crates on a jungle island. Who were the two founders?
context: Gavin and Rubin founded the company as JAM Software in McLean, Virginia; it became Naughty Dog in 1989, with Keef the Thief. Their earlier games included Rings of Power (1991) and Way of the Warrior (1994). After Crash they made Jak and Daxter for the PS2, sold Naughty Dog to Sony in 2001 and left in 2004.

question: Leon Kennedy travels overseas to rescue the U.S. President's daughter in Capcom's Resident Evil 4, released for the GameCube in 2005. Capcom threw out the fixed haunted-house camera angles of the older Resident Evil games and glued a floating over-the-shoulder camera behind him, a single change that reinvented how action video games are filmed. Where does the story take place?
context: Leon S. Kennedy travels to rural Spain to rescue the US President's kidnapped daughter Ashley from a parasite-cult called Los Iluminados. Director Shinji Mikami's over-the-shoulder camera was directly imitated by Gears of War (2006), Uncharted (2007), and Dead Space (2008), defining the post-2005 action-shooter look.

question: An announcer bellows 'He's on fire!' in Midway's 1993 arcade hit NBA Jam when a player sinks three baskets in a row. Two players run a 2-on-2 basketball game full of ten-foot slam dunks and physics-defying jumps that take real NBA stars right off the court, but that voice is the most beloved part. Who voiced NBA Jam?
context: Kitzrow's catchphrases — 'Boomshakalaka!', 'From way downtown!', 'He's heating up!' — were largely improvised in a single Chicago recording session. Kitzrow has voiced almost every Midway and NBA Jam-derivative sports title since. He has no formal sports-broadcast career outside game development.

question: The whole Simpson family fights Springfield's criminals block by block in Konami's 1991 brawler The Simpsons Arcade Game, after Bart accidentally grabs a stolen diamond. Homer swings his fists, Marge whips a vacuum cleaner, Bart rides his skateboard and Lisa cracks a skipping rope. A hidden extra-life donut sits in one exact spot every 90s arcade kid eventually learned. Where does the donut appear?
answer: Behind the bowling alley garbage cans
choices: Behind the bowling alley garbage cans
Inside the Power Plant cooling tower
