On top of the Krusty Burger sign
Down a manhole at the courthouse
context: The Simpsons Arcade is a brawler in the X-Men Arcade / TMNT Arcade tradition — Konami's beat-em-up template. The Bonus Round between stages is the bouncing-on-a-trampoline minigame. Homer's nightmare cutscene featuring a giant donut is one of the more surreal arcade interstitials of the era.

question: Konami built a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles arcade cabinet in 1989 with four joysticks side by side, so four kids could each play a different turtle. Each turtle wears a different color mask, and the purple mask belongs to the team's brainy engineer and inventor. Which turtle is he?
context: Leonardo (blue) wielded katanas. Donatello (purple) wielded a bo staff. Raphael (red) wielded sai. Michelangelo (orange) wielded nunchaku. The Konami arcade is the second TMNT game (after the 1989 NES original), and is widely considered the definitive beat-em-up of the franchise.

question: Disney's 2012 animated film Wreck-It Ralph fills its arcade machines with cameos from real video-game characters, then seats real bad guys together in one famous group-therapy scene. A Pac-Man enemy sits in the chair and runs the meeting. Which ghost is it?
context: Other real-game cameos: Bowser (Mario), M. Bison and Zangief (Street Fighter), Kano (Mortal Kombat), Doctor Robotnik (Sonic), and Neff (Altered Beast). Sonic himself appears with a 'Public Service Announcement' cameo at Game Central Station. Voice direction by John C. Reilly as Ralph.

question: Kids race across the country to a big Nintendo video-game championship in California in The Wizard, the 1989 Fred Savage movie that was really one long Nintendo commercial. Its final round shows off a brand-new Nintendo game that has not yet reached US store shelves. Kids everywhere begged their parents for it. Which unreleased game was it?
context: Super Mario Bros. 3 did not reach US shelves until February 1990. The Wizard's finale shows Jimmy finding a Warp Whistle, and the film also promoted the Power Glove and Nintendo Power magazine.

question: Steve Wiebe, an out-of-work engineer in Redmond, Washington, set up a Donkey Kong machine at home and taped the first game ever to top a million points. Twin Galaxies would not accept it and sent two referees to look over his machine. What did they suspect?
answer: That his circuit board had been tampered with
choices: That his circuit board had been tampered with
That the tape had been sped up to fake his timing
That a friend had played part of the game for him
That the machine was set to its easiest difficulty
context: The board inside Wiebe's machine had been supplied by Roy Shildt, a longtime enemy of Billy Mitchell's, which is why Twin Galaxies feared tampering; it also would not recognize a record made at home on video. Wiebe then took his game to the Funspot arcade in New Hampshire to play in public.

question: A console maker buried piles of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico desert after two of its 1982 games flopped, in the crash of 1983 to 1985 that nearly killed the home console business. One flop was the movie tie-in E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial. The other was a rushed home port of the biggest arcade hit of all time. Which game was that home port?
context: Atari produced 12 million Pac-Man cartridges for a 10-million-installed-base 2600 — they expected to sell to new console buyers. The port's flickering ghosts (a 4-frame palette swap) made it look terrible. Atari sold only 7 million, leaving warehouses full. Combined with E.T., Atari laid off thousands of employees in 1983 and the entire toy aisle stopped stocking games by 1984.

question: Four of Atari's star programmers walked out in 1979 and founded their own studio, Activision. They were angry that Atari, then owned by Warner, refused to put their names on the boxes of the games they had designed. As they later told it, the last straw came from an Atari boss who insulted them at a meeting. What did he say, by their account?
answer: That they were no more important to Atari than the assembly-line workers who boxed the cartridges
choices: That they were no more important to Atari than the assembly-line workers who boxed the cartridges
That Bushnell would refuse to honor their stock-option vesting after resignation
That Atari lawyers would sue them for trade-secret breach if they discussed designs
That Kaplan would be fired for putting his name on the title screen of a game
context: Crane and the others left Atari in 1979 and released Dragster, Boxing, Checkers and Fishing Derby first. The insult rests on the programmers' own later accounts. Atari sued Activision, and the case was settled by 1982 with Activision paying royalties, which set the model for outside publishers; the flood of cheap games that followed fed the crash of 1983.

question: Don Bluth and about a dozen colleagues left a feature unfinished when they walked out of Disney Animation Studios and founded Don Bluth Productions. Their new studio later defined the arcade-game-as-cartoon look. What Disney film were they working on at the moment of the walkout?
context: Steven Spielberg later backed Bluth on An American Tail (1986) and The Land Before Time (1988), both major hits, and Bluth's All Dogs Go to Heaven (1989) opened the same day as The Little Mermaid.

question: Tom Kalinske, Sega's CEO, shocked the industry at E3 on May 11, 1995, by announcing the Sega Saturn at $399 and launching it in North America that same day, earlier than the announced September 2 date. The launch backfired badly. A Sony man stepped up to the microphone, gave one number and walked off. What price did he announce for his own console?
context: Steve Race, the head of Sony Computer Entertainment of America, walked to the microphone, said '$299' and walked off. The Saturn's surprise early launch angered retailers who had been left out of it. Sega left console hardware after the Dreamcast in 2001.

question: Sony proudly unveiled its 'Play Station' at a 1991 electronics show in Chicago: a prototype compact-disc read-only memory (CD-ROM) add-on, built with Nintendo, that would let SNES games ship on disc instead of cartridge. The very next day, on the same stage, Nintendo publicly shocked Sony by announcing it had dumped Sony for another partner. Who was Nintendo's new partner?
choices: Hitachi, which made the Saturn co-processor
context: Nintendo had grown wary of Sony's contract terms — Sony would have kept all the revenue from CD-based games. Switching to Philips humiliated Sony's CES booth team. Ken Kutaragi convinced Sony chairman Norio Ohga to go ahead with the project as a standalone Sony console — the PlayStation. The Philips CD-i went on to be famously disastrous.

question: Microsoft bought a small Chicago studio in 2000 so that its secret science-fiction shooter, later shipped as Halo: Combat Evolved, could launch Microsoft's brand-new console. Bungie was best known for atmospheric first-person shooters on Apple Macintosh computers in the 1990s. Which earlier Mac shooter had already made its name in the game industry?
context: Marathon — Marathon 2: Durandal — Marathon Infinity. Halo was originally a Mac-and-PC RTS, then a third-person shooter, then the FPS Xbox launch we know. Bungie left Microsoft in 2007 to make Destiny under Activision. The Marathon trilogy was open-sourced in 2005 by Bungie.

question: Shigeru Miyamoto led the design of Nintendo's 1985 plumber game, the best-selling game of the decade, but he had a co-designer. That partner stayed with him for the next forty years, working on Zelda, the plumber's later games and Yoshi's Island. Who is he?
context: Tezuka has co-directed almost every major Mario title (he was the producer on Super Mario Maker and Super Mario Wonder). His and Miyamoto's design philosophy — 'design the player's first 30 seconds perfectly' — defines the SMB World 1-1 tutorial, widely studied in game-design programs.

question: Shigeru Miyamoto placed the first enemy of World 1-1, the opening stage of his 1985 plumber game, right beside the first question-mark block. He did it on purpose, so a child holding the controller for the first time would learn one lesson within seconds. What was the lesson?
answer: That Goombas hurt on touch and die from jumps
choices: That Goombas hurt on touch and die from jumps
That enemies are meant to be dodged, never fought
That touching a Goomba from the side defeats it
That a Goomba turns back when Mario runs at it
context: The opening seconds of World 1-1 teach without a word of text: the first Goomba, the first question block and the first mushroom. The level has become a standard example in game-design teaching.

question: Shigeru Miyamoto had wanted a rideable dinosaur for his plumber hero ever since the first NES adventure in 1985, but the older NES was not powerful enough to draw one on screen. Yoshi the green dinosaur finally showed up on the Super Nintendo. On the earliest Nintendo concept sheets he had a long, Latin-sounding scientific name that also punned on his enemies in those games. What was that original name?
context: Yoshi's full name was almost never used in-game. The Mario World manual lists him as 'T. Yoshisaur Munchakoopas' in the US release. Designer Shigefumi Hino. Yoshi has appeared in over 30 Mario titles, has his own series (Yoshi's Island 1995, Yoshi's Story 1997, Yoshi's Crafted World 2019), and is Nintendo's third-most-marketable character behind Mario and Pokemon.

question: One engineer created the cross-shaped D-pad still used on controllers today. As lead engineer of Research and Development 1, the group that designed most of Nintendo's hardware from the 1970s into the 1990s, he also made the tiny handheld Game & Watch, the Famicom and the NES, and a grey handheld with a green screen in 1989. Who was he?
context: Yokoi's 'lateral thinking with withered technology' philosophy — using mature, cheap components creatively — produced the Game Boy and the entire Game & Watch line. He left Nintendo in 1996 after the Virtual Boy commercial failure and died in a car accident in October 1997, age 56.

question: Cloud Strife, the hero of Final Fantasy VII, says he once served in Shinra's elite super-warrior program, whose fighters' eyes glow from the energy pumped into them. The 1997 game sold 9.8 million copies, became the franchise's global breakthrough and put Square at the top of the Japanese role-playing game (JRPG) world. What was the program called?
context: SOLDIER is always written in capitals in the game, and SOLDIER 1st Class is its highest rank.

question: A Final Fantasy VII player plugs glowing orbs called Materia into weapons and armor to grant abilities. The Materia comes in different colors, one for each type: magic spells are green, and command abilities like Steal are yellow. What color are the mighty Summon Materia that call forth Ifrit, Shiva and Bahamut?
context: Five Materia categories: Green (Magic — Fire, Cure, Bolt), Yellow (Command — Steal, Throw, Sense), Blue (Support — All, Quadra Magic, MP Turbo, slotted as a pair), Purple (Independent — passive stat boost), and Red (Summon — Ifrit, Shiva, Bahamut). The system encouraged build experimentation rare for the era.

question: Nintendo's marketers hammered on one big technical advantage when their new console reached North America in late 1996, more than a year after Sony's PlayStation and Sega's Saturn. What was the bragging point?
answer: A 64-bit processor, twice the bit width of its rivals
choices: A 64-bit processor, twice the bit width of its rivals
A built-in modem for playing against other households
A controller with a tiny screen for private menus
Full-motion video streamed from a compact-disc drive
context: The N64's 64-bit MIPS R4300i CPU was technically true but marketing-misleading — the actual bus was rarely fully utilized. The launch lineup of two games (Mario 64 and Pilotwings 64) was infamously thin. Nintendo's choice of cartridge over CD-ROM cost it the goodwill of third-party publishers including Square, who took FFVII to PlayStation.

question: An armored super-soldier races a Warthog jeep up a long collapsing ramp through packed corridors at the close of Halo: Combat Evolved, which launched in November 2001. The game ends in that famously chaotic driving chase, and everyone remembers the level from its ticking countdown music. What is this final level called?
context: The Maw is the tenth and final level of the campaign, and the Warthog run up the collapsing ramp is its most famous stretch.

question: A North American Dreamcast owner dials up over a phone line and plays Phantasy Star Online against people in other cities. The smooth white console is the first home game console to ship with a modem built right into every unit, a 33.6k or 56k card, and it logs into an official online service. What is that service called?
context: SegaNet enabled the first console MMO — Phantasy Star Online (2000), which let players from Japan, US, and Europe play together on shared servers. Dreamarena was the European service. Online play also distinguished NFL 2K1, Quake III Arena Dreamcast, and Chu Chu Rocket. Sega shut down its first-party Dreamcast servers in 2003.

question: Auction bidders pick over the 1999 Base Set's holographic prize for two tiny printing tells: a small stamp on the left of the art, and a thin shadow line down the right side of the card border, which later reprints added. Which printing sells for the most money?
context: The Base Set's first print run had no thin shadow beside the art; the shadow came with later printings. The 1st Edition stamp sits at the left edge below the art. A top-graded 1st Edition Shadowless Charizard has sold for over $400,000 at auction.

question: A composer still in his early twenties built pounding house and techno beats on the sound chip of Sega's 16-bit console for the 1991 brawler Streets of Rage, and they sounded like a real club mix. He had already scored Revenge of Shinobi in 1989 and the Super Nintendo fantasy game ActRaiser in 1990, and he became one of Japan's most famous game composers. Who is he?
context: Koshiro was in his early twenties when he scored Streets of Rage, and his Streets of Rage 2 score is often called one of the best of the 16-bit era. He still composes, including for the Etrian dungeon-crawler games and Streets of Rage 4 (2020).

question: Nobuo Uematsu wrote 'One-Winged Angel,' the final boss theme of Squaresoft's 1997 Final Fantasy VII, as a fusion of Igor Stravinsky and Jimi Hendrix, by his own account. It mixes rock guitar and orchestra with a Latin choir. Where do the choir's Latin words come from?
answer: Carmina Burana, the medieval songbook Carl Orff set to music
choices: Carmina Burana, the medieval songbook Carl Orff set to music
The Dies Irae, the Latin hymn of the Requiem Mass
The Vulgate, Saint Jerome's Latin Bible
The Aeneid, Virgil's Latin epic of Troy
context: The words are taken from poems in the Carmina Burana, a thirteenth-century collection of songs and poems found in a Bavarian monastery and best known through Carl Orff's 1937 setting. Uematsu later played in the rock band The Black Mages, whose arrangement of the piece appears in Advent Children.

question: Konami's 1999 horror game Silent Hill sent a father searching for his missing daughter through a foggy American town where air-raid sirens signaled that the world would shift into a rusted nightmare version of itself. The soundtrack was not orchestral: it was industrial noise, clanking metal, distorted guitars and haunting piano. A 30-year-old Konami sound designer composed every track. What was his name?
context: Yamaoka used metal drums, factory machinery, scraping metal, and distorted electronic beats to create the Silent Hill sound. He has scored Silent Hill 1 through Silent Hill: Shattered Memories (2009) and Silent Hill f (2025). The town's foggy, alternate-dimension Otherworld with its rusted iron and bleeding walls was inspired by the films Jacob's Ladder and Eraserhead.

question: A Sony engineer designed the SPC700 audio chip that ended up inside Nintendo's Super Nintendo (SNES), a rare Sony chip living inside a Nintendo box. When the 1991 Nintendo-Sony compact disc (CD) partnership collapsed on stage in Chicago, he talked Sony's bosses into striking out alone and building their very own gaming console. Who was the engineer often called the father of that machine?
context: Kutaragi was widely called 'the father of the PlayStation.' He led hardware development for PS1, PS2, PS3, and the early PSP. Sony forced him into retirement in 2007 after PS3's troubled launch. His Cell Broadband Engine processor in the PS3 was simultaneously a research achievement and a developer pain-point that hurt PS3's third-party support.

question: An ordinary earthworm stumbles into a super-powered robotic space suit and becomes a hero in Earthworm Jim, the bizarre platformer Shiny Entertainment released for the Sega Genesis and SNES in 1994. A young American cartoonist and animator designed the oddball character, the same man who later created the cartoon Catscratch and worked on Veggie Tales. Who was he?
context: TenNapel sold Earthworm Jim to David Perry's Shiny Entertainment. Perry's team — Nick Bruty, Tom Tanaka, Tommy Tallarico (music) — finished the design. Tallarico's score is considered a high-water mark of Genesis FM synthesis. TenNapel later created Neverhood (1996) on PlayStation, with stop-motion claymation and Terry S Taylor music.

question: Charles Zembillas and Joe Pearson drew the hero of Naughty Dog's 1996 game, an orange marsupial with the placeholder name Willy the Wombat. Naughty Dog wanted a real animal that was appealing but obscure, as Sega had done with a hedgehog and Warner Bros. with one cartoon star. Which star?
context: Naughty Dog bought a field guide to Tasmanian mammals and weighed the wombat, the potoroo and the bandicoot. Willy the Wombat was only ever a placeholder, too dorky to keep, and another company had used the name for a Saturn game.

question: The CEO of Twin Galaxies led a technical investigation himself, and in April 2018 the score-keeping organization stripped Billy Mitchell's Donkey Kong records after concluding that the video tapes he had submitted as proof came from an arcade emulator, not a real cabinet. For decades Mitchell had claimed the first perfect Pac-Man score and the world's highest on Donkey Kong. Who was the CEO?
context: Jace Hall is a Hollywood producer, founder of Monolith Productions (No One Lives Forever, F.E.A.R.), and Twin Galaxies' owner from 2014. The Mitchell investigation used reverse-engineering of arcade-board level-load patterns vs MAME's level-load patterns — a frame-by-frame signature analysis the original Twin Galaxies referees couldn't have done in 2003.

question: Warren Robinett buried a hidden credit reading 'Created by Warren Robinett' inside a home console game in 1979, the first known video-game Easter egg, after his company refused to credit designers on cartridges. In the game a small square hero carries keys and a sword between three castles while dodging three dragons. What was the game called?
context: Robinett's hidden credit was placed in the Black Castle, accessible by carrying a pixel-thin 'gray dot' across multiple screens to a specific spot. Atari executives at first wanted Robinett fired for the secret, then realized players loved discovering it. The term 'Easter egg' was coined by Atari Director of Software Steve Wright in 1980 to describe the phenomenon.

question: Howard Scott Warshaw made his first big hit with Yars' Revenge in 1982, before his E.T. disaster. A fly-like hero, Yar, battles the Qotile cannon behind a force field, and a scrolling band of random colors and pixels runs down the middle of the screen. What is that central band called?
context: The Neutral Zone was a randomly-painted strip of memory bytes — Warshaw used the game's ROM itself as the visual texture. The Yar character was a yellow eight-legged fly-creature; the Qotile alternated between a stationary cannon and a swirly killing-projectile called the Swirl. Yars' Revenge sold over a million copies for the 2600, an enormous hit for the era.

question: Midway hid a secret roster in NBA Jam Tournament Edition, sent to arcades in 1994, which players unlocked by typing certain dates and initials at the title screen. It held TV stars, the developers themselves and even American politicians dunking alongside NBA pros. One hidden player was the person in the White House at the time. Which sitting US president was on the list?
context: NBA Jam TE's hidden characters: Bill Clinton, Al Gore, Tipper Gore, the Beastie Boys, Frank Thomas, Tonya Harding, several Mortal Kombat fighters, and the entire Midway development team. The Mortal Kombat unlocks featured stretchy-arm versions of Sub-Zero, Scorpion, and Raiden. Many cheat codes were leaked in Electronic Gaming Monthly print articles.

question: An American semiconductor company in Pennsylvania released a cheap, fast 8-bit processor chip, easy to program, in the late 1970s. It became the brain of the Apple II, the Commodore 64 and, in a Ricoh-manufactured version with its decimal mode locked out, the Nintendo NES. Almost every classic home computer and console of that era ran on this chip family. Which chip was it?
context: The 6502 was designed by Chuck Peddle's team at MOS Technology in 1975 — explicitly to compete with Motorola's 6800 at one-fifth the price. The 6502 dominated 8-bit personal computing of the late 1970s and the entire NES era. Steve Wozniak picked the 6502 for the Apple I (1976) because it was the cheapest CPU he could find — $25 vs the 8080's $359.

question: Nintendo of America shipped a green-tunic hero's first adventure on a shiny gold cartridge on August 22, 1987, instead of the standard gray plastic used for every other NES cart, to make it look like buried treasure on the store shelf. The trick worked so well that Nintendo gave the same gold cart to one 1988 NES sequel. Which sequel got the gold treatment?
answer: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link
choices: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link
context: Zelda II is the only other NES game in the gold-cart treatment. The Famicom Disk System Japanese version of Zelda used a literal floppy disk in a yellow-and-blue plastic case. The Disk System's audio expansion chip allowed Koji Kondo to use FM synthesis in the original Zelda — capability the NES motherboard lacked.

question: Sega took on Nintendo in America in 1989 with a sleek black 16-bit home console. Under the hood, its main processor was a 16-bit chip made by an American semiconductor company. The same chip family also powered the Apple Macintosh, the Commodore Amiga and most 1980s arcade cabinets, the workhorse of the era. Which chip was it?
context: The Genesis ran the 68000 at 7.6 MHz with a secondary Zilog Z80 handling audio (a leftover from the Sega Master System architecture). The SNES used the 65816 (a 16-bit 6502 successor) at 3.58 MHz — slower clock but more efficient. 'Blast Processing' was Sega's marketing for the Genesis's faster clock advantage.

question: A young orange fox with two tails follows Sonic on every stage of Sonic the Hedgehog 2, which Sega launched worldwide on Tuesday, November 24, 1992, a coordinated release day the company advertised as 'Sonic 2sday.' Everyone calls him 'Tails' because of those spinning tails, but that is just his nickname. What is the fox's real name in the games?
context: 'Tails' is his nickname. The 'Miles Prower' = 'miles per hour' pun is a Sonic-canon-trivia gem. Tails was designed by Yasushi Yamaguchi at Sega Technical Institute. Sonic 2 was the first major game co-developed between Sega of Japan and Sega Technical Institute (Mark Cerny's team), pioneering the trans-Pacific Sega development pipeline.

question: Sega's 1986 arcade racer OutRun puts the player at the wheel of a red Ferrari and offers a left or right path at the end of each stage. The deluxe cabinet pushed the racing beyond the visuals with one piece of hardware. What was it?
answer: A hydraulically actuated motion seat that tilted the player with the car
choices: A hydraulically actuated motion seat that tilted the player with the car
Force-feedback in the steering wheel and accelerator pedal
A 3D stereoscopic LCD shutter set for a glassless 3D effect
Wraparound surround-sound speakers in the bucket headrest
context: Suzuki's 'taikan' (full-body) cabinets defined Sega arcade hardware. After Burner (1987) had a yoke that simulated jet roll. Hang-On (1985) had a motorcycle the player straddled. The OutRun cabinet's bright-red convertible Ferrari shape became an arcade icon — the deluxe version is the holy grail of arcade collectors.

question: Dracula's half-vampire son stars in Konami's 1997 hit Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, the game that pivoted the franchise from linear levels to open-castle exploration. What is his name?
context: Alucard first appeared in Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse (1989). Koji Igarashi, Symphony of the Night's assistant director, went on to lead the series, and the game became a model for the open-castle style now called Metroidvania. Ayami Kojima painted the cover art.

question: A player crouch-jumps into the brick wall above the exit pipe of World 1-2 in Nintendo's original 1985 plumber game, slips through it with precise timing and takes a Warp Zone pipe into a strange underwater level with no exit. The world counter shows a blank tile where a number should be. What did fans nickname it?
context: The Minus World is a copy of the World 7-2 water level that loops back on itself, so Mario can swim forever but never reach a flagpole. On the Japanese Famicom Disk System the same glitch leads through three different levels that can be finished.

question: Fred Savage plays a baseball video game on a home computer in bed at the start of Rob Reiner's 1987 film The Princess Bride, until Peter Falk, his grandfather in the film, arrives to read him a story. The game came out in 1985, though some fans name its 1989 sequel by mistake. What was the real title?
context: Hardball! came out for the Commodore 64 in 1985, two years before the film, so the boy is playing the original and not Hardball II of 1989. Bob Whitehead programmed it for Accolade.

question: Billy Mitchell achieved the first publicly verified perfect game of Pac-Man on July 3, 1999, eating every dot, every fruit, every power pellet and every blue ghost on every level, then dying on purpose at the kill screen. The session took just over six hours. What was the exact perfect score?
context: Mitchell played continuously for 6 hours and 6 minutes without losing a life. The score 3,333,360 is mathematically the maximum possible — 255 levels of 240 dots, 2 power pellets, all four ghosts and bonus fruit eaten on every level. Only a handful of perfect Pac-Man games have ever been verified since.

question: The makers of the 2007 documentary King of Kong: A Fistful of Quarters filmed its climactic Donkey Kong showdown inside the world's largest classic-arcade museum, endless rows of original 1980s cabinets in a lakefront resort town, still coin-operated. Billy Mitchell had rolled the first perfect Pac-Man score there in 1999. Which arcade is it?
choices: Pinball Hall of Fame in Las Vegas
context: Funspot was founded in 1952 by Bob Lawton. It maintains over 600 classic cabinets and is a Twin Galaxies-sanctioned official high-score recording site. The American Classic Arcade Museum within Funspot includes Pong, Computer Space, Asteroids, and dozens of working originals. The Funspot Annual Tournament has drawn world-class scorers for 40+ years.

question: A Konami programmer found his own game, Gradius, too hard to playtest in 1986, so he built in a developer cheat: a button sequence that gave the player full power-ups. The sequence became famous as the Konami Code. What was the programmer's name?
context: Hashimoto died in February 2020 at age 61. The code was supposed to be removed before retail release of Gradius but accidentally shipped. By 1988's Contra, where it gave 30 lives, it had become canon. The code appears in over 100 Konami titles plus easter-eggs across web sites, banks, and Google's old search bar.

question: Dedicated players of Namco's 1981 shooter Galaga found a hidden trick that makes the entire alien fleet stop shooting for good. A player kills every alien on the wave except two of one specific color in one specific row, then survives about fifteen minutes without firing a shot. Every future wave comes in peaceful. Which two aliens does he have to spare?
answer: The two blue aliens of the bottom row
choices: The two blue aliens of the bottom row
The two red aliens of the bottom row
The two yellow flagships of the top row
The two green dragonflies in mid-formation
context: The exploit is a collision-detection bug in Galaga's enemy-state machine — Namco's programmers later acknowledged the bug had shipped. Top scorers exploit it to grind toward the 999,990 score-display rollover before continuing. The bug only works on arcade originals; most home ports patched it.

question: Atari secretly buried a truckload of cartridges in the New Mexico desert in 1983. A film crew dug them up on 26 April 2014, with Howard Scott Warshaw, who programmed Atari's E.T. game, looking on. The crew's leader, Zak Penn, also wrote the script for a 2018 Spielberg film packed with video-game history. Which film?
context: Penn's documentary 'Atari: Game Over' (2014) showed the excavation team finding thousands of buried Atari cartridges — including ET, Pac-Man, Centipede, Asteroids, and Defender — plus crushed manuals and console parts. The dig was sanctioned by Alamogordo NM authorities. Howard Scott Warshaw (ET's developer) attended the excavation in person.

question: Two of the founders of General Computer Corporation, a small startup near Boston, turned existing Pac-Man boards into an unauthorized enhancement kit. Midway then licensed the work, and it reached American arcades in 1982 as Ms. Pac-Man. Who were the two?
context: GCC was founded in 1981 by Doug Macrae, Kevin Curran and John Tylko. Its first product was an unauthorized speed-up kit for Atari's Missile Command; Atari sued, then dropped the case and hired GCC to make games, on condition that it sell no more kits without the original maker's consent. The Pac-Man kit went to Midway, which sold it as the official sequel.

question: The legend of Polybius says a black arcade cabinet of that name appeared in a few Portland, Oregon arcades in 1981; teenagers who played it had seizures, nightmares and memory loss, and men in black suits came to haul it away. No such cabinet has ever been proven to exist. The tale first surfaced online in February 1998, dressed up as real arcade history. On which website?
context: coinop.org's listing for Polybius cited 'unknown manufacturer' and added the conspiracy details over time. No physical cabinet, no manual, no PCB, no flyer has ever been found. The legend has been parodied in The Simpsons (S25 'Married to the Blob,' showing a black cabinet labeled 'PROPERTY OF U.S. GOV'T') and treated as creepypasta canon.

question: A Williams Electronics designer wanted mounts that could flap in midair and still 'look heroic', so he put one knight of his 1982 two-player arcade game on an ostrich and the other on a stork. Each player mashes a flap button to fly around the screen, trying to smash the other knight from above. Who was the designer?
context: Newcomer designed several Williams classics including the dual-button flap mechanic that defined Joust. The cooperative mode where two players could fly together (and accidentally knock each other off) made Joust one of the best two-player arcade experiences of the era. The Pterodactyl appears after 70 seconds; killing it gives 1000 points.

question: Williams' 1981 shooter Defender flies a small ship sideways across an alien planet's surface, rescuing tiny humans before mutant abductors can carry them into the sky. Reviewers said its brutal control panel took a solid hour of practice just to figure out what each control did, let alone survive Wave 1. How many separate physical inputs did the player have to work at once?
answer: Five buttons plus a two-direction joystick
choices: Five buttons plus a two-direction joystick
Three buttons plus an eight-direction joystick
Two buttons plus a 360-degree spinner knob
Seven buttons plus a four-direction joystick
context: Defender's controls: Reverse (flip horizontal direction), Thrust (accelerate forward), Hyperspace (teleport randomly — possibly to death), Fire (shoot horizontally), Smart Bomb (kill everything on screen). The joystick controlled vertical movement only. The complexity made Defender notoriously hard for first-time players and a beloved expertise badge for arcade veterans.

question: Parker Brothers, the American board-game company, licensed Konami's 1981 frog-crossing arcade hit and shipped an Atari 2600 home port in 1982. The cartridge became one of the top-selling 2600 games of the year, helped along by a clever freebie packed inside every box, something a kid could carry upstairs and enjoy separately from the game itself. What did Parker Brothers give away with each copy?
answer: Parker Brothers gave away free Frogger 45 RPM records with the game
choices: Parker Brothers gave away free Frogger 45 RPM records with the game
Parker Brothers bundled it with a glow-in-the-dark frog plush
Parker Brothers added a tournament reply-card sweepstakes
Parker Brothers shipped it in a clear plastic frog-shaped case
context: The Frogger song — 'Time to hop! Look out for the cars!' — was performed by The Buckner & Garcia (also of 'Pac-Man Fever' fame) and shipped on a 45 RPM single included in the 2600 box. The track went to #57 on the Billboard Hot 100. Parker Brothers' Frogger 2600 port sold roughly 4 million units.

question: A DualShock controller vibrates in a player's hands without any in-game input during Metal Gear Solid (1998). The boss Psycho Mantis is showing off his 'psychic power,' and he goes on to taunt the player with comments based on data he reads. Where does he read it from?
answer: The player's PS1 memory card, scanning for other Konami game saves
choices: The player's PS1 memory card, scanning for other Konami game saves
The CD-ROM disc's TOC, reading the user's region code
The PS1's BIOS clock, telling the player the last time played
Sony's PocketStation if connected, reading installed mini-games
context: Mantis comments on Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, Suikoden and other Konami saves he finds on the card. The fight is solved by switching the controller from Port 1 to Port 2.

question: Howard Lincoln, an executive at Nintendo of America, created a small gold-and-black badge for the box of every NES game the company licensed. Shoppers had stopped trusting the label 'video game' after the crash of 1983, when store shelves flooded with low-quality Atari cartridges, and buyers needed a way to tell which games were properly made. What exact phrase was written on that badge?
context: The original 1985 seal said 'Official Nintendo Seal of Quality.' Nintendo dropped 'of Quality' from the seal in 1989 after lawsuits from third-party publishers (Color Dreams, Tengen) over implied quality claims. The seal then read 'Official Nintendo Seal.' Modern Nintendo Switch games no longer use the gold seal.

question: Argonaut Software, a British firm, worked with Nintendo on a processor for Star Fox, which in 1993 put 3D-rendering power on the game cartridge itself. During development the chip carried a codename built on the name of Nintendo's plumber. What was it called when it shipped?
context: The Super FX was a RISC processor built into the Star Fox cartridge to draw 3D polygons, which the console could not manage alone. Its development codename was Super Mario FX, and the chips are stamped MARIO. Argonaut's founder, Jez San, had first shown Nintendo a 3D demo of the space game Starglider in 1990. The faster Super FX 2 later powered Yoshi's Island and the SNES Doom.

question: One publisher flew to Moscow in 1989 to deal straight with the Soviet office ELORG (Electronorgtechnica) for Nintendo. Nintendo had to win a messy legal fight for the worldwide handheld rights to a Soviet falling-block puzzle before the game could come in the box with its new US handheld. Who was that publisher?
context: Rogers had published the role-playing game The Black Onyx in Japan in 1984. Robert Maxwell's Mirrorsoft and its partner Tengen claimed Tetris rights of their own, but only ELORG could grant the handheld rights, and Rogers won them. The 2023 Apple TV+ film Tetris, starring Taron Egerton, dramatises the trip.

question: Rare hid a set of cheats behind speed-run challenges in its 1997 N64 shooter GoldenEye 007. A player who finished the Runway mission on Agent difficulty in under five minutes unlocked one that made every character's head cartoonishly big during play. What was that cheat called?
context: DK Mode, named for Donkey Kong, unlocks on the Runway in under five minutes at Agent. The Dam under 2:40 on Secret Agent unlocks Paintball Mode instead, which leaves paint splats where the bullets land.

question: The armored hero of Halo: Combat Evolved (2001) follows a floating robot guide through identical hallways, floor after floor, while waves of enemies attack, in a notoriously long, repetitive, dimly lit level. Reviewers and fans often name it the dullest stretch of the game. What was the level called?
context: The Chief climbs the Library floor by floor to reach the Index, and players still single it out as the campaign's low point. The level before it is named after the robot guide, 343 Guilty Spark.

question: Up to four players fire shells and drop bananas until only one balloon is left in the beloved battle mode of Mario Kart 64, Nintendo's 1996 N64 game. One arena became famous for how peaceful it looked: a flat platform suspended high in a cloud-filled sky, with four small towers to duck around but no pits, walls or hazards to fall from. What was that arena called?
context: The four MK64 battle arenas: Block Fort (four-corner blocks with ramps), Skyscraper (open platform falling to a kill-zone), Double Deck (two-layer arena with central holes), and Big Donut (ring with no center). Block Fort's relative open-ness made it the dominant tournament-mode arena from 1996 through GameCube's Mario Kart Double Dash (2003).

question: Nintendo released its first vibration-feedback peripheral, the Rumble Pak, alongside Star Fox 64 in 1997. A player plugged it into the expansion slot on the back of the N64 controller, but it had a specific power source that set it apart from later vibration solutions. What was the power source?
answer: Two AAA batteries inside the pack
choices: Two AAA batteries inside the pack
Drew power from the controller's main circuit board
A small lithium cell rechargeable through the cartridge slot
Solar cells on the rear shell of the pack
context: Sony's DualShock (1997 Japan, 1998 US) included rumble motors directly in the controller, drawing power from the console. The N64's battery-powered Rumble Pak was widely criticized for adding weight and requiring battery replacement. Star Fox 64 was bundled with the Rumble Pak in the US — the first game to require external vibration hardware.

question: Nintendo's famous mascots punched each other off floating platforms in Super Smash Bros., released on the N64 in 1999. Eight characters were there from the start, and four more were secrets a player unlocked by finishing challenges. Who was never among those four secrets in the original game?
context: Smash 64's starting eight: Mario, Donkey Kong, Link, Samus, Yoshi, Kirby, Fox, and Pikachu. The four unlockables: Captain Falcon, Ness, Jigglypuff, and Luigi. Marth debuted in Melee (2001). Smash creator Masahiro Sakurai also created Kirby (1992) at HAL Laboratory. The original Smash project was a one-off called Dragon King: The Fighting Game before Nintendo's IP was added.

question: Players of Super Smash Bros. Melee, released for the GameCube in 2001, stumbled onto an unintended trick, and the game's global competitive scene grew largely from it. A fighter who air-dodged diagonally into the ground during a jump kept the sliding momentum and slid across the stage without walking. Pros used it to move faster than the game was meant to allow. What did players name this trick?
context: Sakurai never intended wavedashing: the physics came from the way air-dodge momentum carried through contact with the ground. Later Smash games removed it. Melee tournaments still draw thousands of players.

question: Sonic tears through his zones to a punchy, brassy, buzzsaw tone unlike any other console of the era, the sound of a synthesis technique called frequency modulation (FM). Sega's 16-bit machine, launched in North America in 1989, gave the same tone to the sweeping Phantasy Star adventure scores. One six-channel Yamaha chip generated every note. Which chip was it?
context: The YM2612 had six FM synthesis channels plus a DAC channel for sampled sounds. The companion SN76489 (TI-licensed) provided four PSG channels for sound effects. Hidden inside the architecture: the Z80 secondary CPU handled audio playback while the Motorola 68000 ran the game. The Genesis sound architecture was a direct continuation of Sega's earlier System 16 arcade boards.

question: A Super Mario 64 speedrunner presses Mario against a wall and repeats one specific move, building up enough speed to clip through doors and skip large portions of the castle. What is the move called?
context: The BLJ exploits Mario 64's speed-clamping logic — when long-jumping backwards while running into a wall, the game accumulates negative momentum but caps positive speed. Speedrunners stack BLJ frames against the endless staircase up to Bowser, eventually clipping through. The trick lets a runner finish the game with 0, 1, 16, 50, or 70 Stars depending on what skips they perform.

question: The 23-year-old composer of Squaresoft's 1995 SNES game Chrono Trigger pushed himself brutally on his first major score, sleeping in his studio for nights on end to hit the deadline. Partway through, his health gave out, and Nobuo Uematsu had to finish ten of the tracks. What laid him low?
answer: Stomach ulcers brought on by overwork
choices: Stomach ulcers brought on by overwork
Repetitive strain injuries in both wrists
Pneumonia caught during a winter of all-nighters
A broken arm from a fall on the studio stairs
context: Mitsuda contracted stomach ulcers from the strain, and Nobuo Uematsu composed ten of the game's 64 tracks while he recovered. Mitsuda had threatened to leave Square unless he was allowed to compose.

question: Nintendo showed an adult, dark-cloaked hero swordfighting a real-looking Ganondorf on the GameCube in a tech demo at its Spaceworld show in 2000, and fans went wild expecting a serious, gritty Zelda. The actual game, The Wind Waker, arrived in 2002 with a big-eyed, chibi-style toon for a hero, who looked drawn in a comic book. Angry fans coined a mocking nickname for the style. What did they call it?
context: The Spaceworld 2000 'GCN Demo' showed an adult Link sword-fighting Ganondorf in photorealistic combat — generating immense hype. The reveal of Wind Waker's cel-shaded toddler-Link with floating Tetra pirates produced an internet meltdown. Eiji Aonuma later said the realistic 2000 demo had never been a real game in development — it was a tech demo only.

question: Cortana guides a super-soldier from a chip in the back of his helmet in the Halo series, and her creation story is unsettling. She was built inside the Office of Naval Intelligence (ONI), the future Navy's secret science and espionage branch, from flash clones of a living woman's brain, a legally shaky procedure. Whose brain was it?
answer: Dr. Catherine Halsey, the Spartan program's lead scientist
choices: Dr. Catherine Halsey, the Spartan program's lead scientist
Admiral Margaret Parangosky, head of ONI
Miranda Keyes, daughter of Captain Keyes
Kelly-087, a Spartan who trained with the Chief
context: Halsey made Cortana from flash clones of her own brain, which is why the AI's mind is modelled on hers. She also led the Spartan-II programme that produced the Master Chief.

question: The Last Starfighter, from 1984, follows a trailer-park teenager who beats an arcade high score and is recruited by aliens as a starfighter pilot. Its 27 minutes of computer graphics were rendered on the most powerful supercomputer of its day, kept at a Los Angeles graphics studio, where a single frame could take up to ten minutes. Which machine was it?
answer: The Cray X-MP at Digital Productions LA
choices: The Cray X-MP at Digital Productions LA
The CDC Cyber at the Argonne Lab
context: Digital Productions installed a Cray X-MP/22 in 1983 specifically for rendering The Last Starfighter and Tron 2 (which was never made). The X-MP could render approximately one frame per 5-10 minutes. Despite the technical achievement, the film grossed only $28M against a $14M budget. Director Nick Castle later made The Boy Who Could Fly (1986) and Major Payne (1995).

question: The third season of Stranger Things, in 2019, brings in Robin Buckley, Steve Harrington's workmate at the Scoops Ahoy ice-cream parlor, a bilingual genius who decodes Russian transmissions for Dustin and Steve. The actress who plays her is the daughter of two Hollywood stars. Who is she?
context: Maya Hawke is the daughter of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman. She debuts as Robin in Season 3 — the dynamic between Robin, Steve (Joe Keery), and Dustin (Gaten Matarazzo) became one of the show's best comedy trios. The Stranger Things Palace Arcade scenes were filmed at a real Atlanta reproduction arcade with period-accurate cabinets.

question: Patricia Pulling blamed Dungeons and Dragons for her teenage son's death, and in 1983 she founded a campaign group to warn parents across America about role-playing games. It became one of the loudest voices of the Satanic Panic. What did the group's initials, B.A.D.D., stand for?
context: Patricia Pulling founded B.A.D.D., Bothered About Dungeons & Dragons, in 1983, the year after her son's death. No evidence ever tied his death to the game.

question: John Badham's WarGames, from 1983, follows David Lightman, a Seattle teenager who dials by accident into a military supercomputer that runs nuclear war simulations, and nearly starts World War III. In his bedroom he types on a real 1970s home microcomputer with a metal front panel covered in red toggle switches. What model is it?
context: The IMSAI 8080 (released 1975) was an early S-100-bus microcomputer built by IMS Associates. It used an Intel 8080 CPU and shipped as a kit or assembled.

question: A strong man in a blue suit and red cape lifts a whole car over his head on the cover of Action Comics #1, from 1938. He is an alien baby from dying Krypton, raised on a Kansas farm as Clark Kent. Who is he?
context: Created by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster, both teenagers from Cleveland. The first issue cost ten cents; a copy sold for $6 million in 2024.

question: Detective Comics #27, from May 1939, gives readers a rich Gotham heir who saw his parents shot dead in an alley as a boy. He trains mind and body, then puts on a costume to hunt criminals by night. Who is he by day?
context: Bob Kane is credited as creator but writer Bill Finger contributed the cape, cowl, and detective elements; DC formally added Finger's credit in 2015.

question: Joe Simon and Jack Kirby put out Captain America #1 in March 1941, months before America entered World War II. The cover showed Steve Rogers throwing a right hook in a Nazi bunker. The two Jewish creators got death threats. Who was Cap punching?
context: Joe Simon and Jack Kirby created Cap nine months before Pearl Harbor. The cover drew angry letters from American Nazi sympathizers; NYC mayor Fiorello La Guardia personally called the publisher to offer police protection.

question: Stan Lee and Steve Ditko needed a hero for the last issue of a struggling magazine, Amazing Fantasy, in August 1962. They tried a shy, brainy high-school kid from Queens, New York, bitten by a radioactive spider at a science demonstration. What is his name?
context: Written by Stan Lee, drawn by Steve Ditko. Lee said the publisher, Martin Goodman, thought readers would find spiders creepy. Sales were strong, and Spider-Man had his own title, The Amazing Spider-Man, by early 1963.

question: Four astronauts hit by cosmic rays come home with strange powers in Fantastic Four #1, from November 1961. Its writer was a New York huckster with a knack for slang, and its artist drew as if every panel might explode. Who were the two creators?
context: Lee wrote, Kirby drew. The team — Mr. Fantastic, Invisible Girl, Human Torch, Thing — got their powers from cosmic-ray exposure on a rocket flight.

question: Wolverine lies strapped to a table while the shadowy Weapon X program grafts an unbreakable silver metal onto every bone in his body, including the retractable claws between his knuckles. His mutant healing factor is the only reason he survives. What is that metal called?
context: Wolverine debuted in Incredible Hulk #181 in 1974. The adamantium-bonding was done forcibly to Logan by the Weapon X program. Vibranium is Captain America's shield metal.

question: William Moulton Marston, a psychologist, created Wonder Woman in 1941 and armed her with a golden lasso that makes anyone caught in it tell the truth. Years before, he had built a blood-pressure test for people under questioning. What did that test grow into?
context: Wonder Woman's Lasso of Truth is often read as a nod to the polygraph. Marston's blood-pressure test became one part of the modern polygraph, which John Augustus Larson built in 1921.

question: Stan Lee, writer and editor at Marvel Comics, signed off his letter columns with a booming cry that means 'ever upward,' and he often closed his Stan's Soapbox columns with it too. What was his catchphrase?
context: Lee took 'Excelsior' from the Latin for 'ever upward', which is also the New York State motto. Lee died in 2018 at 95.

question: Jack Kirby filled a Marvel action panel with cracked pavement, cosmic energy and impossible machinery. No artist drew like him before, and everyone imitated him after. Other comic-book artists gave him a one-word nickname of respect. What did they call him?
context: Kirby is widely considered the most influential American comics artist of all time. He also co-created Captain America in 1941 with Joe Simon. His dynamic 'Kirby Krackle' visual style for cosmic energy is still imitated.

question: A bald telepath in a wheelchair opens a private school at his family mansion in Westchester, New York, in Marvel's X-Men comics. Mutant children, born with powers that make ordinary humans fear them, learn there to control their gifts in safety. What is his name?
context: Readers and critics have often compared Xavier and Magneto with Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. The school stands in Salem Center, New York. X-Men: The Animated Series ran 1992-1997 with 76 episodes.

question: Spider-Man first uses his powers for wrestling prize money and TV fame. Then a robber he refused to stop kills his Uncle Ben. The story's last caption states the rule he lives by ever after, later put in Ben's mouth. What is it?
answer: With great power comes great responsibility
choices: With great power comes great responsibility
Never let your guard down against true evil
The strong have a duty to protect the weak
A hero's job is to never stop trying his best
context: The line appears in the closing caption of Amazing Fantasy #15. Uncle Ben's death — Peter failing to stop a burglar who later kills Ben — is the moment that launches Spider-Man's career.

question: Marvel's Thor, son of Odin, raises his enchanted war-hammer to summon lightning. The weapon was forged in the burning heart of a dying star, and only those judged truly worthy can even lift it. What is the hammer called?
context: Thor first appeared in Journey into Mystery #83 in 1962. Only the worthy can lift Mjolnir. Stormbreaker is a separate hammer wielded by Beta Ray Bill.

question: Harry Potter boards a scarlet steam engine at Platform Nine and Three-Quarters, in London's King's Cross Station, bound for a hidden castle in the Scottish Highlands. The castle has moving staircases, a Great Hall with a starlit ceiling and four ancient student houses. What is the full name of the school?
answer: Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry
choices: Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry
context: Hogwarts is in the Scottish Highlands. Beauxbatons is French and Durmstrang is Northern European — both featured in Goblet of Fire. Author JK Rowling wrote the first book in Edinburgh cafés.

question: A pale, snake-faced dark lord murders Harry Potter's parents when Harry is a baby and tries to kill the boy too, leaving him with a lightning-shaped scar. Most wizards are so afraid of him that they refuse to say his name and call him only 'You-Know-Who.' What is his name?
context: His birth name was Tom Marvolo Riddle, an anagram of 'I am Lord Voldemort.' Most characters call him 'You-Know-Who' or 'He Who Must Not Be Named.' Harry's distinctive lightning-bolt scar comes from Voldemort's failed killing curse in 1981.

question: The ancient Sorting Hat sits on Harry Potter's head at Hogwarts and whispers that Slytherin could make him great. Harry begs for a different house, and the Hat gives him the one he asks for. Which house does Harry join?
context: The Sorting Hat almost places Harry in Slytherin but listens to his preference. Gryffindor was founded by Godric Gryffindor; its colors are scarlet and gold, its animal a lion.

question: A British woman was riding a delayed train from Manchester to London in 1990 when the idea of a scrawny orphan who discovers he is a wizard hit her all at once. She wrote the first book in Edinburgh cafés, often broke. Who wrote the Harry Potter books?
context: Joanne Rowling famously wrote much of the first book as a single mother on welfare. The publisher added the 'K' (for her grandmother Kathleen, a name she never had) so the books would appeal to boys.

question: Hagrid takes Harry Potter shopping in Diagon Alley when the boy turns eleven, and in a magical pet store he buys him a pure-white snowy owl as a birthday present. What is the owl's name?
context: Hagrid buys Hedwig for Harry as an 11th birthday gift in Diagon Alley. Errol is the Weasleys' owl, Pigwidgeon is Ron's, Crookshanks is Hermione's cat.

question: A wizard in half-moon spectacles once defeated the dark wizard Gellert Grindelwald in a legendary 1945 duel. Now he runs Hogwarts with a long silver beard tucked into his belt, and he is Harry Potter's guide and protector. What is his name?
context: Dumbledore's full name is Albus Percival Wulfric Brian Dumbledore. He defeated the dark wizard Grindelwald in 1945 and is considered the greatest wizard of his age.

question: Harry Potter would never survive his first year at Hogwarts without the research and quick thinking of a bushy-haired Muggle-born girl. She memorizes textbooks before term even starts and constantly reminds him and Ron Weasley to do their homework. What is her name?
context: Hermione is a Muggle-born witch and the top student in her year. The trio meets on the Hogwarts Express in 1991. Hermione's name is pronounced 'her-MY-oh-nee.'

question: Harry Potter rides a Nimbus Two Thousand around the Quidditch hoops with one job on his team of seven: catch the Snitch, a tiny golden winged ball. Catching it ends the game and scores 150 points. Which position does he play?
context: The Seeker chases the Golden Snitch — a tiny winged ball worth 150 points. Catching it usually ends the match. Harry becomes the youngest Seeker in a century when he joins the team as a first year.

question: An enormous, shaggy-bearded half-giant kicks down the door of the shack where the Dursleys are hiding Harry Potter, and he hands the boy his acceptance letter in person. He works as gamekeeper at Hogwarts and adores dragons and three-headed dogs. What is his name?
context: Hagrid was expelled from Hogwarts as a student in 1943 but allowed to stay as gamekeeper through Dumbledore's intervention. He raises everything from acromantulas to dragons.

question: Thirteen-year-old Harry Potter casts his first full Patronus, a silvery guardian spirit that drives off the soul-sucking dementors of Azkaban. It comes out as an animal tied to one of his dead parents. What shape does it take?
choices: A wolf, like his mentor Lupin
A doe, like his mother Lily
A hare, like his friend Luna
context: James Potter was an unregistered Animagus at Hogwarts, transforming into a stag — earning him the Marauder nickname 'Prongs'. His three best friends were Sirius Black (Padfoot, a dog), Remus Lupin (Moony, a werewolf), and Peter Pettigrew (Wormtail, a rat). Harry's Patronus inheriting the stag form ties him to his father even though James died when Harry was a baby. Lily's Patronus was a doe; Snape's was also a doe, in memory of her.

question: Robert Downey Jr. made his comeback in Jon Favreau's 2008 film, the first of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, as a billionaire weapons designer. Kidnapped by Afghan warlords, the character builds an armored suit in a cave to escape. Which Marvel character did Downey play?
context: Jon Favreau directed the 2008 Iron Man. The casting of Downey — then still recovering from drug-related arrests — was a massive gamble that set the MCU's wisecracking tone for over a decade.

question: A scrawny Brooklyn kid becomes a super-soldier and takes up a round vibranium shield in Captain America: The First Avenger, from 2011. One Boston-born actor plays this Steve Rogers all the way to Avengers: Endgame in 2019. Which actor is it?
context: Evans had previously played the Human Torch in the 2005 Fantastic Four films. He almost turned down Captain America: The First Avenger before agreeing to a multi-film contract.

question: A giant purple warlord from the moon of Titan hunts the six Infinity Stones in Avengers: Infinity War, from 2018. He believes wiping out half of all life with one snap of a gauntlet will bring the survivors balance. What is his name?
context: Thanos is played by Josh Brolin via motion capture. His name comes from Thanatos, Greek god of death. He first appeared in Marvel Comics in 1973 created by Jim Starlin.

question: Chris Hemsworth swings a magical hammer called Mjolnir as a mighty Asgardian warrior in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. The character comes from Norse mythology, where he is the god of thunder and storms. Which Norse warrior god does Hemsworth play?
context: Hemsworth was nearly cut from auditions; his brother Liam read for the part before Chris's mother pushed him to try again. Kenneth Branagh directed the 2011 Thor.

question: Tom Hiddleston plays a horned Asgardian villain in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, the adopted brother of Asgard's thunder god. The character comes from a trickster god of Norse mythology, a sly shape-shifter who loves mischief and clever schemes. Which Norse trickster god does Hiddleston play?
context: Hiddleston originally auditioned for Thor before being cast as Loki. Loki is Thor's adopted brother — actually a Frost Giant raised in Asgard by Odin. He invades New York with the Chitauri in 2012's The Avengers.

question: Peter Quill, a human raider who calls himself Star-Lord, leads a rag-tag team of misfit space heroes in a Marvel Studios film of 2014. A talking raccoon named Rocket and a walking tree fight beside him against cosmic threats. What is this team called?
context: Directed by James Gunn. The team includes Star-Lord (Chris Pratt), Gamora, Drax, Rocket Raccoon, and Groot ('I am Groot'). The soundtrack of 1970s pop hits became iconic.

question: Mark Ruffalo took over the Hulk in The Avengers (2012), after Edward Norton's turn in 2008. The giant green monster is born when a mild-mannered scientist is blasted with gamma radiation. When calm, the man goes by his ordinary human name. What is it?
context: Eric Bana played Banner in 2003's Hulk before Norton's 2008 version and then Ruffalo's. Banner's transformation is triggered by anger; he becomes the green-skinned Hulk after a gamma-radiation accident.

question: DC Comics rebooted The Flash in Showcase #4 in October 1956, swapping the helmeted college student of the 1940s for a brand-new speedster in red and yellow, with no ties to the old hero. Comics historians say that issue launched the Silver Age of superhero comics. What was the new Flash's civilian name and job?
answer: Barry Allen, the police forensic scientist
choices: Barry Allen, the police forensic scientist
Wally West, the teenage fan-club president
context: Barry's costume, red with a yellow lightning bolt, was designed by Carmine Infantino. In the story he is struck by lightning and doused in chemicals in his police crime lab.

question: Hal Jordan, a test pilot, finds a crashed alien named Abin Sur in DC Comics' 1959 reboot of an old hero, and the dying alien gives him a glowing power ring. The ring makes swords, shields and giant fists from his willpower and links him to peacekeepers across space. What is that organization called?
context: The Corps is a force of 7,200 intergalactic peacekeepers run by the Guardians of the Universe on the planet Oa. Hal Jordan was a test pilot when the dying Abin Sur passed him the ring. The Corps oath: 'In brightest day, in blackest night...'

question: Marvel's X-Men gathers five teenage mutants, humans born with strange powers, at a school for gifted students in 1963, each with one signature power. Their field leader wears a special visor because he cannot turn off his eyes, which fire blasts of red force. Which original X-Man leads the team?
context: Scott Summers can't control his optic blasts, so he wears a ruby-quartz visor or glasses. The five original X-Men were Cyclops, Marvel Girl (Jean Grey), Angel, Beast and Iceman. The comic ran only reprints from 1970 until Giant-Size X-Men #1 brought in a new team in 1975.

question: Matt Murdock pushes a stranger out of the path of a truck carrying toxic waste as a boy in Stan Lee and Bill Everett's Daredevil, from 1964. The chemicals blind him but sharpen his other senses to superhuman levels, and by night he fights crime in a red devil suit. What is his day job?
answer: Lawyer in Hell's Kitchen, New York
choices: Lawyer in Hell's Kitchen, New York
context: Matt Murdock practices law with partner Foggy Nelson at Nelson & Murdock. Created by Stan Lee and Bill Everett, Daredevil first appeared in Daredevil #1, April 1964. Frank Miller's late-1970s/early-1980s run redefined the character.

question: Fantastic Four issue 52 brings comics' first major black superhero onto the page in 1966. He is the king of Wakanda, a hidden African nation that sits on the world's only supply of vibranium. He wears a sleek suit and leads a warrior guard called the Dora Milaje. Who is this Wakandan king?
context: The Black Panther Party in California formed independently around the same time. Marvel briefly renamed the character 'Black Leopard' in 1972 to avoid confusion before reverting. T'Challa rules a technologically advanced, vibranium-rich nation. Chadwick Boseman starred as T'Challa in the 2018 film Black Panther, which grossed over $1.3 billion and received seven Oscar nominations including Best Picture, a first for a superhero film.

question: Wolverine first shows up as a Hulk enemy in 1974, short, angry and armed with a healing factor and retractable claws. Giant-Size X-Men #1 puts him on the new team of X-Men in 1975. He calls himself Logan, but that is not the name he was born with. What was his birth name?
context: Wolverine's first full appearance is Incredible Hulk #181 (cover-dated November 1974), fighting both the Hulk and the Wendigo. 'Logan' became his name in Uncanny X-Men; the birth name James Howlett came in the 2001 Origin miniseries.

question: Jean Grey, the X-Men's telepath, is corrupted by a cosmic entity in the most famous story of Chris Claremont's record-setting 16-year run on Uncanny X-Men, drawn by John Byrne. It turns her into a world-devouring destroyer, and her teammates must choose between saving her and stopping her. What is that story arc called?
context: Dark Phoenix ran in Uncanny X-Men #129-137, with John Byrne drawing and co-plotting.

question: Watchmen, the twelve-issue comic by Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons from 1986, turns superheroes into flawed and often dangerous people. One small image becomes the story's signature symbol: it sits on the cover of issue 1 and keeps returning as a reminder of a murdered hero named the Comedian. What is that famous image?
answer: A yellow smiley-face button with a blood splatter across one eye
choices: A yellow smiley-face button with a blood splatter across one eye
A red rose held by a costumed vigilante in silhouette
A black silhouette of a clock with hands at midnight
A blue silhouette of a man against a glowing red moon
context: The smiley face belongs to the murdered Comedian (Edward Blake), whose death opens the series. Dave Gibbons drew all twelve issues.

question: Frank Miller set a gray-haired, 55-year-old Bruce Wayne against street gangs and a fascist government in a near-future Gotham City, in a four-part story for DC Comics in 1986. It changed superhero comics. What was Miller's landmark series called?
context: Miller followed up in 1987 with Year One (Batman's first year, with David Mazzucchelli). The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen, both from 1986, are often cited as the start of the 'mature' comics era.

question: Neil Gaiman's Sandman follows Dream, the pale lord of every story ever told and one of seven immortal siblings called the Endless. Each rules over one part of existence. Dream's elder sister is a cheerful young woman with dark eyeshadow and an ankh necklace, whom the others respect but rarely see. Who is she?
context: The seven Endless are Destiny, Death, Dream, Destruction, Desire, Despair and Delirium, who was once Delight. Death appears as a cheerful young goth woman with an Egyptian ankh necklace.

question: Mike Mignola's 1993 comic brings a bright-red demon to Earth, summoned by Nazi occultists during the Second World War and raised by a kind American professor. With sawed-off horn stubs, a giant stone right hand and a fat cigar, he works as a paranormal detective for a secret US agency. What is he called?
context: Hellboy was summoned to Earth by Nazi occultists in 1944 but raised by Allied paranormal researcher Trevor Bruttenholm. He works for the Bureau for Paranormal Research and Defense (BPRD). Guillermo del Toro directed the 2004 and 2008 films starring Ron Perlman.

question: Garth Ennis and Steve Dillon gave a small-town Texas pastor a divine voice that could command obedience in Preacher, begun at DC's Vertigo imprint in 1995. His traveling companions were his on-and-off girlfriend Tulip and what Irish vampire?
context: Jesse Custer, the preacher, hosts an entity called Genesis — offspring of an angel and a demon. The trio crosses America hunting God Himself, who has abandoned creation. AMC adapted the comic into a four-season TV series in 2016–2019.

question: Rowling published the first Harry Potter book in Britain in 1997, and a year later the American publisher Scholastic changed one word of its title, worried that the word sounded too old-fashioned for American readers. What was the original British title?
answer: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
choices: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
Harry Potter and the Magic Stone
Harry Potter and the First Year
context: Scholastic's editor Arthur Levine thought 'philosopher' sounded too archaic, so the 1998 American edition became Sorcerer's Stone; Rowling later said she regretted the change. The Philosopher's Stone of alchemy is tied in legend to Nicolas Flamel, a real 14th-century Parisian scribe, and he features in the book.

question: A greasy-haired, black-cloaked Hogwarts teacher hates Harry Potter from the very first Potions class and seems cruel and petty for years. The last book reveals that this head of Slytherin house loved Lily, Harry's mother, and secretly served Dumbledore the whole time. Who is this Potions master?
context: Snape is head of Slytherin House. He famously taunts Harry from the first day of Potions class. Alan Rickman played him in all eight films; Rickman knew Snape's full arc from Rowling earlier than the cast or readers did.

question: A dangerous convict has just escaped from Azkaban, the wizard prison, and thirteen-year-old Harry Potter is told the man wants to kill him. The truth in Prisoner of Azkaban turns out to be very different. The convict is Harry's own godfather, framed years ago for a crime he did not commit. Who is this godfather?
context: Sirius can transform into a large black dog, his Animagus form. He was framed for betraying Harry's parents by Peter Pettigrew (Wormtail). Sirius dies in Order of the Phoenix (book five), killed by Bellatrix Lestrange and falling through the Veil in the Department of Mysteries.

question: Prisoner of Azkaban hands Harry Potter the Marauder's Map, an enchanted parchment his father and three friends made as students at Hogwarts. Tapped with a wand, it shows every person moving inside the castle, but only for someone who speaks the correct opening phrase, and a matching closing phrase hides it again. What are the two phrases?
answer: 'I solemnly swear that I am up to no good' / 'Mischief managed'
choices: 'I solemnly swear that I am up to no good' / 'Mischief managed'
'Show me what is hidden' / 'Concealed once more'
context: The Map was made by the Marauders: Moony (Remus Lupin), Wormtail (Peter Pettigrew), Padfoot (Sirius Black), and Prongs (James Potter). Fred and George Weasley give it to Harry in Prisoner of Azkaban after stealing it from Filch's office.

question: Hagrid leads his students out to the paddock for his first Care of Magical Creatures lesson in Prisoner of Azkaban and brings out a rare flying beast with sharp claws. He warns that it is proud and dangerous, and Harry Potter has to walk forward slowly and bow deep before it will let him near. What magical creature is it?
context: A Hippogriff has the front half of an eagle and the back half of a horse. Buckbeak is sentenced to death after attacking Draco Malfoy (who didn't bow). Harry and Hermione later use Hermione's Time-Turner to rescue Buckbeak.

question: Cedric Diggory and Harry Potter race through a magical hedge maze in the last task of the Triwizard Tournament in Goblet of Fire, and they decide to grab the Cup together as joint winners. The moment they touch it, the story turns dark. What happens next?
answer: They are Portkey-transported to a graveyard where Voldemort returns
choices: They are Portkey-transported to a graveyard where Voldemort returns
They are dropped into a flooded chamber to face a sea giant
They are sent back to Hogwarts where the Cup explodes
They are transported to the Forbidden Forest for a centaur trial
context: Cedric Diggory is killed by Peter Pettigrew on Voldemort's orders. Voldemort uses Harry's blood for his resurrection. Mad-Eye Moody (actually Barty Crouch Jr. on Polyjuice) had turned the Cup into a Portkey. Robert Pattinson played Cedric in the 2005 film.

question: Four wizards founded Hogwarts a thousand years ago, and each gave a name to one of its houses. One house prizes cunning and ambition, and its emblem is a green serpent. Which founder started it?
context: Slytherin valued cunning and pure-blood ancestry, leading to his split with the other founders. He sealed a basilisk in the Chamber of Secrets — discovered by Tom Riddle in 1942 and reopened in 1992. Slytherin's symbol is a serpent; house colors are green and silver.

question: Harry Potter goes down into the hidden Chamber under Hogwarts and stabs the giant basilisk through the roof of its mouth. Then he grabs one of its poisonous fangs and drives it into the enchanted object that has been possessing Ginny Weasley. What object is it?
context: The diary is the first Horcrux destroyed — Harry stabs it with the basilisk fang. The seven Horcruxes total: diary, ring, locket, cup, diadem, Nagini, and an unintended one Harry only learns about in book seven.

question: Alfonso Cuarón took over the Harry Potter films from Chris Columbus in the early 2000s and gave the series a darker, more grown-up look, with colder colors, tighter camera work and real weather in every scene. Every Potter film after his imitated that style. Which Harry Potter movie did Cuarón direct?
answer: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004)
choices: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004)
Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone (2001)
Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2005)
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (2007)
context: Chris Columbus directed the first two; Cuarón did Azkaban; Mike Newell did Goblet of Fire; David Yates directed the last four films. Cuarón's work on Azkaban led to his later acclaim for Children of Men (2006), Gravity (2013), and Roma (2018).

question: Fawkes, the pet phoenix Dumbledore keeps in his office at Hogwarts, bursts into flame when he dies and is reborn from his own ashes. He takes his name from Guy Fawkes, the man behind the 1605 Gunpowder Plot in England. What color are his feathers?
answer: Crimson and gold (with a long golden tail)
choices: Crimson and gold (with a long golden tail)
Silver and white with platinum-tipped wings
Black and purple with iridescent feathers
context: Fawkes is named for the English Catholic conspirator Guy Fawkes (Gunpowder Plot, November 5, 1605). The phoenix's tears heal Harry's basilisk wound in Chamber of Secrets. Phoenix tail feathers are wand cores — Harry's and Voldemort's wands both contain feathers from Fawkes.

question: Nick Fury, a one-eyed government agent played by Samuel L. Jackson, appears in Tony Stark's mansion in a hidden scene after the credits of Iron Man (2008). He tells Stark he wants to talk about assembling a team of extraordinary heroes. What does Fury call that team-building program?
context: Samuel L. Jackson played Fury based on his depiction in Mark Millar's Ultimate Marvel comics, which had drawn Fury as Jackson. The scene was added late and cost Jackson a one-day shoot to film. The Avengers (2012) arrived four years later.

question: Two American brothers who had mostly done television comedy sent Steve Rogers after a Nazi secret group hidden inside Marvel's own intelligence agency, in Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014). Marvel liked their work so much that the pair went on to direct Civil War, Infinity War and Endgame. What are the brothers' names?
context: The Russos came from TV comedy (Arrested Development, Community). The Winter Soldier was their first major film. They earned the Infinity War / Endgame gig partly on the 70s-political-thriller tone they brought to Cap 2.

question: Peter Quill gets abducted from Earth in 1988 and grows up as a space outlaw who calls himself Star-Lord, in James Gunn's 2014 film. He carries one thing from home everywhere: a Walkman and a cassette of 1970s pop-rock songs his mom made him before she died. What name is on the cassette label?
context: The mix tape was made by Peter Quill's mother before her death. Songs include 'Hooked on a Feeling' (Blue Swede), 'Come and Get Your Love' (Redbone), and 'I Want You Back' (Jackson 5). James Gunn personally selected every track from his own 70s collection.

question: Thor befriends Korg, a polite rock-monster gladiator, on the planet Sakaar in Thor: Ragnarok (2017), which trades the serious tone of the earlier films for wild comedy and 1980s synth music. The director, a New Zealander already famous for the vampire mockumentary What We Do in the Shadows, voices Korg himself. Who is the director?
context: Waititi had directed Hunt for the Wilderpeople (2016) and What We Do in the Shadows (2014). Ragnarok rebooted Thor's tone toward broad comedy, introduced Tessa Thompson as Valkyrie and Cate Blanchett as Hela, and ended Asgard's existence as a place.

question: Peter Parker, the teenage Spider-Man, starts fading on the planet Titan at the end of Avengers: Infinity War (2018), as half of all living beings crumble into gray dust. He stumbles into Tony Stark's arms, and the first thing he stammers out has become one of the film's most quoted lines. What does he say?
answer: I don't feel so good, Mr. Stark
choices: I don't feel so good, Mr. Stark
Tell Aunt May I'm sorry, Mr. Stark
What's happening to me, Mr. Stark?
I can't feel my hands, Mr. Stark
context: Tom Holland is said to have improvised much of the scene, and the line plays on Peter's youth: he isn't ready for what's happening.

question: Captain America stands alone against an army in the final battle of Avengers: Endgame (2019), the climax of twenty-two Marvel movies. A portal opens and every fallen hero returns to fight. Steve Rogers looks up and at last speaks the rallying cry from the 1960s Marvel comics. What does he say?
context: It's the first time Cap says the full phrase in an MCU film, after the Russos held it back for 22 movies; at the end of Age of Ultron he is cut off before he can finish it. The rallying cry comes from the Avengers comics of the 1960s. He says it once the portals have opened and the returned heroes stand behind him.

question: The Avengers take turns trying to lift the enchanted hammer Mjolnir at a party in Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015), a feat only the worthy can manage. For one Avenger it twitches, a hint he could raise it. Four years later, in Endgame, he grips it and swings it in battle. Who is he?
context: In Age of Ultron, Cap makes Mjolnir budge at a party, hinting he was secretly worthy. The Russos waited four years to pay off the joke. Chris Evans's reaction shot when he wields it — Thor's stunned 'I knew it!' — is one of Endgame's biggest crowd moments.

question: Tony Stark closes his 2008 origin film at a press conference with four famous words. Eleven years later, at the climax of Avengers: Endgame (2019), a wounded Stark yanks the Infinity Stones off the villain's gauntlet onto his own armor. Before he snaps his fingers, he echoes those same four words. What does he say?
context: Tony's 2008 'I am Iron Man' press-conference reveal made Iron Man's identity public — totally inverting comics' usual secret-identity setup. Tony's Endgame line is a bookend; the snap kills Thanos and his army but proves fatal to Tony. Pepper Potts (Gwyneth Paltrow) is at his side as he dies.

question: Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster sold their caped hero to DC Comics in 1938 for $130, split $65 each, with a 10-year contract. The character made DC tens of millions over the following decades while the two men lived in poverty, and they sued in the late 1940s and lost. What development finally got DC to begin paying them small annual stipends?
answer: The publicity campaign around the 1978 Richard Donner Superman film
choices: The publicity campaign around the 1978 Richard Donner Superman film
A successful 1975 federal lawsuit against Warner Bros. parent company
The 1976 Marvel-DC settlement on shared character rights
The 1975 founding of the Comics Industry Code authority for credit
context: Neal Adams led a public-pressure campaign that embarrassed DC ahead of Superman: The Movie. DC settled with each surviving creator for $20,000 a year and 'creators of Superman' credit on all subsequent uses.
