Both Siegel (died 1996) and Shuster (died 1992) finally got their names on Superman's stories.

question: A hulking gray monster emerges from a meteor crater, fights through the Justice League and kills the Man of Steel in DC Comics' now-legendary storyline of 1992. The hero's issue #75 comes with a poster-bag and a black armband. What is the monster's name?
context: Dan Jurgens created Doomsday, and he wrote and drew Superman #75, the death issue, cover-dated January 1993.

question: Frank Miller introduced a deadly assassin during his first run on Marvel's Daredevil, from 1979 to 1983. She had been law student Matt Murdock's college girlfriend before she turned to killing for hire. She wears red, wields a pair of sai daggers and works for the crime boss the Kingpin. What is her name?
context: Elektra first appeared in Daredevil #168 (January 1981). Jennifer Garner played her in Daredevil (2003) and Elektra (2005), and Élodie Yung in the Netflix Daredevil series.

question: Ed Brubaker brought Bucky Barnes back in his Captain America run. Bucky had been Cap's sidekick in World War II, thought dead since 1945, but the Soviets had found his body, given him a metal arm and used him as a frozen assassin for years. What was his code name?
context: Brubaker's Winter Soldier arc, with Steve Epting on art, ran in Captain America (vol. 5) #1-14 (2005). The Russo brothers adapted it as Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014), starring Sebastian Stan as Bucky.

question: Jeff Smith lost three cartoon-looking cousins in a sword-and-sorcery world when he self-published Bone, starting in 1991, through his own Cartoon Books. The black-and-white epic ran to 1,300 pages by 2004. Two of the cousins are Fone Bone and Smiley Bone. Who is the third, the greedy schemer?
answer: Phoney Bone (real name Phoncible P. Bone)
choices: Phoney Bone (real name Phoncible P. Bone)
Sneaky Bone (real name Sneakford P. Bone)
Cranky Bone (real name Crankford T. Bone)
Bouncy Bone (real name Boungo T. Bone)
context: Smith has named Walt Kelly's Pogo, Carl Barks's Donald Duck comics and The Lord of the Rings among his inspirations, and the series won many Eisner and Harvey Awards. Scholastic later released the books in color.

question: A huge man covered in scars, an ex-convict just out of prison, wakes up one morning next to a woman named Goldie in the first story of Frank Miller's Sin City, set in a violent, rain-soaked town called Basin City. When Goldie is murdered in the night beside him, he vows to hunt down her killer and tear the city apart to do it. What is the ex-convict's name?
context: Mickey Rourke played Marv in Robert Rodriguez and Frank Miller's 2005 Sin City film, with Bruce Willis as Hartigan and Clive Owen as Dwight. Miller's hand-drawn high-contrast art with selective color washes (yellow Roark Jr., red Goldie blood) became the film's visual signature.

question: King Leonidas of Sparta kicks a Persian messenger backward into a bottomless pit in the 2006 movie of Frank Miller's graphic novel 300, the retelling of the Battle of Thermopylae. The messenger has come to his throne room demanding Sparta's surrender. As he kicks, Leonidas shouts a line that has become a famous internet meme. What is the line?
context: Leonidas's real ancient retort was 'Molon labe', 'Come and take them', his answer when Xerxes demanded the Spartans' weapons, preserved by Plutarch. Gerard Butler played Leonidas in the film, and the 'Spartan kick' of a foe into darkness became one of the most reused internet jokes of the 2000s.

question: A small-town American Christian pastor suffers terrifying end-of-the-world visions in Kingdom Come, DC Comics' 1996 miniseries by Mark Waid, with painted art by Alex Ross. He narrates a near future in which the old heroes rise against a reckless new generation of super-people. A grim DC hero walks beside the pastor as his supernatural escort through those visions. Which hero?
context: Mark Waid wrote Kingdom Come and Alex Ross painted every page, in a realistic style indebted to Norman Rockwell. Pastor Norman McCay is modelled on Ross's father, a minister.

question: Dolores Umbridge comes to Hogwarts in pink, sent by the Ministry of Magic in Order of the Phoenix, and bans real spellwork in Defense Against the Dark Arts: students may only read theory from a textbook. With the Dark Lord rising again outside, Harry Potter and his friends defy her, meeting in the Room of Requirement to practice real defensive spells. What proud name do they give their study group?
context: The group meets in the Room of Requirement, a magically-revealed chamber on the seventh floor. Hermione enchants a list of members so anyone who betrays them has 'SNEAK' magically appear on the traitor's face — Marietta Edgecombe gets the curse when she reports them.

question: Bellatrix Lestrange kills her cousin Sirius in the Battle of the Department of Mysteries in Order of the Phoenix. He falls backward through an ancient stone archway and is gone. What is this artifact called?
answer: The Veil of Death (or simply 'the Veil')
choices: The Veil of Death (or simply 'the Veil')
context: The Veil stands in the Department of Mysteries, and characters hear voices from behind it. In the 2007 film Sirius's last words, to Harry, who looks just like his father, are 'Nice one, James!'

question: Dumbledore takes Harry Potter into a Pensieve in Half-Blood Prince and shows him a terrible piece of the Dark Lord's past. Tom Riddle, still a student, set out to use the darkest branch of magic to split his soul into seven pieces, hiding each fragment inside an object such as a ring or a locket. To make one he first had to commit a murder. What are these containers called?
context: Creating a Horcrux requires committing murder, the act that splits the soul. Horace Slughorn, the new Potions Master, explains the concept to a young Tom Riddle decades earlier, a memory Harry retrieves with Dumbledore's help.

question: Hermione reads aloud an old wizard fairy tale, The Tale of the Three Brothers, in Deathly Hallows. The brothers meet Death on a lonely bridge and each demands a gift: the first the mightiest wand ever made, the second a Resurrection Stone to bring back the dead, the third a Cloak of Invisibility. What is the first brother's wand called?
context: The Elder Wand passes between owners by being mastered, not gifted — which is why Voldemort dies in the final book when the wand recognizes Harry as its true master via Draco's disarming of Dumbledore. Harry already owned the Cloak (a Potter family heirloom). The Resurrection Stone was hidden in Dumbledore's gift Snitch.

question: Percy Weasley has just rejoined his family after years of estrangement when the Death Eaters storm Hogwarts in Deathly Hallows. He cracks a rare joke in the fighting, and one of his identical twin brothers is still laughing when an exploding wall crashes down on them. Which twin dies?
context: Fred dies mid-laugh, just after making up with his estranged brother Percy. Rowling has said that George later married Angelina Johnson and named their son Fred.

question: Harry Potter dips his face into the stone basin of the Pensieve near the end of Deathly Hallows to view Snape's private memories. Snape has quietly loved Harry's mother, Lily, since they were children playing together. In one memory Dumbledore gently asks Snape whether he still loves her after all these years. What does Snape answer?
context: The one-word answer 'Always' became one of the most quoted lines from the series, especially after Alan Rickman delivered it in the 2011 film. Snape's silver doe Patronus matches Lily's, confirming the depth of his love. Harry names his second son Albus Severus Potter in tribute.

question: James Potter, Sirius and Peter Pettigrew secretly learned at Hogwarts in the 1970s to become Animagi, wizards who can turn into a chosen animal at will. They did it to keep their werewolf friend Remus Lupin company on full-moon nights, and they signed the Marauder's Map with their animal nicknames. What form did Sirius take?
answer: A large black dog (he was nicknamed Padfoot)
choices: A large black dog (he was nicknamed Padfoot)
A grey wolf (he was nicknamed Greybeard)
A black panther (he was nicknamed Shadowpaw)
A great horned owl (he was nicknamed Nightwing)
context: Remus Lupin was a werewolf — 'Moony' — but not an Animagus. James, Sirius, and Peter became unregistered Animagi during their Hogwarts years specifically to keep Lupin company during his monthly transformations. Peter's form was a rat — 'Wormtail' — and he hid as Ron's pet Scabbers for twelve years.

question: Hermione, thirteen, has somehow been attending more classes than her Hogwarts timetable should allow in Prisoner of Azkaban. Finally she pulls a tiny gold hourglass on a chain out from under her robes and shows it to Harry Potter and Ron. Professor McGonagall lent it to her so that she could quietly take two classes at the same hour. What is it called?
context: The Ministry of Magic strictly regulates Time-Turners. Hermione uses hers to take extra classes including Ancient Runes and Muggle Studies. At the climax, she and Harry use it to rescue Buckbeak and Sirius. Rowling has admitted writing Time-Turners into the series was a mistake — it creates plot holes the rest of the books have to work around.

question: Hogwarts brings in a famous wizarding rock band to play the Yule Ball in Goblet of Fire. In the 2005 film the band is played by real rock musicians, among them Jonny Greenwood and Phil Selway of Radiohead. What is the wizard band called?
context: In the film the band's members are all men, and the name comes from the three witches of Macbeth. Jarvis Cocker of Pulp wrote music for the band in the film.

question: Harry Potter writes lines for Dolores Umbridge in Order of the Phoenix with a magic quill that carves the words into his hand. She has taken over Hogwarts as Headmistress and inquisitor. What clever plan does Hermione use to get Umbridge removed from the school?
answer: Tricking Umbridge into the Forbidden Forest where centaurs carry her off
choices: Tricking Umbridge into the Forbidden Forest where centaurs carry her off
Spiking her tea with Veritaserum to expose her Ministry blackmail
Convincing Peeves to flood her office with permanent corridors
Setting Hagrid's Blast-Ended Skrewts loose in her classroom
context: Umbridge had insulted the centaurs as 'filthy half-breeds', and the Forest's herd carries her off after Hermione lures her in with a story that Dumbledore hid a weapon there. Umbridge appears again in Deathly Hallows persecuting Muggle-borns at the Ministry, where Harry stuns her and takes Slytherin's locket from her.

question: Steve Rogers, a frail young man from Brooklyn, volunteers for a secret U.S. Army project run out of a hidden basement lab in Captain America: The First Avenger (2011). A kindly German-born scientist gives him a super-soldier serum that turns him into a super-strong hero. Right after, a Hydra spy shoots the scientist dead so his formula can never be made again. What is the scientist's name?
context: Stanley Tucci played Erskine. The serum's formula dies with him — which is why Hulk (gamma) and Iron Man (technology) become the closest other 'super' Avengers. Erskine had previously experimented on Johann Schmidt (the Red Skull) with an imperfect version that left Schmidt deformed. The serum amplifies a man's character.

question: Joss Whedon's The Avengers (2012) drops the alien Chitauri army onto Manhattan through a swirling rift in the sky, torn open by the glowing cube called the Tesseract. The film's horned villain carries a blue-tipped weapon of his own, and one of the six Infinity gems lies hidden inside it. What is the weapon, and which gem does it hide?
answer: Loki's scepter, with the Mind Stone inside
choices: Loki's scepter, with the Mind Stone inside
Loki's scepter, with the Power Stone inside
Loki's dagger, with the Space Stone inside
Loki's dagger, with the Reality Stone inside
context: Erik Selvig's device on Stark Tower uses the Tesseract, the Space Stone in disguise, to open the portal, and Black Widow closes it with Loki's scepter. The Mind Stone inside the scepter later gives life to Vision.

question: James Gunn's 2014 film gives Star-Lord's ragtag team of space heroes a giant walking, talking tree-alien, voiced by Vin Diesel, who can speak only the same three words over and over. At the climax he sacrifices himself to save his friends, and he is later regrown from a cutting into a tiny dancing sapling in a flower pot. What is the tree-alien's name?
context: Groot first appeared in Tales to Astonish #13 (November 1960) as a one-off alien menace. Vin Diesel recorded 'I am Groot' in many languages for the film's foreign releases.

question: Baron Strucker experiments on twins from Sokovia, Wanda and Pietro Maximoff, with the Mind Stone in Avengers: Age of Ultron. Fox holds the X-Men rights, so the film cannot call the twins mutants, but it can use their comic-book codenames. What are those codenames?
context: Marvel had a complicated rights situation with Fox's X-Men franchise. Fox could call them 'mutants'; Marvel could not. Fox's X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014) also featured Quicksilver, played by Evan Peters. Aaron Taylor-Johnson played Quicksilver in Age of Ultron; the character dies saving Hawkeye and a Sokovian child.

question: Tony Stark and Steve Rogers send their teams against each other at Berlin Airport in Captain America: Civil War (2016), the film that brings Black Panther and Tom Holland's Spider-Man into the series. The two men end up in a private fight in Siberia. What does Tony learn there that destroys his alliance with Cap?
answer: Bucky (the Winter Soldier) murdered Tony's parents on Hydra's orders in 1991
choices: Bucky (the Winter Soldier) murdered Tony's parents on Hydra's orders in 1991
Cap had secretly served Hydra ever since the end of the Second World War
Zemo had built the Winter Soldier program for Hydra with his own hands
S.H.I.E.L.D. had killed Tony's father to seize the Howling Commandos' files
context: Helmut Zemo (Daniel Bruhl) engineers the whole conflict out of grief for his family, killed in Sokovia in Age of Ultron. The 1991 footage of Bucky killing Howard and Maria Stark comes from Hydra's archives, and Zemo's plan is to make Tony watch it with Cap beside him. Cap admits he knew.

question: Stephen Strange, a world-famous neurosurgeon, brilliant, wealthy and unbearably arrogant, smashes his hands in a car crash and loses his career in Doctor Strange (2016). Desperate, he travels to Kamar-Taj in Nepal to study sorcery under a master called the Ancient One. When enemies attack him in the New York Sanctum Sanctorum, one enchanted relic there chooses him and helps him fight when he cannot. What is this relic?
context: The Cloak of Levitation is sentient and chooses Strange during the fight in the New York Sanctum. The Eye of Agamotto holds the Time Stone, which he uses in the film's climax to trap Dormammu in a loop: 'Dormammu, I've come to bargain.'

question: T'Challa takes the throne of Wakanda, a hidden high-tech African kingdom, when the old king dies in Black Panther (2018). Then a fierce American challenger appears, Erik Killmonger, a former U.S. special-forces soldier, who reveals he is T'Challa's cousin, born abroad and long exiled, and fights him for the crown. Which actor plays Killmonger?
context: Coogler had previously directed Jordan in Fruitvale Station (2013) and Creed (2015). Erik Stevens, called Killmonger, grew up in Oakland, the city where Coogler grew up and where the Black Panther Party was founded in 1966.

question: Two longtime partners, a Russian-trained super-spy and a bow-wielding S.H.I.E.L.D. archer, reach Vormir during the 'time heist' of Avengers: Endgame (2019), when the Avengers go after the six Infinity Stones at points in their own past. Both volunteer to die for the Soul Stone. Who actually makes the sacrifice?
choices: Both at once (the Red Skull permitting two souls)
Neither (they trick the Stone into accepting Loki's earlier death)
context: Natasha and Clint struggle over who gets to make the sacrifice, both believing themselves more expendable. Natasha wins the fight and falls. Black Widow got her own film in 2021.

question: Bob Kane signed the first Batman story in 1939 and took full credit for the character until he died in 1998. His overlooked co-creator had actually written that story, given it the cape-and-cowl look that replaced Kane's ski-mask sketches, named Bruce Wayne, made up Commissioner Gordon and supplied the orphan backstory. The publisher finally added his credit in 2015. Who was this co-creator?
context: Finger died poor in his Manhattan apartment in January 1974. Jerry Robinson, an early Batman artist who had a hand in creating the Joker, spent decades campaigning for Finger's recognition. The 2017 documentary Batman & Bill traces the long fight by Finger's family and Marc Tyler Nobleman to get the credit added.

question: The crime boss Kingpin learns Daredevil's secret identity in Frank Miller's 1986 story arc 'Born Again' and ruins Matt Murdock step by step: his money, his home, everything. Broken and half-dead, Matt is nursed back to health by a kind Catholic nun. What is her name?
context: Born Again ran in Daredevil #227–233 with David Mazzucchelli on art. The story is widely considered one of the greatest superhero narratives ever published. The Netflix Daredevil show (2015–18) drew heavily from this run; Joanne Whalley played Sister Maggie in season three. Miller and Mazzucchelli followed Born Again with Batman: Year One in 1987.

question: Alan Moore first pitched Watchmen using heroes his publisher had just bought from a folded rival called Charlton. The publisher blocked him because it still wanted those heroes in its own books, so Moore made stand-in characters instead. Which Charlton hero inspired Rorschach?
context: Rorschach is Moore's deconstruction of The Question, a Steve Ditko hero who shared Ditko's Randian objectivist outlook. Dr. Manhattan is Captain Atom; Nite Owl is Blue Beetle; The Comedian is Peacemaker; Silk Spectre is Nightshade; Ozymandias is Thunderbolt. DC's Charlton heroes were rolled into the post-Crisis DC universe in 1986. Watchmen ran for 12 issues, September 1986 to October 1987.

question: William Shakespeare and his acting troupe perform A Midsummer Night's Dream on a hillside for a real audience of fairy folk, led by Titania and Oberon, in issue #19 of Neil Gaiman's The Sandman. It is still the only comic book to have won the award it took home in 1991. Which award was it?
answer: The World Fantasy Award for Short Fiction (1991)
choices: The World Fantasy Award for Short Fiction (1991)
The Hugo Award for Best Short Story (1991)
The Nebula Award for Best Novelette (1991)
context: Charles Vess drew the issue and Steve Oliff coloured it; the prize, in the Short Fiction category, went to Gaiman and Vess together.

question: Matthew Vaughn's 2010 film of Kick-Ass made an 11-year-old actress a star, playing a small, foul-mouthed, knife-wielding vigilante in a purple wig. Mark Millar and John Romita Jr.'s 2008 comic followed a New York teenager who became a real-life costumed vigilante with no powers at all. What was the actress's character called?
context: Chloë Grace Moretz played Hit-Girl at 11, and Nicolas Cage played her father, Big Daddy, in an Adam West Batman voice. Millar's comic ran for eight issues from Marvel's Icon imprint.

question: Chuck Dixon, Doug Moench and Graham Nolan created a hulking villain, pumped full of a steroid called Venom, expressly to defeat Batman. In the Knightfall storyline he broke Batman's back in Batman #497, from July 1993. What is his name?
context: Bane grows up in the prison of Peña Duro on the fictional Caribbean island of Santa Prisca, and he is as clever as he is strong. Tom Hardy played him in The Dark Knight Rises (2012), and Robert 'Jeep' Swenson in Batman & Robin (1997).

question: A gun-for-hire comes out of an alien parasite incident able to read minds and see through walls in Garth Ennis and John McCrea's Hitman, which ran for 60 issues at DC, from 1996 to 2001. What is the character's name?
context: Tommy is a Gotham hitman, first seen in 1993 in a Bloodlines crossover annual. The series is famous for issue #34, 'Of Thee I Sing', a heartfelt Superman story in which Tommy meets Superman on a rooftop.

question: Brian Michael Bendis rebooted Spider-Man for a new audience with Ultimate Spider-Man in 2000, with Mark Bagley on art. In 2011's Ultimate Comics: Spider-Man he introduced a Black Latino teenager who takes over the mantle. What is the new Spider-Man's name?
context: Miles debuted in Ultimate Fallout #4 (August 2011), co-created by Bendis and the artist Sara Pichelli. He became the lead of the 2018 animated film Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, voiced by Shameik Moore, and he can stun foes with a bio-electric 'venom blast'.

question: Bill Watterson turned down a deal that would have earned him hundreds of millions of dollars, and every other cartoonist was baffled. His newspaper strip Calvin and Hobbes ran for ten years, from 1985 to 1995, about a wild six-year-old boy and a stuffed tiger who came to life whenever the two of them were alone. What did Watterson refuse to do?
answer: License the characters for merchandise (no plush Hobbes, no shirts, no commercials)
choices: License the characters for merchandise (no plush Hobbes, no shirts, no commercials)
Allow Sunday strips to expand beyond the standard four-panel grid
Permit foreign-language translations after the 1991 Italian incident
Hand off the strip to a successor cartoonist after his 1989 sabbatical
context: Watterson believed licensing would cheapen the strip: Hobbes had to stay ambiguous, real tiger or stuffed toy, which no plush on a shop shelf could manage. The ubiquitous Calvin-peeing decals on pickup trucks are all unlicensed, illegal bootlegs.

question: Georges Remi read his initials, R.G., in French and signed himself Hergé. The Belgian cartoonist's Tintin comics ran from 1929 to 1976, and Tintin's white fox terrier goes by 'Milou' in the original French. What is the dog's name in English translations?
context: Hergé's Tintin has been translated into more than 70 languages and sold over 200 million copies. Steven Spielberg directed the 2011 motion-capture film The Adventures of Tintin, starring Jamie Bell. After the war Hergé was criticised for having published in Le Soir under the Nazi occupation.

question: Berkeley Breathed won the Pulitzer Prize for editorial cartooning in 1987 while drawing his newspaper strip Bloom County. Two of its characters became merchandise hits: Opus, a gentle wide-eyed penguin, and a scruffy, tongue-lolling character whose face ended up on T-shirts, mugs and plush toys. Who was that second character?
context: Breathed introduced Bill in June 1982 as a parody of Garfield. His cry of 'Ack! Thbbft!' became a catchphrase, and he ran for president in 1984 and 1988 on the Meadow Party ticket. Breathed ended Bloom County in 1989, drew Outland (1989-1995) and Opus (2003-2008), then revived Bloom County on Facebook in 2015.

question: Rowling's agent spent a year trying to sell the first Harry Potter book, and publisher after publisher turned it down. At Bloomsbury, the small London house that finally took it, the chief executive carried the opening chapters home and handed them to someone else first, who reported that they beat anything else around. Who was that first reader?
context: The reader was Alice Newton, daughter of Bloomsbury's chief executive Nigel Newton. Bloomsbury paid Rowling an advance of £2,500 and printed just 500 hardbacks, 300 of them for libraries.

question: Harry Potter finds the Mirror of Erised in his first year at Hogwarts and reads the inscription on its frame: 'Erised stra ehru oyt ube cafru oyt on wohsi.' Read backward, the letters make an English sentence. What does it say?
answer: I show not your face but your heart's desire
choices: I show not your face but your heart's desire
Mirror of dreams, show me my heart's hidden joy
Within these depths a wish is granted unseen
What you seek the most you shall not find unspoken
context: 'Erised' is 'Desire' reversed. Dumbledore tells Harry: 'It does not do to dwell on dreams and forget to live.' The Philosopher's Stone is hidden inside the Mirror at the climax — only someone who wants to find the Stone but not use it can retrieve it. This is the test Harry passes and Quirrell/Voldemort fails.

question: Rowling built the four houses of Hogwarts around elements and virtues, giving Ravenclaw air and wit. Each founder, a thousand years ago, also left behind a personal relic that later became a treasured heirloom. Which element, virtue and heirloom belong to Hufflepuff?
answer: Earth, loyalty, and Helga Hufflepuff's gold-and-badger-engraved cup
choices: Earth, loyalty, and Helga Hufflepuff's gold-and-badger-engraved cup
Wood, patience, and Helga Hufflepuff's oak-and-honey-bee-engraved horn
Stone, kindness, and Helga Hufflepuff's silver-and-mole-engraved chalice
Mist, humility, and Helga Hufflepuff's pewter-and-fox-engraved goblet
context: The cup is one of Voldemort's seven Horcruxes, stolen from Hepzibah Smith, an elderly witch whom young Tom Riddle murdered. Bellatrix Lestrange hides it in her vault at Gringotts, and Harry, Ron and Hermione break in for it in Deathly Hallows.

question: Peter Pettigrew kills Cedric Diggory on his master's command in a graveyard in Little Hangleton in Goblet of Fire. The Dark Lord's revival in the same scene needs three ritual ingredients. The first is bone of the father, unknowingly taken. The second is flesh of the servant, willingly given, and Pettigrew gives his own hand. What is the third?
answer: Blood of the enemy, forcibly taken (from Harry, with a silver dagger)
choices: Blood of the enemy, forcibly taken (from Harry, with a silver dagger)
Tear of the betrayer, freely shed (from Bellatrix, atop the cauldron)
Hair of the rival, secretly clipped (from Snape, during the gathering)
Tongue of the prophet, unwilling spoken (from Trelawney's grand-niece)
context: Voldemort uses Harry's blood because it carries Lily's protective magic. The act binds Harry and Voldemort more deeply — Harry survives Voldemort's killing curse in the Forest in Book 7 partly because Voldemort's body contains Harry's blood, anchoring Harry to life. Pettigrew sacrifices his own hand and Voldemort restores it as a silver hand of immense strength.

question: Mad-Eye Moody, a scarred old ex-Auror, comes to Hogwarts to teach Defense Against the Dark Arts in Goblet of Fire, and he quietly steers Harry Potter toward victory in the Triwizard Tournament. At the very end of the book this Moody proves to be a hidden Death Eater, who has stuffed the real man inside a magical trunk and drunk Polyjuice Potion every hour all year. Who is the imposter?
context: Barty Crouch Jr. is a Death Eater whose Ministry-official father (Barty Crouch Sr.) had imprisoned him in the family home under the Imperius Curse after Azkaban. Voldemort frees him to engineer Harry's delivery to the graveyard. Brendan Gleeson played Moody; David Tennant played Crouch Jr. in the 2005 film. Crouch Jr. is later given the Dementor's Kiss by Cornelius Fudge, who refuses to believe Voldemort has returned.

question: Cornelius Fudge sends Dolores Umbridge to Hogwarts as High Inquisitor in Order of the Phoenix. Her detention quill uses the writer's blood as ink and carves 'I must not tell lies' into the back of Harry Potter's hand, leaving a scar that stays for the rest of the series. What has Rowling said Umbridge is modelled on?
answer: A blend of people Rowling had met, among them an instructor she disliked on sight
choices: A blend of people Rowling had met, among them an instructor she disliked on sight
Margaret Thatcher in her years as Britain's education secretary
Mary Whitehouse, the British media-decency campaigner of the 1970s and 80s
Enid Blyton's headmistress Miss Grayling from the Malory Towers series
context: Imelda Staunton played Umbridge in the 2007 film. Rowling has written that the real instructor was neither sadistic nor toad-like, and that the two disliked each other on sight for no reason she ever learned. Umbridge returns in Deathly Hallows as a Ministry official under Voldemort's puppet regime.

question: Filch hates Peeves, the Hogwarts poltergeist who plagues students and even staff, but only two figures at the school can keep the poltergeist in line. One of them is Dumbledore. Who is the other?
answer: The Bloody Baron (the Slytherin House ghost)
choices: The Bloody Baron (the Slytherin House ghost)
Nearly Headless Nick (the Gryffindor House ghost)
The Grey Lady (the Ravenclaw House ghost)
The Fat Friar (the Hufflepuff House ghost)
context: The Bloody Baron's bloodstains came from killing the Grey Lady (Helena Ravenclaw) in life — a backstory revealed in Deathly Hallows. Peeves was cut from all eight films. Rik Mayall (of The Young Ones) filmed scenes as Peeves for the first film, but all were ultimately cut by Chris Columbus. Mayall publicly groused about it for years.

question: Ron Weasley takes his turn wearing Slytherin's locket on the run with Harry Potter and Hermione in Deathly Hallows, and its corrupting pull drives him to abandon them. He stays away for weeks before returning. What does he use to find his way back?
answer: The Deluminator left to him by Dumbledore in his will
choices: The Deluminator left to him by Dumbledore in his will
A Howler from his mother delivered through Apparition
Hermione's enchanted DA Galleon she kept on her wrist
The Marauder's Map redirected through the Floo Network
context: The Deluminator, Dumbledore's silver lighter-like device that sucks the light from a room, lets Ron hear Hermione say his name and sends a ball of light to lead him back. In his will Dumbledore left Ron the Deluminator, Hermione The Tales of Beedle the Bard, and Harry the first Snitch he caught and the Sword of Gryffindor, which the Ministry would not hand over.

question: The Dark Lord kills Snape in the Shrieking Shack during the Battle of Hogwarts to claim mastery of the mightiest wand ever made. He believes Snape is its master because Snape killed Dumbledore. Why is the Dark Lord wrong about who really mastered the wand?
answer: Draco disarmed Dumbledore atop the Tower before Snape's curse, then Harry later disarmed Draco at Malfoy Manor
choices: Draco disarmed Dumbledore atop the Tower before Snape's curse, then Harry later disarmed Draco at Malfoy Manor
Dumbledore had quietly passed mastery to Aberforth in a sealed will days before the Tower confrontation
Snape's killing curse was a mercy killing that Dumbledore requested, which voids any wand-mastery transfer
Gellert Grindelwald never actually lost mastery of the Wand to Dumbledore back in their 1945 confrontation
context: The Elder Wand's mastery passes when its current owner is disarmed, not when killed. Draco's disarming of Dumbledore on the Astronomy Tower in Half-Blood Prince — moments before Snape's killing curse — quietly transferred mastery to Draco. Harry's later disarming of Draco at Malfoy Manor (Deathly Hallows) transferred it to Harry. When Voldemort fires the killing curse in the climactic duel, his own spell rebounds off the Wand and kills him.

question: James and Lily Potter switched their Secret-Keeper at the last minute, from Sirius to a new one. The Dark Lord came for them on Halloween of 1981, killed them both and left baby Harry with his lightning scar. Who was the Secret-Keeper who betrayed them?
choices: Caradoc Dearborn (an early Order of the Phoenix member)
context: The Fidelius Charm hides a location/secret in a single chosen person; even those who already knew can no longer find it. Sirius convinced James and Lily that swapping him for the seemingly weak Peter would fool Voldemort. Peter immediately betrayed them. Sirius then went after Peter; Peter cut off his own finger, blew up a street, killed 12 Muggles, and transformed into Scabbers — leaving Sirius framed for the murders.

question: Obadiah Stane, played by a bald and bearded Jeff Bridges, has been quietly selling Stark weapons to terrorists behind Tony Stark's back in the 2008 film that kicked off the Marvel Cinematic Universe. At the climax this father-figure business partner builds his own giant, hulking gray copy of Tony's red-and-gold armor and attacks him in the Stark Industries parking lot. What is Stane's oversized suit called?
context: Stane reverse-engineers the original Mark I suit Tony built in the cave. The Iron Monger is roughly twice Iron Man's size. Bridges shaved his head for the role.

question: Ben Kingsley plays the Mandarin in Iron Man 3 (2013) as a terrifying bin-Laden-styled mastermind, the comics archnemesis foreshadowed through the first two films by the Ten Rings terrorist group. Halfway through the film, Kingsley's Mandarin turns out to be something else entirely. What is he actually?
answer: A drug-addled British actor named Trevor Slattery, hired by the real villain to be a public face
choices: A drug-addled British actor named Trevor Slattery, hired by the real villain to be a public face
An AIM holographic projection driven from a hidden submarine docked off the Miami coastline
Aldrich Killian's hallucination created by the Extremis virus injected into Tony Stark's bloodstream
A shapeshifting Skrull infiltrator using a technology that would later be revealed in Captain Marvel
context: The real villain is Aldrich Killian (Guy Pearce), CEO of Advanced Idea Mechanics (AIM), who hired Slattery as the public face of the Mandarin while he experimented with the Extremis virus. Iron Man 3 was Shane Black's directorial entry into the MCU, his first feature since Kiss Kiss Bang Bang (2005). The film angered some comics fans furious about the Mandarin twist; a 2014 Marvel One-Shot (All Hail the King) walked back the implication that the 'real' Mandarin doesn't exist.

question: The Avengers accidentally give birth to a synthetic android in Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015), a being with a yellow stone set in his forehead who calls himself Vision. The actor who plays him has been the voice of Tony Stark's computer since 2008. Which British actor is he?
context: Bettany had voiced JARVIS (Tony's AI butler, 'Just A Rather Very Intelligent System') since 2008's Iron Man. Paul Bettany is married to the actress Jennifer Connelly.

question: A gatekeeper on the remote planet Vormir demands a soul-for-soul sacrifice for the Soul Stone in Avengers: Infinity War (2018). The Mad Titan, collecting the six Infinity Stones one by one, has come for this one. Who does the Titan sacrifice?
answer: Gamora, his adopted daughter, by throwing her off a cliff
choices: Gamora, his adopted daughter, by throwing her off a cliff
Nebula, his adopted daughter, in a duel-to-the-death ritual
Ebony Maw, his most loyal Black Order servant, with a spell
Drax's daughter, returned to him through Ravager negotiations
context: Zoe Saldana played Gamora. Endgame later resurrects a 2014-era Gamora through the time heist. The Red Skull, banished from Earth by the Tesseract's Space Stone in Captain America: The First Avenger (1945), guards the Soul Stone on Vormir. Ross Marquand voices Red Skull (Hugo Weaving, who played him in 2011, declined). The 'soul for a soul' rule pays off again with Black Widow's Endgame sacrifice.

question: Brie Larson's Carol Danvers, a US Air Force pilot, gains photon-blast powers from the Tesseract's Space Stone in Captain Marvel (2019), a film set mostly in 1995. The story turns on the Skrulls, green shapeshifting aliens, and it contradicts comics canon about them. What does the film reveal about the Skrulls?
answer: They are sympathetic refugees fleeing genocide, not the evil empire they appear to be, and the Kree are the true villains
choices: They are sympathetic refugees fleeing genocide, not the evil empire they appear to be, and the Kree are the true villains
They are revealed to be the source of all human mutation genes throughout history, retconning the X-Men's mutants
They are revealed to have created the Asgardians using genetic engineering, retconning the entire Bifrost system
They are revealed to be Phyla-Vell variants from another dimension entirely, brought through by Captain Mar-Vell
context: Ben Mendelsohn plays Talos, a Skrull refugee leader, with cheek-pouch prosthetics. The Kree — purple/blue antagonists in Guardians of the Galaxy and elsewhere — are framed as the genocidal imperialists. Jude Law plays Yon-Rogg, Carol's mentor-turned-traitor in the Kree Starforce. The de-aging tech used on Samuel L. Jackson for the 1995 Fury sequences was a milestone in MCU VFX.

question: Steve Rogers fights an alternate-timeline version of himself during the 'time heist' of Avengers: Endgame (2019), after he, Iron Man, Hulk and Ant-Man travel to New York in 2012. The fight ends when the present-day Cap whispers two words that throw the past Cap off-guard. What does he whisper?
context: Present-day Cap says 'Hail Hydra' earlier, in the elevator, to walk off with Loki's scepter. The news that Bucky is alive stuns 2012 Cap, who still believes Bucky died in 1945, long enough for present-day Cap to win the fight.

question: Michael Keaton plays a salvager who illicitly builds tech from Battle of New York debris into an armored suit in Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017). Jon Watts's film is Tom Holland's first solo MCU outing, after his debut in Captain America: Civil War (2016). What is Keaton's character called in the comics?
context: Keaton's casting was a meta-joke: he had played Batman (1989, 1992) and, in the 2014 Best Picture winner Birdman, an actor famous for a winged superhero. Adrian Toomes first appeared in Amazing Spider-Man #2 in 1963. Homecoming was a Sony-Marvel co-production made possible by the 2015 deal that brought Spider-Man into the MCU after Sony's two Andrew Garfield films.

question: Joe Shuster drew the Man of Steel lifting a green car over his head while terrified onlookers fled, for the cover of Action Comics #1 in April 1938. A copy graded 8.5 by the Certified Guaranty Company sold at Heritage Auctions on April 4, 2024, for a record-shattering amount. What was the final price?
context: No comic book had ever sold for more. A copy graded 9.0 had sold on eBay for about $3.2 million in 2014. Action Comics #1 cost ten cents, and about 200,000 copies were printed.

question: Jack Kirby left Marvel for DC in 1970 after a fight over credit and ownership, and there he built a huge cosmic saga across four titles known as the Fourth World. Two warring planets sat at its heart: Apokolips, ruled by Darkseid, and what paradise world?
choices: Themyscira (ruled by Queen Hippolyta of the Amazons)
Olympus Major (ruled by Zeus of the New Olympians)
Krypton II (ruled by the survivors of the original Krypton)
context: Kirby's Fourth World ran from 1970 across New Gods, Forever People, Mister Miracle and Superman's Pal Jimmy Olsen. Steppenwolf and the Parademons come from the saga too, and Darkseid became the villain of Final Crisis (2008) and of Zack Snyder's Justice League. Kirby went back to Marvel in the mid-1970s.

question: A godlike alien known as the Beyonder forces the Avengers, the X-Men, Doctor Doom and Magneto to fight each other for his amusement in a huge twelve-issue Marvel crossover, on a stitched-together patchwork planet called Battleworld. The crossover became the template every big publisher would copy for decades. What was it called?
context: Mike Zeck and John Beatty drew most of Secret Wars. The twelve issues were tied to a Mattel toy line, much as DC's Super Powers comics were tied to Kenner's toys. Spider-Man also got his black costume in Secret Wars, the suit that later became Venom.

question: Steve Ditko quietly walked away from The Amazing Spider-Man in 1966, the book he had co-created and drawn beside Marvel writer Stan Lee. The two men had made another iconic hero together, one who wears a red Cloak of Levitation and carries the all-seeing Eye of Agamotto around his neck. Which hero?
context: Ditko died in 2018, aged 90. He lived a famously private life, refusing interviews and publishing essays only through small presses, and his Objectivism led him to create Mr. A (1967), a hero of black-and-white morality, outside Marvel. John Romita Sr. took over Spider-Man and softened its look. Ditko co-created Doctor Strange in Strange Tales #110 (1963).

question: Alan Moore built issue #5 of Watchmen, 'Fearful Symmetry,' as a literal mirror: the panels of the first half were reflected in the second, each page mirroring its opposite, with the centerfold on pages 14 and 15 as the fulcrum. He took the chapter title from a William Blake poem. What is the poem called?
context: The opening lines: 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night; / What immortal hand or eye, / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?' Each Watchmen issue closes with a literary epigraph from sources including Nietzsche, Genesis, Einstein, Carl Jung, and Bob Dylan. Moore is famously meticulous about issue construction; he wrote full prose-style scripts running 40+ pages per issue for Dave Gibbons.

question: Mike Mignola left Marvel and DC, after more than a decade as a high-profile interior artist, and brought out his own demon hero at Dark Horse Comics in March 1994. The comics' mythos gives that hero a birth-name quite unlike the one on the cover. What is his true name?
context: Anung Un Rama is said to mean 'and upon his brow is set a crown of flame.' Ron Perlman played Hellboy in Guillermo del Toro's 2004 and 2008 films, and David Harbour in the 2019 reboot.

question: Frank Castle comes home from Vietnam a decorated Marine and takes his wife and two children on a picnic in New York. They stumble onto a gangland execution, and the mobsters gun the family down to leave no witnesses. Only Frank survives, and he becomes the Punisher. Where was the picnic?
context: The killing in Central Park is the Punisher's origin, first told in the 1970s. Garth Ennis later wrote a long, brutal run on the character for Marvel.

question: Lynn Varley, married to Frank Miller from 1986 to 2005, painted the colors on some of the most famous books he wrote and drew. Miller made his name on gritty crime and superhero comics, and Varley colored several of his books. Which pair of Miller books carries her colors?
choices: Sin City: The Hard Goodbye (1991) and Sin City: A Dame to Kill For (1993)
Elektra: Assassin (1986) with Bill Sienkiewicz and Ronin (1983)
Daredevil: Man Without Fear (1993) and Batman: Year One (1987)
context: Varley also colored Miller's Ronin and Elektra Lives Again, and her watercolors give The Dark Knight Returns its look; she later colored the backgrounds of the 2007 film of 300.

question: Ron Weasley and Hermione sneak away together in Deathly Hallows to finish off Helga Hufflepuff's golden cup, one of the seven objects that hold pieces of the Dark Lord's soul. It had been hidden in a wizarding bank vault. Hermione does the deed. What weapon does she use?
answer: A basilisk fang from the Chamber of Secrets
choices: A basilisk fang from the Chamber of Secrets
Godric Gryffindor's Sword pulled from the Sorting Hat
Fiendfyre conjured by Vincent Crabbe in the Room of Requirement
Fire from the half-blind dragon that guards Gringotts
context: Ron opens the Chamber of Secrets by mimicking the Parseltongue he heard Harry use on the locket, and he and Hermione take fangs from the dead basilisk. The Sword of Gryffindor, which took in basilisk venom in Chamber of Secrets, destroys the locket; Fiendfyre destroys the diadem when Crabbe's curse runs out of control; and Neville kills Nagini with the Sword.

question: Harry Potter gets hold of a used Potions textbook in Half-Blood Prince, and its margin notes improve every potion he brews. The previous owner also wrote in spells of his own invention, among them Sectumsempra, a slashing curse that nearly kills Draco Malfoy when Harry uses it in a bathroom duel. The book is signed 'Property of the Half-Blood Prince.' Whose book was it?
context: Snape's father, Tobias, was a Muggle and his mother, Eileen Prince, a witch: the 'Half-Blood Prince' joins her surname to his mixed blood. Harry hides the book in the Room of Requirement at the end of book six.

question: Walburga Black shrieks from her portrait at 12 Grimmauld Place, the ancestral London townhouse of the Black family and now the headquarters of the Order of the Phoenix. Her son Sirius's nightmarish childhood home is full of family tapestries and dark-arts artifacts. A disgruntled, half-mad old house-elf still serves the place, and at first he betrays the Order. What is the elf's name?
context: Kreacher's loyalty to the Black family, above all to Sirius's younger brother Regulus, explains his bitterness toward Sirius, who detested the family. Voldemort once borrowed Kreacher to test the defences of the sea cave where he hid a locket; Regulus later went there with the elf, drank the potion himself and ordered Kreacher to swap the lockets and destroy the real one. Dobby and Winky appear in earlier books.

question: Garrick Ollivander measures eleven-year-old Harry Potter for a wand in Diagon Alley, and box after box fails until a holly wand sends sparks flying from its tip. Ollivander calls it curious: this wand's brother gave Harry his scar. What do the two wands share?
answer: A tail feather from the same phoenix
choices: A tail feather from the same phoenix
A tail hair from the same unicorn
A heartstring from the same dragon
A branch from the same holly tree
context: Both cores came from Fawkes, Dumbledore's phoenix, who gave Ollivander just two feathers. The twin cores are why the wands lock together in the Goblet of Fire graveyard, the Priori Incantatem effect. John Hurt played Ollivander in the films.

question: Hermione casts a memory charm on her own parents, two London dentists, in Deathly Hallows, and sends them off so that no one can torture them for her location. She erases their memory of having a daughter and gives them new identities. What new names does she give them?
context: Hermione plants in her parents' minds a wish to move to Australia, meaning to find them and lift the charm after the war; Rowling has said she did. Deathly Hallows Part 1 (2010) opens on Hermione casting the charm and vanishing from the family photographs.

question: James Potter spent years at Hogwarts on very hard magic with Sirius and Peter, learning to become an Animagus so that the three could keep Lupin company on full-moon nights. What did each of them have to keep in his mouth for a full month without a break?
answer: A leaf from the Mandrake plant
choices: A leaf from the Mandrake plant
A leaf from the Aconite plant (wolfsbane)
A leaf from the Belladonna plant (nightshade)
A leaf from the Mistletoe plant (Druidic origin)
context: If the leaf comes out before the month is up, the wizard must start again, and the full ritual ends with a potion drunk during a lightning storm. The Marauders managed the change in their fifth year, after about three years of work. McGonagall, a tabby cat, is a registered Animagus; Rita Skeeter, a beetle, is an unregistered one whom Hermione exposes in Goblet of Fire.

question: Harry Potter survives a killing curse in the Forest near the end of Deathly Hallows, and the next chapter finds him at King's Cross in a kind of dream, in conversation with Dumbledore. What does Harry see lying under a bench there?
answer: A flayed, child-sized creature that represents the broken remnant of Voldemort's soul
choices: A flayed, child-sized creature that represents the broken remnant of Voldemort's soul
A silver phoenix feather lying alongside a perfect green basilisk egg
A tarnished mirror reflecting the Forest of Dean's protective enchantments
A torn fragment of the Resurrection Stone wrapped in Harry's mother's handkerchief
context: The King's Cross dream-sequence is one of Rowling's most-debated chapters — whether Harry is dead, dreaming, in limbo, or somewhere else. The flayed creature represents the soul-fragment of Voldemort attached to Harry as the seventh Horcrux, now severed. Dumbledore's appearance allows him to explain the entire Hallows-and-Horcruxes plan to Harry. After the conversation, Harry chooses to return to life; the Forbidden Forest scene plays out with Voldemort believing he'd just killed Harry.

question: Jon Favreau gambled on Robert Downey Jr., still a risky hire after his drug arrests, when he made Iron Man (2008) for $140 million. He opened the film on a Stark Industries weapons convoy in Afghanistan, with Tony Stark getting into the lead Humvee and a now-iconic rock song playing. What is the song?
context: Favreau picked Back in Black to signal Tony's rock-star personality at once. The film's score by Ramin Djawadi, later of Game of Thrones, leans on blues-rock guitar in the same vein.

question: The villain of Joss Whedon's The Avengers (2012) forces a frightened gala crowd in Stuttgart to kneel and asks, 'Is not this simpler? Is this not your natural state?' An elderly German man stands up alone in defiance. What line does he deliver, alluding to a specific historical period?
answer: There are always men like you.
choices: There are always men like you.
We have been ruled by tyrants before.
I have stood in stadiums while men like you raved.
You speak with the voice of those we buried.
context: The full exchange: Loki orders the crowd to kneel. An old German man (played by Kenneth Tigar) stands and says 'Not to men like you.' Loki replies 'There are no men like me.' The old man responds 'There are always men like you.' Captain America arrives at the moment Loki is about to execute the old man, deflecting the blast with his shield. The line and shield-arrival sequence is one of the MCU's most-quoted moments.

question: Robert Redford played Alexander Pierce, the senior S.H.I.E.L.D. official of Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014), a film its writers modeled on 1970s political thrillers. He was cast partly as an homage to one of his own: the film in which an intelligence analyst comes back from lunch to find everyone in his office shot dead. Which film?
context: Redford was cast partly as an homage to 1970s thrillers such as Three Days of the Condor, and as a screen legend playing a villain, the way Henry Fonda did in Once Upon a Time in the West. The writers cited The Parallax View, Three Days of the Condor and Marathon Man as models; Kevin Feige named The Parallax View and All the President's Men. Pierce is revealed as a Hydra agent.

question: General Okoye leads the Dora Milaje, shaven-headed women warriors in red armor with spears, in Ryan Coogler's Black Panther (2018). They are the elite bodyguard of young King T'Challa in the hidden nation of Wakanda. The filmmakers based them on a real army of women from history. Which real army was it?
answer: The Agojie of the Kingdom of Dahomey, an all-female military regiment that existed from the 17th to the late 19th century
choices: The Agojie of the Kingdom of Dahomey, an all-female military regiment that existed from the 17th to the late 19th century
The shield-maidens of Viking-age Norway, celebrated in the sagas of the 9th to the 11th centuries
The Nubian Queens' Guard of ancient Meroe, which trained women warriors from the 5th century BC onward
The Carthaginian Women's Auxiliary that defended the city during the Third Punic War, 149-146 BC
context: The Agojie, called the Dahomey Amazons by European writers and also known as the Mino, were disbanded after the French conquest of Dahomey in the 1890s. The 2022 film The Woman King, with Viola Davis, dramatized them. Danai Gurira played Okoye and Florence Kasumba played Ayo, the best-known Dora Milaje of Black Panther.

question: Thor swings into battle to the hammering rock of 'Immigrant Song' in Thor: Ragnarok (2017). Led Zeppelin almost never lets its songs into films, and Marvel chased the rights through the whole production. The director has said one thing finally won the band over. What was it?
answer: Seeing the first cut of the trailer
choices: Seeing the first cut of the trailer
A handwritten letter from Chris Hemsworth
An offer of a cameo for Robert Plant
A day's visit to the set in Australia
context: Marvel's music supervisor Dave Jordan did most of the work on the deal. Taika Waititi said that when the band saw the first cut of the trailer, they understood how perfect the song was for the character. The band also refused any change to the recording, such as an orchestral version, and the song plays both in the opening fight and in the battle for Asgard.

question: The surviving Avengers track the Mad Titan to a small retirement farm on a distant planet in Avengers: Endgame (2019), weeks after he wiped away half of all life with a snap of the Infinity Gauntlet. They hope to seize the Infinity Stones back and undo the Snap. What moment ends the ambush?
answer: Thor decapitating Thanos with Stormbreaker, going for the head this time
choices: Thor decapitating Thanos with Stormbreaker, going for the head this time
Thor binding Thanos in adamantine chains for Doctor Strange to extract Stones
Thor smashing Thanos's gauntlet to destroy the stones before they can be recovered
Thor calling lightning to teleport Thanos back to Vormir where Gamora could be returned
context: Thor's line about going for the head answers his failure in Infinity War, where he drove Stormbreaker into Thanos's chest and Thanos snapped anyway. Thanos had already used the Stones to destroy the Stones, so the ambush wins nothing back.

question: Sam Wilson, the Falcon, contacts Captain America by radio during the portal scene of Avengers: Endgame (2019), as every previously dusted hero returns. His line is a callback to their old running joke from Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014). What does Sam say?
context: 'On your left' is the line Sam used in Winter Soldier when he repeatedly lapped a running Steve Rogers on the National Mall before introducing himself. The Endgame portal-scene callback turns the joke into one of the franchise's most emotional moments — Steve is alone, exhausted, facing Thanos's full army; the radio crackles; the portals open. Co-director Joe Russo has spoken about the line in multiple interviews as a deliberate emotional payoff.

question: Ben Reilly, a clone of Peter Parker made in the 1970s, roams the country for years under an assumed name in Marvel's Clone Saga, which ran across the Spider-Man titles from 1994 to 1996. When he comes back to New York, he puts on a costume of his own and takes a new hero's name. What is it?
context: The Clone Saga grew far beyond its planned length into a two-year crossover that alienated many longtime readers; the writer J.M. DeMatteis has spoken openly about the editorial chaos behind it.

question: Fawkes the phoenix flies down to Harry Potter in Chamber of Secrets, drops him a sword and blinds the giant basilisk. Two books later, in Order of the Phoenix, he appears in the middle of a duel at the Ministry of Magic between Dumbledore and the Dark Lord. He swoops in front of Dumbledore and swallows one spell whole. Which spell?
context: Fawkes swallows the jet of green light whole, bursts into flame and falls to the floor as a small, flightless chick, to be reborn from his ashes.

question: Bilbo leaves a magic gold ring to his young cousin in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings. The cousin learns it is the Dark Lord's One Ring and agrees to carry it to the volcano where it was forged. What is the cousin's name?
context: Frodo is Bilbo's cousin, though he is often called his nephew, and he sets out from the Shire carrying the One Ring. The first volume, The Fellowship of the Ring, was published in July 1954.

question: Bilbo Baggins sneaks into the Lonely Mountain in J.R.R. Tolkien's tale to see a giant fire-breathing dragon who long ago drove out the dwarves. The beast sleeps curled over their stolen treasure, a mountain of gold coins, jewels and armor. What is the dragon's name?
context: Smaug captured the Lonely Mountain (Erebor) and its dwarven gold-hoard centuries before The Hobbit begins. Tolkien drew Smaug himself for the book's illustrations. Benedict Cumberbatch voiced Smaug in Peter Jackson's 2013 film adaptation.

question: A lonely man sits up late one December night grieving his lost love in Edgar Allan Poe's 1845 poem The Raven. A black raven lands on a marble bust above the chamber door and croaks the same single word in reply to the man's questions. What word does the raven say?
context: The Raven appeared in the New York Evening Mirror on January 29, 1845. It made Poe instantly famous but earned him only $9. The bust the raven perches on is of Pallas Athena. The narrator's lost love is named Lenore.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs's 1912 magazine story leaves an English baby alone in the African jungle after his parents die. A gentle female ape finds the orphan and raises him as her own child, and he grows up climbing trees, wrestling leopards and swinging on vines. What is this jungle-raised hero's name?
context: Tarzan of the Apes debuted in All-Story Magazine in October 1912. His ape name Tarzan means White-Skin in the language of the great apes Burroughs invented. He inherits the title Lord Greystoke from his father.

question: A mysterious crime-fighter prowls the night through the American pulp magazines of the 1930s, in a slouch hat, red scarf and long black cloak, with twin .45 automatic pistols under his coat. His hit weekly radio show opens with a chilling laugh and the line 'Who knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men?' Who is this pulp hero?
context: The Shadow debuted in Detective Story Hour radio in 1930 and as a pulp character in 1931 (written mostly by Walter Gibson under the pen name Maxwell Grant). The radio tagline finished: 'The Shadow knows!'

question: Lovecraft told a 1928 short story through a dead professor's notes and a sailor's diary, and in it he invented the most famous monster of cosmic horror: a green horror the size of a mountain, with an octopus-like face and huge dragon wings. What is the creature called?
context: Cthulhu debuted in The Call of Cthulhu in the February 1928 issue of Weird Tales. The sunken city is called R'lyeh. Lovecraft admitted no human mouth could properly pronounce the name; he suggested 'Khlûl'-hloo.'

question: Robert Howard, writing in the 1930s, sends a black-haired warrior out of the cold northern land of Cimmeria. He wanders the ancient Hyborian world as a thief, a pirate and a mercenary before he seizes a crown and rules the kingdom of Aquilonia. What is this Cimmerian warrior-king's name?
context: Conan first appeared in Weird Tales in December 1932 in the story 'The Phoenix on the Sword', and Howard went on writing him until his death in 1936. Arnold Schwarzenegger played him in the 1982 John Milius film Conan the Barbarian.

question: Raymond Chandler sent a tough, wisecracking private detective down the mean streets of Los Angeles in a rumpled trench coat, in his 1939 novel The Big Sleep. The character became the model for the hard-boiled detective in every book and movie that followed. What is this private eye's name?
context: Marlowe appears in seven Chandler novels. Humphrey Bogart played him in the 1946 film of The Big Sleep. Chandler's other novels include Farewell My Lovely (1940), The Long Goodbye (1953), and The Lady in the Lake (1943).

question: Hari Seldon, a mathematician in Isaac Asimov's book series, watches a vast Galactic Empire begin to collapse thousands of years in the future. He invents psychohistory, math that predicts the behavior of huge populations, to shorten the coming dark age from 30,000 years to just 1,000. What is the series called?
context: Asimov began the Foundation stories in Astounding Science Fiction in May 1942. The mathematician's name is Hari Seldon; his predictive science is called psychohistory. The original trilogy was published as books between 1951 and 1953.

question: A young noble named Paul Atreides is thrown into the deserts of a distant planet in Frank Herbert's 1965 science-fiction novel. Giant sandworms hundreds of feet long slide unseen beneath the sand, and a rare spice called melange lets starship pilots fold space and jump between stars. What is the book called?
context: Herbert based the desert ecology on his research on Oregon coastal dunes for an unfinished article. The book was rejected by 20 publishers before Chilton Books (a manuals publisher) bought it. Sandworms can be over 400 meters long.

question: Ray Bradbury wrote a chilling story in 1953, set in a future where all books are outlawed and firemen no longer put out fires: they start them, burning any book they find. What is the title of the novel?
context: Bradbury wrote the original novella in nine days on a rented typewriter in the basement of UCLA's Powell Library at ten cents per half-hour. The fireman protagonist is Guy Montag; his wife is Mildred. The title's temperature isn't quite accurate — paper actually ignites around 480°F.

question: A wise old wizard in gray robes, with a long gray beard and a pointy blue hat, sends Bilbo Baggins off after a dragon's treasure in J.R.R. Tolkien's tales. Years later he stands at the head of the Fellowship of the Ring. What is the wizard's name?
context: Gandalf is called Mithrandir by the Elves and Tharkûn by the Dwarves. He is one of the Istari, sent to Middle-earth as a Maia (angelic being) in the shape of an old man. Ian McKellen played him in Peter Jackson's films.

question: A narrator swears he is not mad in Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 story. He has hidden an old man's body under the floorboards, and with police in the room he thinks he hears a beating from below. What is the story called?
context: First published in The Pioneer in January 1843, the story is told by an unnamed narrator who is undone by the sound he believes is the dead man's beating heart.

question: An ex-Confederate cavalry officer is mysteriously carried to Mars in a 1912 story by Edgar Rice Burroughs. The planet's lower gravity lets the Earthman leap huge distances and fight like a superhero, and he falls in love with a red-skinned princess named Dejah Thoris. What is his name?
context: Burroughs's first Mars story ran as the serial Under the Moons of Mars in All-Story from February 1912, months before Tarzan, and later became the book A Princess of Mars. Carter is a Virginia gentleman. Burroughs wrote eleven Barsoom books in all, and the 2012 Disney film John Carter was a famous box-office bomb.

question: The heroes of J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings face a dark lord in Mordor who forged the One Ring to rule all the other rings of power. His body is long gone, but his spirit watches as a huge flaming Eye from a black tower. What is his name?
context: Sauron was originally a Maia (servant of the Valar) under Morgoth, the first Dark Lord. His tower is Barad-dûr. His Eye is fashioned in the Eye of Sauron iconography by Peter Jackson; in the books it is more metaphorical. The One Ring contains a fragment of his power.

question: Sam Spade, a private eye, gets caught in the middle as crooks chase a jewelled black bird statue in Dashiell Hammett's 1930 novel. What is the novel called?
context: The novel was serialized in Black Mask in 1929-30. John Huston's 1941 film, with Humphrey Bogart as Spade, is a landmark of film noir.

question: J.R.R. Tolkien published a children's book in 1937 about Bilbo Baggins, a small hairy-footed creature hired by thirteen dwarves as their burglar. Under the Misty Mountains he picks up a gold ring without knowing what it is. What is the book called?
context: Full title: The Hobbit, or There and Back Again. The thirteen dwarves are led by Thorin Oakenshield. The first edition was 1500 copies and sold out by Christmas 1937. C.S. Lewis was one of the first reviewers and praised it warmly.

question: Mickey Spillane introduced readers in 1947 to a brutal, hard-drinking, fast-shooting private eye who works the tough streets of New York City. In Spillane's first novel, I, the Jury, the detective hunts down the killer of his best friend and swears violent revenge. What is this private eye's name?
context: Spillane wrote the first Hammer novel in 19 days. By 1980, seven of the top fifteen best-selling fiction titles of all time were Mike Hammer novels. Spillane himself starred as Hammer in the 1963 film The Girl Hunters.

question: Arthur C. Clarke teamed up with the film director Stanley Kubrick in 1968 to create both a novel and a movie about astronauts flying to Jupiter, an eerie black stone monolith left on the Moon by aliens, and a talking spaceship computer named HAL 9000. What is the shared title of this story?
context: Clarke and Kubrick developed the novel and film together. The book came out a few months after the film's April 1968 release. The story expands Clarke's 1948 short story The Sentinel. HAL stands for Heuristically programmed ALgorithmic computer.

question: Bram Stoker carried a mysterious ancient nobleman out of Transylvania in his 1897 horror novel. This vampire count buys a ruined estate in England, sails there aboard a ghostly ship whose crew die one by one, and begins hunting young English women for their blood. Who is the count?
context: Stoker partly modeled Dracula on the 15th-century Wallachian prince Vlad III, Vlad the Impaler. The novel is epistolary — diary entries, letters, telegrams. Bela Lugosi's 1931 film performance defined the screen image of the vampire.

question: A bronze-skinned scientist and adventurer travels the world in a private plane with his five brilliant helpers, fighting evil masterminds through 181 pulp novels that began in 1933. Every magazine cover calls him the Man of Bronze, and his stories directly inspired Superman and Indiana Jones. What is his name?
context: Doc Savage (Clark Savage Jr.) debuted in March 1933. Lester Dent wrote most of the novels under the house pen name Kenneth Robeson. Doc's headquarters were on the 86th floor of a Manhattan skyscraper modeled on the Empire State Building.

question: Bilbo's young cousin carries the evil One Ring across many dangerous lands in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings. It can be unmade only in the fiery lava of the volcano in Mordor where it was forged. What is the volcano called?
context: Mount Doom (Orodruin in Sindarin, Amon Amarth) is an active volcano in central Mordor. Sauron forged the Ring there in the Second Age. The Ring can be unmade only in the same fires that forged it. The mountain stands within sight of Sauron's tower Barad-dûr.

question: Robert Howard sat in his parents' house in one small central Texas town and wrote his stories. He spent most of his short life there, and the house is now a museum and a pilgrimage site for pulp fans. Which town was it?
context: Howard spent most of his life in Cross Plains, with some years in nearby Brownwood, and his home there is now the Robert E. Howard Museum. He died on 11 June 1936, aged 30; his mother died the next day.

question: Lovecraft left his home city for a short, miserable marriage in New York, then hurried back and spent his last years writing in his attic study. He had been born there in 1890 and lived almost his entire life in that one small New England city. What city was his lifelong home?
context: Lovecraft was born in Providence on August 20, 1890 and died there March 15, 1937 of intestinal cancer. He briefly lived in Brooklyn 1924-26 after marrying Sonia Greene; the experience deepened his xenophobia and informed The Horror at Red Hook. Many of his fictional towns (Arkham, Innsmouth, Kingsport) are based on real New England locations.

question: Chicago newsstands put out a new pulp magazine in March 1923, cheap paper and lurid covers packed with tales of horror, wizards and monsters. Over the next thirty years it printed the best work of Robert E. Howard, Lovecraft and Clark Ashton Smith, and it folded in 1954. What was it called?
context: Weird Tales was founded by Jacob Henneberger. Farnsworth Wright edited it through its 1930s golden age. The signature triumvirate — Lovecraft, Howard, and Clark Ashton Smith — anchored the magazine in the early 1930s while corresponding with each other constantly.

question: J.R.R. Tolkien fought at the Battle of the Somme in 1916 as a young British signals officer, among privates and batmen, and two of his closest school friends were killed in that battle. He later said one loyal, brave character in The Lord of the Rings reflected the ordinary soldiers he served with. Which character?
context: Tolkien described his Sam as a reflection of the English soldier, of the privates and batmen he knew in the First World War. Two of the four friends at the heart of the T.C.B.S. (Tea Club and Barrovian Society), Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith, were killed in 1916; Tolkien caught trench fever and was invalided home on 8 November 1916.

question: Edgar Allan Poe published 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' in 1841, and in it a brilliant gentleman-detective solves the seemingly impossible killings of two women found inside a locked upstairs apartment. He uses pure reasoning to crack a case the police cannot. Critics call this the very first modern detective story. What is the detective's name?
context: The Murders in the Rue Morgue (April 1841 in Graham's Magazine) introduced detective fiction's foundational conventions: the brilliant amateur sleuth, the slower narrator-companion, the locked-room mystery, the dramatic reveal. Conan Doyle named Poe's stories as the direct ancestor of Sherlock Holmes.

question: Don A. Stuart, the pen name of Astounding magazine's own editor, signed a novella in its pages in August 1938. The men of an Antarctic research station thaw out the frozen pilot of an alien spacecraft, a shape-shifting predator, and by the climax the survivors cannot tell man from alien. It was filmed in 1951 and again by John Carpenter in 1982. What is the novella called?
context: Who Goes There? appeared in the August 1938 issue under Campbell's pen name Don A. Stuart. Its expedition numbers 37 men, and its alien can imitate any living thing it absorbs, memories and all, which is why no one at the station can trust anyone else. The story was first adapted as The Thing from Another World (1951) and then as Carpenter's The Thing (1982), which stays closer to the novella. Campbell edited Astounding (renamed Analog in 1960) until his death in 1971.

question: Mutineers maroon two English nobles on the African coast in Edgar Rice Burroughs's 1912 story. The couple die in a jungle cabin before their baby son can speak, and the boy, raised by apes, later learns he is heir to a proud English family title. What is the family's title?
context: Tarzan's father is John Clayton, Lord Greystoke: Clayton is the family surname and Greystoke the title. The she-ape Kala raises the boy. The book Tarzan of the Apes appeared in 1914, and Johnny Weissmuller's 1932 MGM film fixed the famous image.

question: Lovecraft published a story in a pulp magazine in 1928 about a giant tentacled monster older than mankind, sleeping in a sunken stone city called R'lyeh at the bottom of the Pacific, while cults around the world dream of the day the creature will wake. It became one of the most famous horror tales ever written. What was it called?
context: Published in the February 1928 Weird Tales. The story is told in three parts via the papers of Professor George Gammell Angell of Brown University. The Cthulhu mythos vocabulary — R'lyeh, the Necronomicon, the cult phrase 'In his house at R'lyeh dead Cthulhu waits dreaming' — all enter the canon here.

question: Frank Herbert spent years shopping around a strange desert epic, and twenty publishers turned him down before Chilton Books, mostly known for car repair manuals, took a chance on it in 1965. Its hero, the young noble Paul Atreides, sees his family sent by the galactic emperor to rule a scorching, waterless planet full of gigantic sandworms. What is the planet's name?
context: Arrakis is colloquially called Dune. The desert is the only source of spice melange — the substance that enables faster-than-light navigation across the Imperium. The native Fremen people drink water-of-life and ride sandworms called Shai-Hulud.

question: Arthur Machen shocked Victorian readers in 1894 with a short horror novel in which a doctor's brain operation opens a young woman's mind to a glimpse of something wild and pagan, and she loses her reason. Years later a mysterious woman drifts through London society, and the gentlemen who know her begin to die. What is the story called?
context: Arthur Machen (1863-1947) published The Great God Pan with John Lane in 1894, to a storm of scandal. Lovecraft praised it in his 1927 essay Supernatural Horror in Literature, and it shaped his own cosmic horror.

question: An editor gathered the mountain of unfinished notes and drafts the author of The Lord of the Rings left at his death in 1973 and shaped them into a book, The Silmarillion, in 1977. The pages held the ancient creation myths, elf-songs and origin stories of Middle-earth, nearly a lifetime's writing. Who was that editor?
context: Christopher Tolkien (1924-2020) was J.R.R.'s third son and literary executor. He spent the rest of his life editing his father's papers — twelve volumes of The History of Middle-earth (1983-1996) plus Unfinished Tales (1980), The Children of Húrin (2007), Beren and Lúthien (2017), and The Fall of Gondolin (2018). Guy Gavriel Kay assisted on The Silmarillion.

question: Leiber put two swords-for-hire into his first published story in August 1939. One was a giant barbarian from the north, the other a small thief and magician's apprentice, and together they roamed a corrupt city of thieves and wizards. What were the two heroes called?
context: The story appeared in Unknown in August 1939. Leiber went on writing about the pair, the tall barbarian and the small thief, until his death in 1992.

question: Michael Moorcock launched a new hero in a novella for Science Fantasy magazine in 1961: an albino sorcerer-emperor from a dying magical race. He leaned on drugs and on a black sword that drank souls, and he became a founding anti-hero of dark fantasy. What is his name?
context: Elric's sword is Stormbringer. Moorcock developed the larger concept of the Eternal Champion (Elric, Corum, Hawkmoon, Erekosë, etc.) — different incarnations of the same hero across multiple worlds. The original Elric stories ran 1961-1964 in Science Fantasy; Moorcock has returned to the character repeatedly since.

question: A prisoner lies strapped flat to a wooden board in a torture chamber of the Spanish Inquisition in Edgar Allan Poe's 1843 short story, while a huge razor-sharp blade swings closer and closer overhead. The red-hot iron walls of the room slowly slide inward to crush him. What is Poe's story called?
choices: The Masque of the Red Death
context: The story first appeared in the 1843 edition of the annual The Gift. Its narrator is a prisoner of the Spanish Inquisition in Toledo, tormented first by a pit in the dark and then by the swinging blade.

question: Robert Heinlein sent a young recruit named Johnny Rico through brutal boot camp in a 1959 novel, into powered exoskeleton armor that lets soldiers jump like grasshoppers and a war against giant bug-like aliens from a planet called Klendathu. The book won the Hugo Award, and Paul Verhoeven made a famously satirical movie of it in 1997. What was Heinlein's novel called?
choices: The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress
context: Heinlein conceived powered armor (the Mobile Infantry suits) in the novel, influencing every mecha and powered-armor concept since. The book's political philosophy — full citizenship earned only through federal service — provoked decades of debate. Verhoeven's 1997 film satirized the politics; Heinlein's text plays them straight.

question: Robert Howard put a new hero in the pulp magazines in 1928, a Puritan in a slouch hat, armed with a rapier. He wandered the world fighting evil and avenging the innocent, grim and religious. What is his name?
context: Solomon Kane first appeared in Red Shadows in Weird Tales in August 1928, four years before Conan. Howard made him a grim Puritan swordsman who roams the world righting wrongs.

question: C.S. Lewis and other Oxford scholars heard J.R.R. Tolkien read drafts of The Lord of the Rings aloud. The friends met once or twice a week through the 1930s and 1940s, at a pub called The Eagle and Child, nicknamed the Bird and Baby, or in Lewis's rooms at Magdalen, and Lewis's Narnia books got a first hearing the same way. What did they call themselves?
context: The Inklings included Lewis, Tolkien, Charles Williams, Owen Barfield, Hugo Dyson, and Lewis's brother Warnie. They met at the Eagle and Child pub (nicknamed the Bird and Baby) on St. Giles' Street, Oxford. Tolkien read drafts of LOTR to the group; Lewis read drafts of Narnia and Out of the Silent Planet.

question: Dashiell Hammett published his early work in the American pulp magazine Black Mask, the top home for hardboiled crime fiction from 1920 to 1951. His most famous early hero there was a short, tubby private eye who worked as an agent for a big detective agency in San Francisco. What did readers call him?
context: The Continental Op (short for 'Operative') works for the Continental Detective Agency, and Hammett had been a Pinkerton operative himself. Besides his many short stories, the Op stars in the novels Red Harvest (1929) and The Dain Curse (1929). He is short, stout, middle-aged and never named.

question: Lovecraft invented a fake ancient book of forbidden magic and mentioned it in so many stories that many readers believed it was real. He said it was written long ago by a poet he called the Mad Arab, Abdul Alhazred, who went insane from what he learned. What is this made-up book called?
context: Lovecraft invented the Necronomicon for his story The Hound (1922) and wrote a mock History of the Necronomicon in 1927. Several real books have since been published under the name as hoaxes, and libraries still get requests for the original.

question: Two young writers who had been Lovecraft's devoted correspondents started a small book press in Sauk City, Wisconsin, in 1939, to keep the horror stories of their late friend in hardcover print. He had died two years earlier. The press took its name from his fictional New England town. What is that press called?
context: August Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded Arkham House to publish The Outsider and Others (1939), the first big Lovecraft collection. Derleth also wrote Cthulhu Mythos stories of his own.

question: Philip K. Dick published a novel in 1962, set in an alternate 1962 where Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan had won World War II and carved up North America. Inside the book is a forbidden novel called 'The Grasshopper Lies Heavy,' which imagines that the Allies won. Dick's outer book won the Hugo Award. What is its title?
answer: The Man in the High Castle
choices: The Man in the High Castle
Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said
context: Won the 1963 Hugo Award. Dick used the I Ching to make plot decisions while writing. The story is set in 1962 in a Japanese-occupied West Coast (PSA), with a German-occupied East and a neutral Rocky Mountain States buffer. Hawthorne Abendsen is the in-novel author of Grasshopper, the inverse alternate-history showing an Allied victory.
