question: Eric Rucker Eddison, an English civil servant, published a huge, old-fashioned fantasy novel in 1922, written in mock-Elizabethan English. Its noble Demons and treacherous Witches wage war, strangely, on the planet Mercury. J.R.R. Tolkien later admired the force of the prose and disapproved of the cruel morals of its aristocrats. What is the novel called?
context: Eddison's prose imitates the cadence of Jacobean drama; he had translated Egil's Saga from the Old Norse. Tolkien wrote that Eddison was 'the greatest and most convincing writer of invented worlds I have read' but disliked his heroes' outlook. The title's worm is the Ouroboros, the dragon that eats its own tail.

question: Robert E. Howard, writing his Conan stories in his parents' house in Cross Plains, Texas, began a long exchange of letters in 1930 with a horror writer in New England, who stayed his chief correspondent until Howard died in 1936. The two never met in person, but they argued for years over whether civilisation or barbarism was the better state for mankind. Who was that correspondent?
context: Howard and Lovecraft began writing to each other in 1930 and kept it up for the rest of Howard's life, arguing over civilisation and barbarism. Their letters were later collected by Hippocampus Press as A Means to Freedom.

question: An expedition of professors and graduate students from the fictional Miskatonic University flies deep into Antarctica in Lovecraft's longest single tale, a novella of cosmic dread from 1936. There, buried in the ice, they find the frozen corpses of star-headed alien beings that built enormous stone cities on Earth millions of years before humans existed. What is the story called?
choices: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward
context: Astounding ran the novella in its February, March and April 1936 issues. Its Antarctic expedition echoes the real flights of Richard Byrd's 1928-1930 expedition, and the barrel-shaped Elder Things it finds built their cities long before humanity.

question: Robert Howard's earlier hero King Kull, an Atlantean warrior, seizes a decadent throne and becomes king of a dying, pre-human land on a lost continent, long before the age of Howard's later barbarian. What is Kull's fallen kingdom called?
context: Kull debuted in 'The Shadow Kingdom' (Weird Tales, August 1929). Valusia is the most powerful of the Seven Empires of Howard's pre-Cataclysm world. Kull and the snake-people of Valusia inspired numerous later writers including Lin Carter and L. Sprague de Camp. Conan's Hyborian Age is technically a later epoch after Kull's Atlantis sinks.

question: Clark Ashton Smith wrote his dark-fantasy poems and stories in near-poverty, in a rough cabin in the Sierra Nevada foothills of northern California. He was the third pillar of a 1930s pulp magazine beside Lovecraft and Robert E. Howard, but he stayed a near-hermit. Near which small California town did he live most of his life?
context: Smith (1893-1961) lived in a self-built cabin near Auburn, California. He was a teenage prodigy poet first, then turned to weird fiction in the late 1920s. His Zothique, Hyperborea, Averoigne, and Xiccarph cycles each represent different fantastic milieus. Smith ground his own pigments and carved fantastic stone heads in his last years. His correspondence with Lovecraft was nearly as substantial as Howard's.

question: Tolkien built two tongues for his Elves, decades before The Lord of the Rings was even conceived. The high speech, used in formal moments in the book, was meant to sound like Latin or Finnish. The everyday speech, behind most Elvish names there, was meant to sound like Welsh. What are the two called, high speech first?
context: Tolkien was a philology professor at Oxford whose academic work centered on Old English and the West Midlands dialect. He created Quenya around 1915 based on Finnish phonology after reading the Kalevala. Sindarin's Welsh-style consonant mutations come from Tolkien's love of Welsh place-names. Khuzdul (Dwarvish, modeled on Semitic languages) is heard rarely; the Black Speech of Mordor was created by Sauron.

question: Edgar Allan Poe wrote a short poem in 1849 that was first printed two days after his mysterious death in Baltimore. The poem opens 'It was many and many a year ago, in a kingdom by the sea, that a maiden there lived whom you may know by the name of...' — the title is the maiden's name. What is it?
context: Poe's young wife Virginia had died of tuberculosis in January 1847, and the poem is widely read as a memorial to her. Poe died in Baltimore on 7 October 1849, and the poem was first published two days later.

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs took his readers underground with a series of novels set in a hollow Earth, reached near the North Pole. Dinosaurs survive there, primitive humans wage wars with stone tools, and an inner sun lights a world with no concept of time. What did Burroughs call this realm?
context: At the Earth's Core (1914) opens the Pellucidar series, and Burroughs wrote seven Pellucidar books in all. David Innes and his mentor Abner Perry bore down into the inner world in a mechanical 'iron mole'. Tarzan visits Pellucidar in a 1929 crossover.

question: Isaac Asimov began his first robot story in June 1939, about a robot named Robbie who works as a little girl's nanny, the seed of all his later robot tales and their Three Laws. Astounding's editor turned it down, and it finally sold to Frederik Pohl, who printed it in Super Science Stories in September 1940 under a new title that Asimov thought distasteful. What was that title?
context: Pohl renamed the story Strange Playfellow for Super Science Stories (September 1940), a title Asimov disliked; Asimov restored his own title, Robbie, when he collected it in I, Robot in 1950.

question: Tolkien gave a lecture in 1939 called On Fairy-Stories, which became his main statement about how fantasy writing works. In it he coined a special word for the happy ending of a story, the sudden turn of joy that lifts everything. What is that word?
context: Eucatastrophe = 'good catastrophe.' Tolkien argued the Gospels are the eucatastrophe of human history — Christ's resurrection being the supreme unexpected turn from death to life. The essay also developed 'sub-creation' (the artist as imitator of God's creative act) and the primary/secondary world distinction. It first appeared in the 1947 Essays Presented to Charles Williams memorial volume.

question: Young Wilbur Whateley grows at a frightening rate in the lonely farmhouse of his strange family, in the decaying hill country of Massachusetts, and he goes looking for a forbidden book. Lovecraft's story of him was printed in 1929. What is the story called?
context: Published in Weird Tales in April 1929, the story sends Wilbur Whateley to the library of Miskatonic University in search of the Necronomicon. Its Massachusetts hill country is one of Lovecraft's invented corners of New England.

question: Philip José Farmer wrote a mock biography of the pulps' Man of Bronze in 1973, treating the pulp novels as fictionalised memoirs of a real man raised from birth by trainers his father hired to make him a superman in body and mind. The book even fixes the hero's birthplace. Where was he born, according to Farmer?
answer: Aboard a schooner off Andros Island in the Bahamas
choices: Aboard a schooner off Andros Island in the Bahamas
In Hidalgo, his secret Central American haven
In Manhattan, in his father's hospital suite
In the Yucatan, in his father's Mayan refuge
context: Philip José Farmer's Doc Savage: His Apocalyptic Life (1973) places Doc's birth on 12 November 1901, aboard the schooner Orion in a cove off the northern tip of Andros Island in the Bahamas. Doc's full name is Clark Savage Jr.

question: Robert Heinlein, a civilian engineer during World War II, recruited two fellow science-fiction writers, Isaac Asimov and L. Sprague de Camp, to join him at his wartime post in Philadelphia. Among other jobs, the three brainstormed unconventional defences against kamikaze attacks. What was the facility called?
context: Heinlein worked as a civil servant at the Navy Aircraft Materials Center at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard and brought in Asimov and de Camp to work there too. He had left the Navy in 1934 because of tuberculosis.

question: A visitor rides up to a crumbling old family mansion beside a still, dark pond in Edgar Allan Poe's 1839 Gothic horror story, and he notices a thin crack running down its wall. Inside, the nervous last heir of the family lives with his pale, sickly twin sister, and the mansion itself seems to share their gloom. What is the story called?
answer: The Fall of the House of Usher
choices: The Fall of the House of Usher
The Masque of the Red Death
context: Published in Burton's Gentleman's Magazine in September 1839, the story ties the Usher family to the house itself, so that the House of the title means both the mansion and the bloodline. Roger Corman filmed it in 1960 with Vincent Price.

question: Tolkien drew up a writing system for his Elvish languages, with 24 basic letters grouped by the sounds they make, not by ABC order. It appears on the One Ring and on the west gate of Moria ('Speak, friend, and enter'). What is the script called?
context: Tengwar means 'letters' in Quenya. Tolkien invented it in the 1930s. Cirth is a separate runic alphabet used by the Dwarves for stone-cutting. The One Ring inscription is in Tengwar letters but renders the Black Speech of Mordor — 'Ash nazg durbatulûk, ash nazg gimbatul...' Tolkien also invented the Sarati (an earlier elvish script) and various tengwar modes for different languages.

question: Edgar Allan Poe was found at Ryan's Tavern in Baltimore wearing someone else's clothes, and in his hospital delirium, the story goes, he called out one name again and again. He died on October 7, 1849, and his death remains a mystery. What name is he said to have called out?
context: No Reynolds connected to Poe has ever been firmly identified; the explorer Jeremiah Reynolds and a judge, Henry Reynolds, are candidates. Poe's doctor, John Moran, is the main source for his last days, and his accounts changed over the years. One theory, cooping, holds that Poe was kidnapped and forced to vote again and again on election day, October 3.

question: Walter Gibson wrote his cloaked avenger's pulp stories under the pen name Maxwell Grant, starting in 1931. On the radio the avenger is the wealthy Lamont Cranston, but in the pulps Cranston is a real millionaire playboy whose identity the avenger borrows while Cranston is off travelling the world. The avenger's real name was only revealed in 1937: he is a famed First World War aviator. What is his true identity?
context: In the pulps the Shadow is really Kent Allard, a famous aviator who flew for the French in the First World War and was nicknamed the Black Eagle; his name was revealed in The Shadow Unmasks (1937). Lamont Cranston is a rich playboy whose identity he borrows, and the radio show made Cranston the Shadow himself. Henry Arnaud is another of his disguises, and Harry Vincent is one of his agents.

question: A painter keeps getting pulled away from his great painting of a tree, with a forest in the distance, by chores for his lame neighbour Parish in a short story Tolkien wrote around 1939. It first appeared in the Dublin Review in January 1945. Many readers take it as a picture of Tolkien's own struggle to finish his work, though he said it was more mythical than allegorical. What is the story called?
context: Leaf by Niggle first appeared in the Dublin Review in January 1945 and was collected with On Fairy-Stories in Tree and Leaf (1964). Tolkien said the story came to him one morning in 1939 and that he wrote it out almost in a single sitting.

question: Lord Dunsany, an Anglo-Irish baron, set down a whole pantheon and its creation of the world in a 1905 book, in a formal, old-fashioned style modelled on the King James Bible. That book was a major influence on Lovecraft. What was it called?
context: The Gods of Pegana (1905) was followed by Time and the Gods (1906) and many story collections. Lovecraft's Dream Cycle stories, such as The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, are open homages to Dunsany.

question: Edgar Allan Poe published his only complete novel in 1838 — a strange seafaring adventure full of mutiny, starvation, and a voyage toward the southern polar region. Jules Verne later wrote a sequel to it, and Lovecraft drew on it for his own work. What was the novel called?
answer: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym
choices: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym
context: Harper & Brothers published Pym in July 1838. Lovecraft borrowed its cry, Tekeli-li, for the shoggoths of At the Mountains of Madness, and Jules Verne's 1897 sequel was An Antarctic Mystery (Le Sphinx des glaces).

question: Lovecraft's 1931 novella follows a young traveller to a decaying Massachusetts seaport whose people have a strange, staring, fish-like look, and whose fishermen haul in more than they should from a black reef offshore. The traveller stays one night too many. What is the town called?
context: The Shadow over Innsmouth was written in 1931 and published as a small book in 1936, one of the very few Lovecraft books printed in his lifetime. The black reef offshore is Devil Reef.

question: An Oxford undergraduate named Tolkien retold the story of the hapless Kullervo in prose in 1914. He later named that cursed hero as one old source for Túrin, the doomed hero of Men in Middle-earth's First Age, whose long tale came out in 2007 as The Children of Húrin, with paintings by Alan Lee. From which national epic did Kullervo come?
context: Tolkien wrote The Story of Kullervo, a prose version of a cycle from Elias Lönnrot's Kalevala, as an undergraduate at Exeter College, Oxford, in 1914 and 1915, and it became one of the sources for Túrin Turambar. The Children of Húrin came out in April 2007 with illustrations by Alan Lee.

question: Two young readers refused to let Lovecraft's work vanish after his death in 1937, with his stories scattered across old issues of pulp magazines. They had corresponded with him, and in 1939 they founded a small Wisconsin press for the sole purpose of keeping the work in print, publishing his first big hardback collection that same year. Who were the two founders?
choices: Frank Belknap Long and Clark Ashton Smith
Lin Carter and L. Sprague de Camp
context: August Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded Arkham House in 1939, and its first book, The Outsider and Others, gathered stories they selected themselves. Derleth later wrote many Mythos tales of his own.

question: A Brooklyn teenager studying at Columbia University walked into the office of Astounding's new editor in June 1938 to hand over a story in person, and the editor talked with him for more than an hour. In July 1939 the young man's story Trends appeared in Astounding. Who was he?
context: Asimov delivered a story to Campbell in person in June 1938, and Campbell spent more than an hour with him. His first sale went to Amazing Stories (Marooned Off Vesta, March 1939), and Trends appeared in Astounding in July 1939. Campbell's Don A. Stuart stories include Twilight (1934) and Who Goes There? (1938).

question: Edgar Rice Burroughs grew rich on his books and in 1919 bought a big ranch in the hills north of Los Angeles. He founded a company of his own in 1923 to print his books, and he later sold off the ranch land for housing. The neighborhood that grew up there kept the name he had given the ranch. What is it called?
context: Burroughs bought the ranch on 1 March 1919 and named it Tarzana Ranch, after his jungle hero; the San Fernando Valley neighborhood of Los Angeles that grew on its land kept the name. His company was Edgar Rice Burroughs, Inc.

question: Tolkien sailed for France with the Lancashire Fusiliers in early June 1916 and fought on the Somme until trench fever sent him home on November 8. Four schoolboys had been at the heart of the T.C.B.S. (Tea Club and Barrovian Society), his little club at King Edward's School in Birmingham, and two of the four died in the Somme campaign that same year. What were those two friends' names?
answer: Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith
choices: Rob Gilson and Geoffrey Bache Smith
Hugh Cary Gilson and Edward Williams
context: Rob Gilson was killed on 1 July 1916, the first day of the Somme, and Geoffrey Bache Smith died that December of wounds from a shell. The fourth member, Christopher Wiseman, survived the war, and Tolkien later edited Smith's poems as A Spring Harvest (1918). Charles Williams and Owen Barfield were later Inklings friends, not T.C.B.S. members.

question: Frank Herbert researched a magazine article about Oregon's shifting sand dunes and the effort to tame them with grass, and that was the seed of his desert epic. Long before the finished novel, he wrote an outline of a simpler version of the story. In 2005 his son Brian Herbert and Kevin J. Anderson turned the outline into an alternate story for a book. What is that story called?
context: Spice Planet, written by Brian Herbert and Kevin J. Anderson from Frank Herbert's original outline for Dune, appeared in The Road to Dune in September 2005.

question: Philip K. Dick lived through a mystical episode in 1974, and out of it, and out of his idea that reality is a 'Black Iron Prison', grew a 1981 novel about a divine encounter. The novel takes its title from a godlike intelligence. What was the novel called?
context: VALIS stands for Vast Active Living Intelligence System. The novel grew from what Dick called his 2-3-74 experiences of February and March 1974, which he spent years trying to explain in a private journal later published as the Exegesis.

question: Tolkien, then a professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford, was marking School Certificate exam papers when he found a blank page in one candidate's script and scribbled a line on it. He did not yet know what the creature in it was: the word came first. The line became the opening of a famous book. What did he scribble?
answer: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit
choices: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit
Far over the misty mountains cold
There was once a hobbit who lived in a hole
Bilbo Baggins of Bag End was no ordinary hobbit
context: Tolkien told W. H. Auden in a 1955 letter that he had been marking School Certificate papers and scrawled the line on a blank leaf, not knowing why. He read drafts aloud to his children, and C.S. Lewis read the book in manuscript. The first edition (September 21, 1937) had a print run of 1,500 copies.

question: Silver John, a Korean War veteran with a silver-stringed guitar, battles witches, devils and dark fae drawn from real Appalachian folk tales in the mountains of North Carolina. Manly Wade Wellman, who started out as a 1930s pulp writer, began these John the Balladeer stories in 1951. Where did the first one appear?
answer: The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction
choices: The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction
Weird Tales after the Wright era end
Unknown Worlds, the Campbell sister title
Beyond Fantasy Fiction, the Galaxy spinoff
context: Wellman's 'O Ugly Bird!' appeared in F&SF in December 1951. The Silver John stories are characteristically narrated in first-person mountain dialect. Wellman won the British Fantasy Society's August Derleth Award (1975) for Worse Things Waiting; he also won the World Fantasy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1980. He died in 1986 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina at age 82. His Silver John novels include After Dark (1980) and The Lost and the Lurking (1981).

question: Karl Edward Wagner, a trained psychiatrist, published a small-press novel in 1970 about an immortal red-haired swordsman. The hero was a man out of Genesis, marked by God after killing his brother and doomed to wander the Earth forever. What was the hero's name?
context: Kane first appeared in Wagner's novel Darkness Weaves (1970). Wagner held a degree in psychiatry, mixed sword-and-sorcery with horror, and edited The Year's Best Horror Stories from 1980 to 1994.

question: William Hope Hodgson set his most cosmic novel far in the future, on an Earth where the sun has gone out, and he published it in 1912, before he died at Ypres in 1918. The last humans live in a huge pyramid-fortress called the Last Redoubt, ringed by monsters from the outside. What was the novel called?
choices: The Boats of the Glen Carrig
context: The Night Land's prose imitates 17th-century English deliberately — Hodgson considered it formal scriptural style appropriate to the eschatological subject. The novel was reviewed unenthusiastically in 1912 but became a major influence on Lovecraft (who called it 'one of the most potent pieces of macabre imagination ever written'), Clark Ashton Smith, and later Gene Wolfe. Hodgson was a former merchant-marine officer; the sea-horror in his earlier novels The Boats of the Glen Carrig (1907) and The Ghost Pirates (1909) drew from his own North Atlantic experience.

question: Two friends canoeing down the Danube camp on a tiny island of sand and slowly sense that something there is watching them, in a 1907 novella by Algernon Blackwood widely considered one of the finest weird stories ever written. Lovecraft later ranked it as the single best weird story he had ever read. What was the story called?
context: The Willows was published in The Listener and Other Stories (1907). Blackwood himself had canoed the Danube in 1900. His other major weird stories include The Wendigo (1910, the source of the modern North American Wendigo mythos in popular culture) and the John Silence stories — proto-psychic-investigator tales. Blackwood lived 1869-1951 and became a BBC radio personality in his later years, reading his own ghost stories on Christmas broadcasts.

question: A Cambridge professor finds a bronze relic in the ruins of a Templar preceptory on the East Anglian coast, and something starts to follow him, in a tale from Montague Rhodes James's first collection, in 1904. James, a medieval scholar, wrote his ghost stories to read aloud to friends at Christmas, and they defined the antiquarian ghost story: bookish scholars, ancient objects and slow-building dread. What is the story called?
answer: Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad
choices: Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad
The Treasure of Abbot Thomas (1904 tale)
Count Magnus and the Black Pilgrim Tale
context: The story first appeared in Ghost Stories of an Antiquary (1904); James had read it to a King's College Christmas gathering in 1903. The whistle bears the Latin words Quis est iste qui venit, 'Who is this who is coming?', and the professor, Parkins, is staying at the Globe Inn in Burnstow.

question: A Miskatonic University instructor trades letters with a lonely Vermont farmer after the great floods of 1927 wash strange bodies down the rivers, in one of Lovecraft's most science-fictional horror tales, printed in August 1931. The hills hide fungoid, crab-like miners from the planet Yuggoth, who can carry a human brain to the stars inside a metal cylinder. What is the story called?
choices: The Dreams in the Witch House
context: The Whisperer in Darkness was written between February and September 1930 and first printed in Weird Tales in August 1931. Its aliens, the fungoid Mi-Go from Yuggoth, mine the Vermont hills and can carry a human brain through space in a metal cylinder, and the story opens in the wake of the real Vermont floods of November 1927.

question: Gimli cuts down orcs at the Battle of the Hornburg to the Dwarves' ancient war-cry, in the secret language Tolkien invented for them. Khuzdul's sounds are modeled on Semitic languages like Hebrew rather than on the Indo-European roots of his Elvish tongues, and only a few of its phrases appear in The Lord of the Rings. What does Gimli shout?
context: The cry translates as 'Axes of the Dwarves! The Dwarves are upon you!' Tolkien designed Khuzdul to sound angular and stone-like, matching the Dwarves' culture. The Dwarves keep their true Khuzdul names secret from outsiders; the names readers know, such as Thorin, Balin and Gimli, come from the language of Men in the North.

question: Edgar Allan Poe launched the detective genre in April 1841 with a tale in Graham's Magazine. In it, a brilliant French thinker solves the locked-room killing of two women in Paris. Conan Doyle later called the story the direct ancestor of Sherlock Holmes. What was the family name of the two murdered women?
context: Madame L'Espanaye and her daughter are the two women murdered in The Murders in the Rue Morgue, the first Dupin story. Poe followed it with The Mystery of Marie Roget (1842) and The Purloined Letter (1844), and Conan Doyle acknowledged Dupin as an ancestor of Sherlock Holmes.

question: Robert Howard sent the last king of the Picts against Rome's armies in Britain at the head of his dwindling people, and even had him strike at Hadrian's Wall. The Picts were a real ancient people of northern Britain, and most of these stories ran in Weird Tales between 1930 and 1932. What was this king's name?
context: Bran Mak Morn is the last king of Howard's romanticized Picts and fights the Romans in Britain; his final story, Worms of the Earth, ran in Weird Tales in November 1932. Howard's friend and correspondent Lovecraft slipped a reference to Bran into The Whisperer in Darkness.

question: Milton Waldman, a publisher, received an enormous letter from Tolkien late in 1951, explaining how The Silmarillion and The Lord of the Rings fit together into one mythology. Tolkien said all of this material is mainly concerned with three things, and he warned that the urge to make and sub-create, once it turns possessive, ends in the lust for power. Which three things did he name?
context: In his letter to Milton Waldman (Letter 131 in the published Letters), Tolkien wrote that the legendarium is mainly concerned with Fall, Mortality and the Machine. By the Machine he meant using outside plans or devices instead of developing inner powers and talents.

question: Isaac Asimov laid out his Three Laws of Robotics in full for the first time in the short story 'Runaround,' in Astounding Science Fiction in March 1942: laws that told fictional robots never to harm humans, always to obey orders and always to protect themselves. Asimov later said that the magazine's editor had helped him shape the laws into their final form while editing his earlier robot stories. Who was that editor?
context: John W. Campbell edited Astounding Science Fiction from 1937 to 1971 and was a towering — if controversial — influence on the Golden Age of SF. Asimov's earliest robot stories ('Liar!' 1941, 'Robbie' 1940) hinted at the rules; Campbell pushed Asimov to formalize them. The Three Laws first appear in named form in 'Runaround' (March 1942 Astounding). Campbell also discovered and developed Robert Heinlein, A.E. van Vogt, Theodore Sturgeon, and Lester del Rey. Frederik Pohl edited Galaxy and If; Anthony Boucher edited F&SF; H.L. Gold founded Galaxy.

question: Edgar Allan Poe gave the detective genre its toolkit in 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' in 1841: the odd genius amateur, the friend who tells the story, the locked-room puzzle and the big reveal at the end. Dupin solves the case by reasoning step by step from small clues, and Poe called the Dupin stories tales of that method. What did Poe call it?
context: Poe used 'ratiocination' for systematic, reasoned analysis and called the Dupin stories his tales of ratiocination. He published three: Rue Morgue (1841), Marie Rogêt (1842) and The Purloined Letter (1844). Conan Doyle took over much of Poe's apparatus for Sherlock Holmes.

question: The sailor Gustaf Johansen lands on an island newly risen from the South Pacific in Lovecraft's 1928 story, where one angle of the masonry is acute but behaves as if it were obtuse. The young sculptor Wilcox, who saw the city in his dreams, had described its geometry with a word built on the name of an ancient Greek mathematician. Whose name was it?
context: Wilcox said the geometry of the dream-place was abnormal, non-Euclidean, and loathsomely redolent of spheres and dimensions apart from ours. The story's three parts are a dead professor's papers, a police raid on a cult in the Louisiana swamps, and Johansen's account of the voyage of the Emma out of Auckland.

question: Tolkien first wrote the Riddles in the Dark chapter for the 1937 edition of his book about Bilbo, then revised it substantially in 1947 to fit The Lord of the Rings, which he was still writing. In that later book the Ring needed to be a sinister object. What was the most important plot change between the two versions of the chapter?
answer: In 1937 Gollum bet the Ring itself on the riddle game; in 1947 he bet only to show Bilbo the way out
choices: In 1937 Gollum bet the Ring itself on the riddle game; in 1947 he bet only to show Bilbo the way out
In 1937 the cave was located in the Misty Mountains; in 1947 Tolkien moved it to the Iron Hills
In 1937 Bilbo won with a fair riddle; in 1947 Tolkien gave him the trick question about his pocket
In 1937 Gollum had no name; in 1947 Tolkien gave him the Sméagol backstory and the river-folk origin
context: Tolkien explained the rewrite inside the story: Bilbo's first account of the riddle game, the one printed in 1937, was not the true one. The revised chapter appeared in the second edition of The Hobbit in 1951, and copies of the 1937 first edition are prized by collectors.

question: Robert Howard wrote only one full-length novel of his Cimmerian, in 1934, for a British book publisher that went bankrupt before printing it. Weird Tales ran it instead as a five-part serial from December 1935 to April 1936. In it the king of Aquilonia loses his throne to a sorcerer raised from the dead and must find a jewel called the Heart of Ahriman. What was the novel titled?
answer: The Hour of the Dragon (later republished as Conan the Conqueror)
choices: The Hour of the Dragon (later republished as Conan the Conqueror)
The Phoenix on the Sword (the original Conan debut)
Beyond the Black River (the frontier-Pictish horror)
context: Howard wrote The Hour of the Dragon in 1934 for the British publisher Denis Archer, which went bankrupt before printing it, so it first appeared as a Weird Tales serial from December 1935 to April 1936. It was his only full-length Conan novel; its villain is Xaltotun of Acheron, and Gnome Press first published it as a hardcover book, Conan the Conqueror, in 1950.

question: Philip K. Dick, suspicious of the Blade Runner project, saw a 20-minute rough cut at Warner Bros. in October 1981 and was deeply moved. He died of a stroke on March 2, 1982, three months before the film's June release. One writer later set down the making of the film, Rutger Hauer's 'Tears in Rain' speech included. Who recorded Hauer's full account of writing it?
answer: Paul M. Sammon, author of Future Noir
choices: Paul M. Sammon, author of Future Noir
Jerry Pournelle, in his Galaxy column
Roger Ebert, in his 1992 Great Movies
Pauline Kael, in the 1982 New Yorker
context: Sammon's Future Noir (1996, revised 2007) remains the definitive making-of book on Blade Runner. Hauer reduced what was a longer scripted speech to its iconic core: 'I've seen things you people wouldn't believe. Attack ships on fire off the shoulder of Orion. I watched C-beams glitter in the dark near the Tannhäuser Gate. All those moments will be lost in time, like tears in rain. Time to die.' The original script lines (which Hauer kept) were technical descriptions of off-world warfare; Hauer transmuted them into poetry. Ridley Scott has called it the single most moving line ever written for him.

question: Feanor, an Elf of the Noldor, makes three holy jewels in the Blessed Realm in Tolkien's The Silmarillion, published in 1977, four years after the author's death. The jewels are the Silmarils, and they become the cause of long wars. What did Feanor put inside them that no other jewel could ever hold?
answer: The light of the Two Trees of Valinor, silver Telperion and golden Laurelin
choices: The light of the Two Trees of Valinor, silver Telperion and golden Laurelin
The first stars Varda had kindled in the sky during the elves' awakening at Cuiviénen
A drop of the blood of the Vala Aulë, shed during the forging of the Dwarven Seven Fathers
The compressed essence of Eru Ilúvatar's first creative thought before the Music of the Ainur
context: Yavanna made the Two Trees, silver Telperion and golden Laurelin, which lit Valinor before the Sun and Moon, and the Silmarils held their mingled light.

question: C.S. Lewis walked along Addison's Walk at Magdalen College, Oxford, on the night of September 19, 1931, with Tolkien and Hugo Dyson. Tolkien argued that the pagan stories Lewis loved were splintered lights pointing toward the one true story that had actually happened in history. The conversation eventually converted Lewis to Christianity, and Tolkien captured its argument in a poem Lewis called personally important. What is the poem called?
choices: The Lay of Aotrou and Itroun
context: Mythopoeia is a 148-line poem written for Lewis. Its key argument: man is a 'sub-creator' bearing 'the refracted Light through whom is splintered from a single White / to many hues, and endlessly combined / in living shapes that move from mind to mind.' Lewis's account of the conversation is in Surprised by Joy (1955) and in a letter to Arthur Greeves dated 18 October 1931. Lewis converted to theism in 1929 and to Christianity specifically after the Addison's Walk conversation. Mythopoeia was published posthumously in Tree and Leaf (1964) with 'On Fairy-Stories' and 'Leaf by Niggle.'

question: A cardiologist argued in 1996 that Edgar Allan Poe had died of an illness caught from an animal, not of drink. Poe had been found delirious at Ryan's Tavern in Baltimore on October 3, 1849, in shabby clothes thought not to be his own, and in the hospital he struggled even to drink water. He died at 40. Which illness did the doctor name?
context: R. Michael Benitez made the case in the Maryland Medical Journal in 1996, pointing to Poe's delirium and his trouble drinking water, a mark of the fear of water that rabies brings; he thought Poe might have caught it from one of his pets. Other theories run from cooping, an election-day kidnapping for repeated voting, to cholera and a brain tumor. None has been proved.

question: Tolkien had planned one long book in six parts, but George Allen & Unwin split The Lord of the Rings into three volumes, published between July 1954 and October 1955. He was unhappy with the title chosen for the final volume, The Return of the King, because he felt it gave away too much of the story. What title did he prefer for it?
context: Tolkien felt The Return of the King revealed too much and preferred The War of the Ring, but the publisher kept its own title, and the third volume appeared on 20 October 1955. In his six-book plan, Book Five was to be called The War of the Ring and Book Six The End of the Third Age.

question: The young Lovecraft found a major influence in Lord Dunsany, an Anglo-Irish baron and war veteran who wrote in a deliberately archaic, scriptural style modelled on the King James Bible. Dunsany's 1924 fantasy novel is widely considered his masterpiece. What was that novel called?
choices: The Curse of the Wise Woman
context: Lord Dunsany (1878-1957) published The King of Elfland's Daughter in 1924, and his dreamlike invented mythologies were a model for Lovecraft's Dream Cycle stories.

question: The science-fiction novelist behind Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? lived through a series of religious-mystical events in February and March 1974, his '2-3-74 experiences', and they consumed the rest of his life. He spent the next eight years filling an enormous private journal that eventually ran over 8,000 pages. A selection was published in 2011, twenty-nine years after his death. What was the published selection called?
answer: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
choices: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
context: The Exegesis is over 1,000,000 words in total. The 2011 published selection (edited by Pamela Jackson and Jonathan Lethem) ran 944 pages, a 10% selection of the available archive. Dick's experience began with a delivery driver wearing a Christian fish-symbol necklace; from there Dick believed he was receiving 'pink light' transmissions from a Vast Active Living Intelligence System (VALIS). His diagnoses ran from schizophrenia to temporal lobe epilepsy to vitamin overdose to genuine gnostic revelation, depending on his mood. Dick died in March 1982 in Santa Ana, California, of a stroke.

question: Tolkien's wife danced for him among the hemlock blossoms in Roos Wood, Yorkshire, in 1917, and he immediately connected the moment to one of the very first stories of his private Middle-earth mythology: the tragic doomed love between an elf-maiden and a mortal man. What names appear on the joint Tolkien gravestone in Wolvercote Cemetery, Oxford?
choices: Galadriel and Celeborn, the immortal couple
Arwen and Aragorn, the mortal-elven pair
Eärendil and Elwing, the lovers of the Sea
context: After his hospitalization in late 1916 with trench fever, Edith danced for him among the hemlock blooms of Roos Wood in East Yorkshire. They married March 22, 1916 (before his deployment to France). Edith died November 29, 1971; J.R.R. died September 2, 1973. Their joint grave in Wolvercote Cemetery, North Oxford bears the names Christopher Tolkien arranged: 'Edith Mary Tolkien, Lúthien, 1889-1971' and 'John Ronald Reuel Tolkien, Beren, 1892-1973.'

question: Developers bought the land under the Big Ear radio telescope in Ohio, and in 1998 the giant instrument was taken apart. On August 15, 1977, it had recorded a signal from the direction of Sagittarius, roughly 30 times louder than the surrounding background noise, that has never been detected again. What did the developers use the land for?
answer: To expand a nearby golf course
choices: To expand a nearby golf course
To build a regional shopping mall
To lay a new interstate highway
To house a college football stadium
context: Big Ear was disassembled in 1998 after developers bought the site from the university, and they used the land to expand a nearby golf course. The telescope had searched the sky for alien signals since the 1970s; Jerry Ehman circled the 1977 signal on its printout and wrote 'Wow!' beside it.

question: A young Norseman from Thule joins King Arthur's Round Table in Hal Foster's medieval-knight comic strip, launched in 1937, and he later weds Aleta, Queen of the Misty Isles. The strip has run in Sunday newspapers for more than 80 years. What is it called?
context: Foster drew Prince Valiant himself from February 1937 until 1971 and wrote it until 1980. The strip is set in Arthurian Britain but ranges across Europe, Africa and even North America, and King Features Syndicate distributes it. Foster was drawing the Tarzan strip when he dreamed up Valiant.

question: Lee Falk created a costumed jungle hero in 1936, considered the first hero in a purple bodysuit and eye-mask. He lives in a Skull Cave deep in the African jungle and is treated as immortal by the locals. Really, each generation is a new son taking over from his father. Who is this hero?
context: The Phantom debuted in newspaper strips on February 17, 1936 — predating Superman (1938) by two years, making him arguably the first costumed superhero. Lee Falk also created Mandrake the Magician (1934). The current Phantom is the 21st in line. The Skull Cave is in the fictional African country of Bangalla. Native tribes call him 'the Ghost Who Walks.'

question: The Paris police tear a suspect's apartment apart for a stolen paper in Edgar Allan Poe's story of 1844, which may be the most famous detective story of the 1800s, and they cannot find it. Poe's detective cracks the case. Later thinkers like Lacan and Derrida made the tale famous in literary theory. What is the story called?
choices: The Murders in the Rue Morgue
context: Published in The Gift, an annual dated 1845 that came out in 1844. The Minister D. steals a compromising letter from a royal lady, and the Prefect of police brings the case to Dupin after his own men fail. Jacques Lacan's seminar on the story and Jacques Derrida's reply, Le facteur de la vérité, are landmark texts of literary theory.

question: Father Christmas at the North Pole signed the illustrated letters that reached the Tolkien children each year from 1920 to 1943, though their father wrote them. The letters had a running cast of bears and gnomes. Who causes most of the trouble at the Pole?
choices: Snow Bear (the rival of Father Christmas)
context: Tolkien wrote the letters for his children John, Michael, Christopher and Priscilla and illustrated each one himself; the bumbling Polar Bear causes most of the trouble at the North Pole. Baillie Tolkien edited the published collection in 1976.

question: Arthur Conan Doyle worked as a clinical clerk in 1877 and 1878 under a real Edinburgh medical professor, whose way of reading a patient had stunned him as a student. The professor could name a patient's job, home region, illness and recent travels at a glance. Doyle also based Sherlock Holmes on him, and he admitted his debt to Poe in his 1924 memoir. Who was the professor?
context: Joseph Bell (1837-1911) taught at Edinburgh's medical school and amazed students by reading a patient's job and history from small physical clues. Conan Doyle worked for him as a clerk and later acknowledged him as the model for Holmes.

question: Beyond the Black River, Robert Howard's 1935 story, takes his barbarian to a log fort on the edge of a forest held by the Picts, and critics have called it a transplanted Western. They say Howard drew that wilderness from a frontier novel by an American writer better known today for the eerie stories of The King in Yellow. Who was the novelist?
context: The critics Cerasini and Hoffman call Beyond the Black River a transplanted Western, and say Howard modelled his Pictish wilderness on the setting of Robert W. Chambers's frontier novel The Little Red Foot. The story first ran in Weird Tales in May and June 1935.

question: Burroughs ran a magazine serial in 1918 about a captured German U-boat captain and a stranded American who find an island in the South Pacific. Steep cliffs ring it, the only way in is a stream flowing out from a passage beneath them, and life grows more modern the farther north a traveler goes. The 1975 Amicus film was based on it. What do the island's people call it?
context: The Caspak trilogy, The Land That Time Forgot, The People That Time Forgot and Out of Time's Abyss, ran in Blue Book Magazine in 1918. Explorers' charts name the island Caprona; Caspak is what its people call it. Kevin Connor's film The Land That Time Forgot starred Doug McClure.

question: Tolkien called The Lord of the Rings 'fundamentally religious and Catholic' in a 1953 letter, and said he had cut out nearly all references to religion so that it would be absorbed into the story instead. He also translated a medieval devotional dream poem into modern English. Which poem was it?
choices: Caedmon's Hymn, the earliest known Old English poem
The Dream of the Rood, the cross-as-narrator Crucifixion poem
Christ III, the Old English poem of Christ's return
context: Tolkien's translation of Pearl (along with Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and Sir Orfeo) was published posthumously by Christopher Tolkien in 1975. Pearl is by the same anonymous 14th-century Pearl Poet who wrote Sir Gawain. The poem features a grieving father who has lost his two-year-old daughter and dreams of meeting her, now a grown maiden in heavenly bliss. The Pearl Poet's other surviving works are Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (Tolkien co-edited the standard scholarly edition with E.V. Gordon, 1925) and Patience and Cleanness.

question: Alan Jay Lerner and Frederick Loewe turned The Once and Future King, T.H. White's 1958 omnibus, into a stage musical in 1960, with Richard Burton as Arthur and Julie Andrews as Guenevere. White's book had combined four novels into the most-read 20th-century Arthurian work, following Arthur from boyhood under Merlyn's teaching to old age. What was the musical called?
context: Camelot, adapted from The Once and Future King, opened at Toronto's O'Keefe Centre on 1 October 1960 before moving to Broadway, with music by Frederick Loewe and book and lyrics by Alan Jay Lerner. Richard Burton played Arthur, Julie Andrews Guenevere and Robert Goulet Lancelot.

question: Sir Thomas Malory finished Le Morte d'Arthur around 1470, apparently while in prison, weaving French and English sources into one story of Arthur's rise, the Grail quest and the fall of the Round Table. The oldest surviving handwritten copy only turned up in June 1934, when a schoolmaster found it at Winchester College. Before that, every reader knew Malory through one printer's 1485 edition. Who printed it?
context: Le Morte d'Arthur was completed around 1469 or 1470 and first printed by William Caxton in 1485. Walter Oakeshott discovered the Winchester Manuscript, an earlier handwritten copy, in June 1934.

question: R. Daneel Olivaw, a robot, realizes that the Three Laws are not enough to protect humanity as a whole, in the novel that united Isaac Asimov's series into a single timeline, four decades after those laws appeared in Runaround in 1942. There Asimov added a Zeroth Law that supersedes the original three. What novel introduced the Zeroth Law, and what does it state?
answer: Robots and Empire (1985): a robot may not harm humanity, or let it come to harm
choices: Robots and Empire (1985): a robot may not harm humanity, or let it come to harm
Foundation and Earth (1986): a robot must protect the long-term flourishing of human society
The Robots of Dawn (1983): a robot must place the common good above any one person
Forward the Foundation (1993): a robot may serve humanity even at the cost of one person
context: Robots and Empire (1985) joined Asimov's Robot and Empire series into one timeline. In it the robots R. Daneel Olivaw and R. Giskard Reventlov reason their way to a Zeroth Law that puts humanity as a whole ahead of any single human: 'A robot may not harm humanity, or, by inaction, allow humanity to come to harm.'

question: A young writer from Sauk City, Wisconsin, sold his first story to a pulp magazine in 1926 while still a teenager, corresponded with Lovecraft for years, and co-founded the press that kept Lovecraft's stories in print. Yet he considered his most serious work to be something else entirely: an ambitious cycle of novels, stories, journals and poems about his own corner of Wisconsin. What did he call it?
context: August Derleth considered the Sac Prairie Saga, his long series of novels, stories, journals, poems and nonfiction about the Sac Prairie region, his most serious work. He sold his first story, Bat's Belfry, to Weird Tales in 1926.

question: Tolkien gave his lecture Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics in 1936 and transformed academic Beowulf studies. He argued the poem is a coherent literary work, not a quarry for historical data. He said the monsters were the heart of its meaning, and he named a tragic-heroic worldview from Old English at the poem's center. What did Tolkien call this outlook?
answer: The Northern courage of resistance — fighting on though the cause is hopeless and defeat is certain
choices: The Northern courage of resistance — fighting on though the cause is hopeless and defeat is certain
The Anglo-Saxon doctrine of wyrd — fate as the ultimate arbiter of all human endeavor
The Heroic Code of dryht — the warband loyalty above family or kin
The Pagan-Germanic concept of doom — the certainty of cosmic destruction at Ragnarok
context: In his 1936 British Academy lecture, Tolkien argued that the monsters are central to Beowulf's meaning and praised the poem's Northern courage: fighting on even when defeat is certain. The lecture changed how scholars read the poem.

question: Robert Howard launched his Cimmerian in the December 1932 Weird Tales with The Phoenix on the Sword, in which the king of Aquilonia fights off a plot against his throne. He built it by rewriting an unsold story about his earlier hero, the Atlantean warrior-king Kull, and long passages of the two are identical. What was the rejected Kull story called?
context: The Phoenix on the Sword, Conan's debut in Weird Tales in December 1932, is a rewrite of the unpublished Kull story By This Axe I Rule!, with long passages identical.

question: Mary Stewart retold the Arthur story from Merlin's point of view in her Merlin Trilogy, which opened with The Crystal Cave in 1970. She drew on Geoffrey of Monmouth's 1136 History of the Kings of Britain, which invented most of the Arthur legend the West knows, and on the French Vulgate Cycle. The first title points to a real place tied to Merlin's youth. Where is the actual Crystal Cave?
answer: Bryn Myrddin, Merlin's Hill, near Carmarthen in southwest Wales, where local legend puts Merlin's cave
choices: Bryn Myrddin, Merlin's Hill, near Carmarthen in southwest Wales, where local legend puts Merlin's cave
Cadbury Castle in Somerset, the leading archaeological candidate for the historical Camelot
Tintagel Castle on the Cornish coast, the traditional birthplace of Arthur in Geoffrey of Monmouth
Glastonbury Tor in Somerset, the leading candidate for the location of the Isle of Avalon
context: Bryn Myrddin, Merlin's Hill, rises just outside Carmarthen, whose Welsh name, Caerfyrddin, was long read as 'Myrddin's fort', and local legend places Merlin's cave there. The Welsh Myrddin appears in early Welsh poetry, and Geoffrey of Monmouth Latinised the name as Merlinus.

question: Marion Zimmer Bradley retold the Arthur legend from the women's side in her 1983 bestseller The Mists of Avalon, as a struggle between the goddess religion of the island of Avalon and the rising Christian church. She gave the telling to a priestess of Avalon and Arthur's own half-sister, a woman the old romances remember as a dangerous sorceress and his enemy. Who narrates the novel?
answer: Morgaine, known in older tales as Morgan le Fay
choices: Morgaine, known in older tales as Morgan le Fay
Viviane, the Lady of the Lake herself
Igraine, the mother of Arthur himself
context: The Mists of Avalon (1983) is narrated by Morgaine, a priestess defending the old religion of Avalon as Christianity threatens to destroy it; Viviane is the High Priestess of Avalon for most of the story. The novel was a bestseller and was made into a TNT miniseries in 2001.

question: Michael Moorcock asked fellow fans in 1961 what to call the tales of muscle, magic and doomed cities that had grown up after Robert Howard's barbarian. For decades the genre had had no name. An American author of barbarian-and-thief adventures answered in a fanzine with a catchphrase that stuck. Who coined the term sword and sorcery?
context: Fritz Leiber suggested sword-and-sorcery in the fanzine Ancalagon in April 1961, answering Michael Moorcock, who had proposed epic fantasy, and he expanded on it in Amra that July. The genre grew out of Howard's early-1930s work, and his 1929 Kull story The Shadow Kingdom is often called the first true sword-and-sorcery tale.

question: Valentine Michael Smith, a human baby raised by Martians and brought back to Earth as a grown man, founds a religious movement based on Martian ways in Robert Heinlein's Stranger in a Strange Land, published by Putnam in June 1961. His followers learn to understand things so completely that they become part of what they understand. What Martian word did Heinlein invent for this?
context: Grok literally means 'to drink' in Heinlein's invented Martian, but it stands for understanding something so thoroughly that the observer becomes part of the observed. Stranger in a Strange Land won the Hugo Award, and a longer uncut version was published in 1991.

question: A giant, hairy, ape-like creature called Sasquatch walks upright through thick evergreen forests in stories more than a hundred years old. Almost all of the famous sightings happen in one misty, rainy part of the country. Which region of the US is it?
context: Sasquatch lore is concentrated in Washington, Oregon, and northern California. The name 'Bigfoot' was coined by a journalist after construction worker Jerry Crew found large prints in Humboldt County in 1958.

question: A huge, long-necked, plesiosaur-like monster swims in a deep, dark freshwater lake called Loch Ness, or so people have claimed for centuries. In which country does the lake lie?
context: Loch Ness is a 23-mile freshwater lake in the Scottish Highlands. The 'Surgeon's Photograph' from 1934 was the most famous image until a 1994 deathbed confession revealed it was a hoax using a toy submarine.

question: The Yeti, the shaggy giant some call the Abominable Snowman, leaves enormous footprints in the high snow, or so the stories say. Mountain guides have told of seeing it for hundreds of years. In which mountain range is the Yeti said to live?
context: Sherpa folklore long predates Western reports. Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reported strange large footprints on the 1953 Everest expedition, fueling Western Yeti enthusiasm for decades.

question: The long-necked monster said to swim in Loch Ness won over tourists, locals and even some scientists, who gave her a warm, playful, one-word nickname. The name is now used around the world. What is it?
context: The nickname became standard in Scottish newspapers in the 1930s and now appears on everything from souvenir T-shirts to Inverness pub signs.

question: A poor woman with twelve children curses her thirteenth baby in an old colonial legend, and it is born a monster with hooves and bat wings. It is said to haunt a vast, dark forest called the Pine Barrens. Which US state contains that forest?
context: The Pine Barrens is a million-acre stretch of pinelands in southern New Jersey. The legend dates to the 18th century and the creature is said to be the cursed 13th child of one Mother Leeds.

question: A navigator marking the Bermuda Triangle on a chart puts its corners at Miami, Bermuda and Puerto Rico. Writers have claimed for decades that ships and planes vanish inside it in uncanny numbers. What do the loss records actually show?
answer: No more losses than in other busy waters
choices: No more losses than in other busy waters
Twice the losses of other busy waters
Losses of planes but almost no ships
context: The triangle is roughly bounded by Miami, Bermuda and Puerto Rico in the North Atlantic. The lore was popularized by a 1964 Argosy Magazine article. Statistical reviews find no higher disappearance rate than other busy ocean lanes.

question: An ancient Greek philosopher wrote of a huge lost island empire called Atlantis around 360 BC. He said this proud sea-power grew so wicked that the gods sank it in a single day and night. Which ancient Greek thinker first told the tale?
context: Atlantis appears in two of Plato's dialogues, Timaeus and Critias, around 360 BC. Most classicists read it as a moral parable invented by Plato; modern enthusiasts have nevertheless searched for it for centuries.

question: Prehistoric people raised a ring of huge stone slabs, some over 20 feet tall, on the grassy plain of Salisbury more than 4,000 years ago. That ring, Stonehenge, stands in the south of one of the four countries of the United Kingdom. In which country?
context: Stonehenge stands on the Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire. The inner bluestones were quarried in the Preseli Hills of Wales and transported roughly 150 miles to the site.

question: John White, governor of the English colony founded on Roanoke Island in 1587, sailed home for supplies. When he finally returned in 1590, all 115 settlers had vanished. The only clue was a single word carved into a wooden post. What was it?
context: The Roanoke Colony was established in 1587 on the coast of present-day North Carolina. The 115 colonists vanished entirely before White's resupply ship returned. 'Croatoan' was the name of a nearby island and tribe.

question: Mac Brazel, a ranch foreman, found strange metal debris across his sheep pasture near Roswell, New Mexico, in 1947. The Army airfield nearby told newspapers it had a crashed 'flying disc', then changed its story a day later. What did the Army call the debris?
context: The crash site was near Roswell, New Mexico. The Army Air Forces initially reported recovering a 'flying disc,' then retracted to call it a weather balloon. A 1990s declassification revealed it was a Project Mogul nuclear-test-detection balloon.

question: A man in the Nevada desert says he saw strange lights and disc-shaped craft over a secret air base, as others have claimed for decades. The Air Force flies spy planes from it, beside a dry lake bed. What is the base popularly called?
context: The base sits at Groom Lake, about 80 miles north of Las Vegas. The U.S. government first openly acknowledged it in 2013, when the CIA released declassified documents about the U-2 spy plane.

question: Women bathe in green pools among star charts and plants that match no known species, in a handwritten book about six hundred years old. A swirling script captions it all. What has nobody ever managed to do with the book?
context: The 240-page illustrated book dates to the 15th century. It contains an unknown script and drawings of plants nobody can identify. It now lives in Yale University's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library.

question: The Yowie, a tall, shaggy, ape-like beast, walks the deep bush in stories told for many generations. It is a sort of southern-hemisphere Sasquatch. In which country is the Yowie usually placed?
context: Yowie traditions appear across many Aboriginal nations under different names. European settlers in the 19th century recorded their own 'hairy man' sightings, and modern Yowie hunters concentrate in eastern Australia.

question: Khufu had the Great Pyramid of Giza built as his tomb around 2560 BC. It rose 481 feet on the west bank of the Nile, and its size and precision led to wild theories about who built it. In which country does it stand?
context: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC as a tomb for Pharaoh Khufu. Mainstream Egyptology attributes it to Egyptian laborers; alternative theories from Erich von Däniken to modern internet conspiracies persist.

question: A Polynesian carver on Rapa Nui, the South Pacific island outsiders call Easter Island, cut a giant figure from volcanic rock, with a blocky head, long ears and a stern face. His people made nearly 900. What Polynesian word do the islanders use for them?
context: Easter Island, called Rapa Nui by its people, lies in the South Pacific. The 887 monolithic moai were carved between roughly 1250 and 1500 AD. 2012 experimental archaeology showed they could be 'walked' upright with ropes.

question: A London paper ran a photo of a long neck rising from Loch Ness in 1934, and the monster became world-famous. Sixty years later a dying man confessed it was a toy submarine with a putty neck. What is the photo called?
context: Robert Kenneth Wilson, a London gynaecologist, put his name to the 1934 photograph, which is why it is called the Surgeon's Photograph. In 1994 Christian Spurling confessed on his deathbed that his stepfather Marmaduke Wetherell had staged it with a toy submarine and a sculpted putty neck, as revenge on the Daily Mail.

question: A skinwalker, an evil witch who can shape-shift into a coyote, a wolf or a crow, walks unseen at night in the stories of one Native American nation. Many of its people will not say the name out loud. Which people first told these stories?
context: In Navajo language the figure is called yee naaldlooshii, 'by means of it, it goes on all fours.' Speaking the name is widely considered taboo. The modern 'Skinwalker Ranch' in Utah inherits the name without inheriting the religious context.

question: A gaunt spirit of hunger and ice called the wendigo hunts lonely travelers through the winter forests in the stories of the Cree, the Ojibwe and the Innu. All three speak languages from one great family. What is the shared name of these peoples?
context: The wendigo legend belongs to Algonquian-speaking peoples across what is now Canada and the northern United States. The figure is associated with winter, famine, and the moral horror of cannibalism — never with hunger you can satisfy.

question: The gods sink the proud island empire of Atlantis in a single day and night, in a Greek tale written down around 360 BC. The tale sets the island beyond the Pillars of Heracles, now the Strait of Gibraltar. Which body of water swallows Atlantis?
context: Plato placed Atlantis 'beyond the Pillars of Heracles,' i.e. beyond the Strait of Gibraltar in what we now call the Atlantic. The very name 'Atlantic' derives from the Greek 'sea of Atlas,' which the Atlantis story helped cement.

question: A quiet man calling himself Dan Cooper boarded a Boeing 727 in Portland, Oregon, on November 24, 1971, and in midair handed a flight attendant a note claiming his briefcase held a bomb. He collected his ransom in Seattle, and the jet took off again. What did he do next?
choices: Stowed away on the next flight
context: The hijacking happened on Thanksgiving Eve, November 24, 1971. He jumped from the rear airstair of a Northwest Orient Boeing 727 over southwestern Washington and was never identified. The press misheard 'Dan' as 'D.B.,' and the nickname stuck.

question: A tall, faceless figure in a black suit stood behind groups of children in two faked photos that Eric Knudsen posted to a Photoshop contest in 2009. The character soon had his own video games, comics and a 2018 horror movie. What was he called?
context: Created by Eric Knudsen (handle 'Victor Surge') for a Something Awful Photoshop contest about supernatural images. Entrants were asked to alter photos to look like real paranormal documents. Slender Man's documents were photoshopped to look like archive shots of children with a faceless tall figure in the background. The character became a viral creepypasta, then the 2012 indie game Slender: The Eight Pages, then a 2018 movie. A tragic Wisconsin case in May 2014 brought the character to national news and a documentary, Beware the Slenderman.

question: A rancher in the town of Moca found eight of his sheep dead in August 1995, their blood apparently drained. A radio host called the unseen killer the chupacabra, the goat-sucker, and the panic spread. On which Caribbean island did it begin?
context: The first sightings were near the town of Canóvanas, Puerto Rico. Witness Madelyne Tolentino later told folklorists she had recently seen the alien-creature film Species, whose monster strikingly resembles her chupacabra description.

question: Jerry Ehman was reading Big Ear radio telescope printouts a few days after August 15, 1977, when one column from that night leapt far above the background hum. He circled it and wrote 'Wow!' beside it. What was Ohio State's Big Ear built to hear?
context: Astronomer Jerry Ehman, working on Ohio State's 'Big Ear' radio telescope SETI program, circled the printout in red pen and wrote 'Wow!' beside it. The 72-second signal has never been heard again.

question: A ship drifted empty east of the Azores in December 1872, her sails still set and her cargo untouched below decks. Her lifeboat was gone, and so were the captain, his wife Sarah, their two-year-old daughter Sophia and all seven crewmen. What is this famous ghost ship called?
context: The American brigantine Mary Celeste was found by the British ship Dei Gratia east of the Azores on December 4, 1872. Captain Briggs, his wife Sarah, daughter Sophia, and all seven crew were never seen again. The cargo of 1,701 alcohol barrels was intact; the lifeboat was missing. Modern theory: Briggs feared a hold-fire from leaking alcohol vapor and ordered evacuation; the ship sailed away from them. The archetypal ghost ship, referenced by Conan Doyle, Doctor Who, and countless others.

question: Jerry Crew discovered huge footprints at his logging site in California in 1958, made plaster casts of the prints and took them to a local newspaper. The reporter's story gave the unknown creature a memorable new name. What was that name?
context: 'Sasquatch' was already in use, anglicized from the Halkomelem Salish word sasq'ets. 'Bigfoot' was the journalist's invention and quickly became the dominant North American name. The Crew casts are still on display in Willow Creek, California.

question: Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin rode on horseback through the woods at Bluff Creek in northern California on October 20, 1967, hoping to spot a Sasquatch. They filmed what they said was a female one: a big, hairy figure walking across a sandbar and glancing back at the camera. What nickname did Patterson give it?
context: The film was shot on October 20, 1967. Patterson named the subject 'Patty.' Hollywood costume designers and biomechanics researchers have studied the gait, the muscle movement, and the unusual proportions of the figure for decades without consensus.

question: Robert Kenneth Wilson, a respectable London physician, was said to have snapped the famous 1934 shot of a long-necked shape rising from Loch Ness. Because a real Harley Street specialist had put his name on the picture, people trusted it for sixty years. What kind of doctor was he?
context: Robert Kenneth Wilson said he had stopped to look at the loch on a road trip and snapped the photo. He kept his name out of newspaper credits for decades. The image was finally exposed as a hoax in a 1994 deathbed confession.

question: Greek sponge divers exploring an ancient Roman shipwreck pulled up a lump of corroded bronze about the size of a shoebox in 1901. Decades later, X-rays showed what the lump really held. What is this 2,000-year-old device called?
context: Divers recovered it in 1901 off the small island of Antikythera. The lump soon broke into pieces, and on 17 May 1902 Valerios Stais found a gear wheel embedded in one of them; X-ray studies in 1971 and CT scans in 2005 later mapped its gears. The mechanism dates to around the 2nd century BC.

question: Someone in Central Europe filled a 240-page book by hand in the early 1400s with strange plants, star charts and women bathing in green pools, all captioned in a swirling script. A Polish book dealer bought it in Italy in 1912. Which American university keeps it today in its rare-book library?
context: The manuscript lives in Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library. Polish-American antique dealer Wilfrid Voynich bought it in 1912. The script has resisted every cryptographic, linguistic, and AI-assisted attempt to decode it.

question: Ancient people in the desert of southern Peru scraped away the dark surface stones to reveal lighter soil, drawing a hummingbird, a monkey and long straight lines that stretch for miles. Some of these Nazca figures are hundreds of feet long. What puzzling feature makes them so strange to anyone standing on top of them?
answer: They are only fully visible from the air
choices: They are only fully visible from the air
They glow brightly at sunrise and sunset
They move slowly over the course of a year
They are invisible from less than a mile away
context: The geoglyphs were made by the Nazca culture between roughly 500 BC and 500 AD, by removing the dark surface stones to reveal lighter sand. They cover 450 km² in the Nazca Desert. Theories about purpose include religious ritual and astronomical calendar.

question: One column of numbers stopped Jerry Ehman as he read printouts from the Big Ear radio telescope at Ohio State in August 1977: a narrow signal from the night of the 15th, far above the background noise, from near Sagittarius. He circled it and wrote 'Wow!' beside it. Roughly how long did the signal last?
context: The signal lasted exactly the length of the telescope's beam-pass across a single sky position, suggesting an extraterrestrial source. It came from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. Despite repeated listening campaigns, the signal has never been heard again.

question: Igor Dyatlov and eight fellow Soviet hikers slashed their way out of their tent in the middle of the night in February 1959, on a winter trek, and died in the freezing forest below. The event took the name of the twenty-three-year-old leader: the Dyatlov Pass Incident. In the northern part of which mountain range did all this happen?
context: Group leader Igor Dyatlov and his eight companions cut their way out of their tent from the inside and fled into a sub-zero blizzard inadequately dressed. Some bodies showed crushing injuries without external wounds. A 2019 reinvestigation favored a katabatic-snowslab avalanche as the most likely trigger.

question: Five US Navy torpedo-bomber crews took off from a base in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on December 5, 1945, for a routine training flight. All five aircraft, and later a large Martin Mariner flying boat sent after them, vanished without a trace over the stretch of ocean now called the Bermuda Triangle. The lost squadron was Flight 19. What kind of aircraft were the five bombers?
context: The five Avengers left Fort Lauderdale on December 5, 1945. Lt. Charles Taylor reported being lost over featureless water. A PBM Mariner flying boat sent to search for them also vanished, very likely from a known onboard fuel-fume explosion problem.

question: Vincent Gaddis wrote a 1964 pulp-magazine article that gave the name Bermuda Triangle to a stretch of ocean between Miami, Bermuda and Puerto Rico where ships and planes were said to vanish. Ten years later a paranormal author put out a bestselling paperback, The Bermuda Triangle, that made the mystery a household name. Who wrote that 1974 bestseller?
context: Vincent Gaddis coined the term in Argosy Magazine in February 1964. Larry Kusche's 1975 The Bermuda Triangle Mystery — Solved went through individual cases and showed many had been misrepresented or exaggerated.

question: An Arizona logging crew reported in November 1975 that one of their men, twenty-two-year-old Travis Walton, had been struck by a bright beam of light from a hovering flying saucer and had vanished into the woods. Walton turned up dazed on a highway five days later. Paramount Pictures turned his book into a 1993 film. What is the film called?
context: Five of Walton's six fellow loggers passed lie-detector tests about the incident; one man's result was inconclusive. The 1993 Robert Lieberman film stars D.B. Sweeney as Walton and Robert Patrick as the crew boss, Mike Rogers.

question: Sidney Gottlieb, chief chemist of a secret American program, MKUltra, dosed unwitting citizens and soldiers with hallucinogens to test whether drugs, hypnosis and psychological torture could break people's minds. Most files were destroyed in 1973, but a Senate hearing led by Ted Kennedy dragged it into public view in 1977. Which American agency ran MKUltra?
context: MKUltra ran roughly from 1953 to 1973 under chemist Sidney Gottlieb. It involved LSD experiments on unwitting subjects, including drug addicts, prisoners and a US Army biochemist named Frank Olson, who fell to his death from a tenth-floor New York hotel window days after he was secretly dosed.

question: A huge fireball streaked across the sky above the remote taiga near the Tunguska River on the morning of June 30, 1908. The blast flattened roughly 80 million trees in a butterfly-shaped pattern, but scientists who later reached the site could not find any impact crater at all. What does the missing crater show about how the object hit?
context: The airburst occurred above the Stony Tunguska River on June 30, 1908. Eyewitnesses 300 miles away saw a fireball brighter than the sun. No crater was ever found. Most scientists attribute it to a 50-meter stony asteroid airburst at about 8 kilometers altitude.

question: A stewardess on a Northwest Orient Boeing 727 took a note from a soft-spoken passenger on the night before Thanksgiving 1971, saying his briefcase held a bomb. The man, ticketed as 'Dan Cooper', wanted $200,000 waiting for him when the plane landed in Seattle. What else did he demand along with the cash?
context: The FBI recorded the serial number of every one of the 10,000 twenty-dollar bills before delivery. In February 1980 an eight-year-old boy named Brian Ingram found three rotting packets of the bills on a sandbar of the Columbia River near Vancouver, Washington. The rest has never surfaced.

question: A baby girl vanished with the 115 English colonists of Roanoke Island between 1587 and 1590. Her grandfather, John White, returned to discover the entire colony gone. She became famous as the first English child born in what is now the United States. What was her name?
context: Virginia Dare was born August 18, 1587 — nine days after the colony's arrival. She was the daughter of Ananias and Eleanor Dare and granddaughter of Governor John White. When White returned to England for supplies, the Spanish Armada delayed him three years; he returned in August 1590 to find the colony abandoned, fortifications dismantled, no bodies, and the word CROATOAN carved on a fence post. A storm prevented his search of nearby Croatoan Island. Virginia Dare's name remains an American mystery icon.

question: Twelve-year-old King Edward V and his nine-year-old brother went into the royal apartments of the Tower of London in the spring of 1483 for their 'protection', under the care of their uncle, the Lord Protector. Within months the uncle had seized the crown for himself, and the two boys, the famous 'Princes in the Tower,' were never seen alive again. Who was that uncle?
context: Twelve-year-old Edward V and his nine-year-old brother Richard of Shrewsbury vanished from the Tower in 1483 after Richard III had them declared illegitimate and seized the throne. In 1674, workmen at the Tower found a chest containing the bones of two children of the right ages.

question: Eric Knudsen, an amateur artist posting as Victor Surge, entered an online Photoshop horror contest in June 2009. He edited two old black-and-white playground photos and pasted in a very tall, faceless figure in a black suit with long, drooping arms. The mythos exploded from that single thread. Which website ran the contest?
context: Knudsen posted two altered black-and-white photos of children with a faceless tall figure in the background. The character spread across YouTube alternate-reality games like Marble Hornets.

question: An anonymous user posted a single grainy photograph of an empty yellow office in May 2019, and a reply soon imagined slipping through the world into endless rooms exactly like it. The internet ran with the idea, and the scary made-up place became the Backrooms. Which site carried the first post?
context: The photo went up on 4chan's /x/ board, and a reply added the line: 'If you're not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you'll end up in the Backrooms.' The mythos has since exploded into YouTube series, the Kane Pixels short films, and a Lionsgate film deal.

question: The SCP (Secure, Contain, Protect) Foundation, a top-secret organization in an online wiki, locks away a concrete statue that moves only when no one is looking at it. The project grows from that statue and a single 2007 post on an image board, written like a redacted government report. What number does the statue carry?
context: The original post was about SCP-173, a roughly humanoid concrete sculpture by Japanese artist Izumi Kato. The Foundation lore now spans over 8,000 'SCP files' written by thousands of contributors under a Creative Commons license. It is one of the largest fiction projects in internet history.

question: Robert Bauval, a Belgian engineer and amateur Egyptologist, published a controversial idea in the 1990s. He argued that the ground plan of the three Great Pyramids of Giza matched, star for star, three bright stars as they stood around 10,500 BC, a match most Egyptologists reject. Which trio of stars did he mean?
context: Bauval's 1994 book The Orion Mystery argued the three pyramids — Khufu, Khafre, and Menkaure — match the spacing and angle of Orion's Belt. Mainstream Egyptologists reject the precision claim but acknowledge the sky played a role in pyramid alignment.

question: Christian Spurling gave a deathbed confession in 1994 about the famous 1934 Loch Ness photograph, which had run in the Daily Mail as authentic evidence. He revealed that his stepfather had directed the hoax, using a toy submarine with a putty 'neck' attached. Who was that stepfather?
context: The Daily Mail had previously hired Wetherell to find Nessie. He produced footprints, but the British Museum identified them as hippopotamus tracks from an umbrella stand, embarrassing the paper. Wetherell built the toy-submarine hoax as revenge and had family friend Wilson, a respectable doctor, front the image.

question: A large hairy figure pauses mid-stride at Bluff Creek and glances back over its shoulder directly at the camera. That moment in less than a minute of shaky Patterson-Gimlin footage, shot on October 20, 1967, is reproduced more than any other in books, magazines and websites about the creature. What frame number is it?
context: The 53-second 16mm film runs at 24 frames per second. Frame 352 has been analyzed by Hollywood costume designers, biomechanics researchers, and gait analysts for decades. Patterson died of cancer in 1972 still maintaining the film was authentic; Gimlin maintained that position until his death in 2024.

question: John A. Keel, a journalist, investigated the winged-creature sightings at Point Pleasant in 1966 and 1967 and the Silver Bridge collapse of December 15, 1967, and tied them together in a 1975 book that became a classic of high-strangeness literature. What is the book called?
choices: Strange Creatures From Time and Space
context: The book is titled The Mothman Prophecies. Keel had spent most of 1967 in Point Pleasant interviewing witnesses. He also documented Men in Black encounters and prophetic dreams reported by townspeople. Mark Pellington adapted the book into a 2002 film starring Richard Gere.

question: An aerospace billionaire bought a 512-acre ranch from the Sherman family in 1996, two years after their own purchase. The Shermans had reported dead cattle, strange lights and creatures walking on two legs. His group studied the place for over ten years. Who was he?
context: Bigelow runs Bigelow Aerospace, known for inflatable space habitats. He sold the ranch to real-estate developer Brandon Fugal in 2016. The Pentagon's later AAWSAP advanced-aerospace UFO study program included Skinwalker Ranch as a site of interest.

question: A museum archaeologist in Athens examined a broken fragment of corroded bronze in 1902, a year after Greek sponge divers pulled the lump up from a Roman-era shipwreck about 2,000 years old. X-rays in 1971 and CT scans in 2005 later showed it to be the oldest known analog computer ever found. What did this device do?
choices: Calculated tax revenues from temple holdings
Computed harbor tides for trading vessels
context: The mechanism modeled the irregular motion of the moon, predicted solar and lunar eclipses, and tracked the cycle of ancient Greek athletic games.
