context: Dragon was preceded by The Strategic Review (1975-1976), TSR's wargame newsletter, which is where the mind flayer made its debut. Dragon ran until WotC moved everything online in 2007. Sister mag Dungeon (1986-2007) published full ready-to-run modules each issue.

question: Gary Gygax personally brought a general manager into the company he had co-founded, and in 1985 she pushed him out. She had quietly bought up enough shares to become top shareholder and outvote him in the boardroom. What was her name?
context: Lorraine Williams ran TSR from 1985 until 1997, when the company nearly bankrupted and was acquired by Wizards of the Coast (founded by MtG's Peter Adkison). Gygax sued, lost, and went on to design Dangerous Journeys (1992) and Lejendary Adventure (2000). He never returned to TSR.

question: Gary Gygax gave Advanced Dungeons & Dragons spells with wizards' names on them, such as Bigby's Crushing Hand and Tenser's Floating Disc. Bigby, Tenser, Rary and Drawmij became famous archwizards of his world of Greyhawk. Where did those wizards really come from?
answer: Characters from his home campaign, mostly run by his players
choices: Characters from his home campaign, mostly run by his players
Wizards borrowed from Jack Vance's Dying Earth tales
Fantasy authors from the DMG's Appendix N reading list
Saints from a medieval calendar on Gygax's desk
context: Mordenkainen was Gygax's own character, Tenser was played by his son Ernie, Rary was created by Brian Blume, and Drawmij belonged to Jim Ward, whose name it spells backward. Bigby began as an evil wizard in Rob Kuntz's dungeons before Gygax took him over as a player character.

question: An old man in flowing robes sometimes walks the world of Dungeons & Dragons, and he is really a platinum dragon god in disguise. He rules the good metallic dragons (copper, silver, gold, brass and bronze) and stands against five-headed Tiamat, queen of the evil chromatic ones. What is his name?
context: Bahamut's name comes from Arabic mythology — a giant fish-leviathan in some Arabic cosmologies. In D&D he's the patron of dragonborn paladins and good-dragon families. His seven 'Great Wyrm' consorts and the platinum-dragon avatar both became core lore.

question: A young actor starred in Mazes and Monsters, a 1982 CBS made-for-TV movie, as a college student who got so absorbed in a Dungeons-and-Dragons-style game that he lost his grip on reality. The film became a key piece of the 1980s Satanic Panic, which accused D&D of driving kids toward suicide and witchcraft. Who was the actor?
context: Mazes and Monsters was Hanks' first leading film role, based on Rona Jaffe's 1981 novel inspired by the disappearance of James Dallas Egbert III. The film helped fuel the Patricia Pulling-led BADD (Bothered About D&D) panic. Hanks later said he was embarrassed by the project.

question: Heroes hunt slavers raiding the Wild Coast of Greyhawk in a four-module tournament series written for Gen Con in 1980, using Gary Gygax's Advanced Dungeons & Dragons rules. What is the first module, A1, called?
choices: Assault on the Aerie of the Slave Lords
In the Dungeons of the Slave Lords
context: The series was written for the AD&D Open Tournament at Gen Con XIII in 1980: David Cook wrote A1, Harold Johnson and Tom Moldvay A2, Allen Hammack A3 and Lawrence Schick A4. The hunt begins in the Pomarj city of Highport, where a ruined temple serves the slavers as a headquarters, and their raids reached along the coast from Onnwal to the Wild Coast. The four were gathered into one supermodule in 1986.

question: A party of heroes hunts down three enemy chieftains, one lair at a time, in Against the Giants, Gary Gygax's 1978 trilogy of modules. The first module raids a wooden fortress-lodge where a chieftain of the crudest giant kind sits feasting with his brutish retinue at long tables. What is that module's full title?
answer: Steading of the Hill Giant Chief
choices: Steading of the Hill Giant Chief
Glacial Rift of the Frost Giant Jarl
Hall of the Fire Giant King
context: The G-series (G1, G2, G3 — all 1978) sends adventurers up the giant hierarchy. G1 is the hill giants, G2 the frost giants, G3 the fire giants. The trilogy connects directly to D1-D3 (the Drow series), which connects to Q1 (Queen of the Demonweb Pits). Together they're sometimes called the G-D-Q supermodule.

question: David 'Zeb' Cook and Steve Marsh edited the Expert-level Dungeons & Dragons rulebook in 1981. Boxed with it came an adventure module that sent players to a far tropical land filled with dinosaurs and lost tribes. What is it called?
choices: The Master of the Desert Nomads
context: X1 was modeled on King Kong's Skull Island. It established the default Known World (Mystara) setting that Basic and Expert D&D would use through the BECMI line. The island contains thunder lizards (dinosaurs), Aranea spider-mages, the lost cities of the Olman, and other classic pulp elements.

question: Players took one look at a bulette's fin cutting through the dirt and gave the monster a nickname that stuck. The huge armored beast (pronounced 'boo-lay') began as a cheap plastic Chinese toy on Gygax's desk, and in Dungeons & Dragons it swam through solid earth to burst up under adventurers' feet. What did players call it?
context: The bulette burrows fast through earth, surfaces with a dorsal-fin slice, and tries to bite player characters in half. The plastic-toy line that inspired it was sold cheap by the bag. The same line gave Gygax the rust monster and the owlbear, three of D&D's most iconic creatures.

question: Ms. Frost, a game master, draws a teenage player into real witchcraft in a tiny 1984 evangelical comic-book tract, the best-remembered anti-D&D piece of the 1980s Satanic Panic. Whose work is it?
context: Jack Chick's tracts were tiny black-and-white comics handed out at Halloween, on church benches, and in bus stations. 'Dark Dungeons' depicts a fictional Ms. Frost recruiting a player named Debbie into real witchcraft via D&D. The tract became a meme; a 2014 indie film adapted it as a comedic short.

question: One wizard in Gary Gygax's home Greyhawk game grew so strong that he led the Circle of Eight, Greyhawk's top group of mages. He was Gygax's most famous character, played from 1972 on, and several Advanced Dungeons & Dragons spells carry his name, including a magic mansion, a faithful hound and a sword. Who is the character?
context: Mordenkainen was perhaps Gygax's most famous character and also his favorite. He first appeared in print in Eldritch Wizardry (1976), and spells such as Mordenkainen's Magnificent Mansion and Mordenkainen's Faithful Hound carry his name.

question: Lawrence Schick's 1979 module S2 White Plume Mountain sends adventurers into a wizard-built fun-house dungeon to recover three intelligent weapons stolen by the wizard Keraptis. What are the names of the three weapons?
context: Blackrazor is a transparent homage to Stormbringer from Michael Moorcock's Elric saga — a soul-eating sword with chaotic alignment. The module is built around three distinct dungeon mini-environments: an inverted ziggurat, a series of bubbles in lava, and a flooded section with sirens. Schick wrote it as a job-application sample to TSR.

question: Gygax took his heroes down into the Underdark in the 1978 D-series of modules, the first detailed picture of dark-elf culture. The series resolved in a 1980 module that sent the adventurers to confront the spider goddess on her home plane. What is the 1980 module called?
answer: Q1 Queen of the Demonweb Pits
choices: Q1 Queen of the Demonweb Pits
context: Q1 was written by David Sutherland (best known as the iconic D&D illustrator). The module sends the PCs through the entrance plane of the Abyss to Lolth's spider-shaped fortress. Demogorgon and Orcus get cameos. The G1-3, D1-3, Q1 series compiled as a single supermodule is sometimes called the most influential D&D campaign-arc ever.

question: The Village of Hommlet, Gary Gygax's 1979 module, showed heroes a small farming village with a hidden moat-house, a smiling priest with secret loyalties and a budding cult. Gygax promised the full sequel for years but only completed it in 1985, with Frank Mentzer's help, as a 128-page supermodule. What is its title?
answer: T1-4 The Temple of Elemental Evil
choices: T1-4 The Temple of Elemental Evil
T2 The Forgotten Temple of Tharizdun
T1-4 The Caves of Chaos Expanded
context: The Temple of Elemental Evil was famously delayed for years. Gygax kept promising it in Dragon Magazine columns through the late 1970s and early 1980s. When it finally arrived in 1985, fans noticed the dungeon design was less ambitious than expected. The Troika 2003 computer-game adaptation by Tim Cain (Fallout) is well-regarded among CRPG fans.

question: A Black Robe wizard of Krynn, the world of Dragonlance, looks up at a black moon that no one outside his order can see. The white moon serves the good White Robes and the red moon serves the neutral Red Robes, one moon for each of the three orders of wizards. What is the black moon's name?
context: In Dragonlance the three moons are also the three gods of magic: Solinari of the White Robes, Lunitari of the Red and Nuitari of the Black. The Test of High Sorcery in the Tower of Wayreth is the formal initiation a wizard must survive to wear robes of any color.

question: Leiber sent Fafhrd, a barbarian, and the Gray Mouser, a former wizard's apprentice turned thief, across the world of Nehwon, and most of their stories started or ended in one sprawling, corrupt city of thieves and sorcerers. What city served as the duo's home base?
answer: Lankhmar, the City of the Black Toga
choices: Lankhmar, the City of the Black Toga
Sanctuary, the city of the Thieves' World
Ys, the drowned city of Breton legend
Carcosa, the city of the Yellow King
context: Lankhmar lies on the world of Nehwon, whose name is 'no when' spelled backwards. TSR published an official guide to the city for Advanced Dungeons & Dragons, Lankhmar - City of Adventure, in 1985.

question: Lovecraft came back from a short marriage in New York to the hometown where he had been born on August 20, 1890. He spent his last years there, and he died there on March 15, 1937. Where in his hometown is he buried?
answer: Swan Point Cemetery, in his family's plot
choices: Swan Point Cemetery, in his family's plot
Saint John's Churchyard, in his grandparents' plot
North Burial Ground, in its oldest section
context: Lovecraft's name was first carved on the Phillips family monument, beside his parents'. In 1977 admirers added a headstone of his own, inscribed I AM PROVIDENCE, a line from one of his letters.

question: A designer gathered the Basic through Master boxes of Frank Mentzer's line into one 304-page hardcover, years after the 1983 red box that began them. Many fans still call that book the cleanest D&D rulebook ever. Who was the designer?
context: Aaron Allston (1960-2014) compiled and developed the 1991 Rules Cyclopedia, a 304-page hardcover that consolidates the Basic, Expert, Companion and Master sets. He was later best known for his Star Wars X-Wing novels.

question: Heroes at the entrance of Gary Gygax's 1978 Tomb of Horrors find a green devil-face carved into the wall, its mouth looking purely decorative. It is the most infamous of the module's many traps. What happens when a character reaches into or steps into the mouth?
choices: Teleports the character to a random level of the Abyss
Drops the character into a 500-foot pit filled with green slime
Polymorphs the character into a green slime forever
context: Acererak's tomb has multiple devil-face Sphere of Annihilation traps. The tomb's famous false hallway with two false coffins leads to a real trap. Players who survive often find that Acererak himself, in his demilich form, is the LAST encounter. The legendary 'how to play Tomb of Horrors' wisdom: 'Test everything with a 10-foot pole.'

question: Rona Jaffe drew her 1981 novel Mazes and Monsters from a real disappearance at Michigan State, and CBS filmed it in 1982 as a made-for-TV movie. Its lead was a college student who lost touch with reality while playing a fictional game. What was the character's name?
context: Hanks played Robbie Wheeling, a college student whose character in the fictional game is the holy man Pardieu. The film calls the game Mazes and Monsters rather than Dungeons & Dragons.

question: Brian Blume created one of the most iconic villains of Dungeons & Dragons for the 1976 Eldritch Wizardry supplement: an undead wizard-king reduced over centuries to a single severed hand and severed eye. Anyone who attaches them gains terrible magical powers. Who is he, and where does his name come from?
context: Jack Vance's Dying Earth stories inspired the D&D 'fire and forget' spell system, which Gygax adopted directly. Vecna's Hand and Eye relics appeared as iconic AD&D magic items. The 1990 Vecna Lives! supplement and 1998 Die Vecna Die! both featured the lich's attempted ascension. Vecna joined the gods as the god of secrets in Greyhawk lore.

question: Saint Martha tamed a dragon of medieval Provençal legend with holy water and a cross. The 1983 Monster Manual II borrowed its name for the doomsday beast of Advanced Dungeons & Dragons, a scaly, horned, armored colossus that regrows from wounds that would kill anything else. In the original rules only a wish spell could finish it for good. What is the monster called?
context: The tarrasque arrived in the 1983 Monster Manual II as the most destructive creature in the game's world. Its name comes from the Tarasque of Provence, a river dragon that legend says Saint Martha subdued near the town now called Tarascon. In the original rules only a wish could stop it regenerating after it was beaten down.

question: Six kids ride an amusement-park attraction into the Realm and must find their way home, menaced by the sorcerer Venger and the five-headed dragon Tiamat. Their Saturday-morning cartoon, a partnership between Marvel Productions and Gary Gygax's company, runs on CBS from 1983 to 1985. What is the show called?
context: The animated series had voice talent including Don Most as Eric the Cavalier, Adam Rich as Presto the Magician, Sidney Miller as Dungeon Master and Frank Welker as Uni the baby unicorn and as Tiamat. CBS cancelled it before its scripted finale, 'Requiem', was made; the script was later performed as an audio drama for a DVD release.

question: Spelljammer sent Dungeons & Dragons into space in 1989, with ships sailing the 'phlogiston' between crystal spheres that each held a solar system. The setting added a race of war-loving, hippo-headed men who wear tricorn hats and red coats like an old army. What are they called?
context: Giff are widely beloved for their pure Napoleonic-era military aesthetic transplanted to a fantasy-space context. They use smokepowder firearms and prefer line-infantry tactics. The setting itself was a Jeff Grubb design and was famously divisive — beloved by some, rejected as silly by others.

question: A silent figure, tall and slender, with a corona of blades around her head, rules Sigil in the 1994 setting Planescape. The torus-shaped city floats at the top of an infinite spire at the very center of the multiverse, with portals to every plane. It is said that whoever speaks her name vanishes forever. What is she called?
context: The Lady of Pain (often shortened to 'the Lady') was created by designer David Cook. She never speaks; her shadow can flay anyone who threatens her city. The 1999 Black Isle Studios CRPG set in Sigil, with Chris Avellone leading the writing, brought the setting to wider fame. That game is considered one of the greatest RPGs ever written.

question: The 1991 setting Dark Sun throws its heroes onto a post-apocalyptic desert world so short of metal that obsidian and bone weapons have become standard, and psionics has replaced most divine magic. Its signature visual look came from one fantasy artist. Who was he?
context: Brom's painted covers gave Dark Sun a unique 'Frazetta-on-Mars' aesthetic. The setting featured Thri-Kreen mantis warriors, halflings as primitive cannibals, half-giants, and the Sorcerer-Kings — wizard-tyrants of each city-state. The boxed set's first novel trilogy ('Prism Pentad') was written by Troy Denning. Dark Sun won the 1992 Origins Award for Best Roleplaying Supplement.

question: Strahd rules Barovia in the 1990 Ravenloft box set, and he is only one damned lord among many, each bound to a Domain of his own for some signature evil. A strange force creates new Domains by pulling evil souls from across the multiverse. What is it called?
context: The Dark Powers are deliberately never explained or stat-blocked — they're a meta-villain that exists to give the setting its premise. The 1994 Domains of Dread sourcebook lists dozens of Darklords. Vlad von Drakov, Vecna (briefly imprisoned there), Soth from Dragonlance, and Azalin Rex are all famous Darklords. The setting was the model for the 2016 Curse of Strahd 5e adventure.

question: A Boeing programmer who ran a small game outfit from his basement outside Seattle agreed to Garfield's pitch for Magic: the Gathering in the early 1990s. The first set, Alpha, shipped in August 1993 with a print run of 2.6 million cards. Who was the programmer?
context: Adkison founded Wizards of the Coast in 1990, and its first employees worked out of his basement. He published Magic when the collectible card game was a category nobody had tried.

question: Dr. J. Eric Holmes edited a blue-boxed introduction to Dungeons & Dragons for brand-new players in 1977. From 1978 the box also held an adventure built to teach new Dungeon Masters how to fill a dungeon: the rooms came drawn and described, but the monsters and treasure were left blank on separate stocking tables. What is this teaching module called?
choices: Against the Cult of the Reptile God
context: Mike Carr wrote B1 as a teaching module, first printed in 1978 and packed into the Holmes Basic Set from that year. The Caverns of Quasqueton were built by two retired adventurers, Roghan the Fearless and Zelligar the Unknown. From early 1980 the Basic box carried B2 The Keep on the Borderlands instead.

question: A wizard throws a spell at a beholder in Advanced Dungeons & Dragons, and the spell dies in the magic-cancelling cone projected by its huge central eye. The cone does not cover every side of the beholder. From which direction is a beholder still open to magic attack?
answer: From behind or the side — the anti-magic cone covers only a forward arc
choices: From behind or the side — the anti-magic cone covers only a forward arc
Straight ahead — the cone switches off each time the beholder blinks
Directly into the central eye — the anti-magic cone has a blind spot at zero range
From any direction — the central eye closes when it uses its bite attack instead
context: Early Advanced Dungeons & Dragons gave the anti-magic cone a 90-degree arc to the front, so a party that spreads out around a beholder can still reach it with spells, and the beholder must keep turning to aim the cone. Beholders are also famously paranoid: they consider all other beholders heretics, leading to species-wide civil war.

question: The owner of Gary Gygax's old company sold it in 1997, when it was more than $30 million in debt, swamped by returned stock and unable to pay its printers. The buyer was a young publisher from Washington state, grown rich after launching a collectible card game at Gen Con in 1993. Which company took over Dungeons and Dragons?
context: Lorraine Williams sold TSR to Wizards of the Coast in 1997, and Wizards settled TSR's debts as part of the deal. Wizards had launched Magic: The Gathering at Gen Con in 1993, and the card game's success gave it the cash to buy the company that made D&D.

question: I6 Ravenloft, the award-winning 1983 module, began as a vampire Halloween adventure its husband-and-wife authors had run at home for years. One game-mechanical idea became its most-copied feature, changing where the key items lay from one game to the next. What was it?
answer: A tarot-style fortune-telling card-draw system that randomized Strahd's plans
choices: A tarot-style fortune-telling card-draw system that randomized Strahd's plans
A real-time torch system tracking how long player light sources burned
A morale-tracking system causing the player party to suffer Fear penalties
A weather-cycle table that altered the castle's accessible rooms each round
context: In the original module the Dungeon Master draws from an ordinary deck of playing cards to stand in for a fortune-teller's reading. The reading fixes where the Holy Symbol, the Sunsword and the Tome of Strahd are hidden, where Strahd will be found, and what he wants, so every playthrough differs. The 2016 fifth-edition Curse of Strahd kept the idea.

question: Tracy Hickman's Dragonlance story began as a run of Dungeons & Dragons game modules, and his company set him and the book editor Margaret Weis to turning it into novels. Hickman outlined the plot while Weis shaped the characters and the prose. The first book came out in November 1984 and quickly became a bestseller. What was it called?
context: Autumn Twilight came out in November 1984 as a mass-market paperback; Weis and Hickman finished the manuscript in about three months, and it went through several reprints in its first years. The Companions of the Lance (Tanis Half-Elven, Caramon and Raistlin Majere, Sturm Brightblade, Flint Fireforge, Tasslehoff Burrfoot, Goldmoon, Riverwind and Tika Waylan) became the best-known party in D&D fiction, and TSR launched more novel lines on the Chronicles' success.

question: Lawyers for the holders of the Tolkien rights sent TSR (Tactical Studies Rules) a cease-and-desist notice in 1977, after the company put out an unlicensed Tolkien board game. The notice also took aim at Tolkien's names inside Dungeons & Dragons. TSR swapped in replacement names, and those substitutes became permanent D&D canon. Which three names replaced hobbits, ents and balrogs?
context: The legal threat followed TSR's unlicensed board game Battle of the Five Armies. D&D changed hobbit to halfling and ent to treant, and in time its balrog became the balor; the new names have stayed in the game ever since.

question: Gary Gygax built a deadly dungeon for the first Origins convention, held in Baltimore in 1975, packed with traps that killed without warning. It was printed in 1978 as Tomb of Horrors. He had one kind of player in mind. What kind of player was it built to test?
answer: Players who boasted that their heroes could beat any challenge
choices: Players who boasted that their heroes could beat any challenge
Beginners who had never set foot in a dungeon before
Rules lawyers who argued every ruling at the table
Wargamers who scorned fantasy games as child's play
context: Gygax wrote it for tournament play at Origins I in 1975 and to test expert players in his own campaign who claimed their characters could beat anything. TSR published it in 1978 as S1, first of the Special series; S2 White Plume Mountain (1979), S3 Expedition to the Barrier Peaks (1980) and S4 The Lost Caverns of Tsojcanth (1982) followed. Tomb of Horrors has been revisited many times since, among them as the model for the finale of 2017's Tomb of Annihilation.

question: Adventurers in Gary Gygax's 1978 module D3 finally reach Erelhei-Cinlu, the city of the dark elves, in the game's first detailed picture of their society. Its noble houses compete for the favor of their spider goddess. Where in the Underdark did D3 place the city?
answer: In the Vault — a cavern miles wide under a starry, glittering ceiling
choices: In the Vault — a cavern miles wide under a starry, glittering ceiling
In the Pit — a vertical shaft descending three miles into volcanic depths
In the Spire — atop a needle-like stalagmite over a bottomless chasm
In the Web — a network of crystal bridges over the Demonweb itself
context: Erelhei-Cinlu is ruled by competing drow noble houses, each devoted to Lolth, and the Fane of Lolth is its religious center. Crystals in the Vault's ceiling sparkle like stars, and a great mass of glowing stone hangs there like an alien moon. Salvatore's Menzoberranzan for the Forgotten Realms drew on the same picture of rival noble houses.

question: A Kingpriest demands godhood from the gods of Krynn, 350 years before the Dragonlance Chronicles trilogy, and they answer with a disaster that wrecks his capital and reshapes the land. Then the gods leave the world. What has become the central image of that disaster?
answer: The fiery mountain that crashed onto Istar
choices: The fiery mountain that crashed onto Istar
The shadow of the Dragon Queen Takhisis
The shattering of the Graygem of Gargath
The silent fall of the Lostking's tower
context: After the Cataclysm the gods of Krynn withdrew, and true clerical healing vanished with them. The Chronicles open in a world that believes its gods have abandoned it. Istar itself lies sunk beneath the Blood Sea, the new ocean the Cataclysm made.

question: Drizzt Do'Urden came into the 1988 novel The Crystal Shard on a spur-of-the-moment pitch, and he went on to become the Forgotten Realms' most popular character. That novel launched the Icewind Dale trilogy, and he was never meant to be its primary hero. Who was?
answer: Wulfgar, the young barbarian of the Tribe of the Elk
choices: Wulfgar, the young barbarian of the Tribe of the Elk
Bruenor, the exiled heir of Mithral Hall
Regis, the halfling burgomaster of Bryn Shander
Catti-brie, the adopted human daughter of Bruenor
context: Wulfgar's character arc — the young barbarian apprenticed to Bruenor — was the trilogy's main throughline. Drizzt was the gimmick character who walked away with the entire spotlight. Salvatore went on to write over 30 Drizzt novels through the early 2020s, plus film, comic, and game adaptations. The Crystal Shard, Streams of Silver (1989), and The Halfling's Gem (1990) form the original Icewind Dale Trilogy.

question: Gygax wrote up the rules for the beholder, the floating orb with one great central eye, a fanged mouth and ten eyestalks, but he never claimed to have invented it. The idea came from another player at his Lake Geneva table: the brother of Gygax's co-Dungeon Master on Castle Greyhawk. Who dreamed up the beholder?
context: Terry Kuntz, brother of Gygax's co-Dungeon Master Rob Kuntz, created the beholder, and Gary Gygax detailed it for publication. It became one of the most famous monsters in the game.

question: The human witch Iggwilv bears a half-demon son to the demon Graz'zt in Gary Gygax's Greyhawk setting, and that son rules an evil kingdom in the northern Flanaess. He is the closest thing Greyhawk has to a Dark Lord of all evil, a recurring villain through dozens of modules. What is his name?
answer: Iuz, demigod ruler of the Empire of Iuz
choices: Iuz, demigod ruler of the Empire of Iuz
Vecna, lich-god of secrets and ambition
Tharizdun, the forgotten god of eternal darkness
Zagig, the mad archmage of Castle Greyhawk
context: Iuz's mother Iggwilv had bound the demon lord Graz'zt with the help of her tome, the Demonomicon. In the setting's lore Iuz was once imprisoned beneath Castle Greyhawk until the fighter Robilar freed him, and the 1992 From the Ashes boxed set put Iuz at the center of a cold-war standoff with Furyondy.

question: A wizard on Athas, the desert world of Dark Sun, casts one arcane spell and the plants around him die, their life energy drained to fuel it. Surrounding biology suffers too, and millennia of unrestricted casting have stripped the planet. What name is given to this style of magic-use?
context: A counter-school exists: 'preserving,' which draws the energy slowly without destroying plants. Defilers gain spells faster than preservers, creating a moral tension in every magic-user's career. The Sorcerer-Kings who rule the city-states are all powerful defilers, having spent millennia drawing life energy. The Sorcerer-King Nibenay rules from the city of Nibenay, surrounded by drained earth.

question: An immortal Sorcerer-King who has lived for over a thousand years rules Tyr, the Dark Sun city-state where the Prism Pentad novels open, and that immortality has cost him his humanity. He is one of seven such rulers across the Tablelands of Athas, all named in the first boxed set of 1991. Who is he?
context: Troy Denning's Prism Pentad (1991-1993) begins with The Verdant Passage, in which Kalak of Tyr drives his slaves to finish a great ziggurat meant to help him become an immortal dragon. The five novels are The Verdant Passage, The Crimson Legion, The Amber Enchantress, The Obsidian Oracle and The Cerulean Storm.

question: Ed Greenwood began the Forgotten Realms in Toronto in 1967, at about twelve years old, writing short stories for his own amusement about a wandering sage named Elminster of Shadowdale. His 1979 Dragon Magazine articles framed the tales as dictated by Elminster through a magical portal. He sold the entire setting to Tactical Studies Rules (TSR) in 1986. What was the first Realms product?
answer: The 1987 Forgotten Realms Campaign Set, a gray boxed-set with two maps
choices: The 1987 Forgotten Realms Campaign Set, a gray boxed-set with two maps
The 1987 Forgotten Realms Player's Guide, a softcover rulebook
The 1988 Realms Sourcebook, a hardcover supplement
The 1988 Cyclopedia of the Realms, a single-volume reference
context: The gray box (sometimes called the Old Gray Box) is a beloved collector's item among Realms fans. Greenwood has continued writing Realms fiction and lore for nearly 40 years; he's the in-universe canonical authority. Elminster himself has appeared in over 20 novels — Greenwood writes them in first person from Elminster's voice in some volumes.

question: Drizzt Do'Urden wins a magic blade from the treasure of a beast he slays in Icewind Dale, and the blade takes the beast's nickname. It is one of two iconic blades the dark elf ranger carries through the Forgotten Realms novels. What are the two called?
answer: Twinkle (the elven scimitar) and Icingdeath (from the dragon's hoard)
choices: Twinkle (the elven scimitar) and Icingdeath (from the dragon's hoard)
Frostmourne (the cold blade) and Sunrazer (the fire blade)
Shadowfang (the drow blade) and Starfire (the dwarf-forged blade)
context: In The Crystal Shard, Drizzt found the scimitar Icingdeath in the hoard of the white dragon Ingeloakastimizilian, whose nickname was Icingdeath; the blade carries that name. Twinkle is an elven-made scimitar. Drizzt's companion is the onyx panther Guenhwyvar, summoned from a figurine.

question: Expedition to the Barrier Peaks, Gary Gygax's 1980 module S3, sends heroes into a cave in the mountains of Greyhawk that leads somewhere no fantasy hero expects. Inside, robots still patrol the halls and colored cards open sealed doors. What is the 'dungeon' really?
answer: A crashed spacecraft from the stars
choices: A crashed spacecraft from the stars
A buried dwarven forge of iron golems
A clockwork fortress of a mad archmage
A sealed vault of a lost wizard-empire
context: Gygax first ran Expedition to the Barrier Peaks as a 1976 tournament scenario, and TSR published it in 1980. The cave is the entrance to a downed spacecraft whose robots still work; players gather colored access cards to open its restricted areas and use futuristic gear such as blaster rifles.

question: Leiber finally told in 1970 how his huge northern barbarian and his small grey-clad thief first met, on a night when both ambushed the same pair of Thieves' Guild burglars and agreed to split the loot. The novella won both the Nebula and the Hugo. What is it called?
context: Ill Met in Lankhmar, first published in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction in 1970, won the Nebula Award in 1970 and the Hugo in 1971 for Best Novella. In it Fafhrd and the Mouser both ambush two Thieves' Guild members, recognise kindred spirits, and agree to share the loot.

question: The 1995 setting Birthright hands its players kingdoms, not just wandering heroes, with rules for taxes, armies, deals with other rulers and even murder plots. The story follows the heirs of slain gods from an old pantheon. Where do their kingdoms lie?
answer: Cerilia, on the world of Aebrynis
choices: Cerilia, on the world of Aebrynis
Faerûn, on the world of Toril
The Flanaess, on the world of Oerth
Ansalon, on the world of Krynn
context: Birthright was designed by Richard Baker and Colin McComb. It ran from 1995-1997 in print but was canceled when TSR's financial troubles peaked. The bloodline-rulership system was unique — each ruler player character has 'blood points' that can be invested in spells, abilities, or kingdom actions. The 1995 boxed set is now a collector's item. Cerilia's nations include Anuire, the most populous human realm, and Vosgaard, the home of bestial Vos warriors.

question: A traveller in Sigil, the city of the 1994 Planescape setting, uses a portal key, which may be an object, a gesture, a sound or even a thought, and a door opens anywhere in the multiverse. The city is shaped like an inside-out donut at the top of the Spire, so its people live on the inside surface. About how many portals are open in Sigil at any one time?
answer: Tens of thousands, constantly opening and closing
choices: Tens of thousands, constantly opening and closing
Exactly nine, one matched to each Outer Plane
Three hundred sixty-five, one for each day of the year
Twelve thousand, one for each zodiac sign times five
context: Sigil's portals are central to its commerce and politics. The 15 factions of Sigil each have philosophical positions on the nature of the multiverse — the Athar deny the gods, the Doomguard worship entropy, the Bleak Cabal sees the universe as meaningless. The factions occupy specific neighborhoods and run specific institutions (the Athar run the Shattered Temple, the Doomguard run the Armory). The Lady of Pain doesn't take sides in faction politics.

question: A Basic Dungeons & Dragons player reads Dragon magazine in 1991 and finds that the planet he knew only as the Known World has a proper name at last. The same world runs through the Expert, Companion, Master and Immortal sets. What is the planet itself called?
answer: Mystara — the planet whose hollow interior contains preserved cultures
choices: Mystara — the planet whose hollow interior contains preserved cultures
Oerth — the planet of the World of Greyhawk Flanaess
Toril — the planet of Faerûn and Kara-Tur
Krynn — the planet of Ansalon and Taladas
context: The first published use of the name Mystara came in 1991, in Bruce Heard's Voyage of the Princess Ark series in Dragon magazine. Aaron Allston's 1990 Hollow World Campaign Set opened the planet's hollow interior, where lost cultures are preserved, and his 1991 Rules Cyclopedia gathered the Basic rules around the same world. Mystara's nations, among them Karameikos, Glantri, Ylaruam and Thyatis, feature in many Basic adventures.

question: Tom Moldvay sent adventurers into a fog-shrouded chateau in X2, his Dungeons & Dragons module of 1981, where the noble family has been carried off to a magical demiplane. He based the adventure directly on stories he loved by a fantasy author, set in a made-up province of medieval France. Whose stories inspired the module?
answer: Clark Ashton Smith, of Averoigne and Zothique fame
choices: Clark Ashton Smith, of Averoigne and Zothique fame
Lord Dunsany, of the Pegana cycle
Mervyn Peake, of the Gormenghast trilogy
James Branch Cabell, of the Biography of Manuel cycle
context: X2 Castle Amber takes its adventurers into Averoigne, the invented French province of Clark Ashton Smith's stories, and its villains are the decadent Amber family. Smith (1893-1961) was the third great Weird Tales writer of the 1930s beside Lovecraft and Howard.

question: The overgod Ao, angry at the gods' petty quarrels, casts almost the whole pantheon down to walk Faerûn as mortal avatars in the Forgotten Realms' 1989 Time of Troubles, told in the Avatar novels and modules. The last straw is a theft: two gods have made off with the Tablets of Fate. Which two gods stole them?
context: In the Time of Troubles, which TSR's 1989 products used to carry the Forgotten Realms into a new edition, the overgod Ao cast the gods down to walk the world as mortal avatars after Bane and Myrkul stole the Tablets of Fate.

question: Chaosium built its 1981 game Call of Cthulhu around a sanity score that drops as characters witness cosmic horror, and the game has stayed in print ever since. What system did Chaosium use as its foundation, one it also shared with its fantasy game RuneQuest?
answer: Basic Roleplaying (BRP), a d100 percentile-based skill system
choices: Basic Roleplaying (BRP), a d100 percentile-based skill system
Glory and Honor, a d20-based attribute-driven system
FUDGE, an open-source flexible dice-pool system
context: Basic Roleplaying (BRP) was first published by Chaosium in 1978 for RuneQuest. The system is percentile-based — skill checks roll d100 against a target. BRP became the foundation for Call of Cthulhu (1981), Stormbringer (1981), Pendragon (1985), and other Chaosium games. The latest Call of Cthulhu edition (7th edition, 2014) refined the system but kept the core d100 philosophy. Sandy Petersen designed CoC.

question: A tentacled cat stalked a spaceship crew on an abandoned alien world in a story printed in Astounding in July 1939. Gygax adapted it as the six-legged panther of Advanced Dungeons & Dragons, the one that appears shifted from its actual location. The creature in the story was named 'coeurl.' Who wrote the story, later collected in Voyage of the Space Beagle?
context: Van Vogt's 'Black Destroyer' was the cover story of the July 1939 Astounding and is often counted among the foundational alien-monster stories. Van Vogt later sued 20th Century Fox over the likeness of Alien (1979) to his work and collected a $50,000 out-of-court settlement. The Voyage of the Space Beagle (1950) stitches 'Black Destroyer' together with other stories into one novel.

question: Gary Gygax co-founded the Gen Con convention in August 1968, renting the Horticultural Hall in the Wisconsin town where he lived. About a hundred people came. It soon outgrew the town, moving to Kenosha in 1978, Milwaukee in 1985 and Indianapolis in 2003. What was the name 'Gen Con' short for?
answer: Geneva Convention — a play on the international-law treaty
choices: Geneva Convention — a play on the international-law treaty
General Convention — a generic name for gaming gatherings
Generation Convention — a name for the new generation of gamers
Genuine Convention — emphasizing its hobby-gaming authenticity
context: The 'Geneva Convention' name was Gygax's pun: the gathering began in Lake Geneva, and the Geneva Conventions are treaties about war, the subject of many early games. A year earlier, in 1967, about a dozen gamers had met at Gygax's home. Gygax met Dave Arneson at the second Gen Con, in 1969, and Gen Con remains one of the largest tabletop gaming conventions in North America.

question: An artist painted the full-color hex map of the Flanaess, the eastern continent of Oerth, for the 1980 World of Greyhawk folio, and it appeared again in the 1983 boxed set. It became one of the best-loved maps in tabletop gaming, known simply by its maker's first name. Who painted it?
context: The map was credited simply to 'Darlene'. It was printed in the 1980 folio and again in the 1983 boxed set, was later reissued as a poster, and remains a collector's item.

question: Gary Gygax began a run of sword-and-sorcery novels in 1985 about a boy from the slums of the City of Greyhawk who grows into a master thief. His old company printed the first two, and after it pushed Gygax out, the small press New Infinities Productions published the rest. Who is the hero?
context: Gord the Rogue novels: Saga of Old City (1985), Artifact of Evil (1986), Sea of Death (1987), Night Arrant (1987), City of Hawks (1987), Come Endless Darkness (1988), Dance of Demons (1988). The Gord novels remain in print as PDFs through various small presses.

question: Lareth the Beautiful, a handsome young evil priest, commands the bandits in the ruined moathouse outside Gygax's 1979 module T1 The Village of Hommlet, a sleepy frontier village that hides an evil cult. The module warns that anyone who harms him had best not boast of it where word could reach the demon who favors him. Which demon is that?
answer: Lolth — the Demon Queen of Spiders
choices: Lolth — the Demon Queen of Spiders
Orcus — the demon prince of the undead
Demogorgon — the two-headed Prince of Demons
context: Lareth the Beautiful, a fifth-level cleric, is the new master of the moathouse bandits outside Hommlet. The module warns that whoever harms him had best not brag of it before anyone who might inform the demoness Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders, a thread that ties Hommlet to the drow and the later Q1 module.

question: Gygax kept psionics, a second system of mental powers alongside magic, in his 1978 Advanced Dungeons & Dragons Player's Handbook only as optional rules, open to characters who made lucky rolls. Those powers had arrived in the 1976 Eldritch Wizardry supplement, and they brought a new monster that stalks dungeons and eats minds. Which monster is it?
answer: The Intellect Devourer — a walking brain on four legs
choices: The Intellect Devourer — a walking brain on four legs
The Ulitharid — a giant elder-form mind flayer
The Cerebrilith — a demon-form psionic predator from the Abyss
The Elder Brain — the vast ruler of a mind flayer colony
context: The intellect devourer first appeared in Eldritch Wizardry (1976), the supplement that introduced psionics, as a brain-shaped creature on four legs that feeds on minds. In the first-edition Player's Handbook (1978) psionics were an optional appendix, available only to characters who qualified with lucky rolls.

question: Howard and Leiber both made the list Gary Gygax printed at the back of his 1979 Dungeon Masters Guide, of the authors whose books inspired Dungeons and Dragons. Many of the names are American pulp writers, but one is a titled nobleman. Which lord made Gygax's list?
answer: Lord Dunsany, of the Pegana mythology and 'The King of Elfland's Daughter'
choices: Lord Dunsany, of the Pegana mythology and 'The King of Elfland's Daughter'
Lord Tennyson, of 'Idylls of the King' Arthurian poetry
Lord Macaulay, of 'Lays of Ancient Rome' historical poetry
Lord Byron, of 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage' Romantic poetry
context: Lord Dunsany (1878-1957) appears among the authors of Gygax's Appendix N, alongside series such as Howard's Conan and Leiber's Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser. Dunsany's 1924 novel The King of Elfland's Daughter is the classic picture of Faerie as a strange and beautiful realm.

question: A staff designer began answering readers' tricky rules questions in 1987 in 'Sage Advice', a monthly column in the official Dungeons and Dragons magazine. He stayed with it until 2004, through grappling, spell components, monster stats and every edge case gamers could invent, and he became the rules oracle for a whole generation. Who was he?
answer: Skip Williams, who later co-designed 3rd Edition D&D
choices: Skip Williams, who later co-designed 3rd Edition D&D
Roger E. Moore, a longtime magazine editor at TSR
Kim Mohan, a TSR magazine editor of the 1980s
Bruce Heard, who wrote the Voyage of the Princess Ark column
context: Skip Williams started at TSR in 1976 as a part-time clerk in its Dungeon Hobby Shop and wrote Sage Advice from 1987 to 2004. He later worked on the 3rd Edition design team with Monte Cook and Jonathan Tweet.

question: A pilot sits down in a magical helm in Spelljammer, a chair-shaped device that turns his spell energy into ship motion, and his vessel sails the strange medium called the phlogiston. Helms range from cheap minor helms to powerful major helms. Who sells the high-end major helms?
answer: The Arcane — gigantic blue-skinned alien merchants who sell helms throughout the spheres
choices: The Arcane — gigantic blue-skinned alien merchants who sell helms throughout the spheres
The Scro — orc admirals who sell helms from their black shipyards
The Neogi — spider-slavers who manufacture helms via dark magic
The Elven Navy — armada-builders who grow their own living ships
context: In Spelljammer the Arcane, towering blue-skinned humanoids, are the premier merchant race of wildspace, dealing in helms and other gear across the crystal spheres. Lore holds that they sell the major helms but do not build them, and they keep the helms' true source secret.

question: The spirit of a long-dead pharaoh, cursed to roam the desert until someone robs his tomb, haunts the 1982 module I3 Pharaoh, first of the Desert of Desolation trilogy. Its husband-and-wife authors also wrote Ravenloft. What is the pharaoh's name?
context: The Desert of Desolation trilogy runs I3 Pharaoh, I4 Oasis of the White Palm and I5 Lost Tomb of Martek, and TSR later gathered all three into a single supermodule. The pharaoh's spirit seeks heroes who will rob his tomb and so end his curse.

question: The 1974 Dungeons and Dragons box hands its buyer three small booklets: one for making characters and casting spells, one listing creatures and loot, and one for running games below ground and out in the wilds. Collectors still prize all three. What are the three booklets titled?
answer: Men & Magic, Monsters & Treasure, and The Underworld & Wilderness Adventures
choices: Men & Magic, Monsters & Treasure, and The Underworld & Wilderness Adventures
Heroes & Spells, Beasts & Gold, and The Dungeon & Outdoor Campaigns
Fighters & Wizards, Creatures & Loot, and The Labyrinth & Wilderness Guide
Characters & Sorcery, Dragons & Hoards, and The Castle & Countryside Book
context: The original 1974 set held three booklets: Men & Magic, Monsters & Treasure, and The Underworld & Wilderness Adventures. It sold for $10, and the first print run was 1,000 copies.

question: Bigby, an evil low-level wizard in another referee's dungeons, was subdued by Gary Gygax's own wizard and forced into service. Later Gygax played Bigby himself, and the wizard's 'hand' spells became iconic, including Bigby's Interposing Hand, Grasping Hand and Crushing Hand. In whose dungeons did Bigby begin?
answer: Rob Kuntz, Gygax's co-DM and an early TSR employee
choices: Rob Kuntz, Gygax's co-DM and an early TSR employee
Tim Kask, the original editor of Dragon Magazine
Brian Blume, Gygax's TSR business partner
James Ward, of Metamorphosis Alpha fame
context: Bigby started life as an evil low-level wizard in Rob Kuntz's dungeons of Greyhawk. Gygax's Mordenkainen subdued him and made him a servant, and after Bigby changed his ways Kuntz ruled that Gygax could take him over as a player character. Kuntz co-refereed the Greyhawk campaign and played the fighter Robilar.

question: A staff artist at Gary Gygax's company gave early-1980s Dungeons and Dragons its most distinctive look, with bright, strangely proportioned creatures and covers. He was one of a small group who set the game's visual identity around 1980, and his style was psychedelic, weird and slightly Gothic. Who was he?
answer: Erol Otus — cover painter of the 1981 Basic Set
choices: Erol Otus — cover painter of the 1981 Basic Set
David Trampier — DMG and Monster Manual interior art
Jeff Easley — covers of 1983-1989 AD&D hardcovers
context: Erol Otus joined TSR's art department in the late 1970s and was on staff by 1979; he was one of the two staff artists left after the May 1981 layoffs. He painted the cover of the first Deities & Demigods (1980) and the color cover of Tom Moldvay's 1981 Basic Set rulebook.

question: A Call of Cthulhu investigator witnesses one cosmic horror too many, reaches zero Sanity points and goes permanently insane. Chaosium's 1981 game made that score its iconic mechanic, and it has spawned over 40 years of supplements. Who designed the game?
answer: Sandy Petersen, who later did level design on id Software's Doom and Quake
choices: Sandy Petersen, who later did level design on id Software's Doom and Quake
Steve Perrin, the original RuneQuest fantasy-game system designer
Marc Miller, the designer of the science-fiction game Traveller
Ken St. Andre, the designer of the game Tunnels and Trolls
context: Sandy Petersen, born in 1955, designed Call of Cthulhu for Chaosium and later worked on RuneQuest III. He then joined id Software, where he designed levels for Doom (1993) and Quake (1996). He returned to tabletop games in the 2010s with his own company, Petersen Games, making Lovecraftian board games.

question: Chaosium's 1978 game RuneQuest dropped its heroes into a Bronze Age fantasy world of cult-based religion, dragon-newts, dwarves who were living machines, talking ducks and warring Lunar and Solar empires. One man made the whole setting himself. Who was he?
answer: Greg Stafford, founder of Chaosium and Glorantha mythologist
choices: Greg Stafford, founder of Chaosium and Glorantha mythologist
Steve Perrin, the RuneQuest rules designer
Ken St. Andre, the Tunnels and Trolls designer
Lynn Willis, the Chaosium editor and designer
context: Greg Stafford (1948-2018) built Glorantha as a personal worldbuilding project starting in the 1960s, much as Ed Greenwood built the Forgotten Realms, but with a deeper interest in myth and religion. He spent his life refining the setting, and later games such as HeroQuest and 13th Age in Glorantha drew on his lore.

question: Marc Miller built one famous rule into Traveller, the science-fiction role-playing game Game Designers' Workshop published in 1977. A new character served careers in the Navy, Marines, Scouts, Merchants, Army or Other for four-year terms, gaining skills along the way. What was this signature rule?
answer: Survival rolls — a hero could die before play began
choices: Survival rolls — a hero could die before play began
Reincarnation tables — a dead hero returned in a new body
Point-buy careers — players bought every skill with points
Alien heritage — every recruit rolled a random species
context: Traveller's death-during-chargen mechanic became famously controversial — some saw it as adding gritty realism, others as just frustrating. Later Traveller editions made the rule optional. The game's setting, the Third Imperium, has been a constantly-developing universe since 1977. Marc Miller still oversees the line, now published as Mongoose Traveller (2008+). Traveller is considered one of the most influential RPGs ever, alongside D&D, RuneQuest, and Call of Cthulhu.

question: A 1981 superhero role-playing game hands its players a stock of points and lets them buy custom powers, perks and drawbacks, one of the first games built that way. The same rules later ran fantasy, spy and science-fiction games. What is the shared system called?
answer: The Hero System, also called Champions Hero System
choices: The Hero System, also called Champions Hero System
The GURPS System, the Steve Jackson Games universal mechanic
The Storyteller System, the White Wolf World of Darkness mechanic
The FATE System, an early Fudge-derivative game
context: The Hero System reached its definitive form in 4th Edition (1989), with revisions through 6th Edition (2009). Its signature is the granularity of power design: every superpower or magical effect can be broken into pieces bought separately. Champions itself remains the flagship Hero System game, and the same rules ran Fantasy Hero, Star Hero and Pulp Hero.

question: Greg Costikyan, Dan Gelber and Eric Goldberg set their 1984 comedy role-playing game Paranoia in a future totalitarian complex ruled by an insane AI Computer. Players are Troubleshooters, whose job is finding traitors while being traitors themselves, each carrying a clearance color. What was the player handbook's notorious cover slogan?
answer: 'Stay Alert! Trust No One! Keep Your Laser Handy!'
choices: 'Stay Alert! Trust No One! Keep Your Laser Handy!'
'You Are Safe! The Computer Is Your Friend! Report Everything!'
'Welcome To Alpha Complex! Have A Nice Day! Don't Die!'
'Service The Computer! Report All Mutants! Watch Out For Communists!'
context: Paranoia's tone was deliberately satirical, a comic jab at authoritarian bureaucracy: the Computer thinks it is helping, and the players must lie and betray to survive. The game spawned multiple editions through Mongoose Publishing (2004 onwards). The phrase 'The Computer is your friend' became a tongue-in-cheek meme outside the gaming hobby.

question: Leiber and his college friend Harry Otto Fischer invented two heroes in letters in the 1930s: Fafhrd, a giant red-haired barbarian of the north, and the Gray Mouser, a small thief and magician of the city. Their first published story appeared in August 1939 in Unknown, John W. Campbell's new fantasy pulp, and later collections renamed it The Jewels in the Forest. What was its original title?
context: Two Sought Adventure appeared in Unknown in August 1939 and was later retitled The Jewels in the Forest. Leiber went on writing about the pair until his death in 1992.

question: Mary Kirchoff, a book editor, was about to pitch The Crystal Shard in 1987 when her novelist, needing a new companion for its hero, offered a drow off the top of his head. Drizzt Do'Urden stole the entire trilogy and went on to anchor over thirty more novels. The same writer later told Drizzt's full origin in Menzoberranzan in a separate set of prequels. What are those prequels called?
answer: The Dark Elf Trilogy: Homeland, Exile and Sojourn
choices: The Dark Elf Trilogy: Homeland, Exile and Sojourn
Legacy of the Drow: The Legacy, Starless Night and Siege of Darkness
The Cleric Quintet: Canticle, In Sylvan Shadows and Night Masks
The Hunter's Blades: The Thousand Orcs, The Lone Drow and The Two Swords
context: The Dark Elf Trilogy is widely considered Salvatore's best work and the definitive depiction of drow society. Homeland (1990) showed Drizzt's youth in House Do'Urden in Menzoberranzan; Exile showed his banishment into the Underdark wilderness; Sojourn (1991) showed his journey to the surface and the early friendship with the blind ranger Montolio DeBrouchee. Salvatore's portrayal of Menzoberranzan as a matriarchal drow city-state — with its noble houses, the Academy, and the constant intrigue in Lolth's name — became iconic Forgotten Realms canon.

question: Debbie, a fictional teenage girl, joins a D&D group under a 'Dungeon Master' named Ms. Frost in a 1984 evangelical comic tract. The group plays a session where Debbie's character earns levels of magic, and Frost then invites Debbie to a real witchcraft circle to learn real spells. The tract names one spell Debbie casts on her father. What does she cast on him?
answer: A 'Mind Bondage' spell, to stop him banning D&D
choices: A 'Mind Bondage' spell, to stop him banning D&D
A 'Charm Person' spell directly copied from D&D
A 'Cause Disease' spell that makes him fall ill
A 'Curse of Failure' spell that destroys his business
context: In the tract Debbie says she used the 'mind bondage' spell on her father because he was trying to stop her playing D&D; the spell is Chick's invention, not a D&D spell. A 2014 short film directed by L. Gabriel Gonda and written by JR Ralls took its plot and dialogue from the tract.

question: Tom Lazarus wrote the teleplay of Mazes and Monsters from Rona Jaffe's 1981 novel, the story of a college student who lost himself in a fantasy role-playing game. CBS aired the made-for-TV movie on December 28, 1982. Who directed it?
context: Steven Hilliard Stern directed Mazes and Monsters, which CBS aired on December 28, 1982. Tom Lazarus wrote it from Rona Jaffe's 1981 novel, and it was Tom Hanks's first lead role.

question: Charmander, the small orange lizard among the starter Pokemon, carries a small flame on the tip of his tail. The Pokedex, the trainer's Pokemon encyclopedia, carries a warning about that flame. If it ever goes out, what happens to Charmander?
choices: Charmander loses the ability to use Fire moves
context: The flame burns brighter when Charmander is healthy or excited and dims when he is weak or sick. Trainers shelter the tail from rain. It is the most iconic life-force symbol in the franchise.

question: Little orange Charmander grows up in two steps in Pokemon Red and Blue, first into the sturdier Charmeleon, then into the huge dragon-like Charizard, tail blazing. Charizard's Pokedex entry lists two types, and one of them is Fire. What is the other?
context: Venusaur is dual-typed too, Grass and Poison, while Blastoise is pure Water. Despite his dragon looks, Charizard was never Dragon-type until Mega Charizard X (Pokemon X and Y, 2013) gave him a Fire and Dragon form.

question: A young trainer in the Pokemon games runs into a wild creature in tall grass. He plucks a small red-and-white ball from his belt and throws it, and it snaps open in a burst of light and pulls the creature inside. What is this capture ball called?
context: The standard Pokeball is the baseline catch device. The Master Ball is the rarest, with a 100% catch rate, and is famously given once in each main-line game.

question: Ash Ketchum, ten years old, leaves home in the 1997 Japanese Pokemon anime, battles gym leaders in Pewter City and Cerulean City, and finally competes in the Indigo League tournament. All of it lies inside one starting region modeled on real east-central Japan. What is the region called?
context: Kanto is the original 151-Pokemon region from Pokemon Red and Blue. Each later generation introduced a new region: Johto (Gold/Silver), Hoenn (Ruby/Sapphire), and so on.

question: A scientist on Cinnabar Island in Pokemon Red and Blue spends years splicing the genes of an ancient myth Pokemon and makes a tall purple psychic Pokemon. He waits in a cave for trainers who have already beaten the Elite Four. What is his name?
context: Mewtwo's origin is told in journals scattered through the burnt-out Cinnabar Mansion, and his Pokedex entry says a scientist made him after years of horrific gene splicing and DNA engineering. He is found in Cerulean Cave.

question: A young trainer in Pokemon Red and Blue beats Brock of Pewter City, Misty of Cerulean City and Erika of Celadon City, and each hands over a shiny metal Gym Badge. Only the full set opens the way to the Elite Four. How many badges make up that set?
context: The Kanto gym badges, in order, are: Boulder (Brock), Cascade (Misty), Thunder (Lt. Surge), Rainbow (Erika), Soul (Koga), Marsh (Sabrina), Volcano (Blaine), and Earth (Giovanni).

question: Jessie and James of Team Rocket catch up with Ash Ketchum in the Pokemon TV cartoon and, as before every fight, recite a rhyming motto together. What words does Jessie use to open the motto?
context: The full opening is 'Prepare for trouble! / And make it double!' James follows Jessie, then they introduce themselves and Meowth caps it. The motto became one of the most recognizable bits of dialogue in 90s anime dubbing.

question: Game Freak, a tiny Japanese studio, released Pokemon Red and Green for the Game Boy in February 1996. The Pokedex numbers the creatures from the grass-lizard Bulbasaur at 001 to the rare psychic legend Mew in the final slot. How many Pokemon appeared in that first Pokedex?
context: The 151 became the cultural canon. Mew was added in development as an Easter egg by programmer Shigeki Morimoto with only days left before the master disc shipped. The number 151 was later memorialized by the Pokerap.

question: Ash, Misty and Brock find a Charmander huddled on a rock in a rainstorm in an early Pokemon episode, shielding the tail flame his life depends on. His trainer had told him to wait there, then abandoned him with a cruel lie. What was the trainer's name?
context: Damian told Charmander to wait on the rock and would come back, knowing he would not. The Pokemon was too loyal to leave. Ash takes Charmander in, and the dynamic that produces Ash's most famous Pokemon arc begins right there in the rainstorm.

question: Blaine, a bald old showman who loves stage-magic gags, faces Ash Ketchum in the Pokemon anime as the seventh gym leader of Ash's journey, and Ash wins the deciding match against Blaine's ace. Which gym leader is Blaine?
answer: The Cinnabar Island fire gym leader, hidden behind a riddle door
choices: The Cinnabar Island fire gym leader, hidden behind a riddle door
The Saffron City psychic gym leader of Silph Co. fame
The Fuchsia City poison gym leader who trains ninjas
The Vermilion City electric gym leader, an American soldier
context: In the games Blaine's gym stays locked until the trainer finds its key in the burnt-out Pokemon Mansion, and its doors open only to right answers in a quiz. In the anime he battles with Ninetales, Rapidash and Magmar.

question: Brock, the rock-type gym leader of Pewter City, beats Ash Ketchum at their first match in the Pokemon anime. At the second, Ash's electric partner triggers the gym's overhead sprinklers and drenches Brock's ace, a giant rock snake of chained boulders, and once wet it is vulnerable to electricity. What is that rock snake called?
context: Brock travels with Ash for most of the original anime as a cook and aspiring Pokemon breeder. He has many younger siblings whom he raises in Pewter City after his father Flint leaves. Brock's signature gag is fainting over every Nurse Joy and Officer Jenny he meets.

question: Ash Ketchum's electric partner jolts a red-haired girl in the very first episode of the Pokemon anime, and something of hers ends up a smoking wreck. She is Misty, the water-type gym leader of Cerulean City, and she follows Ash from then on, demanding that he replace it. What does Misty want Ash to pay her back for?
context: Misty's fried bike is the running gag of the early series. Pikachu wrecked it with a Thundershock that scared off a flock of Spearow chasing Ash, and Misty follows them for repayment and never collects.

question: Nintendo re-released Pokemon Red and Green as Red and Blue in North America in September 1998. Japan had also seen a third version, Blue, an enhanced port. Each cover shows one starter in its final form: Red the fire lizard, Green the plant dinosaur, Blue a giant turtle with cannons on its shell. Which Pokemon is on the Blue cover in both countries?
context: Pokemon Red and Blue launched in the US on September 28, 1998 for the Game Boy. Japanese Pokemon Red had Charizard, Green had Venusaur and Blue had Blastoise. For the Western release, the localization team used the Japanese Blue version's improved code base and renamed the second version 'Blue' with Blastoise on the cover, replacing the Japanese 'Green/Venusaur' pairing.

question: Pikachu follows the player around outside his ball in a special anime tie-in of Pokemon Red and Blue, released in the US in 1999. The game starts the player with Pikachu instead of one of the three usual starters. What is the game called?
context: Pokemon Yellow Version: Special Pikachu Edition launched in Japan on September 12, 1998 and in the US on October 19, 1999. Jessie, James, and Meowth replaced certain Rocket grunts. All three Kanto starters could be obtained over the course of the game.

question: A tall purple psychic Pokemon wakes in a glass tank at the start of the first Pokemon movie, released in 1998 in Japan and 1999 in the US. When he learns that he was made as an experiment, he flies into a rage. What does he blast to rubble?
answer: The island laboratory where the scientists cloned him
choices: The island laboratory where the scientists cloned him
Professor Oak's research lab in Pallet Town
The Indigo Plateau Pokemon League stadium
The Pokemon Center in Viridian City
context: In the film Mewtwo wakes in a laboratory on New Island, where Giovanni had hired Dr. Fuji to clone the myth Pokemon Mew. In the games his story is told in journals left in the burnt-out mansion on Cinnabar Island.

question: A trainer in Pokemon Gold and Silver, out in Japan in 1999, watches the sky and the wild Pokemon change as the actual hours pass, driven by the cartridge's internal clock. He also meets 100 brand-new Pokemon and travels a brand-new region just west of the original one. What is that region called?
context: Johto introduced breeding via Day Care couples, the Pokegear watch device, and 16 gym badges (Johto's eight plus the original Kanto eight in the post-game). Crystal (2000-2001) added a female protagonist option named Kris.

question: Tim Goodman, played by Justice Smith, finds his vanished detective father's Pikachu partner in Ryme City in Detective Pikachu, Warner Bros' 2019 live-action film. To Tim's shock, the little electric mouse talks to him in the deadpan, wisecracking voice of an adult man. Which actor, best known for playing Deadpool, gave Pikachu that voice?
context: Detective Pikachu was directed by Rob Letterman and based on the 2016 Japanese 3DS spinoff game. Reynolds's Pikachu drinks coffee, wears a deerstalker hat and snarks his way through Ryme City's mysteries.

question: Niantic launched a mobile augmented-reality game on July 6, 2016, and turned real-world parks and landmarks into Pokemon hunting grounds. People walked into traffic, climbed fences and gathered in parks at 2 a.m. by the thousands. What was the game?
context: Niantic had built the GPS-walking framework with its earlier game Ingress (2013). Pokemon GO hit 500 million downloads in its first eight months. The cultural sensation included serious news coverage of Lapras and Snorlax sightings in Central Park.

question: Two partners on a Japanese fanzine founded the game studio Game Freak in Tokyo in 1989. One had collected beetles as a boy in Machida. The other, a talented young illustrator, went on to draw the concept art for every main-series Pokemon monster from Red and Blue in 1996 on. Who was the illustrator?
context: Ken Sugimori is the lead character designer who has drawn the canonical art for every Pokemon since 1996. Junichi Masuda became the music director. Tsunekazu Ishihara runs The Pokemon Company, the licensing arm. Shigeru Miyamoto greenlit the project at Nintendo when no one else would.

question: Pokemon X and Y, on the 3DS in October 2013, hand Charizard two different Megas, temporary in-battle super-forms, because he is so popular. Mega Charizard Y keeps his original typing. Mega Charizard X drops his second type, turns his scales pitch black and his flames electric blue, and shifts into a new dual type. What is Mega Charizard X's dual typing?
context: Mega Charizard X answered the long fan argument that Charizard should have been Dragon-type. It comes from the Charizardite X stone, exclusive to Pokemon X, while Charizardite Y in Pokemon Y gives Mega Charizard Y, which keeps Fire and Flying and grows much larger wings.

question: Ash Ketchum's mother Delia stays home while her son travels the world in the Pokemon anime, and she keeps a strange helper around the house: a tall pink-haired clown Pokemon who cleans, cooks meals and weeds the garden. What species is it?
context: The Pokemon's nickname is Mimey. Delia adopts him after Ash and friends help out in an early-season episode. Mr. Mime's Pokedex skill is to project invisible walls, which Delia uses to keep dust out of the house. He is a household staple in the Ketchum home for the rest of the anime.

question: A trainer named Tad takes on Ash's stubborn Charizard in the Orange Islands episode Charizard Chills, and Charizard ignores Ash's orders. Tad's Pokemon douses Charizard's tail flame with Water Gun and freezes him solid with Ice Beam, and Ash stays up all night keeping Charizard warm. Which of Tad's Pokemon is it?
context: In Charizard Chills, Tad's Poliwrath shrinks Charizard's tail flame with Water Gun and freezes him with Ice Beam, and Ash spends the night keeping Charizard warm.

question: A Japanese voice actress took on Pikachu in 1997. Local actors gave Ash and his friends new voices in English, French or Spanish, but the dubs of the Pokemon anime kept her in every language, so that Pikachu sounded the same all over the world. Who is she?
context: Ikue Ōtani has voiced Pikachu since the anime began in 1997, and unlike other Pokemon voice actors she plays the role in all languages. Even her brief cameo in the 2019 film Detective Pikachu was kept in nearly every language version.

question: Ash's Charizard grabs an opponent in his front claws, soars high and slams it spinning back into the ground. This is the signature finishing move he develops in the Pokemon anime, and he uses it to knock out opponents, Articuno among them. What is the move called?
context: Seismic Toss became the trademark of Ash's Charizard in the anime. One famous win came against Noland, the Battle Factory's Frontier Brain, and his Articuno.

question: A wild fossil Pokemon, revived by Team Rocket, snatches Ash Ketchum from a cliff in the Pokemon anime and carries him away. His Charmeleon chases after them and evolves into Charizard mid-pursuit to save him. Which fossil Pokemon is the kidnapper?
context: Aerodactyl, the prehistoric Flying/Rock-type, was revived from an Old Amber fossil by Team Rocket on Grampa Canyon. Charmeleon's mid-air evolution into Charizard, slashing Aerodactyl with newly grown claws, is one of the most-replayed evolution scenes in the original anime.

question: Charizard stops obeying Ash Ketchum altogether for a long stretch of episodes in the Pokemon anime, sleeping in the middle of battles and roasting Ash with flamethrower for laughs. Charmander had adored Ash, and Charmeleon was already stubborn. What one clear in-universe reason does the anime give for the change?
answer: Charizard sees Ash as too weak to command a fully evolved Pokemon
choices: Charizard sees Ash as too weak to command a fully evolved Pokemon
Charizard misses his original trainer Damian and resents Ash
Charizard has been corrupted by exposure to Aerodactyl's primal aura
Charizard requires a higher-tier Pokeball than Ash's standard one
context: In Pokemon lore, a Pokemon may stop obeying a trainer below its level if the trainer lacks the appropriate gym badges. The anime adapts this into Charizard's pride: he tests Ash by sleeping through gym battles or burning him with Flamethrower until Ash earns his respect.

question: Red arrives in Lavender Town in Pokemon Red and Blue and finds Team Rocket occupying the upper floors of a building where people go to remember their deceased Pokemon. Ghost Pokemon appear on every floor. What is the building called?
context: The Pokemon Tower includes the ghost of a Marowak killed by Team Rocket while defending her child Cubone. Red can only see and battle the ghosts after acquiring a Silph Scope from Saffron City. The Marowak ghost is the most haunting NPC encounter in the original Kanto games.

question: Cubone, a small ground-type Pokemon in the original Red and Blue Pokedex, stands upright on two legs, carries a bone as a club and wears an oversized animal skull like a helmet that hides his face. The entry nicknames him the Lonely Pokemon. What is the skull he wears?
choices: A defeated rival's skull from his first battle
The skull of an Aerodactyl ancestor
A ceremonial mask handed down through Cubone generations
context: Pokemon Red's Pokedex entry: 'Wears the skull of its deceased mother on its head. Its cries echo inside the skull and come out as a sad melody.' The lore ties directly to the Marowak ghost on the Pokemon Tower's seventh floor. This is one of the darkest pieces of canon in the entire franchise.

question: Lt. Surge, the electric-type gym leader of Vermilion City, styled like an American army veteran, brags that he evolved his Pikachu the moment he caught it, before it could learn key moves. That evolved form is his ace. What is Lt. Surge's signature Pokemon?
context: In the anime, after Raichu beats him, Ash offers Pikachu a Thunder Stone in episode 14, Electric Shock Showdown, and Pikachu refuses to evolve. He beats Raichu in the rematch by using his speed.

question: Ash Ketchum lets go of the first wild Pokemon he ever caught, in one of the most emotional episodes of the first season, aired in 1997. Its species migrates across the ocean to find mates. The episode's title is a farewell phrase. What is the episode called?
choices: The Path to a Pokemon Master
context: Butterfree had been Ash's first wild catch, as a Caterpie on Route 1. In the episode he falls for a pink Butterfree in the migrating swarm, and Ash lets him go to follow her across the ocean.

question: Ash and his friends were zapped inside a computer network in the Pokemon episode that aired in Japan at 6:30 in the evening on December 16, 1997. The flashing red lights on screen caused seizures in many children, and 685 were sent to the hospital. The flashes came from Pikachu's own attack, yet a different Pokemon, the blocky digital creature at the center of the episode, was banned from the show for good. Which one?
context: Ironically, Porygon was banned despite the seizure-inducing effect coming from Pikachu's Thunderbolt explosion, not from Porygon itself. The incident, dubbed 'Pokemon Shock,' delayed the anime's return by four months and led to Japanese broadcast standards reducing strobe-cut rates. Porygon, Porygon2, and Porygon-Z have not appeared in the anime since.

question: Red stops to talk to one non-player character in Pokemon Red and Blue, then surfs along a coast, and a corrupted-data Pokemon called Missingno appears. That chat stores his name where the game later reads it as a species. Where does Red meet this character?
answer: On the docks of Viridian City, the Old Man who demonstrates catching
choices: On the docks of Viridian City, the Old Man who demonstrates catching
In the Celadon Game Corner, the rocket grunt at slot machines
On Cinnabar Island, in front of the Pokemon Mansion's main door
In the Pewter City Museum, the curator with the Old Amber
context: The Old Man demonstrates the catching tutorial, which writes the player's name to a buffer used to load wild Pokemon when surfing. Surfing the Cinnabar Coast — east edge of the island — then loads garbage data as the species, summoning Missingno. The glitch duplicates the player's sixth-slot item by 128, the famous Master Ball / Rare Candy duplication exploit.

question: Giovanni runs the very last gym of Pokemon Red and Blue, the eighth, in Viridian City. A trainer must beat him there before entering Victory Road and challenging the Elite Four. What badge does Giovanni's gym award to the trainers who beat him?
context: Viridian's gym stays shut until near the end of the game, and its leader trains ground-type Pokemon. His Rhydon is said to be the first Pokemon Game Freak ever designed.

question: An American kid recites a whole song from memory at the late-1990s peak of the Pokemon anime, the order of the names and all. It played at the end of every episode, naming every one of the original Pokemon at rapid-fire speed over rotating animations. What was the song called?
context: The Pokerap aired at the end of US episodes during the Kids' WB Saturday morning lineup. It was split into four parts, each cycling a quarter of the Pokemon. Adult Pokemon fans can still recite the order from memory, especially the climactic Mew-ending of the fourth and final segment.

question: Sabrina, the psychic-type gym leader of Saffron City, telekinetically turns Ash, Misty and Brock into living toys on display, in one of the early anime's most surreal episodes. The lore explains her cold powers as the result of an old trauma. Who lives in her gym as her family?
answer: Her father and a doll inhabited by her childhood-self psyche
choices: Her father and a doll inhabited by her childhood-self psyche
Her trainer-mother and twin sister, both also psychic gym leaders
Her grandmother and a Mr. Mime who acts as a butler
Her brother Sabri, a younger non-psychic challenger
context: Sabrina's father explains that her powers grew so strong that her childish side split off into a doll.

question: A trainer sets out across Pokemon Red and Blue after three legendary birds, Zapdos the electric bird, Moltres the fire bird and Articuno the ice bird, each waiting in a hidden lair on the map. Articuno waits at the bottom of a multi-floor labyrinth at the southwestern tip of the region. What is the name of that lair?
choices: Victory Road on the way to Indigo Plateau
context: Articuno (Seafoam Islands), Zapdos (Power Plant outside Cerulean), and Moltres (Victory Road, later Mt. Ember in remakes) form the legendary bird trio. Each can be caught at level 50 and is famously hard to keep awake long enough to throw a Pokeball without first running out of them.

question: Meowth, a scrawny alley cat, teaches himself human speech and an upright walk in the episode Go West, Young Meowth, a look back at the days before he did the haggling and the scheming for Jessie and James. What is he trying to do?
answer: Impress a female Meowth he had fallen for
choices: Impress a female Meowth he had fallen for
Earn a place in Team Rocket's elite squad
Win a talent contest for show Pokemon
Escape the city pound that had caught him
context: In Go West, Young Meowth, Meowth tries to learn to talk and to stand upright to impress a female Meowth, who only thinks him a freak for it.

question: One Pokemon alone walks behind the player on the overworld in the special anime tie-in edition of 1998 in Japan and 1999 in the US. The next mainline game to fully bring back that walk was set in the region just west of the first games' map, and it let any Pokemon follow. What game was it?
context: HeartGold and SoulSilver, the DS remakes of Gold and Silver, let the lead Pokemon of the party follow the player on the map, each with its own sprite and lines. The Pokewalker pedometer that came with the game let players take a Pokemon on real-world walks.

question: Red explores the abandoned Cinnabar Mansion in Pokemon Red and Blue, half burnt and full of locked doors and hidden switch statues, and finds a scientist's journal pages. Read in order, they tell of a new Pokemon found deep in the jungle and named Mew, and of the newborn named Mewtwo. In which country does the first entry place that jungle?
context: The entries run in order: a new Pokemon discovered deep in the jungle in Guyana, South America; the new Pokemon christened Mew; Mew giving birth to a newborn named Mewtwo; and a warning that Mewtwo is far too powerful. None of them is signed. In the first film the scientist who makes Mewtwo is Dr. Fuji.

question: Ritchie, a trainer who looks just like Ash Ketchum, faces him at the Indigo League conference. Ritchie gives each of his Pokemon a nickname, and his team mirrors Ash's at the time, down to a counterpart of Ash's Charmander. Ritchie's Pikachu is named Sparky. What does Ritchie name his Charmander?
context: Ritchie, a trainer who looks a lot like Ash, gives his Pokemon nicknames, which Ash never does: his Pikachu is Sparky and his Charmander is Zippo.

question: A young Pokemon photographer rides an automatic tracked buggy called the Zero-One through six wildlife courses across Pokemon Island, in Nintendo's 1999 game for the Nintendo 64. He photographs wild Pokemon in their natural habitats, and Professor Oak grades the pictures back at the lab. What is the photographer's name?
context: Pokemon Snap reached the N64 in 1999. Blockbuster Video stores in the US carried Snap Station kiosks that printed players' photos as stickers.
